channel.title: Personal News Feed — Other

item.title: Thousands of African birds are missing from sound libraries. A massive grassroots effort hopes to change that
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.78
Thousands of African bird species remain missing from the sound libraries that train AI-powered research and conservation tools. Now, the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and BirdLife South Africa are leading an ambitious continent-wide grassroots effort to fill in the gaps. Alexandra Owens reports.

item.title: This Indigenous-led tour in BC is part of a Canada-wide initiative to put First Nations tourism in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.54
Seven in 10 Canadians say they’d enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures on their travels, but many don’t know how or where to find a tour. Indigenous-owned Talaysay Tours and B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel are hoping to fix that. “We are on the unceded territories of the Squamish and Lil’wat people,” says Talaysay Campo, whose name translates to ‘ocean breeze’, ‘wind blowing on the water’ or ‘whispering winds’. “There’s one thing I want to share, and that’s that the land is absolutely everything.” We’re just outside Whistler Village in British Columbia about to embark on a forest trail walk to Lost Lake (Sḵwiḵ), a critical stopping point for Indigenous communities to gather resources and fish when traveling between the coast and the interior. Today we’re on a preview of Campo’s new ‘We Are The Land’ tour. “The reason we chose this name for the tour is something my Aunty Talaysay would tell me when I was a little girl: ‘We are the land’. It means that we are the caretakers of the land,” she says. Campo is co-owner of Talaysay Tours, an Indigenous, women-owned tourism company offering Indigenous-led experiences across British Columbia. Founded by her mother Candace Campo, in 2002, the company is rooted in the traditions and knowledge of both the Shíshálh (Sechelt) and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) Nations, of which the women are members. Walking beneath a canopy of towering old-growth Western Hemlock trees, Campo points out the Devil’s club, a woody shrub used by her ancestors for pain relief. “It’s important to have Indigenous tourism so our local guests and out-of-town guests can build a stronger relationship with the land,” says Campo as we pause by a babbling brook, where glimmers of sunlight dance on the slow-moving creek. “There’s so much going on with logging, global warming—one thing I’ve realized is that if (people) don’t have a relationship with the land, how are they going to take care of it or know how to take care of it?” It’s a question that sits at the heart of a growing conversation about what responsible travel in Canada should look like. As part of this conversation, Talaysay Tours has partnered with B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel on this new ‘We Are The Land’ experience. It’s aim is to help bring place-based learning, cultural ecology, stewardship and storytelling to Intrepid’s 10-day Grand Canadian Rockies itinerary beginning in 2027. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism. We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” - Christian Wolters, Intrepid Travel Canada President The Talasay partnership is part of a broader initiative by Intrepid to include more Indigenous tourism across its Canadian itineraries, with the goal to have an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of Canada tours by the end of this year, and one on every Canadian itinerary by the end of 2031. According to new research from non-profit foundation Angus Reid, commissioned by Intrepid Travel in July this year and surveying a group of 1,507 Canadians, 57 percent say they are interested in participating in an Indigenous-led tourism experience within Canada, yet fewer than one in five have ever done so. Part of the problem may be visibility. Among Canadians who have never participated in an Indigenous-led experience, 42 percent say they have not encountered one while planning a trip, while another 30 percent say they don’t know where to find one. According to the survey, seven in 10 Canadians would enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures, while more than four in 10 would be more likely to choose a Canadian trip that includes an Indigenous-led tourism experience. The appetite is certainly there. For Intrepid Travel Canada President Christian Wolters, who has joined us on the walking trail, making these experiences easier to access is more than a business opportunity. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism,” he tells me, after stopping to taste a few reddish salmonberries, native to the Pacific Northwest. “We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” Intrepid is also working closely with the Indigenous Tourism Association of Canada (ITAC) and has committed over USD$350,000 over five years to support the growth and promotion of Indigenous tourism in Canada. This includes adding Indigenous experiences to existing tours, as well as developing new, bespoke experiences alongside Indigenous tourism operators. “Partnerships like this create tangible opportunities and ensure communities gain direct economic and cultural benefits, while supporting our vision of Canada becoming a world leader in Indigenous tourism by 2030,” said Keith Henry, chief executive officer and president of ITAC in a press release. Coming up in 2027, a Huron-Wendat experience in Wendake, Quebec, will be added to Intrepid’s Eastern Canada by Rail itinerary, which will include a guided visit to the Huron-Wendat longhouse at the Huron Traditional Site. This addition will see Intrepid reach its goal of an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of their Canada itineraries—a significant milestone on the road to integrating Indigenous-led experiences across every Canada trip. “When it comes to Indigenous tourism in Canada, we only take up five percent of tourism and that’s such a small percentage,” says Campo, as we stand before the lovely Lost Lake with its mountainous backdrop. “So this partnership with Intrepid and other Indigenous companies throughout Turtle Island—these are the partners I wanna work with.” As she distributes traditional ‘hush’ tea made with soothing raspberry leaf, refreshing mint sweet licorice root and vibrant rose hips, we talk of the importance of stories. “When it comes to a lot of Indigenous history and our government, they try to write our story for us,” she says. “We’re redirecting that chapter so we can write and share our stories ourselves.” The writer was hosted by Intrepid Travel **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Journalist and wanderluster Charmaine Noronha is a travel writer with a penchant for adventure, culture and chocolate. She started her career as a reporter with The Toronto Star before becoming the EIC of Vervegirl Magazine for five years then reported on Canadian news for The Associated Press for 11 years. Most recently, she was a Lifestyle reporter/editor at HuffPost Canada.

item.title: Traditional gumbo, kettle-boiled bagels, Chelsea buns: What do ‘endangered dishes’ tell us about the world today?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.71
Globalization, overtourism, climate crisis, and social change can all contribute to the loss of beloved cultural practices—including what we eat. But what does this mean for cultural and food heritage? And how can travelers help preserve the flavors that make our experiences so much richer?

item.title: Dark sky camp-out one day, zebra migration the next. Alternative adventures in the salt flats of northeastern Botswana
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.64
Camping on cracked earth in the middle of one of the world’s largest salt pans followed by a zebra migration across a dried-up riverbed prove to be an unexpected safari combo in this pocket of Botswana. “Makgadikgadi means ‘dry and thirsty place’,” our guide Metal Matmos tells us. No kidding. This is cracked earth indeed. We’ve arrived at one of the world’s largest salt pans to spend a night under one of the planet’s darkest skies. Bar our group and guides, there’s no-one around in this southern section of the lunar-like Makgadikgadi Salt Pans. Here, in northeastern Botswana, southeast of the Okavango Delta in the Kalahari Basin where the ancient Lake Makgadikgadi (pronounced Mah-caddy-caddy) once stood, salt denies grass and trees cannot germinate. It is barren, vast and surreal. As we drive closer to where Metal’s colleagues are setting up trestle tables and chairs, I spot our ‘rooms’ in the distance. Five cozy ‘bedrolls’ with a thick duvet inside bivvy bags—a tent-like covering we can crawl into—a couple of storage stands, and each bedroll a sizeable distance apart. Camping is not in my comfort zone—mostly down to an ick for shared bathrooms as opposed to sleeping outdoors, which is the good bit. But one thing travel does is test, and stretch, comfort zones. Perhaps falling asleep under a dark sky resplendent with stars on this flat, crater-like landscape with a 360-degree view of the horizon will do just that. An equally fair distance away in the opposite direction is the ‘bathroom’, a tented toilet with a washing bowl outside. It’s clean, far enough for privacy, close enough to (mostly) avoid middle-of-the-night Salt Pan Scaries. It passes the inspection. As Metal, full name Mathale Mosheti, gets the campfire going, I grab a moment to take in the vastness around us. I’ve traveled to remote spots before: The Kalahari Desert in South Africa’s Northern Cape province; the salt desert of Kutch, Gujarat in northwestern India; Churchill, Canada, the polar bear capital of the world. But I’d never felt this distant from life, so completely off-grid, surrounded by a silence that’s both unsettling and soothing. Within minutes, I fall asleep. When I wake, it’s to the most exquisite sunrise, a soft orange glow rising from the flat horizon ahead. This Makgadikgadi Salt Pans sleep-out is a seasonal experience from Desert & Delta’s Leroo La Tau lodge, one of 11 lodges and camps in their Botswana portfolio. A four-hour drive from the salt pans, I’d already spent one night there, and would return for another, if I survived the camping. 100 percent-Botswana-owned, all properties are managed by local people with staff empowerment woven in; Chobe Game Lodge, further north, home to Botswana’s first all-female-led guiding team. “The Makgadikgadi Pans are visible from the Moon,” Metal says as he hands me a bottle of local St Louis lager to accompany sunset. It’s not hard to believe; Lake Makgadikgadi, long evaporated, once covered an area larger than Switzerland. During the wet season, water surrounds the edges of the pans, attracting zebra, wildebeest and antelope en route to greener pastures, and flamingoes to the saltwater lakes that spring up. Metal, who has worked for Desert & Delta Safaris for nearly 18 years, is also a walking encyclopedia, whether it’s geology, birdlife or conservation. He’s one of those enigmatic guides you don’t forget and I feel lucky to have met a fair few on my travels; like others, he has a natural calling to share the joy of the landscapes, people and wildlife around him. After cold beers at sunset and a barbecued meal under the southern skies, bed beckons. The bedroll is cozy, and looking up is like being in a planetarium. I take out my phone, purely to bring up an offline stargazing app. I find the Southern Cross and a haze of stars that form the Milky Way. It’s utterly mesmerizing. While other constellations elude me, just staring up into the night, with zero light pollution, is satisfying enough. Perhaps a cliché for a reason, but I realize that sometimes we need such moments to remember how insignificant we are, to come outside of our own heads. I doubt this late-night philosophizing lasts long and I’m sure I fall asleep within minutes. When I wake, it’s to the most exquisite sunrise, a soft orange glow rising from the flat horizon ahead. At breakfast, we trade stories of our first salt pan camping experience. I admit, despite craving a hot shower, I leave the salt pans with a slight pang. When it’s a daily challenge to quieten the busy mind, this one night had done exactly that. Back on the road, a movement in the grasslands catches Metal’s attention. We all squint and ‘tune in’ with our eyes; I see something vaguely stripy scampering across the savannah. Metal’s eyes glint. “It’s an aardwolf.” It’s a rare sighting—it’s only the fourth time he’s seen one. “They’re from the same family as hyenas,” he tells us. Despite their somewhat feral carnivorous appearance, I learn they’re actually insectivores. An aardwolf’s idea of a good feast is munching around quarter of a million termites in one night, using their signature long sticky tongue to catch them. It’s a joy to return to my room at Leroo La Tau, perched above the seasonal Boteti River, the main outflow of the Okavango Delta, and along the western boundary of Makgadikgadi Pans National Park. Its 11 thatched-roof chalets and one suite are glass-fronted, so wherever you sit, stand, lie down—or even shower—there’s a Royal Circle view of the riverbed and watering holes. The river had began to recede in the mid-1980s, due to fewer flood waters from the delta and low rainfall. By the mid-1990s, it had dried up entirely, leaving just a few waterholes for crocodiles, hippos, zebras and wildebeest. In 2009, record rainfall arrived, reinstating this watercourse, albeit with a degree of unpredictability. Today, some 15,ooo zebras move 310 miles (510 kilometers) between the Okavango Delta/Moremi region and the Makgadikgadi Pans. We’re towards the end of the May-October dry season, the rainy season looming, and this river-turned-ravine, following a shift in tectonic plates, is teeming with herds of zebra, wildebeest, oryx, impala, elephants. Sat on the deck looking over the Boteti River Valley, I enjoy the scene unfolding in front of me. What I am sure is a vulture flies past then swoops below. Moments later, a monkey appears on the railings. I eyeball him or her, while guarding my cookie and sipping my tea. “When you reach a herd of elephants, you should pass by when they’re behind you, so you can drive forward if you need to and not in reverse which is slower. If guests want to die, they can die somewhere else.” - 'Metal' Mathale Mosheti, Desert & Delta Safaris guide Later, I head to the lodge’s hide, past the campfire and pool, for a closer close-up. It’s extraordinary to see zebras, wildebeest and the gang this close, and in such numbers. Walking back to the restaurant, an impala wanders across the lawn. They pause, I pause. For urbanites like me, these moments are (almost) as enchanting as the mightier scenes below. It’s also a reminder you are on the edge of a national park. When darkness falls, staff escort you to the rooms, and we’re advised to be vigilant. A windstorm blows outside, an eerie combination of piercing shrieks and deep gusts. Later, what we’re convinced is a leopard, comes close to camp. It’s exciting when you’re inside four walls and cocooned under a duvet and mosquito net. It’s definitely not the time to step onto the balcony to test your camera’s ‘night mode’. No matter what ‘people’ say about the early-morning game drive, I’ve always rated the late afternoon one. The bleary eyes of the dawn safari are long gone, it’s still warm, wildlife is mooching about, and golden hour is kicking in. As we drive through Makgadikgadi Pans National Park with our ranger Kets, Metal shares some of his road safety tips. “When you reach a herd of elephants, you should pass by when they’re behind you, so you can drive forward if you need to—and not in reverse which is slower,” he tells us. “If guests want to die, they can die somewhere else.” It sounds perfectly logical. We bookmark this advice in our heads for the next time we’re driving and come across a herd of the largest living mammal on earth. As we head down to the riverbed itself, the scenes from our decks are magnified. African savanna elephants on the move, dazzles of zebras sip at watering holes, a confusion of wildebeest join their stripy friends for a drink, and above, a kori bustard, the largest flying bird native to Africa. From a ridge, we spot crocodiles lurking at the water’s edge and grunting hippos enjoying their late afternoon dip. Alongside elephant health and safety, Metal tells us why zebras and wildebeest can happily graze together; zebras like taller grass while wildebeest go for shorter grass. “And you see how the impalas have an M-shape on their back?” he asks. We nod, expecting some mystical interpretation. “We call it McDonald’s for the lions.” We know our chances of seeing lions are slim, due to human-wildlife conflicts. “Lions used to go beyond the gate and kill goats in the villages; then they’d be killed,” says Metal. The river is the boundary, with the national park on one side, and community land and the lodge’s private land on the other. Communities live close to and around national parks and reserves, and their livelihoods and food security is vital. It’s something Desert & Delta are acutely conscious of, and part of their work involves investing in local education, community empowerment, and research. I’m reminded of a talk I attended back in London: “When an animal destroys someone’s garden, that person doesn’t have a Waitrose at the end of their road.” On my final morning, I stand on the deck and watch the scene in front of me for the last time. Zebras yap like puppies reuniting at Doggy Daycare, elephants arrive majestically at the watering hole, giraffes stroll along the ravine, while wildebeest, who look like they picked up the last remaining body parts in a fancy dress shop, move en masse. Between this sensory overload and the quiet emptiness of the salt flats, I feel my senses have had the full workout. ** The writer’s trip was supported by Desert & Delta Safaris and African Pride who curate a variety of packages in their properties across Botswana including Leroo La Tau and the salt pans sleep-out (dry season/June to October). **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. London-born-and-bred with a Ugandan-Indian heritage, Meera Dattani is Adventure.com's executive editor and an award-winning freelance travel journalist. Her stories center on food and cultural heritage, wildlife and conservation, and soft adventure, often through a lens of decolonizing and modernizing travel writing. Her work has been published in National Geographic Traveller, BBC Travel, Condé Nast Traveller, Olive magazine and many others.

item.title: These 6 Gear Trends Took the Long Trails By Storm in 2026
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.15
(Photo: Zoe Gates) On long trails, gear and clothing trends can seem as fad-driven as they were in high school. Caps are out, bucket hats are in. Heavy boots are so 2005. And if you aren’t dressed in a hooded, collared shirt with donuts all over it, are you even a thru-hiker? Show up to the trailhead with the wrong setup, and just like when you were a teenager, you might feel like you risk being laughed all the way back to town for a resupply. Not that every trend exists across every trail, of course. Trail culture—and the gear that contributes to it—varies from place to place. For example, “Ultralight felt very ‘in’ out west in a way that it didn’t out east,” says thru-hiker Madelyn Dukart, who has trekked long trails across the country. When something is hot in the thru-hiker community, it’s only a matter of time before it trickles down to the rest of the backpacking world. And while some gear crazes only stay in vogue for a season or two, plenty of fresh gear and apparel becomes popular thanks to its practicality or innovation. Here are the trends that took the long trails by storm this past season. To say the ultralight material Alpha Direct swept the thru-hiking community off their feet may be an understatement. “Just a year or two ago [thru-hikers] were all about microgrid hoodies, but they definitely have moved on to Alphas,” notes Mary Pillsbury, owner of 2 Foot Adventures outdoor stores located along the PCT in Julian and Kennedy Meadows. It makes sense: Alpha Direct is lighter, more compact, breathes better, and still insulates well when layered under a windproof jacket. Hoodies made from the material have been popular for a few seasons, but this year’s hikers aren’t stopping there: pants, hats, socks, even gloves have been hot ticket items this year for their gram-consciousness and versatility. Head to any trail town and there’s one thing you’re practically guaranteed to find in every hiker box: a quarter-full IsoPro fuel canister or three. After all, no one wants to leave town with one day of fuel left in their canister then have to carry it empty to the next resupply. Enter fuel transfer devices. These pocket-sized wonders allow hikers to combine fuel from multiple partially empty containers into one. They aren’t new this year, but they were formerly built of hefty metal materials. But a 2.4-gram plastic version is becoming ubiquitous: “Almost every hiker carries a fuel transfer device thanks to Alpenglow Gear. They are so light and inexpensive; 3D printing is changing the market,” says Pillsbury. “This is the first year I’ve heard thru-hikers talk about microplastics,” says Pillsbury. Where Smartwater bottles were once the go-to, more hikers have made the swap this year to using reusable CNOC or M!Go bottles, she’s noticed. Smart, since studies have shown that reusing single-use plastic bottles results in ingesting more microplastics. Plus, reusable bottles are designed to last for years and are only marginally heavier. “Most people that get involved in outdoor recreation begin with their love for nature, and it can feel dissonant to preach respecting nature while relying on single-use plastics for such a crucial piece of gear. Seeing multiple brands with thru-hiker-friendly water bottles seems to alleviate some of that dissonance,” Dukart says. Long gone are the days of huffing and puffing into your inflatable sleeping pad every night thanks to the rise of ultralight pad pumps. In fact, the gadgets have gotten so small and light––thanks in part to the rise of 3D-printed gear and the cottage industry––that there’s little reason not to pack one. After all, there’s an option to suit every hiker, from the stupendously light Alpenblow that you plug into a power bank to the battery-powered Flextail Zero Pump. Wander into any thru-hiker camp this season, and you’re unlikely to see many people inflating their pad the old fashioned way. While Durston has enjoyed a loyal cult following for several years now, this past thru-hiking season brought an explosion in popularity. “It feels like you can hardly walk through a campsite without seeing an X-Mid,” says Amber Rae Hedman, a thru-hiker who completed the PCT in 2022 and 2025, among other trails. It makes sense: The unique offset design of the trekking pole tent offers a more spacious layout and for staggering low weight. Plus, while they were once difficult to get as limited batches were often released months apart, more regular production has allowed hundreds—if not thousands—more hikers to become instant die-hard fans. A more surprising piece of gear that’s made an appearance on long trails in the last year are standalone cameras. Be they digital, film, or disposable, more thru-hikers are ditching the photo capabilities of their phones for a dedicated image-capture experience. “Documenting the journey has become such a big part of the thru-hiking experience,” Hedman says. To do so, many modern hikers are turning away from their smartphones. Is it worth the weight? That’s a personal choice. But compact cameras take measurably better photos than phones (and without draining your battery).

item.title: PCT’s Northern Terminus Reopens, to Thru-Hikers’ Delight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.08
Monument 78 and the Canada/ US border marks the northern end of the Pacific Crest Trail (Photo: eppicphotography via Getty Images) The northern terminus of the Pacific Crest Trail is accessible again following a weekslong closure that foiled the plans of many northbound (NOBO) thru-hikers. The 50-mile stretch from Hart’s Pass to the Canadian border reopened on September 9 after having been officially closed since July 31 due to the Ptarmigan fire. Since then, finishing northbound thru-hikers have commemorated the finish line in a number of ways: In late July, some built a makeshift monument at the trailhead for Rainy Pass, just south of the closure. Others rerouted to the west, converging on a little-known obelisk at the Canadian border in the Mount Baker Wilderness. As of today, NOBO hikers still on the trail will be able to take the standard route to the border. “We’re overjoyed to know that the PCT up to the Northern Terminus is open again, as it is such an iconic and symbolic portion of the trail,” says Chris Rylee, Director of Marketing and Communication for the Pacific Crest Trail Association. “Appreciation and gratitude goes out to the Methow Valley Ranger District of Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest and all of the other partners, responders, and firefighters who coordinated massive efforts to keep PCT hikers and communities safe.” As thru-hiking season winds down on the PCT, the reopening comes at a difficult time for many hikers who recently left the trail. Last year, the average finish date for NOBO thru-hikers on the PCT was September 12, according to a survey by Halfway Anywhere. “For me it’s tough because all last month I’ve heard that there’s no possible chance they’d open to the terminus, despite the Ptarmigan fire being more and more contained. Because of this I changed my plans to skip that section and go east to the other monument,” says Reed “Steezy” Patricelli, a thru-hiker from Portland, Oregon who reached the Canadian border on September 6, just three days before the terminus reopened. “As much as it’s a bit annoying, to me its also not a huge deal,” he adds. On his reroute to monument 90, a spot on the Canadian border east of the official terminus, Patricelli says he spotted three black bears and 12 mountain goats: “I firmly believe that the trail is a different journey for everyone, and if the end of my journey had to be a different terminus, so be it!” For others still in the final stretch, the reopening means they’ll be able to cross the trail in the way they’d always imagined. Nicola “Sunflower” Whitbread, a NOBOer from England, is one of those hikers. Whitbread was on the trail in northern Oregon when she heard from another hiker that the terminus had reopened. “The PCT for me has always been about the journey and not the destination, but I won’t lie, I’m stoked that I’ll have the finish I’ve dreamed of for a decade.” In an Instagram post, the PCTA noted that lands east and west of the trail remain closed due to ongoing firefighting operations.

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape”: Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.84
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from an order by the BLM this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in the first place in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to re-categorize the definition of livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said that removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species away from its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led to the cancellation of American Prairies public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.10
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston says. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW teams have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without breaks. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the 5-year average, and euthanizations are up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as we spoke on the phone. “It’s been a busy year,” he says. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he says: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston points to the record-low snowpack that has caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston says, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he says. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explains. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston points out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them, and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also says that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston says. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: How chislic became a South Dakota obsession
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.44
How a Crimean meat kebab travelled thousands of miles to become a South Dakota obsession Chislic may look like a simple meat skewer, but its journey from the Black Sea to the American Great Plains tells a much bigger story. At Meridian Corner, a roadhouse amid the corn and alfalfa fields of Freeman in South Dakota, my lunch took about 40 seconds to arrive at the table: five sticks of lamb and five of mutton, deep-fried and served with garlic salt and crackers. This is chislic – South Dakota's most beloved light bite, often eaten as an appetiser or snack between meals. Here in the town of Freeman, it's ubiquitous, served in bars, restaurants, and homes across this south-eastern pocket of the state. Drive much beyond it, however, and people may have no idea what you're talking about. "I grew up eating chislic and never thought much about it," town archivist Marnette Hofer told me. "Then I went to college in Kansas, and nobody knew about it. I don't think people in the Black Hills – in South Dakota! – had a clue." Chislic may be distinctly South Dakotan, but its roots lie thousands of miles away, around the Black Sea. So how did it become so thoroughly local that, in 2018, the state legislature made it the official state "nosh"? From Crimea to Dakota In the 1870s, Germans from Russia began arriving in what was then Dakota Territory, bringing with them traditions from their former homes around the Black Sea. Hofer, who grew up in the area and serves as the executive director of its Heritage Hall Museum & Archives, took me through its exhibits chronicling the historic passage. As she showed me around its exhibits, we discussed chislic and the unlikely chain of events that brought it here. While roasting meat on sticks is an ancient technique, peoples living around the Black Sea and the Caucasus traditionally cut their meat into small chunks before skewering it on metal rods, or even swords. Russian troops encountered this style of cooking among Tatars in Crimea and the Caucasus as the empire pushed south towards the Black Sea from the late 17th Century. Called "shashlyk", it was typically made with mutton, marinated in onions or vinegar and grilled on skewers – quick to prepare and easy to eat on the move. By the late 18th Century, shashlyk had become fashionable in parts of the Russian Empire and was enthusiastically taken up by German settlers who had been encouraged to settle in Russia under Catherine the Great, many of whom later established communities around the Black Sea. But in the 1870s, as Tsar Alexander II revoked privileges long granted to its German settlers, including their religious freedom and exemption from military service, many began emigrating. Among the things they carried with them were recipes. "And President Abraham Lincoln had eight years previously enacted the Homestead Act of 1862, promising cheap land on the American frontier," recounts Tim Waltner, the Heritage Hall's education and communication coordinator. "If you stayed on five years, the land was yours." The timing proved irresistible to immigrants from all over Europe, including some 115,000 Russo-Germans – or "Germans from Russia" as they would become known. Among them was farmer-turned-carpenter Johann Hoellwarth, who arrived in the growing town of Freeman in the 1870s. According to the earliest records available, said Hofer, Hoellwarth was the first to introduce shashlyk to Dakotan palates. "Only," she adds, "his accent was so thick people thought he was saying 'chislic'." How shashlyk became chislic The new name stuck, and more changes were ahead. Hoellwarth quickly discovered that the windswept Great Plains were very different from Crimea's milder landscape. While sheep farming was well established in the Dakotas by the early 1800s, there was no metal for skewers, no vinegar for marinating, and on the treeless prairies, hardwood was far too precious to burn. Even onions were relatively new. Like many immigrants before him, Hoellwarth made do with what he had: a cauldron, lard, garlic salt, hand-length sticks whittled from willow bushes, and 10ft (3m)-tall wild grasses that burned fast but hot. This is how a meal that was once marinated, grilled on a sword and eaten with flatbread became a deep-fried, salted bite-sized snack served on a glorified toothpick and eaten with crackers. "He would serve it during Fourth of July celebrations in Freeman," said Hofer. And just as Russian soldiers had discovered generations earlier, "it was popular." Inside the Chislic Circle At Meridian Corner, the chislic is traditional and the gossip, as the saying goes, could rip the paint off a barn. The roadhouse sits at the heart of the Chislic Circle, a term coined by writer Richard Preheim in 2005 for the roughly 30-mile radius around Freeman where devotion to chislic runs deep. It has also become something of a culinary bastion. Even after chislic was named the state's official "nosh" and chefs began serving beef, goat and pork versions, the Circle largely held to lamb and mutton. The legislature chose "nosh" rather than "dish" or "meal" because it considered the term a better fit for the snack-sized food. "When it became the state nosh, the definition of what chislic is really expanded," said Abby Streyle, Meridian Corner's manager, who is of German-Russian ancestry. "It's fun when people do different twists on a food, but it is important to keep some things old-school." More like this: But chislic has been evolving almost from the start. From Hoellwarth's introduction, as it passed down family lines the recipe picked up local peculiarities reflected in eateries across the area today. In the nearby town of Kaylor, the Kaylor Locker, the butcher supplying most of the Circle for the last 65 years, serves a venison version, the Circle's only acceptable stand-in for lamb or mutton. At Pep's Pub across the street, the chislic is griddled – not fried – with onions. In the town of Dimock, locally made cheese is added as a side along with crackers, while Bud's Tavern in Marion adds jalapeños to the onions and uses only "dirty oil" (previously used) to enhance the flavour. Some adaptations have been economic. Pep's Pub and Bud's Tavern serve their chislic "loose" – without skewers – a practice Cindy Fischer, owner of The Schnitz Bar in the town of Menno, says helped keep prices down. Others were practical. Over-fried chislic comes out hard as a rock, which may help explain the rise of griddles and air fryers to keep the meat juicy and evenly cooked. How far can chislic stretch? "When we began, we had a tasting competition and divided it into traditional and 'New Age Nosh' categories," she recalled. "Even then, there were some who scoffed that nothing other than traditional sheep chislic earned the name. But in the New Age Nosh category, someone wanted to enter alligator! That was going too far." Beyond the Chislic Circle, however, the rules remain loose. I tried beef chislic at the Blarney Stone in Sioux Falls – an hour's drive from Freeman – that bucked tradition further with horseradish and Carolina BBQ sauces. Delicious, but Hoellwarth's head would likely be exploding. "They called it steak tips before 2018," Streyle muttered. While the recipe continues to evolve, what chislic represents has remained remarkably consistent. "Chislic is hospitality in a simple, unassuming dish," Hofer told me. "Kind of a 'come as you are, we're glad you're here' type of food. It is a simple experience that reminds people of a community where hard work and honesty are important values. Where being real, down-to-earth and welcoming are just part of life." And one day, maybe even with alligator. --

item.title: Six US drive-ins where you can stay the night
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.22
Six places in the US where you can sleep at a drive-in From retro 1950s properties to modern glamping sites, these places are reviving one of the US's most enduring pastimes – and offering travellers one last classic summer experience. At the Frontier Drive-Inn, there are no televisions in the guest rooms. Instead, as the property rather cheekily puts it, the biggest TV in southern Colorado is right outside your door. That would be the outdoor screen left over from the Frontier's first life as a drive-in cinema, which opened in 1955 and went dark three decades later. Today, the former cinema anchors a retro-inspired hotel where guests sleep in Quonset-style yurts and vintage trailers, then gather outside for films beneath the famously dark skies of the San Luis Valley. As Labor Day (7 September) approaches, the Frontier and other properties like it are providing a fresh take on one of the US's most enduring warm-weather pastimes – and offering one last classic summer experience before the season winds down. For generations of Americans, drive-ins have been inseparable from summer. The country's first drive-in opened in 1933, but they exploded after WWII, when rising car ownership, suburban expansion and the baby boom helped push their number to nearly 5,000 by the late 1950s, according to April Wright, a drive-in historian and director of Going Attractions: The Definitive Story of the American Drive-In Movie in which she visits roughly 500 open, abandoned or former drive-in sites. "Going to the drive-in was just something you did every summer," Wright said. Though their heyday may have passed, Wright says the appeal of drive-ins isn't purely nostalgic. Plenty of younger visitors are experiencing them for the first time, drawn to the fact that a night at the drive-in is as much about the ritual around the film as the film itself. "What it's always been about, and what it is still about today, is spending time with friends and family, and creating an experience," Wright said. Now, a handful of hotels, motels and campgrounds around the US are turning that experience into an overnight stay. Some have revived long-shuttered drive-ins, while others let guests sleep within sight of giant screens that have been showing films for decades. At these properties, film night doesn't end with the final credits. Frontier Drive-Inn – Center, Colorado Luke Falcone, co-owner of Frontier, said the screen had survived decades of the San Luis Valley's harsh weather and was too important to the site's history to lose. "When doing historic preservation projects, if you come across something that isn't broken, you've hit the jackpot," he said. Despite the name, the Frontier is no longer a traditional drive-in: guests don't pull up in their cars, but settle into lawn chairs or onto blankets to watch fan-favourite films under the stars. "By bringing folks out of their rooms (and cars), we provide an entirely different experience that we can all bond over," Falcone said. The programming leans into nostalgic cult classics, while the accommodation is decidedly modern. Best Western Movie Manor – Monte Vista, Colorado The motel was built beside The Star Drive-In Theatre, which opened in 1955 as drive-ins were booming across the US, and many rooms face one of its two screens through large picture windows, with the film's audio piped inside. Each room is named after a movie star, from Cary Grant to Robert De Niro, and guests can also head outside and watch from their cars. More than 70 years after The Star first lit up, it still shows films seasonally (generally from spring to the end of September). Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday – Sutherlin, Oregon The Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday campground occupies the former Cloverleaf Drive-In, where the original 100ft (30m) screen survived long after the cinema itself closed. When the current owner bought the property in 2006, they chose to keep the screen and eventually added a digital projector and FM transmitter, bringing films back to the site. Today, films are shown most weekends. Some RV sites sit directly in front of the screen (or have private patios angled towards it), allowing guests to watch from their rigs and tune into the film over their radios, much as they would at a traditional drive-in. Tent campers and guests in the rest of the RV sites can bring chairs or blankets to a grassy viewing area just in front of the screen, where the sound plays aloud. Hotel Caravana at Four Brothers Drive-In – Amenia, New York Unlike most of the places on this list, Four Brothers isn't a survivor from the golden age of the silver screen. The Hudson Valley theatre opened in 2013, reviving the format decades after thousands of its predecessors had disappeared. Since then, the family-run property has added mini-golf, fire pits and Hotel Caravana, where guests can sleep in vintage trailers within the drive-in grounds or even pitch their own tent. Ofland Escalante – Escalante, Utah Set along Scenic Byway 12 in southern Utah, Ofland Escalante occupies a former drive-in site within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. Guests spend the day hiking, exploring slot canyons or visiting nearby Bryce Canyon and Capitol Reef national parks, then return in time for the nightly film. "The movie starts just after dusk and it anchors the whole evening," said Noah Ellis, CEO of Ofland Hotels. "It's a key amenity, not an add-on." The old drive-in comes with its own fleet of vintage cars – including a 1957 Chevrolet and Ford Thunderbird – that are parked facing the screen. Guests grab complimentary popcorn and classic sweets from the concession stand, choose a car and settle in beneath the desert sky. "The site was a drive-in long before it was a hotel, so keeping actual cars in the mix mattered to us," Ellis said. "There's something about a row of vintage cars, climbing in with a bag of popcorn, that stays with people." Overnight options range from modernised vintage Airstreams to a variety of cabins. Tiger Drive-In – Tiger, Georgia Tucked into the mountains of north-eastern Georgia, the Tiger Drive-In first opened in 1954, went dark in the 1980s and then sat abandoned for roughly two decades. It returned to life in 2004, and today guests can stay after the movie in one of three vintage 1960s campervans parked on the drive-in grounds (each with a private deck facing the screen), or camp in a tent or RV. --

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.67
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Why visitors to Prague should drink in a 'hospoda'
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.00
Why visitors to Prague should drink in a traditional pub Prague is synonymous with pubs – but for the real thing, travellers should venture away from its touristy centre and seek out an old-school "hospoda". My wife and I were sipping beers at a pub in Prague's Žižkov district when the bartender plopped two foamy pints of pilsner in front of us. We hadn't ordered them. We weren't even finished with the ones we were drinking. "Oh, we're in one of these pubs" I said, quickly covering my pint with a cardboard coaster. "When you've had enough, just do this." Most visitors to Prague are likely to linger in its Old Town Square, marvelling at its Gothic and Baroque splendour. They'll zigzag through the narrow cobblestone streets to the 14th-Century Charles Bridge and then trudge up to Prague Castle. Everyone should do this on a visit to Prague. But if you only explore its tourist-mobbed centre, as many people do, you'll miss out on one of the most quintessentially Czech cultural experiences: whiling away a few hours in a real Czech pub, where the beer only stops coming if you know the code. A city synonymous with beer It's no secret that Czechs love beer. After all, they drink nearly 150 litres of it per capita every year, making the Czech Republic the top beer-consuming nation in the world. Prague itself boasts the most pubs per person of anywhere on the planet. Your local expert David Farley is a food and travel writer who lived in Prague for three years and regularly writes articles for the BBC, The New York Times, The Guardian and other publications. He has probably spent a year or two of his life in Czech pubs. But just as most New Yorkers don't dine in Times Square and most Londoners don't eat in Piccadilly Circus, you'll rarely find Praguers drinking in Old Town, where bars cater largely to outsiders. Instead, to really get under the skin of Czech culture, you should venture to one of Prague's most atmospheric areas: Žižkov (pronounced Zheezh-kof), a gritty, working-class neighbourhood that has long had a proud reputation for its salt-of-the-earth pubs, and where the bartender's job is to make sure your glass is never empty. Home to hilly cobblestone streets and graffiti-tagged 19th-Century blocks of flats, Žižkov is home to classic pubs such as U Vystřelenýho Oka and U Slovanské Lípy. Despite its relative proximity to the centre of town – tram number 9 will get you there in about 20 minutes – you won't find a lot of guidebook-clutching tourists wandering around. "If you want to understand Czech pub culture, it's hard to find a better place than Žižkov," said Martin Havlin, co-founder of Prague Craft Beer Tours and a born-and-bred Žižkov denizen. "The big difference is that pubs in Žižkov are still mainly for locals. Nobody is trying too hard to look 'authentically Czech' for tourists. You'll find people having a beer after work, old guys at the same table they've probably occupied for 30 years, and a tapster who already knows what half the room is drinking." Žižkov's traditional Czech pubs, called hospoda, are one of the few places where people from all walks of Czech society mix naturally. Hospoda etiquette • If you you're sitting at a table, you're expected to wait for the server to take your order. Unless it's clearly indicated otherwise, don't order at the bar yourself. • Glasses are served wet at a hospoda, so always take the beer mat. It goes under your beer and will save you a wet table – and probably a few looks from the staff. • In Czech lager, foam is part of the beer, not something stealing space in the mug, so don't send it back because you think the glass hasn't been filled to the line. It has. "You can have a construction worker, lawyer, university professor and pensioner sitting at neighbouring tables drinking exactly the same beer," said Jakub Neužil, Havlin's colleague at Prague Craft Beer Tours. "Most importantly, though, they would understand that going to the pub in Czech culture isn't necessarily about 'going out drinking'. Historically, the hospoda has been an extension of the living room: somewhere to meet friends, discuss football, politics, work and life. Beer happens to be at the centre of it." These "living rooms" are great places for travellers to meet English-speaking regulars. A simple "how long have you been coming here?" may soon lead to stories about how hospoda have played an instrumental role in Czech history. Prague was the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and until World War Two, German was widely spoken here alongside Czech. By the latter half of the 19th Century, Czech speakers had begun separating themselves from the German population, and the Czech National Revival, which would eventually result in the creation of Czechoslovakia in 1919, was fomented in Czech cafes and pubs. "At the time, pubs played an important role as gathering places for revivalists, patriots, politicians, writers, artists et cetera; they became centres of associational and cultural life and were one of the few places where Czech was commonly spoken," said Dr Jiří Vinopal, a Senior Fellow at the Institute of Sociology at the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. During the heavily oppressive socialist period from 1948 to 1989, Vinopal explains that Czech pubs were "used more as an environment for escape". More like this: Today, pubs are as much a part of Czech life as ever – and a big draw for tourists – but it's increasingly harder to find the kind of old-fashioned hospoda where historical conversations flow as easily as the beer. The city's modern offerings tend to be cleaner and smoke free, with classic fried cheese sharing menu space with dishes like pumpkin soup and cauliflower pancakes. How to drink at a real Czech pub? Havlin's advice is to simply find a busy pub in Žižkov, sit down, order a beer and don't rush. "Watch how people behave, how the beer is poured, order some Czech pub food and maybe start a conversation – and definitely don't leave after one beer." He adds, "That’s the beauty of a real [hospoda]. You're not being shown Czech culture – you're just sitting in the middle of it. And after the second or third beer, you might even start feeling like a local." While sipping your beer and meeting regulars, you may also notice the way Czech bartenders treat Czech beer differently than the more touristy pubs in Prague's historical centre. It starts with the bartender taking a chilled mug and re-rinsing it using a counter-top spray device to ensure there's no fat residue. Then they use the Czech-invented Lukr side-tap to pour the beer, ensuring there's at least three fingers' worth of foam; the side-tap allows the bartender more control of the foam and emits far less gas into the drink than the traditional top pull, making the beer from the Lukr side tap less likely to bloat the stomach. "This developed because beer has been such an important part of Czech culture," said Lucie Janečkova, co-founder of Institut PIVO, a Prague-based school providing beer-focused bartender training. "We've learned that brewing a good beer is only half of the job. What happens to it between the brewery and the guest can completely change the final experience." There is a common saying among Czech bartenders: 'The brewer brews the beer; the bartender makes it.'" There's also an etiquette to drinking once your beer arrives. "When you get a beautifully poured beer, drink it while it's fresh – don't leave it sitting on the table for half an hour," added Janečkova. "And if you're drinking with others, clink glasses with your first beer and say 'cheers' in Czech – 'na zdraví!'" She adds, "And perhaps the most Czech rule of all: if someone says, 'Let's go for one beer,' you probably shouldn't make any plans for the rest of the evening." And, as my wife learned, if you're in a pub in Žižkov, even the bartender won't let you go until you finally put that beer mat atop your empty mug. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.96
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.46
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent.
