How much jam was the recipe supposed to yield? Thank you for this recipe and challenge. I will definitely make it again. It's a showstopper. Here are pictures of my process putting it together." And Mark sends us a beautiful little grid of six photos. JS: Mark's Karpatka looks so good. SU: It looks so good. He got a really dramatic top hat. JS: Yeah, it's crazy wonky and big. SU: And in the picture, Mark has a glass container of plum jam, which is kind of half full. He seems to have maybe at least a cup, if not a little bit more of plum jam leftover, but you can tell from the way it's on the sides of the container, that it does seem a bit thinner than maybe what you intended. JS: Yeah, because the top of the jam was completely flat. SU: Yes. JS: And I think if it was cooked longer, it would have a more texture. SU: Chunky. JS: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think the jam is just one of those things that's like a recipe can only tell you so much, and then you have to cook it to your instinct. And looking at your jam, it does look like, perhaps, it was a little loose. It could have gone longer. So, I think you were very smart and had good baker instinct holding back on not using it all. And it looks like it cut clean. So, yeah, I would just enjoy the extra jam. But for those who haven't made it yet, when you're making the jam, it's almost like you have to cook it until it's dry enough, that when you drag a spatula through it, it kind of holds the streak for a second. SU: Oh, okay. JS: You know what I mean? SU: Yeah. JS: You're not making caramel, but it needs to have body. SU: Yeah, yeah, yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. Mark, essentially, you did amazing. Next time, reduce the compote a bit further. JS: Yeah, but I think your instincts were spot on. SU: Yes. And that top hat of your Karpatka looks so good. JS: No, yeah, it looks really good. SU: Okay. And while we're on the compotes, Meg reached out to say, "I feel so accomplished after making this. This is the plum side. The other half is peach compotes." JS: Oh, wow. SU: "They're both tasty, so I'm glad I didn't go back to the store, but I realized half my plums had gone bad. Really fun project. And my teenage son says this is his favorite Bake Club recipe to date." JS: Wow. SU: "Perfect for summer." JS: Okay. First of all, Meg, you're a real one. You've been with us forever. SU: Yes. JS: I think it's absolutely crazy cool that you have a half peach, half plum side. SU: I love that. And rather than swirling it all together, Meg really kept it two different sides. JS: I think, again, this is like your baker's instincts was spot on. Don't go to the store to get more. Just use what you have and make it work. And this was really smart. Also, your puff is good too. SU: Yeah, Meg's cake. Meg took it in a really beautiful light. It's very dramatic and the filling is so tall and beautiful looking. JS: It looks great. SU: Jesse, what other fruits do you think would work well? Taking Meg's example of using peaches instead of plums. JS: I'm trying to think of fruits that wouldn't work well. SU: Oh. JS: And it's harder. I think raspberries would be exceptional. SU: Yeah. JS: Any berry, to be honest, would be really impactful. Any stone fruit would be great. I don't know. What do you think? SU: I am inclined. A berry or a stone fruit, yes. JS: Those are the easiest ones, I feel like. SU: Those are the easiest. I don't think we would do something like a citrus. JS: That would take a little more work, I feel like. SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Maybe a store-bought, like a citrus marmalade. JS: You could totally use that. SU: Maybe. JS: Yeah, or even a curd could probably be swirled in there. SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. And I do think if you wanted to take a shortcut, just buy a jar of really nice jam, and that would totally work. SU: Okay. We have a question about choux pastry from Katie. Jesse, this actually was a question that came in from a Paris-Brest episode, and we didn't get to answer it then, but I think it's perfect timing now. And Katie writes to us saying, "When cooking the dough on the stove, I felt like my dough was done really fast. Is it possible to overcook at this point?" What do you think, Jesse? JS: I think that it does happen really fast, actually, or it can. I think you can overcook. I think that it's not likely. Some people treat it like more of an instinctual kind of thing, where it's like the recipe's written flexible with the amount of eggs to account for this exact issue, because sometimes your choux pre-eggs is drier. Sometimes it is more wet, and the eggs are supposed to account for that. So, mine doesn't give a range, but I think it'd be hard to overcook it, to be honest. SU: Yeah, it would probably burn before it's overcooked. JS: Yeah. And I feel like for the things we're using it for, it's going to be fine. SU: Okay, that makes sense. JS: Yeah, and it can happen fast. So, this makes sense, Katie, that you felt that this was rushed, because it can be. SU: Especially if your pot is whiter than what you maybe intended for. JS: Totally. SU: Okay. That's amazing. And now, we're moving on to the filling, Jesse, where we have two questions from Rachel L. She writes, "The plum jam is perfection. Made the Karpatka with some gorgeous plums that I got at the farmer's market. I will be making seasonal fruit riffs of this recipe in the future." "I ended up making the filling twice. The first time I tried to substitute the gelatin with three-quarter teaspoon of agar. However, the filling wasn't light and fluffy. It was liquid. Because it was late and I didn't have any more cream cheese, I ended up having to wrap my choux overnight to retry making the filling the next morning. The filling in the pictures was made with whipped cream folded into the whipped cream cheese mixture." "I have two questions," says Rachel. "Do you have any advice for working with agar or other gelatin substitutes?" And her second question is, "My choux looks a little gummy towards the center tip of the slice. It tasted great, but should I have mixed it longer after the final egg, or could it be because I let it sit overnight wrapped on the counter? Is it also possible to re-crisp the choux before assembly?" These are all fantastic questions, actually. JS: These are good. I'll start with the choux questions. They're a little easier. SU: Yeah. JS: I will say, can you re-crisp choux? Yes, famously so, a lot of times, bakeries and restaurants will do that. You can bake them, and then if you put them in a hot oven for a few minutes, they come right back to life. However, if your Karpatka is a little gummy towards the center, for me, that just indicates that it could have been baked longer. For the assembly here, because it's refrigerated with this filling, you want to really bake it, and choux can take it. It can be cooked, as we say every episode, bien cuit, just quite dark. So, don't be afraid to cook it until it's like a medium wood shade, not just golden brown, a touch darker, and then it's going to be more resilient and hold up to that refrigeration and filling. For the agar, I got to be real. I don't have so much experience with agar. It's a whole different beast. SU: Yeah. JS: Shilpa, do you have experienced the agar? SU: Not really. Not very much. I remember- JS: It's very like molecular gastronomy in my mind. SU: It is. It is. It's pliable ganache. JS: Pliable ganache, fluid gel, espuma. SU: Jesse and I are going to put that in a T-shirt, by the way. If you're willing to purchase it, let us know. JS: Yeah, please reach out to us. SU: No, I don't have much experience with agar. I just know it's- JS: It's fascinating. It holds up at any temperature, I know that. SU: Yes. JS: Yeah. SU: It is not thermoreversible, and it makes a very brittle set. JS: It's firm. Yeah, it's different. SU: And it's used a lot in the making of the fluid gels that we just mocked, because what agar can do is, after it sets it like a solid sort of jello brick, I want to say, then you can blend it, and it forms this nice sort of- JS: Glossy? SU: Yeah, a glossy- JS: Ketchup. SU: Ketchup consistency. It's like if jello was a sauce, and somehow held its shape. So, it's great for that, but unfortunately, I don't have experience working with it as a gelatin substitute. JS: Yeah. I know it is the go-to gelatin substitute, so it makes sense, but it's ... SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah, you'll have to tell us. Yeah. SU: I mean, I did like Rachel's solution where she ended up using whipped cream. JS: Yeah, it looks like it held up fine enough. Yeah, these are great questions. SU: Fantastic questions, Rachel. I'm sorry we don't have more experience on the agar, but if any of you are listening out there and you do have experience, you can always write them to us on our Substack. Okay. And a question about getting the swirls of compote, and this one is from Holly. Holly says, "Delicious. I was concerned about the choux pastry, but it puffed up in the oven nicely. I needed to remove it a few minutes early as it did get a little past golden brown. The cream cheese mixture seemed runny at first, but set overnight. The plum jam is yummy. We sampled it on toast too. I think I need help with the swirling part. Any suggestions? Maybe a little less jam as the filling looked more red and less ribboned. The choux pastry was tasty, and when combined with the cream cheese mixture, amazing." JS: I mean, the picture, it looks very nice. SU: Yeah. JS: And I think the color of the choux is what I want people to do, actually. SU: I agree with you. JS: Yeah, so a beautiful tan. Swirling, actually, I do have advice, and my advice is you have to have kind of restraint, dollop it in, and just barely drag it through. In fact, I'd rather you didn't drag your dollops versus swirling too much. If you swirl to the point where it looks how you want it to be, by the time you cut into and set, it's going to look overswirled. SU: It's too swirled. JS: Yeah, so just have a light hand. Yeah. SU: And you do advice doing it in stages, right? You say do a layer of the cheesecake, then do a layer of the plum. JS: Yes. SU: Do a little light swirl, then do more filling. JS: Yes. And since you're building a pan, what I like to do is take a spoon you don't care about, and bend it so it's- SU: Like at 90 degrees, like an L. JS: Yeah, like an L. And then I use that to assemble the inside, and it really helps. And you can bend it back, whatever. It's fine. SU: You can't. JS: It's a work spoon. I'm not paying for it. SU: It's a little freak of a spoon. JS: Save it for later. SU: It is very helpful in this application. JS: Yeah, you can use it for other things. SU: Yes. If you make a lot of layer cakes, you should definitely be bending your spoon into an L shape. JS: I agree. I agree. SU: Okay. And finally, from Christina, "What is the leftover situation for the cheesecake? Should I wait to make it until I have enough people to eat it all at once, or can it last in the fridge for a bit?" JS: It totally lasts. Yeah. I think since it's that we're leaning into the crisp/gone soggy of it all, I think that it will last for several days, and you're good. SU: Ooh, okay. Okay, perfect. And before we take a break, it's time for our new tradition. JS: Okay. SU: The Baker of the Month Award, in which you get nothing but a shoutout. Jesse, who gets the shoutout this month? JS: Okay. Listen, I know Mark, you didn't cook your jam far enough, but that top choux you got, that looks like a nasal cavity. It is giant, and I feel like you get the award because your choux is the wonkiest, the craziest. I love it. SU: Wonderful. JS: Yeah. Mark, you win. SU: Mark and your nasal cavity, Karpatka won our Baker of the Month Award. JS: We're having the wonkiest bake. You win. SU: Okay. We are going to take another break on that note. JS: And when we get back, we're going to introduce you to a baker we think you should know. SU: Welcome back to BA Bake Club. JS: And it is time to meet a baker that we think you should know, although she might already be a familiar face to many of you, if you are online, or if you watch the British Baking Show. SU: We have a lot of British Baking Show fans. JS: A lot of fans. SU: Ruby Bhogal survived the Bake Off tent. She was a finalist on season nine of the show, and she now has a very exciting, very beautiful book called Around the World in 80 Cakes. JS: So, Ruby, we are so excited to have you. Ruby Bhogal: Thank you so much for letting me gatecrash your podcast today. JS: No, not a crash. It is an enrichment. SU: Oh, God, enrichment is really lovely. RB: You're being too kind. SU: No, thank you for sending the book, Ruby. We both really love the book, and I love that there's such a nice variety of things in there. JS: Yeah. I'm curious what the inspiration was, because it sounds really difficult to write, honestly. SU: Yeah. RB: Yeah. I didn't make my life easy for myself when I started the second book. And in all honesty, the series started online, I can't believe I'm going to say this, three years ago, which is mind-boggling, because people have followed the journey from the very start and have now had kids who are three years old. And that honestly makes me, A, very happy, but B, also mortified that I've taken so long to make 80 cakes. JS: You can't think about it too much. RB: No. You know what? It's done, it's done now. It's fine. But I initially started the series as a bit of light relief. I had just finished writing my first book, and was looking for something to kind of reignite my baking mojo. I had poured every last bit of me into my first book, and I was talking to one of my friends, and she was like, "Oh, have you seen this list? This is the top 10 cakes in the world." And I was like, "Oh, this would be really fun just to try out on social media. No pressure, just having a little bit of fun with it and see what we can do." And then my brain was like, "Well, 10 doesn't sound really exciting, and 10 also sounds like I could do that in a weekend. Why not make it 80, because it's obviously a catchy title?" And honestly, when I first thought of that, "I thought this is going to be easy. I will get 80 cakes made in about a couple of months, seriously, we'll be done, and then I'll move on to something else." Lo and behold, it's taken me three years to make 80 cakes. And I've done my best to deep dive really quickly into the history of each cake and learn about the origins. And it's so much more than just my sassy quips that people normally see on Instagram. SU: What was the most challenging, or maybe unfamiliar, region of bakes that you tackled? RB: Honestly, all of it. Even the cakes that I'm familiar with, I think, especially in the UK, like our beloved Victoria Sponge and Lemon Drizzle, I really wanted to go above and beyond just what we normally get or what we normally know. I really wanted to understand the history about it, and learn a bit more about where it originated from, and the initial variations that people used to make of it. And that was quite hard. And people are very patriotic about their cakes, which has honestly been endearing, but also mind-boggling, because people get really upset if you don't make it how their nan has made it. And I think for me, in my book, I've tried to be respectful to tradition, but then also wanted to add my own tweak to it, my own kind of twist to a recipe, because otherwise then it's just me regurgitating a lot of stuff that already preexists. But it's been a really wild journey. I really have loved being able to explore different continents and different countries all from the comfort of my own kitchen, and really being able to showcase cakes from regions that really just don't get shown enough or people are aware of. For instance, there's this Fijian honey cake, which features in the book, which is stunning. It's so easy to make. It's a real distillation of that country in carb form, and I really love that. JS: Not to overaggrandize, but it's almost like you're kind of decolonizing baking education, because I feel it's so rooted in French technique, and that's "The proper thing we're taught." But it's like the world is huge. SU: Yeah. JS: Yes, and this is such a beautiful tone. SU: An encyclopedia. JS: Yeah, so I love what you're doing. RB: Thank you. JS: Okay. Taking it back to Karpatka. RB: Yeah. JS: So, you made a traditional one, and you liked it. And as a proud Polish person, I say thank you. But you also made a PB&J ones. So, I also riffed on Karpatka for this. So, I'm wondering where your riff, the inspiration came from. RB: I have wanted to make one for so long. Love choux pastry, think it was delicious, and then have seen iterations of it on social media for a very, very long time. Because I think the first time I made it, I just rippled through a rhubarb and strawberry compote in there. And it was so delicious, but people got so mad at me because, obviously, you can't beat tradition, you can't beat what's original. But honestly, I think you can in certain circumstances. And then the PB&J one was really just a bit of fun. It was just something where I wanted to bring classic flavors, or a classic flavor combination of a peanut butter and jelly, into something that is quite traditional. Choux pastry is such a wonderful vehicle for stuffing with lots of wonderful things. So, yeah. JS: I'm excited to try it. SU: Yeah, and I think it's brilliant. It's like PB&J, like a PB&J sandwich essentially. JS: How can you not like it? SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: I think it's great. We endorse, and I think that really governs a lot of stuff we do at Bake Club, which is we take- JS: Yeah, if you give credit and you honor it- SU: Yes. JS: ... yes, you can riff. SU: Yeah. Since we're in the Karpatka zone, Ruby, we have a listener question that Jesse's going to- JS: Sure. Yeah. So, this comes from a listener named Ashley, and she wrote, "I loved making this recipe. The Karpatka was stunning. One slight issue was the weather. It's been really hot lately, and it started to look a bit sad in the heat. I don't have air conditioning. Any tips to help deal with hot weather?" We thought you might be perfect, as I feel like everyone's like, "The tent, it's so hot." RB: And also, no one in the UK has air conditioning. Let's be real. That was a whole topic on social media over the summer. But especially, when it comes to something like choux pastry, I don't really feel like there is much movement for it, in terms of choux pastry is akin to something like a sponge. It loves moisture, and so the only way you can really keep choux pastry nice and crisp for a long time is to only fill it before you're about to eat it. So, maybe this is, you tackle it in a way of making smaller Karpatkas, or individual Karpatkas, where it's essentially just a filled choux bun. But another way you can maybe tackle that, in a not so traditional way, is by adding craquelin on top of there, which will kind of give the top of the choux pastry a bit more of a crunchy texture, which may work if you're eating it straight away, or you are eating it the same day. But then, alternatively, again, if you are going to be putting it in the fridge, once again, it will still soak up and locks that moisture. So, my tip would be maybe make smaller Karpatkas, or smaller choux buns, if that's what you want to do and keep them for a longer time period. And then before you're about to eat them, pop them back into the oven for about 5, 10 minutes, just to crisp up again, just on something low and slow, just to help draw out any of that excess moisture. But choux pastry is choux pastry. How you've got anything left over once you've made it is beyond me, because that stuff goes within a blink of an eye. JS: I like the idea of making tiny Karpatkas too, because then you just eat it before the filling will melt too if it's crazy hot. SU: Yeah, that's true. RB: Absolutely. JS: And I wonder if you could use a little muffin tin and make little baby ones. SU: That would be so cute. RB: That would be so cute. JS: Yeah. SU: That is cute. JS: I've never tried. SU: Thanks, Ruby. That was actually a very helpful tip. JS: I want to make little baby ones now. RB: I know, me too. SU: Okay. Now, we're going to talk about Bake Off stuff, which I'm sure a lot of listeners want to hear about. And we want to know what the experience taught you about yourself. RB: Oh, I mean, what a phenomenal experience, particularly, as I'd only started baking, I'd say a year before I got in the tent. I honestly applied, I remember filling out the application form in a very jokey manner. It was like I was having a conversation. It's also a very rigorous application to get into Bake Off. So, if you're not serious about baking, you'll get found out pretty quickly. But I had just gone through a period of unemployment. I was like 28 years old, 30 was on the horizon, started to have a bit of a mild panic about that. Spoiler alert folks, she did not find a job. She was unemployed for about 12 months. And then, for some reason, and I don't know why, because neither my mom or my dad bakes, but there was a baking book on the shelf. And I hate to credit him with this, but it was a Paul Hollywood book. I would never say this to his face, but it did teach me the foundations of baking. And I literally baked my way from my unemployment. I tackled everything from making croissants to attempted sourdough very terribly, but I did everything just to wow my days away because I had so much time. It would make me feel good that I was actually doing something useful. Fell into a job, and then I remember seeing the Bake Off audition, the bit of fun that I had with the application form turned quite serious when then they called me up and was like, "Oh, loved your application. Just got a few questions for you." And I was like, "Great. I literally know nothing about baking. How am I going to get through these questions?" And then they were asking me these questions, and every time they'd ask me something, I'd be like, "Oh, I'm really sorry. My phone line has gone so bad." Put them on mute, and I was furiously typing away on Google like, "Oh my God, please help me. What is this? What are they talking to me about?" Sorry, Bake Off if you hear this, but yes, I did cheat my way for the- JS: Fraud. RB: Loud and proud, can I just say? And then next thing I know, I was in the tent with people who had been baking since they were five, or been baking with their granny all their life. And everyone was like, "Oh, so how long have you been baking for?" And I was like, "About a year." But I think my inexperience actually really helped me in the tent because I had no expectation. I had none of this. I want to get to halfway point, or I want to get to the final, or I want to win. I was like, "I'm just counting my lucky stars that I made it into the tent." So, it was wonderful. I've made some incredible friends from there. I've had an incredible experience, and it's given me such a wonderful, joyful platform, that it will always be one of my most cherished memories, I think. JS: Are you still in touch with your fellow bakers? RB: There's one in particular who, no matter what I do, I just can't get rid of him. This guy is invited to my family weddings. He came to my cousin's wedding. He baked a cake for my own wedding. He's my best friend, and I couldn't see my life without him. Antony, he was only in the tent for about three weeks, but we bonded from the minute that we first met. Very, very grateful for that. JS: I'm like, "Damn, I need to fill out an application." SU: I know. RB: It's an incredible experience. SU: Is it safe to say that Paul Hollywood doesn't get invited to any family weddings? RB: Oh, absolutely not. That guy will be lucky if he gets a hello here and there. JS: Damn. SU: Okay. We'll move on to a rapid fire question. JS: Yeah. Are you down to answer some? RB: Oh, yeah, absolutely. Let's go for it. JS: What are you bringing to a bake sale? RB: Oh God, this is like asking someone who their favorite child is. This is terrible. Chocolate cake, something like my Brooklyn Blackout from my book. JS: Crowd pleaser, yeah. SU: Yeah. Who do you call in a baking emergency? RB: My friend Antony, for sure. I mean, very rarely will he give me good advice, but he will calm me down. JS: That's me for Shilpa. RB: Yeah. SU: That's both of us. JS: What do you think the best baking smell is? RB: Oh God, laminated pastry, for sure. It's just that waft of butter in the kitchen that really just gets me every single time. Just nothing but butter. Fantastic. SU: Do you have a motto or words that you live by in the kitchen? RB: What's the worst that can happen? JS: Fair enough. Yeah. RB: Literally, every time I have a disaster in the kitchen, I take it as a lesson and a step closer to perfecting something that I wanted to. So, yeah, definitely that. JS: I like that. SU: A great lesson for life. What is the best compliment you've ever received on something you've baked? RB: I remember on Bake Off, everyone would strive for getting a Hollywood handshake, or some praise from Paul, but for me, Prue was a tough cookie to crack. And there was one cake that I made, and she said that she wanted the recipe for it afterwards, and then she came up to me afterwards and said, "Please send that to me." And that for me was a huge compliment. Someone who I've admired in the food industry, she's a strong, fierce woman, who's really made a name for herself in the food industry. And so, to get a compliment like that so early on in what I didn't know then was my baking career was phenomenal. JS: That's a good one. SU: Did you send her the recipe? RB: Well, I sent it on to the production company, so whether she got it or not- JS: Who's going to say? RB: I don't know. But you know what? I did my bit, girl. SU: Yeah, yeah. You certainly did. Okay, that's the end of our rapid fire. Ruby, we really loved having you. JS: Yeah, thank you so much. RB: Thank you. SU: This was such a good conversation. JS: Where can our listeners find you if they want to follow you? RB: You can find me on Instagram and TikTok @rubybhogal, where you can keep up to date with the latest cakes. Hopefully, by the time you hear this, I've finished the cake series, but you never know. We could have another three years in it. Or you can also grab a copy of my new book, which will be out in the States towards the end of September at your local bookstore, on Amazon, at Barnes & Nobles, or your local independent. JS: Beautiful. Thank you so much. SU: Thank you. RB: Thank you. Thank you so much for your time today. JS: That's it for this month's edition of BA Bake Club. Shilpa, do you want to tell our bakers about the September Bake Club recipe? SU: Okay. September's Bake Club recipe is probably the one recipe that we're not actually baking. JS: Oh. SU: September's recipe is for glazed apple pie fritters, because I'm thinking of state fair fritters, and I've never been to a state fair, and I've always wanted to go to one. JS: They're fun. SU: Oh my God, I'm so jealous that you've been to one. How many have you been to state fairs? JS: A handful. SU: Oh my God. JS: Yeah. SU: Anyway, I've always been thinking about these state fair fritters and how they have these big chunks of fruit in them, and I wanted that same sort of chunkiness, but in the texture of a cider donut that you get at the farm stand. JS: Oh, yes, yes, yes, yes. SU: So, this is my version of that. JS: I can attest to their deliciousness. And is there any special equipment or ingredients that bakers should have on hand? SU: Ingredients, I would say get some nice ricotta. I generally like the ones that are in a tin with some holes. JS: Oh, with a big bulbous top? SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Can I just name the brand? JS: Yeah, sure. SU: It's Calabro. Calabro has the best ricotta that I had. JS: Yeah, sure, sure, sure. SU: So, that's as far as ingredients go. Get yourself some nice apples. Jesse and I are very partial to Honeycrisp apples, after a few failed attempts with Granny Smith, and you should be good. JS: Yeah. SU: Yeah. JS: Cool. Well, Bake Clubbers, once you bake through the fritters, send us your pictures and questions. There are so many different ways to get in touch. SU: You can comment on the recipe on the Epicurious app, or on the Bon Appétit website. You can comment on our Substack, or you could email us at [email protected]. And if you've made it and loved it, please rate and review the recipe on our site. JS: Or you can tell a friend. If you have a buddy that should be in the Bake Club, share this episode. SU: Oh, good. Are we buddies, Jesse? JS: Oh, baking buddies. We got a package sent to us that said Shilpa and Jesse today. SU: I know. That was our first joint package. JS: Yeah. SU: I'm so touched. JS: Okay. Well, we're your hosts, Jesse Szewczyk. SU: And Shilpa Uskokovic. JS: This month's episode was produced by Emily Elias. SU: Pran Bandi is our studio engineer, and we had editing by Rhiannon Corby. JS: Research editing by Ryan Harrington. SU: This episode was mixed by Amar Lal at Macro Sound. JS: If you like this show, leave us a rating and review, and hit that follow button so you never miss an episode. SU: And if you're not already part of the club, head to bonappetit.com/bakeclub to find all the information you need to join. JS: Thanks for listening to BA Bake Club, and we'll see you next month.

item.title: I've Tested 41 Rice Cookers and Swear By These 4 (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.23
In college, I was introduced to the world of rice cookers when my roommate bought one for our house. I didn't fully realize how spoiled I'd been until we graduated and she moved across the country, taking her rice cooker with her. I was left to make do with the finicky stovetop method that never turned out quite right. In the years since, I've never been without one. Having consistently fluffy, well-cooked rice means I can turn my attention to the other components of the meal, and that convenience is well worth the price tag and the extra storage space a rice cooker comes with. Besides, there's nothing as humbling as cooking a big pot of rice for company only to find it's turned into a pile of mush. Our top picks - Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker - The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) - Best small rice cooker (that's also PFAS-free): GreenPan Advanced 4-Cup Rice Cooker - A great stainless steel rice cooker: Tatung Electric 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Steamer The best rice cookers are like a kitchen cheat code, a helping hand that ensures at least one part of your meal goes off without a hitch. But they vary a lot in performance. I've tested 41 rice cookers and cooked over 120 cups of rice (and that's just in the Test Kitchen), so I'm here to give you the lowdown and help you choose the right one for your lifestyle, budget, and household size. I believe the best rice cooker for your money is the Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker. It's the right size for most people (making up to 14 cups of cooked rice), and at $70 it's a great price. But I also have picks for PFAS-free options, small cookers for tiny spaces, and the Zojirushi NP-HCC10 that makes the absolute best rice, as long as you're willing to pay for it. We think it's worth it. New in this update: I tested the GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup (Cooked) Rice Cooker and found it to be a good option for those looking for a small rice cooker with a ceramic, PFAS-free nonstick inner pot. I also tested the new KitchenAid Compact Grain and Rice Cooker, but didn't think its performance merited its price tag. Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Consistently good rice - Affordable - Handy features Cons: - Rice can get scorched on the bottom - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 7 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10.75" x 10.75" x 11" Weight: 4.8 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, whole grain, hot cereals, steam cook, heat/simmer You don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to make great rice. The Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker has consistently impressed me throughout years of testing, and at under $70, I think it’s the best option for most home cooks. What I love: The Hamilton Beach ranked right behind the Zojirushi (our splurge pick below) in a side-by-side blind tasting of white rice. It excelled in the brown rice test, producing individual and intact grains that had a satisfying amount of bite to them (though if you prefer your brown rice on the softer side, I'd recommend adding a bit more water than the recommended amount). It also fared well with long-grain basmati, producing a pot of fluffy rice on par with (if not better than) some of the more expensive cookers I tested. It cooked each pot of rice significantly faster than the Zojirushi, too: 35 minutes for a pot of white rice as opposed to the Zojirushi’s 50, and an hour for brown rice as opposed to 90 minutes. But what I really loved about the Hamilton Beach is that despite its low price tag, it doesn't sacrifice some of the helpful features the more high-end cookers tend to have. Besides a standard Keep Warm function, there are also six presets to choose from (white rice, quick rice, whole grain, heat/simmer, steam cook, and hot cereals), a handy delayed start feature (great if you want to prep a pot of rice before work and have it ready by the time you get home in the evening), a cook time countdown, and an audible beep when the rice is done cooking—all things most other options at this price point lack. Its 7-cup (uncooked) capacity is also larger than that of many of the other rice cookers I tested, but the machine's footprint is comparably compact. It's also technically a multi-cooker thanks to the heat/simmer and steam cook settings, though I was primarily interested in its rice-making capabilities for this review and will not vouch for those other functions here. I named the Hamilton Beach our budget pick two years ago, but after continuing to test it against the previous overall winner and countless other new-to-me models over the past couple of years while watching the price of the Zojirushi climb closer to—and oftentimes above—$400, I can confidently say that it’s the best choice for most home cooks for its balance of performance, features, and affordability. What I'd leave: While I found the Hamilton Beach to be well-made for a $70-ish machine, it didn’t feel quite as sturdy as the higher-end models we tested. I also didn’t love the design of the lid: It requires you to press and hold a button while manually opening it, and it opens sideways rather than front to back. The inner pot is also relatively thin, which contributed to a scorched layer of rice at the bottom in some of my tests—something that wasn’t a deal-breaker for me in the end but is worth noting. And, unlike many other models we tested, there is no differentiation in the recommended amount of water for different types of rice. I didn’t find that this negatively impacted the resulting rice, though the brown rice, which had a nice bite to it, could be a tad al dente for some with the recommended amount of water. The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) Pros and cons Pros: - Consistent results - Wide range of capabilities Cons: - Expensive - Bulky cord is not retractable Specs Capacity: 5.5 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10" x 14" x 8" Weight: 9 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Micom technology, induction heating, delay cook, automatic keep warm function Menu settings: white rice (regular, softer or harder), jasmine rice, mixed rice, sushi rice, porridge/congee, sweet rice, brown rice, GABA brown rice and quick-cooking, rice paddle and measuring cup, nonstick pot. Zojirushi is to rice cookers what Vitamix is to blenders, and KitchenAid is to stand mixers. That is to say, it's the brand everyone knows to buy if you want the best. We've tested seven of Zojirushi's 19 models, and I've been most impressed by the NP-HCC10, which has won our blind taste tests every time. If you're serious about your rice and willing to invest in a perfectly fluffy pot, this is the model for you. What I love: BA staffers have crowned this machine the winner time and time again in blind taste tests, noting the way it produced grains that were not too soft, not too hard, and never mushy. In my own testing, it turned out evenly cooked, perfectly fluffy rice every time. That comes down to two technologies working together. Micom (short for microcomputerized) technology, found in many of Zojirushi's cookers, uses built-in sensors that adjust temperature and cook time according to real-time feedback, acting as a safeguard against imprecise water-to-rice ratios. Induction heating, more specific to this tier of Zojirushis, lets the cooker maintain a precise temperature and conduct heat evenly across the whole pot, rather than from the bottom only, as non-induction cookers do. Rice quality was my number one criterion in evaluating these cookers, but I also gave points for design and features. The NP-HCC10 has a 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, enough to feed six people. Its nonstick pot is a breeze to clean, and the interior is clearly marked in white with the water levels for various types of rice. I loved that this model counts down the total cook time, a surprising rarity among the rice cookers I've tested, though the Hamilton Beach does it too. Its extended Keep Warm setting, on top of the standard automatic one, prevents rice from yellowing or drying out when it's left to sit. A delayed start setting lets you set your rice to be done cooking at a certain time. And nine programmed settings cover several types of rice, including jasmine, brown, and sushi (the White Rice setting on a Zojirushi refers to short-grain white rice). For other grains like quinoa or oats, Zojirushi has a guide here. What I’d leave: The main downside to the NP-HCC10, and the reason it's no longer my top pick, is the price. This model has gotten steadily more expensive over the years and now sits around $400, which makes it a definite investment piece. Still, our testers could tell the difference in rice quality during every blind tasting, so if rice is something you care about, that's what you're paying for. Zojirushi also tends to fall short on brown rice across the board. I found the brown rice this model produced to be a touch soft for my liking, though using a bit less water than the recommended amount fixes it. There's also no retractable cord, which makes storage more of a hassle. Another thing to know if you’re new to the world of precision rice cookers, is that it takes a very long time to make a pot of rice. Depending on the volume, white rice can take up to an hour and brown rice up to two. That's not a shortcoming. It's part of the reason they work so well. Get in the habit of starting the cooker before you begin the rest of your cooking and you won't notice. On weeknights when you're tight on time, the timer function guarantees your rice will be done when you need it. For more information about Zojirushi’s line of rice cookers, read our guide. Instagram content The best small rice cooker: GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Easy to use - Decent rice - PFAS-free ceramic nonstick inner pot Cons: - White rice was a touch unevenly cooked - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 4 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 9.8" x 7.5" x 8.7" Weight: 5.2 lb. Warranty: Lifetime limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, brown rice This sleek little rice cooker makes a good pot of rice and takes up less counter space than the other models on this list—plus it's got a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot that makes cleanup a breeze. What I loved: This new rice cooker from GreenPan is lightweight, relatively compact, and quite sleek, with a straightforward interface that’s intuitive to use. It made serviceable white and basmati rice in testing and excelled in the brown rice test, producing extremely individualized grains with a satisfying amount of bite, similar in texture to the batch made in the Hamilton Beach. While the GreenPan doesn’t offer a ton of presets, it’s got everything you need if your main use case for it is cooking rice: dedicated white and brown rice settings, a Quick Cook setting, an automatic Keep Warm function, and a Delay Timer. The ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot cleaned up easily with a sponge during testing, but it’s also dishwasher-safe. What I’d leave: While the GreenPan made acceptable rice, it wasn’t perfect—the white rice was a bit unevenly cooked according to some blind taste testers, and the brown rice was too firm for some tasters’ preferences (though others disagreed). Unlike the Hamilton Beach and the Zojirushi, the GreenPan is limited when it comes to settings. I also wish it had a carrying handle, though it’s so lightweight that it’s relatively easy to move around anyway. The best PFAS-free rice cooker: Tatung Electric Rice Cooker and Steamer Pros and cons Pros: - PFAS-free - Makes great rice Cons: - Stainless-steel pot is hard to clean - Lid gets very hot - Lid rattles around when rice is cooking - Pricey given lack of features Specs Capacity: 6 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 12" x 9.8" x 9.8" Weight: 7.1 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Automatic keep warm function Menu settings: None Tatung has been a leading manufacturer of rice cookers and steamers in Taiwan for over 60 years. With its straightforward on/off switch and cook/warm lever, the company's signature rice cooker looks like some of the simpler Zojirushi models, but it features a unique inner and outer pot system that steams the rice as it cooks. What I loved: In my testing, the Tatung produced fluffy pots of rice that earned praise from blind taste testers. The white rice had a nice amount of bite to it and a pleasant, slightly sticky texture. The brown rice was a good middle ground, al dente but not as dry as the rice from the Hamilton Beach. And the basmati was fluffy, the delicate grains all relatively intact. One major plus? Each pot of rice was done in about half the amount of time as the Zojirushi NP-HCC10. The Tatung is all stainless steel, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. That nesting design is what makes it work differently from most rice cookers. Rice and water go into the inner pot as usual, then you add more water to the outer pot, which heats up and steams the rice from the outside in. The Tatung features an all-stainless-steel construction, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. To make a pot of rice, you'll add rice and water to the inner pot as per usual, and then add more water to the outer pot before covering with the lid and setting to cook. What I'd leave: Because it's made of stainless steel, the Tatung can get quite hot while cooking—especially the lid, which I burned my hands on a few times during testing. The lightweight lid and addition of water surrounding the inner pot also meant that this model rattled quite a bit as it cooked, and water occasionally bubbled up over the edge when making large batches of rice. The stainless-steel inner pot is, as expected, much harder to clean than a nonstick pot, and required some soaking and serious elbow grease in order to scrub clean. The other thing to note is that at $210 at the time of writing, this is not a cheap appliance, but it doesn't come with the kinds of features (like delayed start or multiple settings) you might expect from a rice cooker at this price. How we tested rice cookers Many rice cookers these days try to position themselves as do-it-all appliances (the Instant Pot-ification of the category), but we were here to see how each model performed at one all-important function: making rice. We’ve spent years testing over two dozen models and have held numerous taste tests among Bon Appétit staffers, abiding by the following testing process each time: Each rice cooker was first put through a white rice test. We used Nishiki Japanese medium-grain white rice, cooking two cups worth in each full-size cooker and one cup in the mini cookers (models with 4-cup uncooked capacities or less). Models that performed adequately in this test then moved onto short-grain brown rice, and finally to long-grain basmati rice. Our tasters were on the lookout for fluffy pots of rice made up of nicely individualized grains that had just enough bite and didn’t mush together. Cookers that fared well in our initial testing were then given to several different editors to use in their own homes. Those editors have and will continue to provide feedback on how these models perform in the long-term. What we looked for in the best rice cookers Let’s start with the obvious: How was the rice? While we evaluated rice cookers based on several factors, no amount of fancy features or high-tech claims mattered if the resulting rice wasn’t up to par. Our testers and tasters scored models on the quality of all three kinds of rice, and they were looking for evenly cooked grains that were neither over- nor undercooked, not too wet and not too dry, and fluffy rather than gummy or mushy. How’s the user experience? The whole point of having a rice cooker is to make your life easier, so we were looking for rice cookers that were straightforward and intuitive to use. We valued clear instructions on how to wash and measure rice, guidance on water ratios and selecting settings, and automatic Keep Warm functionality. A timer function was an added bonus that we appreciated in some of the more advanced models. We also looked at the accessories each model came with. Every rice cooker comes with a few necessities, which usually include a rice paddle and a measuring cup. Every model we tested, save for the Cuckoos, came with a built-in paddle holder, and many came with an additional steamer basket insert. While we didn’t test out steamer or synchro cooking functionality in our initial tests, our long-term testers were encouraged to report back on how such functions performed. How easy is it to clean? Nearly every model we tested had a nonstick coating on its inner pot, and the few that didn’t were a bit of a nightmare to clean. We wanted to be able to cleanly scoop rice out of the cooker without leaving any residue behind, and looked for pots that were easily washed with a soapy sponge and some warm water (if you are really trying to avoid PFAS coatings, note that most rice cooker pots are not dishwasher-safe). Some models have removable, cleanable lids, something we appreciated and noted where applicable. How easy is it to store? We took note of the footprint of each model, but found that most full-size options were around the same size. Is it worth the price? The rice cookers we tested ranged in price from $25–$750. While we think a great model like our winning Zojirushi is worth its $300 price tag, we awarded points to models like the Hamilton Beach that provide a great value, performing better than their cost might suggest. Other rice cookers we tested and liked Cuckoo 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Warmer CR-0655F This model from Cuckoo is a great rice cooker for the price. Tasters ranked the rice it made nearly as highly as our winning Zojirushi, which is a feat considering the Cuckoo is a third of the price. It’s also much faster than the Zojirushi, finishing in 15 minutes less, and a bit larger, with a 6-cup capacity. Why didn’t it take the top spot, you might ask? A couple of reasons: The lid jerks open with so much force that it can knock the whole appliance off the counter (as well as any objects surrounding it), and it doesn’t have a countdown for the total cook time. Tiger Micom Rice Cooker JBV-A10U This former best budget pick is made by Tiger, another Japan-based company with over 100 years of history making many of the same kinds of products Zojirushi does. It’s one of the most affordable Micom models out there, ringing in at $99 (at the time of writing). And while it doesn’t have all the fancy bells and whistles of our winning Zojirushi, it still makes consistently great rice. In our blind taste tests, staffers picked the Tiger over several more expensive models. We also loved this cooker’s generous 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, the fact that it’s easy to clean, and that it offers something a step above a simple one-button, non-Micom model. This is still a dead-simple, no-frills rice cooker though. You get what you pay for: There is no alarm, timer, or digital interface, and fewer settings than you’ll get on something like our winning Zojirushi or some of the fancier Tiger models. In our most recent round of testing, the Hamilton Beach model edged it out by producing slightly better rice and having more helpful features, all while ringing in at practically half the price. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-JEC10 The Zojirushi NW-JEC10 is like if Apple made a rice cooker: It’s sleek, high-tech, and expensive. It’s the most expensive home rice cooker in the brand’s lineup, as a matter of fact. Of its host of features, the one that sets it apart from the other high-end models Zojirushi offers is the My Rice setting, which uses artificial intelligence to learn your preferred rice texture based on inputs you give it after cooking through each batch of rice. Commerce writer Wilder Davies has been testing the NW-JEC10 for over a year and has come around to the view that the My Rice functionality is no gimmick. He found that his batches of rice evolved for the better over time as he gave the machine more feedback (specifically, it will ask you to input whether the stickiness and firmness of the previous batch you made was “not enough,” “okay,” or “too much”). What’s more, this rice won its initial taste test with our staffers. But the difference in rice quality was not enough to merit the $750 price tag, hence our recommendation for the average rice eater remains the (nearly $450 cheaper) NP-HCC10. Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-TSC10A This model is similar to our top pick in design and functionality, but rings in at about $100 cheaper. The main reason for that is likely that it lacks the induction heating capabilities of the NP-HCC10. While it produced good rice across all of our tests, it never quite achieved as perfectly textured results as our winner. Our testers found the rice to be a bit too soft across the board (though this could be remedied by adding a bit less water than the recommended amount). We did, however, appreciate the retractable cord—plus the silver-and-light gray design is rather chic. Toshiba TRCS01 Rice Cooker This model performed exceedingly well in our initial blind taste test, producing fluffy grains that won over our testers. We also loved its suite of programmable features, the way it gave us a timer countdown from the start of cooking as well as the option to delay cooking until later, its audible alarm, and its use of fuzzy logic to make minute temperature and time adjustments according to real time sensor feedback (something more typically seen in higher priced models). We found it easy to use, with helpful presets for a range of rice types and a Quick Rice function that worked well for grains like quinoa, farro, and polenta, and an included steamer basket. But our long-term testing of this product revealed a major flaw: We found that the timer would repeatedly freeze (sometimes for 20 minutes or longer) while the machine continued to cook. This issue was particularly prevalent when using the Mixed Rice and Quick Rice settings. It’s worth noting that the timer function on a rice cooker is typically more of an approximation, and it’s not uncommon for it to change or stall momentarily—but not to this extent. It resulted in overcooked or even burned rice. It was not a consistent problem, but a problem nonetheless, and a big enough one to give us pause about recommending this model as our top budget pick. Zojirushi Neuro Fuzzy Rice Cooker and Warmer NS-ZCC10 The Zojirushi NS-ZCC10 didn’t make as nicely textured and fluffy rice as our winning pick. It does include many of the features we loved in our winner at a lower price point, like the intuitive interface, sturdy inner pot, Keep Warm function, and array of presets. It also had some additional features our winner lacked, like a retractable cord and handles on the sides of the pot that allow you to lift it out from the cooker while it’s still hot. However, at over $240 at the time of publication, we just don’t think this cooker produced rice that merited the still-high price tag. Toshiba TRSH01 Low-Carb Digital Programmable Multi-Functional Rice Cooker This sleek model from Toshiba has an intuitive digital interface and eight different settings, including one for “low-carb” rice that uses a colander-like insert to drain away starchy water as the rice cooks (which Toshiba claims “can remove unhealthy digestive starch by up to 37% and increase healthy resistant starch by up to 34%”). We aren't going to vouch for the low-carb claims, but we can tell you that this model fared relatively well in testing. We found the white and jasmine rice to be a tad soft for our liking, which ultimately kept it out of our top picks (though this could be remedied by using a touch less water than recommended). It excelled in the brown rice test, producing rice with just enough bite—the Goldilocks of brown rice, as one of our taste testers put it. If you’re a brown rice fiend, this may be the model for you. Tiger 5.5-Cup IH Rice Cooker JKT-D10U This model performed similarly to our winning pick from Zojirushi, scoring just a few points below it in our taste test. It has a 5.5-cup uncooked capacity, a sturdy nonstick inner pot with handles for safely lifting it out of the machine while hot, and all the other features we’d expect from a rice cooker with its price tag: A bevy of settings (12 to be exact), automatic logic technology, an audible chime, and an automatic Keep Warm functionality. It produced beautifully cooked white rice that was nearly on par with the Zojirushi NP-HCC10, but fell a bit short in the brown rice test, where the grains were on the mushier side. All in all, it’s a great rice cooker that any home cook would be happy to use, but for just a few dollars more, we’d recommend you go with our winning pick from Zojirushi. Zojirushi Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-QAC10 This model is part of Zojirushi’s newest line of rice cookers, and it looks similar to the pricey NW-JEC10 model we mentioned above. It is similar to our winner in terms of functionality, but it couldn’t match up to the NP-HCC10’s results in the white rice test. Our tasters found the rice this model produced to be soft and less intact than they’d have liked. That said, the NW-QAC10 features quinoa and oatmeal settings, which makes it a good rice cooker for anyone with a particular affinity for either of those grains. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NP-NWC10 With Micom technology and induction heating, this model is very similar to our top pick. If you’re wondering why it’s over $100 more expensive, that’s because, unlike our winner, it uses pressure when cooking rice. While intended to produce a more tender grain, our testers preferred the rice the NP-HCC10 churned out, deeming the NP-NWC10’s rice a bit soft for their liking when cooked on a standard setting. It’s worth noting that this model allows you to adjust texture and consistency with relative ease, which worked well in our long-term testing, but we cannot recommend you shell out an additional $100-plus for it based on its overall performance. Rice cookers we don’t recommend Whether because of how they fared in our taste test or because of their design, these are the rice cookers that we don't recommend buying. - Aroma Digital Rice Cooker ARC-914SBD: This affordable 4-cup model performed well in the white rice test, but failed with brown rice. It leaked starchy water onto the lid that would have spilled everywhere had we not mopped it up. The rice itself was wet and oh-so-mushy. - Aroma 2.5-Cup Rice Cooker ARC-753SG: This model from Aroma has a stainless-steel inner pot that we found difficult to clean. It made white rice in near record time (20 minutes or so), but it tended to be a bit underdone. The same can be said for the brown rice test—the rice was good, but certainly not great. This model also exhibited some leakage through the steam vent even when just cooking one cup of rice, which we imagine would only get worse if you filled it to capacity. - Beautiful by Drew Barrymore 14-Cup Rice and Grain Cooker: I’ve generally been impressed by Drew Barrymore’s line of appliances, but this rice cooker was disappointing. It produced mushy, gummy white rice and didn't make it past the first round of testing. - Cosori 5-Cup Rice Cooker: Standard settings on this model produced rice that was a bit undercooked, according to most of our testers. This machine does have a whopping 18 settings, including a range of different grains, so it could be a decent option for anyone who frequently cooks steel-cut oats, barley, farro, and the like. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Heating Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-P0609S: The rice this Cuckoo made was incredibly sticky. It also suffered some design flaws: the lid snaps open aggressively, the control panel is unintuitive, and there's no countdown timer. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Micom Rice Cooker CR-0675F: This model made great rice. However, unresponsive buttons, a confusing interface, and a poorly translated manual made it frustrating to use. So while this cooker checks the "Makes Great Rice" box, the same cannot be said for the "Is a Joy to Use" box. - Cuckoo 6-Cup HP Twin Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-ST0609F: Like the other Cuckoos, this model made decent rice. However, its control panel was irritatingly unresponsive. It also talks, and in a voice that can only be described as Barbie DreamHouse-core—which may be amusing to some, but aggravating to others. - Cuisinart 4-Cup Rice Cooker: This mini model didn't move past the white rice test–the rice it produced looked very wet and undercooked at the time it finished cooking and switched to the Keep Warm function, and it tasted too firm in the middle. - Dash Mini Rice Cooker: This one-button model has a lid that is too light to stay sealed, allowing steam and heat to escape during cooking. - Imusa GAU-00011 Electric Nonstick Rice Cooker: This is one of the cheapest rice cookers you can get these days. Was the rice edible? Totally. But we found the white rice to be undercooked, and the brown rice it made was sort of wet, as if not enough water had been cooked off. - Instant Pot Duo: The beloved Instant Pot Duo is a multi-cooker that claims to do it all—including make rice. It was one of the fastest models to do so, but the grains it produced were gummy and decidedly un-fluffable. - KitchenAid Rice and Grain Cooker: This model from KitchenAid has a unique design that comprises an integrated scale and attached water tank. It uses that scale and whichever of the 21 preset functions you've chosen to determine how much water to add, eliminating the need to futz around with measuring cups and ratios. While it's an interesting concept, we weren't impressed enough by this model's performance to recommend it. The first batch of white rice we made was painfully dry, though the second batch we made using the Softer setting was an improvement. The brown rice was serviceable, nicely textured if still a touch dry. We spent time in 2025 testing its other capabilities as well and found them hit or miss. You can check out our complete KitchenAid rice cooker review here. - KitchenAid Compact Rice and Grain Cooker: This new version of the KitchenAid model above eliminates the attached water tank for a more compact footprint. While it made decent rice, we found the workflow of pouring water into the inner pot while it was attached to its base (rather than filling it to a designated line at the sink) somewhat annoying, and ultimately weren't impressed enough by the quality of the rice to justify the somewhat steep price tag. - Nutribullet EveryGrain Cooker: This cooker has settings for specific grains like white rice, quinoa, and oats, plus other nice-to-have features like a Delay Start button and Steam option. While we can't comment on how this cooker performs with other grains, we can say that it did not fare well with rice. The white rice we made was wildly inconsistent, even within the same batch. - Our Place Rice Cooker: This rice cooker is cute as can be. It's intuitive to use and looks nice on a countertop—an attribute most rice cookers lack; however, the appliance is bulky and pricey considering the small, 3-cup uncooked capacity. After some long-term testing, we found that the rice cooked inconsistently, either too mushy one time or too dry another, despite the fuzzy logic, so ultimately we don't think it's worth the price tag. - Tiger Microcomputer Controlled Rice Cooker JAX-T10U: Despite its promising features, this model produced white rice that was a bit wet and soft for our testers' liking. The brown rice had a nice bite to it, but its exterior was a tad mushy. We found that the less expensive Tiger JBV-A10U outperformed this pricier model. - Tiger 10-Cup (Uncooked) Rice Cooker JNP-1800-FL: This is a straightforward, single-button rice cooker that makes enough rice for the whole family (and a large one at that). Unfortunately, the rice it produced proved some of the softest of the bunch. With few features and lackluster performance, it's hard to recommend. - Toshiba TRCS02: This 3-cup model from Toshiba fared relatively well in the white rice portion of our taste test, but produced overcooked brown rice that kept it from earning a top spot. - Yum Asia Panda: This cooker is a bestseller on Amazon, so we wanted to see what all the fuss was about. It remained a promising contender through the first round of taste testing, in which it produced excellent white rice. However, the brown rice this model made was overcooked and mushy. But if brown rice isn't your thing, you might still consider this model. - Zojirushi 3-Cup Rice Cooker: This dead-simple mini model from Zojirushi uses a single button to start cooking. Unlike some competitors we tested, it didn't leak starchy water, but it produced inconsistent results. It also lacks a Keep Warm function, and we found it didn't handle brown rice well. - Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-LGC05: This 3-cup version of one of Zojirushi's micom models ultimately failed to impress us—especially compared to the other mini models we tested, which performed much better even despite being lower tech. The white rice made in this model was quite sticky and mushy, as was the brown rice. Because of that micom technology, it also took longer to cook than the other small models. - Zojirushi NL-EAC10: This newest model in Zojirushi's lineup is cute, but it lacked the helpful carrying handle that most other Zojirushis have, took longer to cook rice than our winner, and produced white rice that was overcooked and a touch mushy. FAQs Should you rinse your rice? To make a long story short, you probably should. Washing rice strips the grains of their starchy coating and keeps them from sticking together and becoming a gummy mess when cooked—something you want for most types of rice (exceptions to this rule include arborio rice used for risotto, where the excess starch is necessary to create that creamy texture). In testing these cookers, we followed each model’s instructions with regard to rinsing rice. In general, you’ll want to swish your measured rice around in some water, pour that water out, and repeat until the water runs clear. Do you need a rice cooker? What about stovetop rice? You don’t need a rice cooker, but there’s no denying that having one makes getting weeknight dinners on the table or cooking rice for a crowd infinitely easier. That said, making great stovetop rice is a skill worth mastering—and the food editors in our test kitchen can help you with that. How much rice can a rice cooker make? You’ll notice that many of the rice cookers on this list have cup capacities in their names. That number refers to the amount of uncooked rice a given cooker can make at a time, measured in 180-ml rice cooker cups rather than standard US cups (which are 237 ml). Rice approximately doubles in size after cooking, so a 5.5-cup rice cooker like the winning Zojirushi will make a maximum of about 11 cups of cooked rice (which is enough to feed around 5–6 people). If you’re cooking for just yourself, note that the minimum amount of rice most rice cookers can make is one rice cooker cup’s worth. This will likely be more rice that you need for a single serving meal, but we’d advise against trying to make less rice than the cooker is designed for. And besides, the leftovers will make for excellent fried rice the next day.

item.title: What Are Budget-Friendly Recipes I Can Make for My 60-Person Wedding?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.70
There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here. My 60-person wedding is going to be a DIY affair at a small inn-turned-Airbnb. The big meals are going to be handled by professionals, but there’s a couple meals—Friday breakfast and lunch, Saturday breakfast—that we’re hoping to cobble together ourselves in the inn’s commercial kitchen. While we regularly host groups of 20ish at our apartment, 60 people feels like an entirely different beast. How can we (simply! not-too-expensively!) scale up and make sure everyone is well-fed? We’re nominating some friends to help prep and serve food for each meal, but where do we start with the menu? How do you think about how much food you need? —I Do Congrats are in order! Thanks for writing in about your big day—I’m honored. This is a great size for a guest list. My husband and I invited a similar range (scandalous in pre-pandemic times) and the room was overflowing, bountiful, raucous at times. The funny thing about a small wedding is…it’s still a lot of people. And you’re right, it’s an entirely different beast than your everyday dinner party. I applaud you for tapping in friends. Delegation is—begging my editor to let me keep italics here—of the utmost importance. Not just because, unless you are a Top Chef contestant, feeding 60 people should not be a one-person endeavor. But also because, ahem, you’re the one getting married! As corny as it sounds, I hope that the top item on your to-do list is: Have fun. Everything else can wait, or should be someone else’s problem. Okay, speech over, taking a sip of pét-nat, onto the recipes! Breakfasts Not actually a recipe: My family has a reunion at the Shore every summer and our foolproof feed-a-crowd breakfast is bagels plus fixings. Can’t be beat. BA Bake Club has a wonderful homemade bagel recipe, which you should save for later and not use for this occasion. Now is the time to buy and assemble: bagels (if they’re fresh, skip toasting; if not, broil on a sheet pan); a few flavors of whipped cream cheese; smoked salmon (skip if this breaks the budget); sliced tomatoes and onion; capers; pickles. Optional fruit alongside. The math: - 1¼ bagels per person = 75 bagels - 1½ oz. cream cheese per person = 90 oz. (12 eight-oz. containers) - 2 oz. lox per person = 7½ lb. (Costco is your friend) - ⅓ tomato per person = 20 tomatoes - ⅙ onion per person = 10 onions - 1 tsp. capers per person = 1 giant jar - Who can say how many cornichons per person = 4 jars Ham-and-Cheese Croissant Bake. A charming, crowd-pleasing dish that you can assemble in advance, then bake the next day. Serve with some store-bought prewashed mixed greens splashed with Three-Minute Vinaigrette. Simple and chic. Mix the custard in two batches, each in a humongous bowl. (I have one of these and, honestly, can’t recommend it enough. Sure, it only comes in handy two-ish times a year, and my family makes fun of me for it, but when you need it, nothing else will do.) Bake in disposable aluminum pans. The math (recipe times eight for 64 servings): - 80 croissants (cheap supermarket ones! Lidl is known for them) - 3 lb. Gruyère (could do cheddar for a cheaper alt) - 3 lb. ham - 40 eggs - 8 pints heavy cream - 1 cup Dijon mustard - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt* - 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2 tsp. freshly grated nutmeg - 2 handfuls thinly sliced chives *Please get Diamond Crystal for this measurement or adjust the quantity for another brand. The type of salt always matters, but especially so in large batches. Lunches Olive Bar Pasta Salad. As my colleague Rebecca Firkser writes, “The beauty of this pasta salad is its flexibility.” In your case, I would actually avoid the supermarket olive bar; it can get pricey in large quantities. Instead, find a Trader Joe’s or Costco and make the most of their shelf-stable antipasti offerings: marinated artichokes, roasted peppers, pitted olives, white beans, etc. More cost effective and just as yum. If you have an ambitious pal who wants to grill or sear chicken for a crowd, that would be a nice addition, estimating ½ breast per serving, or 30 breasts total. But not needed by any means! The math (recipe times 10 for 60 servings): - 20 garlic cloves - 5 cups finely chopped oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes - 2½ cups sun-dried tomato oil (cut with olive oil if you don’t have enough) - 3 cups plus 2 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (optional) - 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper - 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt - 10 (1-lb.) boxes short pasta - 5 lb. small mozzarella balls or torn mozzarella - 10 quarts (40 cups) mixed antipasti (see above) Marinated Mixed Beans. I can hear someone scoffing in the distance at the audacity of the suggestion that you serve your beloved guests canned beans. But hear me out. They are delicious and cheap, can be assembled days in advance, and can confidently anchor an unfussy menu. Serve the beans in the same bowl linked above (see? Already coming in handy again), along with: crusty sliced bread; one to three cheeses (burrata, Brie, whatever strikes your fancy); soft-boiled eggs; olives and pickles; maybe some charcuterie. Nosh-y and fun. The math (recipe times 15—gasp—for 1 cup per person): - 15 shallots, finely chopped (use a food processor if you have one) - 2¾ cups plus 1 Tbsp. white wine vinegar, plus more to taste - 7½ cups finely chopped tender herbs (again with the food processor) - 5 cups olive oil - 30 (15.5-oz.) cans beans (bride’s pick!) - 5 Tbsp. Aleppo-style pepper or gochugaru - Kosher salt, to taste Drinks For breakfast, get some travel boxes of joe from a nearby coffee shop and call it a day. For either lunch: If one of your friends (read: not you) wants to go the extra mile, set up a vermouth-spritz bar with: bottles of rogue and blanc vermouth; cans of seltzer; lots of ice; lemon and lime wedges. Celebratory but won’t have everyone sloshed in the middle of the day. Readers, what’s the best wedding food you’ve ever had? (Yes, sure, it can be from your own wedding. But only if you’re telling the truth!) Share in the comments. Warmly, Emma Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

item.title: 43 Easy 30-Minute Dinner Ideas for Busy Nights
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.67
When you need dinner on the table fast, these 30-minute dinner ideas deliver. They’re the recipes Bon Appétit editors turn to when it’s 7 p.m., we’re already hungry, and we haven’t even made it home yet. But quick doesn’t have to mean boring. These easy 30-minute meals include spicy chicken lettuce wraps, sizzling shrimp fajitas, creamy carbonara, crispy tofu with peanut sauce, and plenty of one-pan dinners that minimize cleanup. Some lean on smart shortcuts like rotisserie chicken, canned tuna, or store-bought dumplings; others take advantage of naturally quick-cooking ingredients like shrimp, ground meat, tofu, and eggs. Every recipe here can be made in 30 minutes or less, start to finish. Really pressed for time? Our 15-minute meals round-up includes even speedier options. More easy dinner ideas:

item.title: 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.64
This dead simple, three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat. It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You’ll Fall For. Recipe information - Total Time 30 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 1 2 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

item.title: Everyone Seems to Be Taking a “Fallcation” This Year—What Does That Mean for Travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.67
Fall was always my favorite time to travel. It’s when the crowds have loosened their grip on Paris, the weather is better in Italy, and the hotel rates are lower in Marrakech. But over the last few years, I’ve noticed more and more travelers at airports near and far in September, October, and November. Indicating demand, plane tickets haven’t been dipping in the same way that they used to when the leaves turned. Open any news app, and you’ll see the headlines shouting from the rooftops: We are in the era of the “fallcation.” “Savvy travelers are establishing autumn as the new peak season for global trips,” says John Clifford, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and founder of International Travel Management. He attributes this to the fact that more people are traveling than ever in the summertime, leading to crowded destinations. On top of that, summers are only getting hotter. All this, Clifford says, leads to people looking to take their big annual vacation outside of the summer season. The data backs it up: According to Virtuoso, the global network of luxury travel agencies and advisors, bookings for fall travel this year have increased by 59% compared to last year; the network’s agents report a 77% increase in September sales, making it a peak month for travel. October and November sales are up 54% and 71%, respectively. Fall travel is increasing even to destinations in Asia, where the window between September and November is already the peak season. Catherine Heald, another CNT Top Travel Specialist and founder of Asia-focused Remote Lands, says her company has been seeing around 15% more fall bookings in the last few years. But nowhere is it more pronounced than in universally loved Italy, where September and October have become the height of the season, when it’s still “summer-like” in Southern Europe, says Gary Portuesi, a CNT Top Travel Specialist and a co-managing partner of Authentic Explorations. To Portuesi, fall in Italy now means November and December—and yes, they’re seeing a surge in bookings for those months too, when temperatures are cooler, crowds have dwindled, and hotel rates tend to drop. As he puts it, “It’s the new shoulder season.” To learn more about the rise of the fallcation, I tapped a host of Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists to weigh in: Who’s actually traveling in the fall? Where are people going? And will we eventually have to avoid traveling in the fall, too? In a few years, will we be craving “summercations”? Here’s what the experts had to say. What is leading to more “fallcations”? At this point, it’s conventional wisdom that September, October, and November are more comfortable times to travel because, in most destinations, you get more temperate weather and fewer crowds in the fall. “Autumn has outperformed summer for at least the past two years,” says Tom Barber of UK-based Original Travel. For Barber, September and October departures are up by 53% and 45%, respectively, compared to August departures. He explains, “People still want the classic summer destinations—Greece, Italy, Spain, Egypt, Morocco—but they increasingly want to experience them without the intense heat.” September is now one of the busiest months for travel company Red Savannah, says Camilla Davidson, its head of destination management for the UK, France, and Ireland. The relentless summer news cycle is also playing a part in this behavioral shift. “It’s all dominated by headlines around European wildfires, unlivable temperatures, endless lines on arrival at airports, overtourism, and elevated prices,” Davidson says. “Many savvy travelers are looking to shoulder seasons to avoid these pitfalls, with the fall seen as a more ‘reliable option’ than the spring.” On the other hand, Cari Gray of Gray & Co., which focuses on private active trips, says that fall has always been her clients’ preferred travel period over the summer season. “So many folks have well-established summer routines like going to their cabins and annual visits to favorite lodges,” Gray says. “They break free in the fall when kids are in school—both in grade school and college—and the weather is perfect for outdoor activities.” Who are the people actually taking “fallcations”? Travelers with kids in school are often tied to the academic calendar—back to school in the autumn, big vacation periods in the summer. So fall travel has historically been the domain of empty-nesters, young couples without dependents, parents bringing along adult children (or vice versa), friend groups, and solo adventurers. This has largely remained the case in our current era of the fallcation. “Couples and adults traveling without children have the most flexibility,” says Jonathan Alder of Jonathan’s Travels. But he notes that a good chunk of parents aren’t opposed to their kids missing class for the right family trip. “It really depends on the age. Pulling a child out of kindergarten for a week is very different from pulling an older child out during an important academic period,” Alder says.
