Rather than simply recreating a summer itinerary at a different time of year, fallcation travelers are looking for activities and experiences that are better suited to the autumn season, says Mark Bonte of France-based French Side Travel. Foodies in particular love to travel in September and October to catch various harvests, Bonte says: “Wine aficionados enjoy the mid-October fête des vendanges in Bordeaux’s Saint-Émilion. Champagne is another popular fall destination. Although the exact date varies annually, harvest typically begins in late summer and lasts several weeks.” More broadly speaking, Bonte says travelers who choose the fall tend to be keen on moving “more deeply” through a destination, “whether that means focusing on wine, gastronomy, culture, or a specific region rather than trying to see all of a country in one trip.” Are travelers swapping out summer for fall? The rise of the fallcation doesn’t necessarily spell the doom of the summercation. “Rather than give up the traditional summer vacation, travelers are adding a second vacation later in the year,” says Julie Durso, a private travel manager at Scott Dunn. “We’re seeing an increase in both summer and fall travel,” says Red Savannah’s managing director for villas Nick Westwood. The company’s villa bookings in June this year were up 24%, compared to the same month in 2025; July and August were up by 65%. Other travel advisors agree that summer travel is not going extinct, but have indeed noticed shifts in terms of where—and when—people are going. “There’s definitely some substitution happening,” says Barber of Original Travel. He observes that the UK market is increasingly staying closer to home during the summer, and their big international trips are instead happening in October or even the Easter season. Alder of Jonathan’s Travels says clients from the United States are saving places like Europe for later in the year: “Europe is fading as a summer destination for our clients, as it should be. When you have the flexibility, there’s little reason to fight the extreme heat and enormous summer crowds when you can experience many of the same destinations beautifully in September or October.” Authentic Explorations is seeing the same trend, says Portuesi; a wine tour in late October was sold out quickly, and past summer trips were more difficult to fill up with travelers who were largely staying in the US. Where are people going for “fallcations”? The short answer: People are going everywhere. Some fall trips, though, are certainly trending among the travel specialists I consulted. Going to Japan for the autumn is big right now, where the fall colors are just as spectacular as the cherry blossoms in spring. Of course Italy and Greece are big, especially for non-beach trips: the Peloponnese and Tuscany in the fall, Athens and Venice in winter. But for travelers insisting on jumping into the Mediterranean, October is still a good time to go. Overall the conventional wisdom holds: weather is better, crowds are fewer, and costs are more manageable outside of the summer season. Whether that pattern will hold as more people eye autumn remains to be seen. As for domestic travel, Clifford of International Travel Management says his clients are “focused on places where you can easily escape the crowds: the historic coastal estates of Newport, Rhode Island, the open spaces and private ranches of Big Sky, Montana, and the high-desert mountains of Santa Fe, New Mexico.” How is the travel industry meeting the moment? Now that September is squarely part of the summer travel schedule, “shoulder season” and “off season” are being pushed later into the year. This means some seasonal destinations and hotels are staying open longer. Gray of Gray & Co. name checks popular destinations that used to shutter at summer’s close, like the Amalfi Coast in Italy, where hotels like Palazzo Avino in Ravello welcome guests until late October, and Le Sirenuse in Positano until November 1. Gray says that the task of hoteliers and restaurateurs extending their seasons is to keep up the level of service and energy as one would expect in the summertime. The cruise industry, too, is investing in fall and winter travel. Cruise lines like Regent Seven Seas and Explora Journeys are operating their first full winter seasons in the Mediterranean this year. Cruises expert Mary Jean Tully of Tully Luxury Travel sailed with Explora in November last year and says, “It was fabulous. No crowds. The weather was fresh but not cold. It’s a great time to go.” Additionally, airlines are making moves for the fall and even the winter, extending seasonal flight routes beyond their usual September cutoffs. For example, United Airlines will operate its thrice-weekly flight between Newark International Airport and Palermo, Sicily, until mid-December this year. Delta is operating flights from New York-JFK to Catania in Sicily and Porto in Portugal through January 2027. What are the potential repercussions of the “fallcation”? The fallcation began as an escape from the heat and crowds of high summer, but its longer-term effect may be to redraw the entire travel calendar. Barber expects that seasons will shift: “September and October will stop being the ‘shoulder season.’ In the most popular parts of southern Europe, they’ll increasingly become part of the main season, with higher hotel rates, tighter availability, and fuller flights. Destinations will stay open longer. Hotels, beach clubs, restaurants, guides, and seasonal flight routes have a commercial reason to extend their seasons.” We’re already seeing this happening, though the adjustments currently seem like temporary novelties. There’s a world in which fall becomes a high-traffic season too. “That could be hugely positive for local employment, making tourism less dependent on an eight-week summer bonanza,” Barber says. “If fall travel continues to grow, certain destinations could eventually face some of the same pressures we're seeing in peak summer,” says Bonte of French Side Travel. He makes the case for cultivating travel programming that does not simply repeat its old mistakes—“reshuffling by destination” rather than the creation of “a single new peak season.” Regions could start reverting to the seasons that actually suit them, Bonte says, rather than times of year into which they’ve been pigeonholed. As opposed to a summer spree, the French Riviera could become hot for winter again, as it historically had been; the Alps could pick up as a summer destination. “Each region in France has a season where it truly shines, and the opportunity is to match travelers to that, rather than pushing everyone into the same few months,” he says. It’s work that falls on travel specialists to accomplish as well, to spread the travel traffic around—to bring it not only to the destinations that need it, but the parts of the calendar that do too. Is there still an off season in the age of the “fallcation”? Every part of the calendar is largely claimed by a good reason—and a good place—to travel. Put another way, one place’s “off season” may be another destination’s perfect window. Portuesi says the dead-of-winter months of January and February are still considered the low season in Europe, save for ski destinations like the Dolomites. Meanwhile, that’s one of the best times to go to the Caribbean because hurricane season is usually over by Christmas. For other places, what we might traditionally assume to be peak season is actually low season. Take Asia, for example. “Rainy periods in Southeast Asia and Japan also generally coincide with the summer months,” says Heald of Remote Lands. “But even then, some travelers will visit because it is the only time their schedules allow. In Japan, summers can be extremely hot and humid, yet travelers continue to go.” “I really don't think there is such a thing as an off-season anymore,” Alder says, adamant that the idea of everyone going to the same place at the same time of year is not sustainable or desirable. Besides, there’s a whole world out there and an entire calendar to consider. As Alder puts it, “There's almost always a great place to go, and increasingly we're helping clients identify when a destination is at its best for them, rather than simply when it's traditionally considered peak season.”

item.title: Newport, Rhode Island, Is New England’s Gilded Jewel—Here’s Where to Eat, Stay, and Play
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.38
Newport, Rhode Island, has certainly been having a moment as of late. You can attribute it to the Gilded Age dramas taking over small screens, the old-money aesthetic taking over TikTok, the Real Housewives of Rhode Island taking over Bravo, or just the fact that it’s beyond beautiful all year long. Either way, it’s undeniable that this compact coastal city has become a mecca of sorts for travelers eager to live out their East Coast fantasies—seafood, seersucker, sailboats, and all. But truth be told, Newport has never been a bad idea. The charming city has been a popular summer destination since the early 19th century, first as a playground for America’s elite, with families like the Vanderbilts and Astors building massive mansions along the water to serve as vacation homes (more on those later). Today, it’s a little less exclusive and a hot spot year-round, with New Englanders and international visitors alike spending sunny days becoming one with the sand at Easton’s Beach, breezy afternoons hiking the Cliff Walk, and chilly nights imbibing their way through Bowen’s Wharf before retreating to shingled cottages and luxurious hotels across town. If all that sounds like your kind of bliss, keep reading for a guide to seeing Newport in all its glory, as compiled by two New Yorkers who have been returning over and over again for the past decade. Here’s where to eat, stay, and play in the City by the Sea. Where to eat We’d argue the food and drink scene in Newport is reason enough to come to town, boasting old favorites and newer hubs that have given the city’s dining scene some fresh energy. Early birds, hit up Cru Cafe for a cozy bistro vibe and elevated comfort dishes like smoked salmon avocado toast. If you’re willing to wait in line, The Nitro Bar is a newer favorite (especially among influencers) with coffee and pastries that just might be worth the hype. Or, head to locally loved Franklin Spa, a legendary diner that hasn't changed its retro greasy-spoon energy in decades, and still serves one of the best lunches in town. Speaking of lunch, if the weather calls for it, take yours alfresco. Use Bowen’s Wharf as your hub: Belly up at 22 Bowen’s outdoor bar-restaurant area, have a casual seafood lunch at The Mooring, or get your clam chowder fix at The Black Pearl, with its lively dockside setting. You'll also find Clarke Cooke House, one of Newport's most popular restaurants, at the wharf. Its ship-like setting is one for the books, and the bistro offers a big menu spanning summer sushi to burgers, native cod, and even steak frites. For something less serious, Wally’s Weiners is another classic, and the kind of place you'll want to work into a day of wandering around Thames Street, known for being the center of the city. For harbor views and a Mediterranean-inspired menu, head to Flora, one of the newer names in town housed within the Gardiner House hotel. White Horse Tavern, on the other hand, offers classic Americana, with upscale farm-to-table dining (and stellar rum drinks) inside a building dating back to 1673. Crossing the bridge into Jamestown? Head to Beech if you want dinner to be the main event, with tasty, seasonal American fare headed up by locals. Where to stay Newport has no shortage of gorgeous hotels scattered from busy Thames Street to breezy Castle Hill Cove. Most guest rooms fall on the smaller side—this is a compact city, after all—but the best properties go big on glamour, offering gobsmacking views, old-world interiors, and exceptional in-house eateries and wellness facilities. Those looking for a taste of the Gilded Age should opt for spots like The Vanderbilt, an Auberge property built by a member of the Vanderbilt family in 1908, or Francis Malbone House, a Georgian-style mansion that dates back to 1760. If you’re all about location, location, location, book The Chanler at Cliff Walk for easy access to the popular waterfront hiking trail, Hammetts Hotel if you want to be steps from some of the city’s best bars and restaurants, or Forty 1º North Hotel Marina Resort to be so close to the water you’re basically swimming. Whether you’re staying there or not, you don't skip a stop inside Castle Hill Inn, a landmark Victorian mansion and one of the most iconic hotels in town. With an incredible location atop rocky bluffs that overlook the sailboat-studded ocean, the property’s Lawn Terrace is where you’ll want to grab a glass of Sauv Blanc and pretend you’re an Astor. Of course, hotels in Newport can be pricey, so if you’re on a budget or traveling with a group, an Airbnb might be a better bet—especially if the sound of a kitchen or common hangout space tickles your fancy. You can find smaller homes and apartments in Newport proper, like this four-bedroom with harbor views right downtown or this minimalist waterfront condo in the Historic District, but many visitors look to Middletown, Rhode Island—a town right outside Newport—for bigger, more affordable rentals. This adorable three-bedroom cottage with a shingled façade, for example, is technically in Middletown, but just five minutes from downtown Newport. Where to play The soul of Newport is rooted in the very concept of play. It’s a family-friendly destination and a romantic coastal escape; a place where sweet boutiques meet cool bars and Gilded Age history meets a working harbor. In the warmer months, chase the sea: Easton’s Beach is the most convenient option near town, Gooseberry Beach is tucked along Ocean Drive, and Second (or Sachuest) Beach offers a long stretch of sand and Atlantic surf. Post up at Second for a lobster roll and fries (sold from a beachside concession stand, the best), then grab an icy, refreshing Del’s Lemonade served from its iconic truck before heading home. Oh, and before you go, buy your next beach read at Commonwealth Books of Newport in the Historic Hill neighborhood. If you time it right, you can hit Newport's renowned Jazz Festival and the Newport Folk Festival, both hosted annually at the end of July (and sometimes running through early August). Plan in advance to secure tickets, as they can go quickly. For a more last-minute excursion that's completely free to the public, walk the Cliff Walk on the southeastern shoreline. The scenic coastal path threads between the Atlantic and the Newport Mansions, which, of course, you'll want to go inside and tour. If you’d rather be on the water than beside it, Sail Newport offers a Try Sailing experience, as well as afternoon-to-sunset sails. For something further from the coast, the International Tennis Hall of Fame is a great rainy day pit stop for exploring the history of the beloved sport and sniffing your way through the gardens surrounding the iconic grass courts. The Preserve in Blackstone Valley offers guided horseback tours, carriage rides, and sunset strolls, while Shephard’s Run Winery is a dreamy estate that gives you an excuse to head inland in South Kingstown for a tasting. As for a great Irish pub, The Fastnet has frosty beers on tap, while O’Brien’s is ever-abuzz and makes a mean house mudslide. If you want to make a night of it, have a drink and bites at Hotel Viking’s French-inspired Pescadou restaurant, then dance to the live DJ at its rooftop bar, Cap Club. Midtown Oyster Bar is perfect for a nightcap.

item.title: TSA’s New PreCheck Perk Allows Non-Ticketed Visitors to Accompany Friends and Family at the Gate
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.06
TSA’s newest PreCheck perk is intended for people who aren’t flying at all. Gateside by TSA PreCheck, which began rolling out this month at 13 US airports, allows eligible non-ticketed visitors to pass through security after receiving advance approval. That means they can accompany someone to a departure gate, meet an arriving traveler airside, visit a friend or relative during a layover, or access the restaurants and shops beyond the checkpoint. The program marks an expansion of an idea that several individual airports have experimented with in recent years: allowing some people without boarding passes back into the secure side of the terminal. But Gateside also raises a more practical question—who actually wants to go through airport security on their own volition when they don’t have a flight to catch? Jennifer Yellin, managing editor at travel rewards platform Points Path, expects the answer to be mostly people helping or meeting someone they know. “I think families will be the ones to use this the most,” Yellin says “I foresee this being the most beneficial for parents accompanying their child for an outbound flight as well as welcoming home family members.” She also sees potential for older travelers, nervous or infrequent fliers, and people navigating unfamiliar airports with the help of a friend or relative. In those cases, Gateside could make it possible for someone to stay alongside a traveler all the way to the gate, rather than saying goodbye before security. “If you have a child, parent, spouse, or even friend who is a nervous flier, being able to walk them to their gate and see them off could help put their nerves to ease,” Yellin says. “It can also be useful to help the same younger or older family member navigate an airport, which might otherwise be challenging. For some travelers, having someone there with you to the very end can put them at ease.” That doesn’t mean Gateside will replace existing assistance available to travelers who need it. Airlines already issue escort or gate passes in certain circumstances, including unaccompanied minors, and airports and airlines offer assistance for travelers with disabilities. Gateside is broader: A visitor doesn’t need to be escorting someone who qualifies for one of those services. Instead, access is based primarily on the visitor’s eligibility for TSA PreCheck screening and approval for Gateside. How Gateside by TSA PreCheck works Gateside is currently being offered as an “operational assessment” at 13 airports, including major hubs such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and Salt Lake City International Airport. To use it, visitors need to be eligible for TSA PreCheck screening and have a Known Traveler Number. That includes TSA PreCheck members as well as eligible members of trusted traveler programs such as Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI. The pass itself is free, but visitors have to apply online one to three days before their intended airport visit and select the participating airport they plan to enter. Those who are approved bring an acceptable form of identification to the airport and go through a TSA PreCheck checkpoint; they are still subject to normal security screening and restrictions. An approval is valid for the designated calendar day and allows the visitor to leave and re-enter the secure area that day. Gateside isn’t the first way for a non-ticketed visitor to get beyond airport security. Airports including Seattle, New Orleans, Orlando, Tampa, Palm Springs, and Tulsa already operate their own visitor-pass programs, each with its own rules. Detroit and San Diego have existing visitor programs in addition to being among the first Gateside airports. The distinction with the new TSA program is that Gateside is tied to PreCheck eligibility and gives approved visitors access through the PreCheck screening lane. For the average traveler, Yellin says, the program is still likely to remain fairly niche. “While it's a meaningful change, it's only beneficial for a small group of travelers,” she says. “For the average traveler, it won't change the airport experience since this is limited to a very small subset of airports and advance approval is required.” Seeing off a family member is perhaps the most obvious use for the program, but Gateside could also make it easier to spend time with someone who isn’t beginning or ending their trip in your city. “If you have a friend or family member traveling with a long layover in your home airport, meeting them during their connection is the perfect situation,” Yellin says. “This allows the traveler to stay near their gate without having to leave security.” Currently, meeting a connecting passenger generally requires the traveler to leave the secure area of the airport, then go through security again before continuing their trip. That may not be practical on a shorter connection, particularly at a large airport where getting between the gate and terminal exit can itself take time. With Gateside, the local visitor goes through security instead. Still, Yellin doesn’t expect non-ticketed visitors to start heading to airports simply because they now can. “The airport experience today is tiring for many and extremely different than what it once was,” she says. “Because of that, I do not believe too many people are going to choose to park their car and navigate their way through security, without actually traveling that day, unless they have a very real reason.” The program’s arrival also comes 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed who could access US airport gate areas. Before 9/11, people without tickets could generally accompany passengers through security; afterward, access to the secure side of terminals became largely limited to ticketed passengers and those with specific authorization. However, Yellin doesn't believe Gateside is a signal that TSA is returning to the old airport model. “Now that it's been 25 years, TSA is experimenting to see how the overall experience can be better for travelers, while still keeping safety in mind,” she says. Airports offering Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Ohio - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Texas - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Michigan - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indiana - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Nevada - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in California - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) in California - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Utah

item.title: Thousands of Flights Disrupted at UK Airports Due to Air Traffic Control Issue
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.73
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following an air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday, September 8. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue through Wednesday as airlines and airports work through backlogged flights. The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologized for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken “longer than hoped.” An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” London Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before traveling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before traveling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday, September 9 have already been canceled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by the disruption are repositioned. Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or canceled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 (approximately $300) per person to £520 (approximately $700) per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is canceled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Or, if your flight departs from an EU country and arrives in the UK (operated by either an EU or a non-EU airline). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruptions: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport This is a developing news story and will be updated with more information. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: An Ode to Gander Airport, 25 Years After 9/11
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.44
Twenty-five years ago, the remote Newfoundland town of Gander found itself becoming an unlikely haven at the edge of the North Atlantic. In the wake of 9/11, more than 4,000 airborne flights were forced to divert when the Federal Aviation Administration closed American airspace—and 38 of those aircraft landed in Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of just 10,000 people. Brian Mosher, a Gander resident and TV reporter, filmed practically non-stop in the days following September 11, in an attempt to share what was happening on the ground with the world. “There were 7,000 different reasons why people had to get home,” says Mosher. “We were their shoulders to cry on.” The “come from aways,” the Newfoundland term for out-of-towners, were welcomed into the community with warmth, love, food, and anything else their hosts could provide. Buffet tables were set up to feed the new arrivals, and accommodation arranged in homes, schools, and churches. “We thought we’d give them a bite to eat before we put them back on their planes, not realizing they were going to have to stay here five days,” he says. The events of these confusing, confounding days went on to inspire a hit Broadway musical, Come From Away, with Ganderites immortalized in song. Today, Gander International Airport feels smaller and sleepier than its reputation might suggest. Most travelers who find themselves here are on brief stopovers en route to or from other destinations in Newfoundland and Labrador. Others have made a special visit, drawn by the extraordinary architecture and design of the former International Departures Terminal, a Modernist time capsule dating back to 1959. Gander Airport’s legacy actually far predates the events of 9/11–in fact, going all the way back to a time when global aviation was, literally, just taking off. It was the late 1930s, just three decades after Orville and Wilbur Wright’s first flight took off from Kitty Hawk beach in North Carolina. With long-haul air travel underway, and Newfoundland’s location on the Great Circle Route—930 miles closer to Europe than anywhere else in North America—positioned Gander as the perfect staging point for refueling, maintenance, and emergencies at a time when flying was far more unpredictable and potentially unreliable than we know it to be today The first plane to land in Gander touched down on a snow-packed runway in 1938. By 1940, it was already the world’s largest airport, and in World War II served as the main maintenance point for Allied aircraft flying to Europe. Eventually, Gander would go on to welcome commercial flights from Europe and the Soviet Union for refueling stops, but it couldn’t throw off its military past. Until 1959, arriving travelers still found themselves disembarking into a hangar designed for WWII. The opening of the Gander Airport International Departures Terminal by Queen Elizabeth II in June that year changed everything. The new terminal was a showcase for an ambitious, modernizing, young nation featuring Canadian Modernist art and design, as well as stylish furniture by some of the design world’s greatest names like Charles and Ray Eames and Arne Jacobsen. Gander was now ready to welcome world leaders, celebrities, royalty, and rock stars to this little outpost in remote eastern Newfoundland, and was determined to put on a show. Major stars of the day passed through—Marilyn Monroe, Albert Einstein, and Elizabeth Taylor—and could be seen drinking martinis at the Big Dipper, Newfoundland’s only 24-hour bar. As the Jet Age advanced and aircraft became more powerful with increased ranges, trans-Atlantic flights no longer needed to make refueling stops. Arrivals into what was once the “crossroads of the world” began to slow, and Gander’s fortunes declined. The glamorous international terminal and lounge, no longer a necessity, was at risk of being lost to a newer, smaller, more economical option. Eventually, an outpouring of support led to its rescue, and in 2022 it reopened as a museum space with a small movie theater, gastropub, and souvenir shop. Today, it is preserved largely as it was in its heyday. The Mondrian-esque terrazzo floor in shades of salmon, slate, and jade still carries the sheen of 1950s glamour. Clocks on the wall still tell the time in London, Montreal, New York, and Moscow. Stylized bird sculptures by Arthur Price welcoming arriving passengers to Canada still gather in a flock. But the most dramatic feature is the 72-foot Flight and Its Allegories mural by Canadian artist Kenneth Lochhead, featuring a dynamic scene of activity and abundance. A matronly figure stands with arms outstretched. A bearded man feeds airplane-shaped bluebirds. A boy peers through binoculars. Stylized birds burst into the air, some Concorde-like in form, predating the iconic supersonic aircraft by over a decade. Gander-born Todd Saunders, the celebrated architect behind Newfoundland modern icon Fogo Island Inn, credits the International Departure Terminal as being his first exposure to contemporary architecture. “The Canadian government invested in architecture because this was the first face of Canada, and that first impression was really important,” he says. But the airport’s pull went beyond architecture alone. Saunders still recalls the smell of Cuban cigars that lingered after flights stopped in en route between Havana and Moscow. “In a way, it was like Penn Station in New York, but for the world,” he says. The international terminal used to be open to the public at the time, and in doing so, held a cosmopolitan allure for the people of Gander. “My dad worked there as an airplane mechanic and he would call me and say, ‘The [Rolling] Stones are here’, and I’d get on my BMX and head down. You’d be looking at Mick Jagger because they’d had to stop for gas," he recalls. For local textile artist and designer Janet Langdon, whose father worked as an aircraft refueler in Gander in the 1950s and 60s, the airport offered an opportunity to see the world come to town. “I was making my own clothes at the time, and through my young eyes it was super exciting to see worldly fashions.” As a teenager, she would hitchhike to the airport to see the exotic arrivals, including off the many Aeroflot flights that touched down in the early 1970s. “A passenger once gave me a small container of yoghurt,” Langdon says. “It was my first time enjoying it.” Today, flights use the more modern, but less romantic, building next door to the original, but for aviation geeks and history lovers, the museum space is still worth the flight to Gander, not least of all for the history it documents. One display highlights all the most unusual cargo to have moved through the airport, including an aircraft load of ping-pong balls en route to Moscow, a Boeing 747 full of toothpicks, and a shipment of live alligators. Another features episodes like the rescue of George Bush Sr. when he got stuck in a local bog, and Frank Sinatra being admonished for jumping the bar queue and being told to wait his turn. My favorite display is the photo of Fidel Castro sledding in Gander in December 1976: a cadre of heavy-coated officials looking on with concern as a giddy Castro is about to topple off into a heap of snow. But it’s not all about the history. The airport is still a vital part of the Gander community. “An economic impact study concluded last year shows that one in five jobs in the town of Gander are associated with the airport,” Reg Wright, President and CEO of Gander International Airport, says. “It’s nice to see Gander and its guests gather in the lounge again.” For Langdon, the airport is synonymous with what it means to be from this small aviation town in Newfoundland. “Originally it brought people together from all over for employment, and during 9/11 it brought the world to our town,” she says. “Today, people come for the history, some because of Come From Away, and of course the aviation geeks. I just met a retired Lufthansa flight dispatcher who was going to spend time at the lounge before heading back to Luxembourg.” Langdon is hopeful that the airport and departures lounge will remain thriving community spaces. “To quote Reg Wright, we as Ganderites have jet fuel in our veins.” For the town and its people, the airport will never be just a place people pass through; it is woven into their identity and history—and, despite the changing tides of aviation, will remain part of their future. And if there is ever another time when they must heed the call of the world's travelers again, the airport and the community will no doubt stand ready.

item.title: Where Was 'Practical Magic 2' Filmed? Coastal Massachusetts Moves Over for Southern England
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.14
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Practical Magic 2. In 1998, Hollywood starlets Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock played Gillian and Sally Owens, two sisters in possession of special powers in Practical Magic, a film adapted from the eponymous Alice Hoffman novel. Set in the witch-rich state of Massachusetts, the outcasted siblings attempt to lift their ancestral curse, which strikes dead any man who falls in love with an Owens woman. As they embark on this harrowing journey, spells are cast, midnight margaritas are made, and matriarchy reigns supreme. At the time, the film’s reception was middling at best—with a New York Times review describing it as “Barbie Joins a Coven”—and its performance at the box office not much better. With a little room to breathe and bask in nostalgia’s rose-colored glow, the movie has transformed into a feminist cult classic with Gen X and Gen Z fans alike. From 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple to The Devil Wears Prada 2, the past year has been a boon for follow-up films. In that same vein, Kidman and Bullock have reunited in Practical Magic 2, a sequel directed by Susanne Bier that promises to delight fans and take us across the pond to a whole new continent of spooky locales. Another generation of the coven-loving lives on in Practical Magic 2, which picks up after a sizable time jump but with more of the same kooky hijinks. A generous interpretation of time—and a little movie magic—lands Sally’s daughters Antonia (Maisie Williams) and Kylie (Joey King) in their early 20s. Up until now, they have lived their lives ignorant to their powers, which their mother has deliberately shielded them from. Medical student Antonia most closely resembles her mother, while Kylie, now a Harvard student, is a bit more of a free spirit. When Kylie falls for sweet Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) and then he falls into a coma, she follows her mother’s path of attempting to right things. Counseled by the recently uncovered Book of the Raven, Kylie sets off to her family’s ancestral home of England, bringing much of the story to English territory. While the original movie used Washington State's Whidbey Island as a stand-in for New England, production for the sequel moved to the United Kingdom. Here are all the places where Practical Magic 2 was filmed. Leavesden Studios – Hertfordshire, England The Owens women remain the main characters in this film, and fans of the original film will recall the outstanding Victorian-style Owens family home. The house itself has reached a cult status with its cutesy cottage core aesthetic, and its recreation was crucial to the making of the sequel. Practical Magic 2’s production notes explain the importance of the revival of the house. Producer Denise De Novi felt that bringing the house back to life was one of the most rewarding components of making this movie. “The house in this movie is just a phenomenon,” she noted. In the first film, the exterior of the house was built on San Juan Island in Washington state, and the interiors were created on a soundstage in Los Angeles. Those structures no longer exist so this time around, production designer Tom Burton determined that the most economical option was to build the house from scratch on the back lot at Leavesden Studios. Great care was taken to ensure that the replica was consistent with the original home, including establishing the same positioning to the sun so that the sun would set in the same position as it did in the original film. Once the house’s construction was almost complete, the greens team descended upon the set to bring the renowned garden to life, with over 4,000 plants brought in. While about half of the 55 shooting days were spent at Leavesden Studios, the remainder were shot at several notable locations in and around the London area. Village of Hambleden The quaint village of Hambleden, just west of London, served as the town Thornfield. The center of the village is filled with old, picturesque brick and flint cottages, all with the signature dormer windows. The Royal Standard of England, Beaconsfield British viewers might take notice of this historic pub, which serves at the exterior of the fictional Thornfield Inn just northwest of London. The Royal Standard, which has been around for over 900 years, claims to be the oldest pub in Great Britain. Located in the Chiltern Hills, the scenic old pub is filled with charm and has been featured in numerous films and television shows, including The Theory of Everything, Hot Fuzz, and Too Much. Oysters, fish and chips, and a robust beer list are on offer, and Quiz Night is every Tuesday. Langleybury Mansion in Hertfordshire Langlebury is a vacant 18th-century period house that has served as a backdrop for several notable productions including Downton Abbey, The Crown, and Paddington. The crew utilized this mansion to stand in for rooms at Harvard University as well as some of the UK lodgings. Wormsley Estate in Buckinghamshire The private 2,700-acre estate boasting an opera pavilion, cricket grounds, and a walled garden served as the backdrop for the cottage of Tom Lockland (Solly McLeod), a longtime magic student at Thornfield. Black Park Country Park Practical Magic 2 features sweeping views of the British rolling hills and conifer forests. Black Park, a large park with woodland trails, horse riding, and a lake, was filmed as the forest surrounding Thornfield. The Royal Chelsea Hospital The historic Royal Hospital Chelsea in London is a retirement and nursing home for British Army veterans who have reached the state pension age. The hospital was founded by Charles II in 1692, and it has maintained its grand property while modernizing to fit the present-day needs of its inhabitants. The impressive grounds with brick buildings and Roman columns were used in the film for a flower market and shots meant to be Harvard University exteriors. The Victorian flats of Cromwell Buildings The tattoo-covered Professor Ian Wright (Lee Pace), who quickly becomes Sally’s love interest, is one of the more charming updates in this sequel. His apartment was shot in these flats.

item.title: Boston’s Best Lobster Rolls Include a Secret Off-Menu Pick
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.88
New Englanders grow up on unfussy seafood like lobster rolls the way other people grow up on tacos or barbecue—foods so embedded in the way of life of a particular place that you don’t realize how special they are until you start traveling. Now, when I’m away from home, I find that lobster rolls are seen as an expensive delicacy. Yes, lobster rolls are special; they exist in the city’s glitzier and fine-dining restaurants, and their prices have skyrocketed in more recent years. But they’re also just as common at fast food counters in the suburbs and fishmonger docks up and down the coast. And just like paying $6 a gallon for gas on a California road trip, or $43 for a martini at Bemelman’s Bar in Manhattan, having a lobster roll in Boston is a worthwhile investment every once in a while. It's simply what you do when you’re here. That being said, not all lobster rolls are created equal—and many (sometimes controversial) variations exist. A purist will say that a proper one must—must!—be served on a split-top bun that’s been griddled until golden brown, while others make compelling arguments for fancy swaps like brioche rolls. Then there’s the lobster meat itself, served either as a simply dressed cold salad (Maine style) or warm and buttered (Connecticut style)—but that’s more of a personal preference. The good news? There are many, many lobster rolls to experience in Boston, ranging from textbook classics to more chef-driven interpretations. Here's where to find the best. Row 34 Chef Jeremy Sewall knows a thing or two about good fish, and his popular Row 34 restaurants (with locations in Fort Point and in Cambridge’s Kendall Square) are where you go for excellent beer, interesting wines, and a chef’s sensibility. Here, the lobster roll is surprisingly personal, with lobster sourced from chef Sewall’s cousin Mark, who captains a boat in York Harbor, Maine. There are two versions here: a warm buttered roll with steamed tail, claw and knuckle meat and tucked into a traditional split-top bun; and the other, the Ethel’s Creamy Lobster Roll, named for Sewall’s grandmother and folded together with celery, red onion, pickles, mayonnaise, crème fraîche, lemon, celery salt and black pepper. The cold, creamy one comes on a rosemary brioche bun that is griddled to order and is nothing short of heavenly. James Hook & Co. James Hook & Co. is the alpha and omega of Boston lobster rolls; a platonic ideal of what a lobster roll should be. The family-run seafood business operating on the Boston waterfront for over 100 years is an adorable, unassuming shack on shiny, transformed Atlantic Avenue downtown—this is where any good lobster roll tour of the city should begin (or end). The company ships over 50,000 pounds of lobster daily, both online and to wholesale distributors nationwide, so they know a thing or two about quality. The rolls here come in two sizes and two styles, either chilled or warm with butter. While you’re here, don’t overlook the other seafood specialties; the double-stuffed scallop, clam chowder, and lobster mac and cheese make for a perfect shared side. Saltie Girl If James Hook is the lobster roll in its natural habitat, Saltie Girl is its glamorous, city-slicker cousin. This stylish Back Bay restaurant slings some of the best seafood on Newbury Street, in an elegant yet playful dining room overlooking the boutiques of Newbury Street. Its classic New England-style lobster rolls arrive perfectly coiffed, alongside a charmingly branded bag of Saltie Girl potato chips (add some caviar from the raw bar if you like). But the real insider move here? Ask your server about the secret, off-menu version of the lobster roll: the meat comes fried, sprinkled with Korean chili flakes and sweet corn butter, resulting in something richer, spicier, and considerably more decadent than a traditional version. It’s a sterling reminder that, even in a historic city like Boston, we don’t have to take our classics so seriously. The Banks Seafood and Steak The Banks is a crowd-pleaser of a restaurant—a perfect location in Back Bay, a lively bar scene, and an elevated menu of New England classics. The lobster roll here is an example of a perfectly adventurous recipe where the chef has improved on the original with a few tweaks, but none so heretical that they feel like a major departure from tradition. It comes on a house-made brown-butter bun, sprinkled with sea salt and chives, and served with Old Bay potato chips. The hot lobster roll is a standout—it’s par-cooked, then warmed in a “lobster beurre monté,” a classic French technique that glazes the meat and also helps infuse more lobster flavor into it. The result is a roll that is deceptively simple, yes, bursting with flavor. Eventide Fenway Originally from Portland, Maine, Eventide brought its contemporary take on New England seafood to the Fenway neighborhood as a seafood counter in 2017 before evolving into a full-service restaurant in 2023. The experience here is decidedly more Boston than Maine—it’s a bustling, popular spot for pre-Fenway Park drinks and snacks, less of a cozy, James Beard-recognized eatery than its progenitor in Portland—but Eventide did one key invention with it for the Hub: its brown butter lobster rolls. They come on a fluffy, bao-style steamed bun, drenched (in a good way) with browned butter and flecked with sliced chives. The Sail Loft Nestled on the fringes of the North End within steps of the Freedom Trail, Faneuil Hall and the restaurants of Hanover Street, this institution feels like it’s been here forever. The Boston Sail Loft’s lobster roll is classic, with chilled lobster salad lightly dressed with mayonnaise and piled generously into a toasted bun. The thick, crispy fries that accompany it are a departure from the canonical bag of chips, but they’re a nice touch. There are fancier lobster rolls in Boston—but with perfect execution, stiff drinks and waterfront views, what else would you need? Red’s Best at Boston Public Market A great, no-frills option for travelers who want to understand where their seafood actually comes from, this counter inside Boston Public Market is dedicated to small, independent New England fishermen. And that direct connection to the local fishing community is what makes this experience special. The market itself—just steps from the Freedom Trail—is an easy stop while sightseeing, especially if you’re in the Faneuil Hall, North End, or Beacon Hill areas. The lobster rolls fresh and unfussy. While there’s no waterfront view or white tablecloth, there is something very Boston about enjoying solid seafood in a bustling public market surrounded by Bostonians going about their everyday lives. Plus: Save room for a doughnut from Union Square Donuts, or a popover from The Popover Lady. The Barking Crab Right across Fort Point Channel from James Hook & Co., you’ll find The Barking Crab, another old-school spot where the lobster rolls are classic, but the atmosphere is decidedly more festive. This ramshackle seafood restaurant feels like a relic from the old Seaport, before the neighborhood redeveloped into an epicenter of glass towers and luxury condos. The location makes it especially appealing on warmer days, and the vibe is a little rowdy (in a good way). The lobster roll here is a straightforward expression—toasted roll, available either tossed with mayo or “naked” with warm, butter-poached lobster meat—but if you’re really feeling like splurging, opt for the “One and Done”: whereas most rolls come with about one-fourth a pound of meat, this one comes with a solid one pound, for a whopping $150. Worth it? After a few beers or cocktails, you bet. Yankee Lobster Co. Venture into the Seaport, keep cruising past all the newfangled developments, and you’ll eventually find yourself at Yankee Lobster Co., which has been serving seafood here for roughly 75 years, making it one of the increasingly rare links to the city’s working waterfront in this part of town. That history is part of the appeal, and the lobster roll is comfortingly old-school: generously portioned, straightforward, crafted from the freshest lobster. Come here if you want a classic Boston seafood experience without the polish or price tags of the Seaport’s flashier restaurants. Sullivan’s Castle Island A visit to Castle Island—which is actually not an island, but the tip of the peninsula known as South Boston, or “Southie”—is a beloved Boston ritual. You walk or bike to the far edge of Southie, go for a waterfront stroll around Fort Independence, the oldest continuously fortified site in British North America, then stop for a refueling at Sullivan’s, so much a part of the fabric of Boston life that it received a James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award. This is not the lobster roll to choose if you’re looking for culinary drama—it’s the one you choose when you want to eat seafood like a Boston local.

item.title: The Quiet Magic of Greece in the Off Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.62
Few eras of Greek history compare to the ancient times that the country has become so synonymous with—the cinematic fables of Odysseus, comic-book lore of Leonidas, and philosophic creeds of Socrates are ever-present in pop culture. But anyone who’s been to Hellas in the past few years can tell you that something new is brewing here—current-day Greece is coming close to a similar precipice, one that could be nearly as definitive as the Bronze Age, as visitors arrive in droves higher than ever before. Arrivals to the nation of 10 million people were up by 38% in the first few months of 2026, the highest increase on the continent for that period by far (Italy was second, with a 21% rise). Now, more than ever, it feels like everyone is planning a seafaring escape or mountain adventure to Athens and the islands—or, if you’re in-the-know, to the serene coastal towns of the Peloponnese peninsula or the northern Aegean’s sparkling Thermaic Gulf. One decade after the country’s financial crisis peaked, and a half decade since the pandemic-era halt in tourism that had so many here pleading for the long-despised cruise ships to return, you would think this is good news for a state as tourism-dependent as Greece. And you could be right—but the unfortunate reality, according to the Bank of Greece, is that the crescendo coincides with mounting climate disasters that threaten the infrastructure of a nation still in the throes of recovery; a particularly harrowing warning ahead of this year’s El Niño; not to mention during their Mediterranean neighbors' unprecedented fire seasons. The seasonal pressure has become a balancing act. The good news, though, is that summer is far from the only time to visit. Outside the grip of sweltering summer heat lies some of Greece’s most delicious adventures: tasting early spring’s olive oils straight from the groves right after harvest; fall parties with small-island locals celebrating another season of panigiria wrapped; perusing the treasures of Athens’ open-air ruins in the soft, pre-winter light. There is so much more to Greece than the postcard islands—and the packed ferries to get to them—and with the mainland about to have its moment in the sun (we’re looking at you, Christopher Nolan), there’s no better time than the off-season to uncover every corner’s most spectacular self—the one without the heaving crowds. To prove it, we’ve tapped the best local creators to share how they do it, and how you can, too, siga siga (more slowly). —Shannon McMahon, senior destinations editor Over the last 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has made Ammos Hotel (and its beloved on-site Red Jane Bakery) one of Crete’s most talked-about hotels. Born and raised in Chania, the owner’s joyful, design-led approach to hospitality is rooted in his hometown, with 80% of his staff also locals. From its high-quality cuisine to its warm, home-away-from-home atmosphere, Ammos reflects Tsepetis’s deep connection to Chania. Here, he shares why spring is his favorite time to experience the city. For Dutch artist Christiane Smit, a vacation on Paros in 2008 changed the course of her life. Drawn instinctively to the Cycladic island, she stayed and has lived in villages across Paros ever since. Today, she runs a ceramics atelier in Lefkes and owns minimalist clifftop villa Moonhouse, while restoring a century-old stone house in Kostos. Here, Smit shares the shoulder-season pleasures that keep her on the island year-round, and where to eat and stay. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, moving to Santorini from Greece's mainland 11 years ago was an easy choice: “It is the mecca of Greek white wine.” Since then, he has worked across the island’s wineries before launching Orycton, a small-batch Assyrtiko made with grapes from old vines. Now based in quiet Monolithos, Kouloglou has lived throughout Santorini, gaining an intimate understanding of its villages, landscapes, and rhythms. Here, he shares why autumn is his favorite season to explore the island. Greek family recipes are often passed down by instinct rather than instruction—a pinch here, a glug there, learned at the kitchen table. Food writer Anastasia Miari has spent nearly a decade documenting these dishes and the older generations and remote villages that have kept them alive. Her cooking celebrates Greece’s culinary traditions, while her latest book, Mediterranea, expands the journey across the region, from Moroccan tagines and Turkish breakfasts to Sicilian pasta. “Alive. That’s how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. Having lived in the capital since she was 18, Sbokou has watched the city continually evolve, while retaining its irresistible energy. For her, the joy of visiting somewhere lies in understanding its local rhythm. Here, she shares why autumn is so magical in Athens, alongside some of her favorite places to explore in the city. Lead editors: Sarah Allard, Shannon McMahon, Arati Menon, Lisa Riehl Writers: Shannon McMahon, Chadner Navarro, Noo Saro-Wiwa, Olivia Morelli Visuals and social media: Sophie Knight, Mercedes Bleth, Lucy Bruton Syndication editors: Kat Chen, Skyli Alvarez This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Shoulder Season on Paros: Ceramicist Christiane Smit Finds Inspiration at a Slower Pace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.55
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision, it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her unplanned move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse—both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round as well as her favorite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery, and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbors greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most. It changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colors, textures, and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colors of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea—those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travelers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer vacation, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship—from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming, and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favorite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged—a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine—dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages—Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos—that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures; crisp, sunny days; and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both! This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: You Can Now Book the 'Sterling Point' Cottage on Airbnb—and the Inside Might Surprise You
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.41
Great news for anyone who fell in love with Muskoka after watching Sterling Point but didn't inherit a lake house from their estranged grandfather: Gordon Bay Cottage, the actual property at the center of the hit show, is officially coming to Airbnb. In the Prime Video series, protagonist Annie Rubin makes a pilgrimage to the property—located on a fictional island called Sterling Point—after finding out it has been willed to her after the death of her grandfather, Gordon. Now, fans will be able to call this same cottage home, at least for a few nights, thanks to an Airbnb sweepstakes allowing guests to request one of three special stays at the five-bedroom lakeside lodge this fall. Bookings open on September 15 at 9 a.m. ET, and the stays will take place October 2 to 5, October 9 to 12, and October 16 to 19, with a price tag of $180 a night. If you're looking to cosplay as Annie, Ellis, Connor, or Ramona, set your alarm now—these dates are going to go quick. While Gordon Bay Cottage serves as the façade for Gordon's cottage, interior scenes were filmed on a soundstage in Toronto, about two hours south of Muskoka. That means while the outside of the home will look familiar—cedar-shingled gables, wraparound porch, stone steps leading down to the water, Muskoka chair–dotted dock—the interiors aren't what you'd expect. In fact, they're way more upscale. While Gordon's place in the show looks like it hasn't been updated in a few decades, the property up for grabs on Airbnb appears fresh and modern, with hardwood floors, bright white walls, and contemporary but comfortable furniture. Probably not Ramona's style, but definitely ideal for a luxurious long weekend on the lake. The real Gordon Bay Cottage also sits right on Lake Joseph, one of the most popular and sought-after lakes in the Muskoka region, which means a stay here will come with all the trappings of a classic Canadian summer getaway. Sweepstakes winners should come with their Roots sweatpants and be prepared to “shower” in the lake, drink some Steam Whistles around the firepit, drive their boats to dinner, and gulp down some fresh air while staring at the stars. Ready to experience all that cottage country has to offer but afraid you won't be able to score a stay at Gordon Bay Cottage? Lucky for you, there are plenty of other incredible rentals in Muskoka, and we've found the best of the best. Between Sterling Point, Heated Rivalry, and Every Year After, this stunning slice of Ontario is more popular than ever (no, really, Airbnb searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 are up nearly 110% year over year, according to the vacation rental brand), so if you want to secure a lakeside spot for next summer, you'd be wise to start looking—and booking—now.

item.title: The Best Rentals and Airbnbs Near Disney World Have Private Pools, Themed Bunk Rooms, and More Fun Amenities
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.31
I've been visiting Walt Disney World my entire life. I've snacked my way around EPCOT, waited out afternoon storms in Magic Kingdom, and celebrated more special occasions at the parks than I can count. But some of my favorite Disney trips happened once I committed to leaving “the bubble” and chose to book a rental property just outside the gates. Staying in a vacation home or Airbnb near Disney World means access to a full kitchen to cut down on pricey park meals, more room to spread out after a long day, and a home base within easy reach of other attractions like Universal Studios, SeaWorld, and Central Florida’s freshwater springs and lakes. Whether you're traveling with a big group, crave a private pool to wind down in post-park, or just want more space than a standard hotel suite allows for, these are the best rentals near Disney World to book for families, friend groups, and solo travelers alike. We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. FAQ: Is it cheaper to stay off-property at Disney World? It is usually cheaper to stay off-property when visiting Disney World. For big groups or families that require additional space and amenities outside of park access, booking a vacation rental is a great option. Before you book though, there are a few extra costs to keep in mind, including rental cars and Disney World parking. You also won't have access to some of the special perks that on-property hotels receive, like early entry to the parks, free park and resort parking, and priority access to booking Lightning Lanes skip-the-line services. How do you get to Disney World? Walt Disney World is about a 30-minute drive from Orlando International Airport. If you're staying at a vacation rental, you'll likely also need access to a car to get to and from the parks. There are a few rentals above, however, that partner with resorts to give you free shuttle access to the parks, which can come in handy if you're an out-of-towner. You can also book ride-shares to and from the park if necessary, but that can add up depending on how far away you're staying. Plus, wait times can be long, especially if you're staying further away or trying to leave at peak times, like after the fireworks show. Once on property, you'll be able to take advantage of Disney's free internal shuttle transportation to get around.

item.title: How to Make the Most of Greece’s Shoulder Season, According to Condé Nast Traveler Specialists
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.23
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Condé Nast Traveler's Top Travel Specialists about how to decide which off-season destination in Greece for you. As we continue to spread the good word of traveling outside of summer—peak season for most destinations, but most of all European—let us convince you that this advice is especially prescient for Greece, which is also magical in late fall, winter (skiing, anyone?), and early spring. But you might ask, how do you even travel to Greece in the off season? This country of many island groups, from Aegean to Ionian, is not just to be experienced at its peak in the summer, when ferries are run to and fro, and your social feed becomes awash with selfies from white-plastered Mykonos. Nay—Όχι! For reasons climate- and crowd-related, certain sides of Greece shine brighter when the brutal Grecian sun lets up and Zeus’s calming clouds roll in, when you actually have breathing room at the Parthenon and can even potentially commune with Athena herself in the soft winter light of Athens. Or, hey, why not just take advantage of the cheaper hotel rates and airfare while most families are wrapped up at school? For these reasons and more, locals and in-the-know visitors know that, in Hellas, “off season” truly means “game on.” To learn what it takes to make the most out of the off season, we tapped some of our favorite Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists who are experts on visiting Greece: Julie Durso of Scott Dunn, Lisa Kusak of Kusak & Co., Emily Rister of Original Travel, and Laura Plansky of Audley Travel. Here they tell us the pros of visiting outside of summer, where to take a city break, and what to pack so that you’re prepared for your own off-season odyssey to Greece. Why you should visit Greece in the off season After an entirely too-hot Eurosummer this year (every year now, it seems), the pros of visiting Greece in the cooler off season have never been more evident. “Visiting off season is perfect for avoiding crowds and the heat,” says Rister of Original Travel. “Generally, Greece can be quite mild, even in winter, so it’s still pleasant to visit and be out and about exploring. Cultural sites are much quieter and you don’t have to book restaurants weeks in advance.” Rister also says that hotel rates massively drop at this time of year, outside of the peak summer travel months, so the off season is a chance to experience luxurious properties for a fraction of the cost. Beyond the weather and value-for-money factor, Kusak of Kusak & Co. says there’s a human element too: “In the off season you find a certain authenticity. With fewer people present, you can get a real connection with the local community—the pace is gentler for everyone.” To top it off, the off season is perhaps the best time for foodie travelers, given the bounty of the winter harvest. “The olive harvest runs from November into December, and some estates will welcome visitors to watch or take part,” Kusak explains. “Citrus season follows in the Peloponnese and Crete, when the orange and lemon groves are at their most vibrant." Of course, no rose is without its thorns: many establishments in Greece do close for the winter, and it’s not exactly prime time for beachgoers—so be sure to calibrate your expectations to cultural and culinary adventures. “It's not the peak season for swimming and boating, if guests have that as a priority,” says Durso of Scott Dunn. While there are locales where restaurants remain open year-round thanks to universities and locals (Athens, Corfu, and Crete among them) it depends where you are: “Many restaurants will also begin closing for the season, so I tend to recommend resorts with restaurants on property, so guests don't feel like they're missing out” if the small tavernas, cafés, and bakeries are shuttered until the spring. The cultural and culinary prowess of Greece in the off season First, the culture and history buffs will greatly appreciate Greece in the off season, Planksy says, because fewer people crowd the main tourist sites and the sun isn’t beating down on travelers as aggressively. Lines are shorter, and there’s more room to breathe in museums and at archaeological locations like the Acropolis or the Agora in Athens. Plus you’ll be able to relish the hike up to the Parthenon without melting in the heat. Of course don’t just waltz in anywhere without tickets or reservations—traveling in the off season still requires the usual due diligence as a traveler. You’ll just have less competition for tables at the best restaurants in Athens. “This time of year is also great for guests who are excited to interact more with locals in the small towns,” Durso says, “those who prefer a relaxed pace rather than enduring crowded tourist areas during high season.” Whether you go to romantic Nafplio in the Peloponnese with its neoclassical mansions or seaside Galaxidi with its cobblestoned alleys, locals will be pleasantly surprised to see out-of-towners passing through, happy for your business and company in the off-season. As Kusak puts it, the off season in Greece is for “someone who wants authenticity and a genuine connection to the place, rather than just boat days and beaches.” There’s no shame in wanting boat days and beaches, of course—we at Traveler love partying and seaside time when we go to Greece too. But just know that if that’s what you’re looking for, summer really is your best bet, Durso says, when all the restaurants and beach clubs are open. How to do it: practical tips When visiting Greece in the off season, one of the first things we need to talk about is the climate. “As the weather starts to shift, you get more wind and cooler evenings,” says Durso. “So it’s important to pack layers,” like lightweight sweaters, linen that you can wear on top of each other, a rain jacket, maybe a little bit of cashmere while you’re at it. Take it from me: Even in May of this year on Corfu, I found myself reaching for my denim jacket more than once, even on a beach day. The next thing to be mindful of is the country’s schedule, from the timetables for ferries to the opening hours of restaurants, tourist and archaeological sites, and even whole islands. “Ferry schedules are reduced in the off season and the weather is more likely to impact those journeys,” says Plansky. Don’t go to Greece in the off-season hoping for the typical island-hopping style vacation, because many of the smaller islands close between November to April. “So it’s better to explore the mainland of Greece and some of the bigger islands like Crete, Corfu, and Santorini during that time,” she says. And double check with your hotel if they’ll be open during your visit. Chances are that a hotel won’t accept your booking if they see that you’re in town when they’re not, but it never hurts to be sure. “It is worth planning around what is genuinely open rather than where you want to go on the map,” Kusak says. “This is where I lean on my team in Greece. They know which properties are running, which restaurants stay open through the winter, and where a January afternoon is best spent. It isn't information you can always find online, and it changes from year to year.” Are you, conveniently enough, hoping to spend a January afternoon in Greece? “A January afternoon in Athens is best spent on foot,” Kusak asserts. “I’d wander a few of the neighborhoods—Plaka, Monastiraki, Thisio, Kolonaki—just to get a feel for how the city lives, pausing at a small shop for a warm koulouri or a slice of spanakopita along the way. Then the Acropolis, which in the off-season is blissfully unhurried. With the crowds thinned, there's room to take it in properly.” Where (else) to go in Greece in the off season In the off season, while many places in some smaller islands and destinations may “shut down,” Greece does not close uniformly. Athens, the rest of the mainland, and many of the larger islands carry on much as usual. In addition to Athens, Corfu, Crete, Santorini, and Paros—as recommended by locals we admire and trust—our Top Travel Specialists also gave their own additional recommendations for where to go in Greece in the off season: Thessaloniki and the Peloponnese. Thessaloniki: Culinary heritage on the Thermaic Gulf Waterfront Thessaloniki is designated a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, with a dining scene informed by a long history as a crossroads of ancient and modern trade. Given its position in Northern Greece, Thessaloniki has played host to Greeks, Ottoman Turks, Sephardic Jews, Armenians, and Slavs for centuries, resulting in meals and dishes that pull influences from all over the continent. And because Thessaliniki is also the second largest city in Greece, it has more in common with Athens schedule-wise and stays open even after the summer is over. Kusak has two restaurant recommendations: “For something traditional, I suggest The Rouga. It’s a good place to share meze and a few Greek classics. For a quieter, more polished evening, there’s Olympos Naoussa inside the ON Residence, a Small Luxury Hotels of the World hotel. It sits in a restored heritage building overlooking the Thermaic Gulf, and suits a special occasion or a last-night-before-we-go-home dinner.” As for where to stay, Rister often books clients at The Modernist Thessaloniki set in a 1920s heritage building; The Excelsior, just a block away from the harbor; and Electra Palace Thessaloniki, a grande dame on Aristotelous Square. When it comes to cultural excursions, Rister recommends a walking tour of the city with a private guide—“Great for fans of Alexander the Great.” and a day trip to Vergina, home to the tomb of Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great’s father. Rister at Original Travel can help put these offerings together for those who are keen. The Peloponnese: Homeric outdoor adventure In lieu of the typical Greek islands vacay, a road trip that traces the coast of the rugged and mountainous Peloponnese peninsula could scratch that itch to be near some water, as long as you’re okay with the fact that it may be too cold to go in. Kusak recommends a few seaside towns in the Peloponnese: “On a rocky islet just off the coast, Monemvasia is a medieval town you reach almost by surprise, where you can wander the cobbled streets and stay in one of the restored stone houses,” she says. “And Pylos gathers around a waterfront square and an old natural harbor.
