It’s the way into the Costa Navarino resort area, with its beaches, golf, and resorts, though Pylos holds its own quiet history and lends itself to a slower coastal stay.” Kusak also recommends Nafplio for its proximity to Athens—under two hours apart by car—and the beautiful Venetian architecture in the area, souvenirs from when Venice held trading posts in Greece. Plansky also loves to send travelers to Nafplio: “It has a little bit of everything—history, culture, coastal beauty, plenty of food and wine. And there are some fantastic sites nearby including Mycenae, Epidavros, Ancient Corinth, and the Nemea wineries that are easy day trips.” Where to stay If you’re a fiend for a good hotel, Durso recommends Amanzoe, considered by Aman junkies to be one of the brand’s very best properties. “Plus it stays open through the second week of November, offering a luxurious option at sometimes less than half its peak-season rates,” Durso says. Conveniently it’s also close to villages like Nafplio and historic sites like Mycenae. “Another lovely property is Kinsterna in Monemvasia, a boutique hotel with fantastic farm-to-table cuisine,” Durso says. And for those seeking quiet, Rister suggests an easy-going stay in some of the most relaxing spa hotels in the Peloponnese for some true rest—Euphoria Retreat in Mystras and Manna Arcadia. The former is a wellness retreat located near epic Sparta and the UNESCO-listed Archaeological Site of Mystras, or castro (fortress), for those who like their relaxation with a side of historic adventure; the latter is surrounded by moody fir forests ideal for hiking, giving it the feel of a remote getaway. “They can be easily combined with a city break in Athens at any time of the year,” Rister says.

item.title: I Spent Four Days Touring Scotland’s Whisky Island—and It Was Better Than I Expected
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.15
My dad’s 60th birthday was coming up, and as an avid whisky drinker with a particularly sharp nose, his dream trip has always been to explore the coastline of Islay, a Scottish island famed worldwide for its smoky, peated single malt whiskies. I often travel solo and am fond of organized tours, so when I came across Rabbie’s four-day Islay and whisky tour—with pickup from Edinburgh, a selection of historic stops, a maximum group size of 16 people, and plenty of opportunities for drams—it sounded ideal for us both. Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, with a landscape of rugged beaches and peat bogs, and traveling through it usually involves many small logistics. I was thrilled to see that this tour handles all of the planning for you—including transportation, accommodations, attractions, and providing a local guide for the four-day trip. It starts at just $609 per adult without accommodations or distillery tours, or around $1,464 all-in, which seemed like a great deal. I was convinced, so I booked it! Our trip began with an evening in Edinburgh to recover from jet lag. The next morning, we made our way to the Edinburgh bus station to meet our driver and group. A 16-seat Mercedes mini coach pulled up, and we all piled in as our guide’s Celtic music played and we said goodbye to the city. Our first stop was the historic town of Falkirk, just 25 miles from Edinburgh, where we saw the iconic towering Kelpies sculptures and grabbed a coffee. I knew I was going to like our Glaswegian guide, Peter McShane, from the excitement in his voice as he told us about Scottish folklore. We then rode through the Lowlands and mountainous regions surrounding Loch Lomond and Trossachs National Park en route to the town of Oban, known as the “Gateway to the Isles.” There, we browsed local shops and grabbed some fresh seafood. Bellies full and a dram or two later at Oban Distillery, we hopped back on the coach and drove to Kennacraig to make our evening ferry to Islay. For two hours, we sailed along the glass-like Sound of Jura before the Paps of Jura mountains came into view, signaling that the island was just ahead. Arriving in Islay was like nothing I’d experienced before. At just 240 square miles, the island felt entirely remote yet surprisingly homey. We settled in for the evening in the town of Bowmore. We didn’t know what to expect when our itinerary said accommodations would be shared, but we were pleasantly surprised by the setup we were met with at Bowmore Distillery Cottages. There were four bedrooms, and my dad and I each had our own room, while two others from our group took over the other two rooms and shared the communal kitchen and living spaces with us. Our first full day on whisky island started with a short two-minute walk to the distillery that would kick off our tour: Bowmore Distillery. We learned about the distillery’s 240-year history on the island, which was a great starting point for the days ahead. Then came a tasting (straight from the cask!) in the cellar, and another tasting upstairs to end the tour, this time with whisky, chocolate, and views of the sea. Since Islay is a very small island with a population of a little over 3,000 people, it’s important to be flexible on these types of trips and just roll with the punches. Depending on the days of your tour, some distilleries may be closed or not open to full tours. Our itinerary said we’d be visiting Kilchoman on day one, but instead, we diverted to Ardnahoe for a lively tour and quick tasting before driving through the countryside to Bunnahabhain. With sweeping views of the clear blue waters, we explored the facilities and sampled four drams at Islay’s most remote distillery. While it's always great to meet new people and travel around with them, I appreciated that lunches and evenings were free for us to explore at leisure. After full days of sampling whiskies, it was a nice respite to just enjoy some quality time with my dad. That said, by day two, our group was buzzing as we became more comfortable with each other—and this second day was the big one for most of us as we took on the villages of Ardbeg, Lagavulin, and Laphroaig, each with their own distilleries. Though the island is small, the differences between the West Coast and Southern Coast became evident as we left Bowmore toward Ardbeg. Because it was a Saturday, our itinerary mentioned our visit to Ardbeg would not include a tour—but, as I said, roll with the punches. We did, in fact, get to see some of the facilities and end with a five-dram tasting. This experience was probably one of the most memorable moments of the trip for me—sitting around a table in the sunshine with people I’d just met, laughing, and sampling some of the finest whiskies in the world. We made a quick stop at Kildalton Church, home to an eighth-century cross and one of Scotland’s finest early Christian monuments, before continuing toward Port Ellen, a tiny town built around Loch Leòdamais, for a lunch break. Again, these parts of the tour are not organized, so if you have a restaurant or attraction in mind you want to visit, make an early reservation or chance your luck at walking in. At Lagavulin Distillery, our visit didn’t include a tour or tasting, but we chatted around the bar with our new friends and strolled down to the coast. In under five minutes, we made it to Laphroaig—our last whisky tasting of the trip. Here, we enjoyed an immersive tour of the peat kilns, stills, and warehouses before sampling a few more of their whiskies, our Glencairn glasses conveniently attached to lanyards around our necks. On day four, we had an early start and set sail again for a two-hour journey from Islay to Kennacraig. We treated ourselves to a full Scottish breakfast and explored the ferry, this time passing strangers-turned-friends. After an hour’s drive, we stopped in the castle town of Inveraray for lunch before making our way through the rugged Arrochar Alps to the “Rest and Be Thankful” mountain pass viewpoint. Our final stop was the quintessential village of Luss, where we, of course, found yet another distillery to visit. There was something heavy yet appreciative in the air during our last stop—we were sad it was our last day, but incredibly thankful for the new connections, laughs, and memories we’d made along the way. I’ve done Rabbie’s day tours in the past, but this one was particularly immersive because we were with the same people for the entirety of the trip—and we lucked out with our guide. All in all, this experience came at just the right time for my dad and me, and it was amazing learning more about his passions. According to him, a man with a collection of over 200 whiskies, “it was well worth the money.” How to book Rabbie’s Islay & the Whisky Coast tour Founded in Edinburgh in 1993, Rabbie’s specializes in small-group tours throughout Scotland, the UK, Ireland, and Europe. The four-day Islay & the Whisky Coast tour departs from Edinburgh and includes transportation, ferry crossings, entrance fees, and three nights in Bowmore (some distillery tours and tastings are available for an additional fee). You can book the tour on Rabbie's website, Viator, or GetYourGuide.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: To Avoid the Crowds on Crete, Hike and Ski in Early Spring
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’s improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning, year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city." Yet, 80 percent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience, because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity." Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favorite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favorite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains]—you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation, so spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here—not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favorite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern, it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous Restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages, because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs, and liver. We normally eat it at home—it’s not so much a restaurant dish—but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens—we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes—and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini, and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called dakos, a barley rusk with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in village Maza, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring, the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski, and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased, but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2:00 p.m., I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane, and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays, it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighborhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favorite open-air theater is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there, you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path—not for the faint-hearted—to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 13 Best Hotels in Key West, From Historic Inns to Private Islands
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.93
Long known for its free-spirited vibe and its identity as the iconoclastic “Conch Republic,” Key West welcomes you to come as you are, whether that means strolling past street-roaming roosters in your finest cowboy hat and Daisy Dukes, joining the revelers on Duval Street à la Mardi Gras, enjoying family time on the beach, or just staying put around your hotel pool “wasting away again in Margaritaville.” (Jimmy Buffett actually wrote the final verses of the song circa 1977 while stuck in traffic on the Seven Mile Bridge heading back to the Florida Keys, then debuted it on Duval Street shortly thereafter.) It’s definitely a place that caters to hedonistic tendencies at land’s end, especially during Fantasy Fest and other wild celebrations throughout the year, but it’s equally suited to soaking up the sun and embracing an IDGAF attitude. Beneath the more recent commercialization of Key West lies a deeper charm, reflected in its eclectic mix of resorts. The most sought-after stays are in Old Town, which occupies the island’s western edge, touching both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Old Town is remarkably walkable, with fabulous restaurants, historic sites, and kitschy dive bars never more than a short stroll away. True, there are plenty of places to stay in New Town, often at lower rates. But why rely on an hourly shuttle to Old Town or stare at a chain mall parking lot from your room when so much of the fun of Key West is crawling back to your hotel through picturesque neighborhoods and lush gardens after a night of debauchery? There’s also something to be said for actually sleeping in one of the historic cottages and buildings that speak to Key West's earlier days, recalling the words of Hemingway and lyrics of Buffett. Whether you’re after a romantic retreat, a fun weekend with your besties, a gay nudist escape, or a laid-back family vacation, you’ll find it among our picks for the best hotels in Key West. Explore our complete Key West travel guide, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Key West - The Best Restaurants in Key West - The Best Beaches in the Florida Keys How we choose the best hotels in Key West Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: At Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, Exploring Eastern Indonesia by Boat and Board
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.74
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell, and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach—good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels—a few hundred miles apart—front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track, and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night, I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance; storytelling; and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew, and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the fire pit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders—and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile—on the harbor, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: Come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free, go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land, and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “selamat datang" (meaning welcome) or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution. One is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year, there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling gasoline in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones, and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese—a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade—resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles and the ti’i langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs, and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats. I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel and fast-float in the choppy current to spy on triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colors of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls, and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags, and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene. “No drugs, no nightclubs," as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet." Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote." “Here you feel you can give back. Life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s Bo’a Vida resort, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Where to stay Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), the 21-villa Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travelers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex, and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. Bo'a Vida owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs the café Indika in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5:30 p.m., when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Nat and Matt Thistlewaite of Rote Island Huts came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channeled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise, and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. At Sardine Beach Rote, they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, paneled walls, and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of Mick’s Place Rote, three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens, and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. There's a one-week stay minimum, and the lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built 81 Palms and its six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas, and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded. This story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: How to Make the Most of the Venice Film Festival, According to a Critic Who Goes Every Year
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.68
When one thinks of the Venice Film Festival, a few indelible, almost impossibly exotic images spring to mind. The most recent may be Lady Gaga with her legs coyly crossed over the side of a water taxi as she announced her arrival to town for the premiere of A Star Is Born. (Or, I suppose, Harry Styles maybe spitting on his Don’t Worry Darling co-star Chris Pine.) But there has been a wealth of such moments for many decades: Venice is the oldest event of its kind, first held in 1932 and running near continuously since then—minus a few gaps during the Second World War and during some severe political strife that rocked Italy in the 1970s. The festival’s origins are, well, not great: it was founded by fascists loyal to Mussolini and, eventually, Axis powers. But in the many decades since, the festival has evolved into one of the so-called “Big Three” festivals of Europe, alongside winter’s Berlin Film Festival and the mid-spring glitz and madness of Cannes. It is a premier showcase for art-house international fare and, on a good year, glossy Oscar bait sent across the Atlantic by American studios debuting their latest prestige fare. Compared to Cannes, Venice is more relaxed—its screening schedule not so densely packed, its staff not quite as snooty, its dress codes more lax. The climate may often be punishing—high temperatures in baking sun, 100% humidity, mosquitoes suddenly filling the air at dusk—but Venice is nonetheless regarded by many people on the festival circuit as the jewel in the crown, one of high programming quality and easy glamour. Lido v. San Marco: The Eternal War It’s not hard to be glamorous when your event is held in one of the world’s most beautiful cities, that floating tangle of red buildings and snaking canals. Well, that’s where a lot of the nighttime events are, anyway. All of the screenings, meanwhile, are held on the Lido, a barrier island dotted with low-key beach clubs (and one decidedly high-key one, at the ritzy Excelsior Hotel, where cabanas can go for hundreds of Euros per day). A small town center with a few restaurants and lots of retirees is home to the festival headquarters. Some people—industry professionals, veteran critics, publicists, and awards strategists—are near-religiously committed to staying on the Lido, where you can walk (or bike, or e-scooter) to screenings without having to deal with the vaporetti, the lurching water buses that ferry people around Venice’s many islands. Me, I figure that if I’m going to be in Venice, I want to be in actual Venice. In the years that I’ve been going to the festival (as the chief critic of Vanity Fair until last year), I’ve always stayed on San Marco island, the center of the city’s tourism industry and the host of its most iconic images: the eponymous Piazza with its tall brick tower and ornate palace, the Bridge of Sighs, that cute gondolier you keep seeing as he poles his boat under the Rialto Bridge. Traveling between San Marco and the Lido is one of the more grumbled-about aspects of the festival, though I’ve mostly found it easy enough over the years. One simply hops on the number 20 vaporetto at San Zaccaria (just a tiny bit south and east of Piazza San Marco) and, maybe 20 minutes later, the boat drops you off on the festival grounds. Lines can get long if you don’t time things right—a crush of people all trying to make the same movie in 45 minutes can be a harrowing mess—but if you give yourself a wider berth, the boats are calm and manageable and then you can while away your extra time on the Lido by having a bite at one of the festival’s snack bars or a drink on the charming terrace of the old-school Albergo Quattro Fontane, right across the street. (Hopefully in the shade; again, that sun is brutal.) Carb City Staying on San Marco can be way less expensive, due to the abundance of hotels and rental apartments, and it affords you far more opportunities to eat not only well but also surprisingly diversely. Seafood, pasta, and pizza still dominate most menus, but there are other kinds of cuisines to be found, like Chinese and Indian and North African—I even had a complex vegan tasting menu at the highly rated Bistro de Venise, located in a tiny alleyway off of an only slightly less narrow street that leads pilgrims on the well-trod path between the Rialto and Piazza San Marco. If one is busy covering the festival, one may not always have time for a long sit-down meal, preferring instead to grab a few cicchetti (little tapas-like crostinis that are a staple of Venetian cuisine) or a sandwich. The best place that I’ve found to do the latter is L’ Bacaro de’ Bischeri, tucked into one of the market stalls right across from the Rialto, on the island of San Polo. The most popular item on the large menu seems to be the Don’t Tell William, two massive squares of focaccia with a generous heaping of stracciatella, mortadella, and pistachios piled in between. Eat it on the street outside, or do what I did and take it back to your little garret apartment in Campo San Luca (right near the H&M!) so no one will see you make a mess. But if you do want to sit down, one classic option is Al Covo, just to the east of San Zaccaria, in a slightly quieter neighborhood. It’s a Michelin-recommended, seafood-heavy favorite among festivalgoers looking for a more elevated but affordable meal than they might get on the Lido. I know several journalists who make a point of going there every year, and have been doing so for decades. If you want something fancier, that’s both old and new, the Four Seasons has just reopened the iconic Hotel Danieli after a years-long remodel, and you can enjoy a posh lunch or dinner on the well-shaded fifth-floor terrace overlooking the lagoon. Just be careful that when you order the pinot grigio, the waiter knows you don’t mean the glass that costs €80. I made that unfortunately delicious mistake this year, on a placid afternoon when I’d had enough movies for the day. But again, most people attending the film festival have little time for such a luxury. It’s mostly foraging for food between screenings and writing assignments, scarfing down that same sandwich over and over again, or darting back to your apartment to eat the groceries you bought at Supermercato Punto, a nearly American-sized market that also has a lovely little cocktail bar off to one side. (Where I stopped before my big shop to enjoy my go-to Venice drink, a Cynar spritz, on the tiny balcony perched over a canal.) Where to Party If You Can Get In, or If You Can’t There is certainly elegant fun to be had, though, if you knock on the right doors. (Or email the right publicists.) American studios often hold pre-premiere parties in the garden of the Excelsior, steps away from the Pala Grande, where celebrities walk the red carpet and scores of onlookers—from matinee idol-crazed teens to elderly looky-loos—gather to gawp and take pictures. This year, I journeyed to the Excelsior garden to brush shoulders with Oscar-winning filmmaker Martin McDonagh, who has followed up his lauded film The Banshees of Inisherin with a dark comedy about CIA spooks called Wild Horse Nine. His life partner, the actor and writer Phoebe Waller-Bridge of Fleabag fame, was with him, as were several members of his cast, including Steve Buscemi, who looked perhaps a little perplexed to be there among the Euro swells and various influencer-type hangers-on. Those afternoon events are brief amuse-bouches compared to what comes later in the evening, when Italian and French fashion houses flex their resources and throw exclusive dinners or parties at palazzos around the city, or at revered Grand Canal-side hotels like the Gritti Palace and the St. Regis. At the former, two friends convinced hotel security to let me into the tail end of a dinner for Cartier, where I sat a stone’s throw from a pleased-looking Orlando Bloom in the hotel’s lavishly appointed bar and chatted with Kate Mara about the wild, weird Bucking Fastard, the Werner Herzog movie that she and her sister, Rooney, debuted at the festival. At the St. Regis, on another night, I sat one couch over from Robert Pattinson, who seemed relaxed and no doubt happy with the rave reviews for his award-worthy performance in A24’s big Venice premiere Primetime, in which Pattinson plays To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen. The party was jam-packed and the bar lines were long, but one barely minds such things when one has a view of the canal and of Edward Cullen himself, dapper in a white dinner jacket. That said, Venice is not quite the party-hopping, champagne-guzzling bacchanal that Cannes tends to devolve into. It’s a more restrained affair, partly because the city of Venice shuts down pretty early—unless, of course, a local points you in the direction of the good late-night spots. At least one of those places, one that’s a staple of many attendees’ film festival experience, is easy to find on your own: Ai Do Leoni, a compact and jovial bar right off of Piazza San Marco that stays open until 1:30, friends and potential lovers and a few awkward critics spilling out into the square (or, near the square) to talk and carouse and flirt while the rest of the city goes to sleep. You’ll be hungover on a boat the next day, but hey, you’re still in Venice.

item.title: 23 Best Airbnbs in Florida for Disney World Trips, Beach Getaways, and City Excursions
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.35
From the Gulf Coast to the Atlantic and all of the beautiful landscapes in between, Florida is a natural playground for travelers of all interests. I’ve called the Sunshine State home for more than 25 years, and I make time for a staycation along these fun-filled shores every chance I get. Whether I’m in the mood to stay in a tropical cottage in the Florida Keys; go someplace quiet along one of the state’s freshwater lakes; or plan an urban getaway in Tampa, Orlando, or Miami, the wide range of Airbnbs and vacation rentals in this state means there’s always a stylish place to bed down. Below, find some of the most unique, stylish, and exciting stays across the Florida Keys, Orlando, Tampa, Naples, and the Panhandle, with options for every type of traveler. For families, enjoy spacious homes with pools near theme parks; for couples, charming coastal cottages and hideaways; and for groups, large, entertainment-packed villas designed for fun. With warm weather year-round and endless activities from sunrise to sunset, you can rest assured these Florida vacation rentals are perfect for exploring, relaxing, and adventuring, all under one roof. We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. Our top picks: - For a girls getaway: Adorable townhouse on Anna Maria Island - For a lakeside stay: Lovely lakeside cottage near Gainesville - For city-slicking: Vibrant, artsy one-bedroom - For Disney-goers: Four-bedroom villa near Orlando’s best theme parks FAQ: What are the best areas in Florida to book an Airbnb? The state’s gorgeous beaches—from those in the Florida Keys and West Palm Beach to 30A in the panhandle—are always a hit with vacationers. But don’t sleep on a city escape here, either; in cities like Tampa (my town), Jacksonville, Miami, and Orlando, there's plenty to do and see for all ages. While beach lovers might prioritize proximity to sand in Destin, Key West, or Clearwater, theme park enthusiasts will want easy access to Tampa or Orlando’s attractions. If you have specific activities or restaurants in mind, look beyond the Airbnb photos and check the map view to see what's nearby before booking. Depending on your travel needs, search the reviews for more information about noise levels, parking, and walkability, and consider whether the property provides amenities that complement your trip, such as beach gear, bicycles, or a fully equipped kitchen for longer stays. What is the average cost of an Airbnb in Florida? Rates for individual rentals in Florida depend heavily on the time of year you're visiting and the specific location you're headed to. If you're planning a trip for high season (winter or summer), expect rates to be higher than usual. Similarly, if you're headed to a popular location like South Beach in Miami or 30A, many vacation rentals will feature steeper rates. In general, Florida rentals start from around $250 a night, but it’s possible to find less expensive stays, too, if you're flexible with location and timing. How should you prepare for your trip to Florida? Before heading on your trip to Florida, you can do a few things to prepare. While in general you'll want to pack warm-weather clothes like shorts, bathing suits, and sun hats, it's a good idea to check the weather before your trip to see if you'll need anything specific (like a rain jacket). Also, depending on where you're headed and what activities are on your roster, you may want to arrange transportation, like car rentals or airport transfers, ahead of time. For theme-park visitors, book your tickets in advance so you can avoid any confusion or difficulty day-of. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Madison Flager and Paris Wilson.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: Fall in Santorini Through the Eyes of Winemaker Michael Kouloglou
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.34
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards. On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing. He’s currently settled in Monolithos, a quiet seaside village in the east—but has historically lived all over Santorini, which has offered him great insight into the rhythm of the island. “Each village has its own unique character,” he says, “far beyond the image [of Santorini] that most visitors see.” Here, the longtime Santorini local shares why autumn is his favorite time of year—and all the treasures of the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins. What do you love most about being there during the off-season? Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know. By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time, there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin. Friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? During autumn, you'll still find some travelers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini. They enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next. By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that the last boat has sailed. From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals. Conversations become longer, people have time for each other again, and everyday life feels calmer. I think that's the Santorini most visitors never get the chance to experience. What’s notable about the locals in Santorini? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? One thing that has always impressed me about the locals is how deeply everyday life is connected to the Orthodox Church and its traditions. Almost every small chapel on the island has its own patron saint, and every saint's feast day is celebrated with a panigiri, a traditional village festival. During the summer, many of these celebrations continue late into the night with traditional music, dancing, and plenty of local wine. What I also find fascinating is that many of the locals still organize their year around the feast days of the saints. They won't say, "I'll start pruning in late November." They'll say, "I'll start after Saint Philip's Day and I have to finish before Saint Alexius's Day." That's how they measure time. It's a tradition that has been passed down from generation to generation, and it's still very much alive today. Where would we find you eating during this time? During the off-season, you will most likely find me at Pentozali, a traditional taverna that serves authentic mezze from both Santorini and Crete. I absolutely love it for its relaxed atmosphere, its genuine food, and its people. What I appreciate most during this time of year is that it becomes a gathering spot almost exclusively for locals. It is very common for me to run into someone who has just finished a hard day's work in the vineyards. We’ll sit down together for a glass of wine and a little chat, with absolutely no rushing around. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? If you are lucky and the spring timing is right, the dish to order is definitely an omelette with wild asparagus. It’s a rare treat because you can't just find it every day; it completely depends on whether someone woke up early in the morning and gathered the wild asparagus fresh from the countryside. Another staple that is almost always on the table is our traditional Santorini fava topped with sautéed onions. It is incredibly simple, but when cooked properly, you truly don't need anything more. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? As the summer venues close, the life of the island doesn't disappear; it just shifts to the places where people actually live year-round. Areas like Karterados and Messaria become the real hubs. They are central points on the island that stay busy and full of life all year. The local closing parties of fall range from wild gatherings by the beach bars to more laid-back evenings in traditional cafés and small local hangouts. Later, in the winter, as people begin gathering more at homes, these central areas remain the heart of our social life. But if you want to talk about a completely hidden side of Santorini that comes alive in a very quiet, spiritual way, it’s the Askitaria. These are old stone monk lodgings perched right on the edge of the cliff on the mountain between Perissa and Kamari. In the spring, you will find many locals sitting there for hours, doing nothing in particular but gazing out at the endless blue, the passing ships, and distant islands like Anafi, Ios, and Anydro. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Autumn and winter are much warmer and sunnier than most people expect. They bring a rare, beautiful peace. For us winemakers, even the rain is a blessing, not bad weather. It’s a relief to see the vines finally get a drink after months of summer drought. The main disadvantage—if you can call it that—is the unpredictability. March, for instance, is a strange and stubborn month with strong winds, cold snaps, and constant weather shifts. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect off-season Saturday starts slowly, without checking my watch—perhaps walking through the narrow paths of the caldera in Fira or Oia. Later, I would meet up with friends. There is always an excuse for an impromptu barbecue, either with meat or, even better, fresh seafood; almost every group of friends here has at least one good fisherman. We would share a coffee or wine, talk without any rush, and if we are lucky, someone might randomly pick up a lute, a tsampouna, or a violin. No big plans or appointments needed, just letting the night unfold naturally. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? My favorite activities are tied to the water. The Aegean is ideal for kitesurfing due to its consistent winds, and as paradoxical as it may sound, specific weather systems often generate great surf here during the winter. We have a small but tight-knit community of surfers on the island, and when the conditions are right, we all head out into the water. Even though the water is still cold, the feeling is incredible. Sometimes you might even catch people paddleboarding inside the Caldera with absolutely no sea traffic, no cruise ships or catamarans, just you traveling parallel to the old quarries and rusty iron piers that hold the island’s history. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Author Anastasia Miari on Corfu's thriving food scene and why spring is the best time to savour the isle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.32
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to food writer and author Anastasia Miari. Whenever I’m feeling disconnected from myself or from Greece—the place my mother’s family is from and whose traditions I grew up with—I muster up the energy to make a comforting Greek meal. But, whether it’s my yia yia’s old-school-style avgolemono soup, my mom’s traditional pastitsio, or my thea’s Americanized spanakopita, the recipe is rarely ever already written down. As with so many other cultures’ time-tested family dishes, they’re usually passed on by doing; surmising how many box grater’s-worth of tomatoes you'll need or eyeballing the number of glugs of olive oil to add. Enter Anastasia Miari, a food writer and author who has spent the better part of a decade traveling all over the Mediterranean to document not only Greek recipes but create an extensive, photographic encyclopedia of the many octo- and septuagenarians (and their often-remote villages) who passed those very dishes—and their way of life—to younger generations. Nowadays, when I want to try a new or lighter Greek dish than the handful of rib-sticking ones I know, I crack open my stained copy of Yia Yia, Miari’s first cookbook. Better yet, when I want to explore the cuisine of the broader region—Moroccan tajin, Turkish breakfast, Sicilian pasta—there’s now also her newer iteration, Mediterranea. To say Anastasia is an expert in all things Greek would be an understatement—she was born and raised on the Ionian island of Corfu in Greece’s northwest, and is currently renovating a historic cottage on the Cycladic island of Tinos to enjoy with her family in the summers (and filming a web series about it all). Here, the British-Greek Corfiot shares her guide to the Italian-leaning island’s Venetian traditions, natural splendor, and seasonal dishes—all of which are best experienced in the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? I would say May, springtime. Because of all this rain that we get then, the island is fully in bloom in May—it's stunning. It's like being in a Disney movie here. What do you love most about being there during this season? If you have in mind to do the Corfu Trail, which is a hiking trail that runs all the way from the south of the island to the north of the island, the month of May is a particularly incredible month to come in, because you tend to have the best weather, but it's also not incredibly hot. You're still able to hike, especially in the morning and evening hours. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? Corfu is really interesting, because it doesn't have this sort of off-season, on-season vibe as much as the Cycladic Islands do. What I mean by that is the island doesn't shut down when it isn't summertime. We have a university, and we have a music school on the island, and because it is very cosmopolitan, and because it's so big, we tend to retain our residents. People don't tend to move to Athens or to Saloniki as much as they might in more remote Cycladic islands. So, of course, there are a few travelers, but it's not as many as you'll find in July and August. And I think it's usually people who love to hike and people who like to be in nature, so it's a different kind of traveler. What’s notable about the locals? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What's notable about the locals in Corfu is that, supposedly, we're the craziest in all of Greece? Other Greeks tend to say that Cretans and the Corfiots are the crazies of the nation. But I do think we are quite distinct in Corfu, because we have this incredible heritage that comes from Italy, and we love to align ourselves with the Italians. The Venetians came and colonized 500 years ago, and many vestiges of our Venetian past are still visible, not just in the architecture and in our food. Where would we find you eating? The places that eat in the summer tend to also be open in the winter, and I think that's great because you are always able to rub shoulders with local clientele. One of my favorite places to eat is Marina's Tavern in Corfu Town, because they do all of the classic yia yia, home-cooked dishes in a really great style. So I love eating a pastitsada or a stifado at Marina's, and all of the traditional home-cooked dishes that they serve. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? The dish to order is tsigarelia, which are like wild greens that you find at that time of year. And here in Greece, we sauté them with lots of spices. Again, this is a sort of vestige of the Venetians, and [a result of] our being put on the spice trail by the Venetians. So it includes lots of spices like cinnamon, cloves, and cayenne pepper. So cigarella, that's a great dish to have. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? In the off-season, I think Corfu Town is the place to be because even everyone else from the rest of the [surrounding] island tends to sort of congregate in Corfu Town. It’s really popping off, especially because of the universities there. There's a high concentration of people hanging out in town, it's very much alive. Any coffee shop you go into will be full of people. Again, Corfu isn't one of those sort of Disneyland islands that shuts down in the winter and opens up this sort of like fake display of life in the summer. It's very much alive all year round. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Corfu is one of the wettest islands in Greece, so if you try and come in May, you’ll have the occasional rain shower. But generally, it's just a very pleasant temperature and really great to experience the best of the island, which is its nature. September or October can be the trickiest months. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? It's fantastic to go into the mountains and visit mountain villages on weekends, because I think much of the coastline has been marred by mass tourism. The real secret and beauty of this island is actually inland, in the mountains. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? It absolutely has to be hiking. And I think the most incredible way to live and experience this island is by doing the 112-mile Corfu Trail. You don't have to do the whole of it, of course. You could just pick one part of the whole trail because it takes like seven days to hike it in full. It took me a bit longer, but you can pick a section of the trail and do just that. It's unmissable, really. Where to stay: Snugly in a pine-studded cleft beneath Mount Pantokrator, the island's tallest mountain, The Merchant's House has six guestrooms carved out of the stunningly renovated stone-walled shell of a 14th-century Venetian building. High ceiling rooms with chunky stone walls are far from medieval; however, there are Coco-Mat mattresses and large balconies with spectacular views over to the Albanian coast opposite. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Ready for a Euro Fall? Travel Experts Weigh In on the Best Destinations for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.31
Lower the beach club umbrellas and check on Dua Lipa: Euro summer is coming to an end. Maybe you, like Dua, went all in, losing track of days as you plunged in and out of the Mediterranean Sea. Or perhaps you didn’t get a chance to partake in Europe’s sunniest season, and the last few months have involved lots of envious scrolls on Instagram. Whether you still have room for more, or are making up for lost time, hold on to that last bit of PTO, because we’re entering what’s arguably an even more rewarding travel moment. Fall in Europe brings with it brisk temperatures that make sightseeing an utter joy, thinner crowds that leave room for locals, and an opportunity to experience cities in their most authentic light. You might find yourself falling in love with the version of Vienna that’s settling down after the tourist rush, or chasing new destinations entirely, whether that’s Denmark’s North Zealand coast or Italy’s “green heart” of Umbria. “I’m seeing people looking far more off the beaten path this season,” says Kimberly Davis of Trouvaille Travel. “Even if they want to travel to major European cities, it’s places like Copenhagen rather than the typical London, Paris, or Rome.” To help you plan your autumnal sojourn, we gathered expert-suggested itineraries, from the food haven that is the Basque Country to the moody Irish countryside. Below, the seven best places to travel to in Europe this fall. Copenhagen and the Danish Riviera, Denmark “Copenhagen just makes sense to me in the fall,” says Christine Andraus of Partenza Travel. “The food, the bakeries, candles everywhere, beautiful design, people actually embracing being cozy instead of trying to pretend it’s still summer.” Andraus is right: There’s no better place to embrace hygge than Denmark’s capital, where afternoons might look like strolling through golden-hued Assistens Cemetery or bundling up in a fisherman’s sweater at a harborside food hall like Reffen or Broens. Davis says she’s seeing clients opt for more design-forward hotels—think Hotel Sanders instead of Hotel D’Angleterre—to better lean into the city’s artsy edge. For a more comprehensive trip, Andraus suggests adding a couple of nights in North Zealand, otherwise known as the Danish Riviera, where historic palaces like Shakespeare-famous Kronborg Castle collide with vast forests and wild coastlines—plus, of course, the seaside stunner that is the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art. Where to stay in Copenhagen and the Danish Riviera: Vienna, Austria Things are changing in Vienna, the old-world city Nadine Fedorenko at Fora Travel cites as a top destination this fall. For the past few years, the capital has been welcoming a new crop of contemporary museums and galleries, restaurants moving beyond the farm-to-fork template, and a few luxury hotels, including a Mandarin Oriental and Rosewood. While Viennese gardens are lovely to stroll around any time of year, there’s added romance with a little chill in the air. This is the ideal time to visit vineyards just outside the city limits for glasses of biodynamic wine, house a schnitzel at an old-fashioned café, or catch a screening of The Third Man at the cozy Burg Kino movie theater. And while the city might be embracing change, Fedorenko points out that its cultural and artistic history forever looms: “Hotel Sacher turned 150 this year, the Albertina Museum turned 250, and even Mozart celebrated a big birthday [his 270th]!” Where to stay in Vienna: San Sebastian, Spain For travelers intent on planning their trips around food, there’s no better time to visit San Sebastian, a city with one of the highest numbers of Michelin-starred restaurants per square mile and a rich bar culture. In the fall, temperatures hover comfortably in the 60s, and quick spurts of rain lend the city an atmospheric mist. “San Sebastian in October gives you pintxos, the coast, Rioja nearby, and temperatures where you actually want to walk around all day,” Andraus says. This fall also marks the 50th anniversary of New Basque Cuisine—it’s being celebrated at San Sebastián Gastronomika (October 5–7), which will host the legendary chefs who pioneered avant-garde Basque cooking in the ‘70s as they engage attendees in masterclasses and tastings. As for where to stay, Andraus points travelers to Hotel Maria Cristina if you want to be right in town, or Akelarre for its world-renowned restaurant. Where to stay in San Sebastian: Midland Region, Ireland If you’re into the occult, there’s a certain draw to fall in the Irish countryside, where Samhain, the earliest version of Halloween, was first celebrated. Serious spooksters might visit the sacred sites of County Meath, including the ancient Hill of Ward and Hill of Tara, where ancient Celts first lit fires over 2,000 years ago to scare off spirits, or stick around for the holiday’s biggest celebration, the annual Púca Festival (October 29–November 1). Perhaps carrying a copy of Bram Stoker’s Dracula in your pocket while taking in the moody landscapes is more your vibe: “Ireland is one of those places where a little bit of weather almost makes the trip better,” Andraus says. “Give me a gorgeous country house, boots, a long walk, a fire, a great dinner, and maybe a little rain, and I’ll be very happy.” She recommends checking in at Ballyfin Demesne for a romantic, old-school stay, as well as combining the countryside with a few days exploring the island’s remote western region, from the counties of Clare and Mayo to the Connemara Coast, where you’ll encounter dramatic limestone formations and glacial lakes. Where to stay in the Midland and western region: Paris, France There’s something to be said about traveling to a familiar favorite in the off-season. When you visit Paris in the fall, you’ll be treated to temperatures that sit between the mid-50s and low-60s, shorter museum lines, and a few more vacant pistachio-green chairs at your favorite public parks. Known as the “rentreé,” the French version of back to school, this is when residents return to the city after their summer holidays, and everything comes alive again, from local shops to museum exhibits—including recent favorites like “Auguste Bartholdi and Mary Cassatt" at the Musée d’Orsay and “Cézanne and Us” at the Grand Palais. “Paris is always a hit, especially now with Celine Dion singing there this season,” Fedorenko says, referencing the star’s residency at the Paris La Défense Arena (running until October 17). There’s no shortage of excellent hotels to stay in either—like the affordable Hotel Rochechouart, which starts at around $300 per night—but for a trip you’ll simply never forget, consider renting an apartment with a view of the Eiffel Tower. Where to stay in Paris: The Dolomites, Italy “Everyone thinks of the Dolomites for skiing or summer hiking, but fall there is spectacular,” Andraus says. “The larches turn this crazy golden color, the air is crisp, the summer crowds are gone, and you can still spend your days outside before coming back to an amazing spa and a long dinner.” Be sure to plan your trip around mid-to-late October, when autumnal foliage is at its peak, and hit hiking trails that come alive with color, like the Croda da Lago Circuit and its reflective alpine lake, Lago di Federa. Or, visit the famous emerald-green waters of Lago di Braies when it’s not overrun with summer crowds. When it comes to where to stay, there’s an abundance of spa-forward hotels specializing in hydrotherapy and treatments that take inspiration from the surrounding nature. “I love Hotel Hubertus here—it’s dramatic and incredibly beautiful, but still has that cozy Alpine feeling,” Andraus says. “This is one I recommend to clients who want nature and wellness but still want a real five-star experience.” Where to stay in the Dolomites: Umbria, Italy Andraus believes Italy’s “green heart” is finally having its moment. Umbria, the underrated, landlocked region in central Italy, is famous for its lush landscapes, medieval palaces, and rustic trattorias. “I plan so much Italy, and I’m definitely seeing more clients who have either already done Tuscany or just want something a little quieter and less ‘on the circuit,’” she says. “Fall is when Umbria really shines—truffles, wine, olive harvests, tiny medieval towns, fireplaces, and amazing food.” Spend your days visiting museums, from the National Gallery of Umbria to the contemporary Fondazione Burri; visit the famous basilica in Assisi; or hike in the National Park of Montecucco. The region has also seen a growing interest in estates-turned-hotels: “Castello di Reschio is the dream here,” Andraus says. “It’s obviously a splurge, but it’s one of those rare hotels where I could happily send someone for four nights and almost tell them not to make plans.” Where to stay in Umbria:

item.title: How a Homecoming to Jamaica Helped Author Marlon James Write 'The Disappearers'
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.31
This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books. In this installment, Booker Prize-winning author Marlon James describes returning to his hometown of Kingston to write his new novel The Disappearers. In it, a group of queer men gathered to rehearse a play experience an anti-gay hate crime, and the story follows the survivors as they navigate the 1980s and ’90s in Jamaica. The riotous 640-page door stopper grapples with homophobia then and now, the lingering specter of colonialism, the tumult of the AIDS crisis, and frameworks of power that demand dominance or submission. To develop the Booker Prize-nominated book, James conducted research in Jamaica to better understand a queer history and heritage he had refused before coming out. Below, he describes how his travels across the Caribbean nation shaped his most personal work to date. “I went to Kingston in 2023 and 2024 to do research for The Disappearers. For my books, I like to interview dozens of people, especially when I'm writing about something I don't know a lot about. I grew up in Jamaica in the 1980s, but I didn’t experience queer life there—I was in the church, praying away the gay. So I looked into those years, but also from the early 2000s all the way back to the 1940s. I get curious about my characters’ lives before the novel even begins. Most of what I uncover in research never makes it directly into the book, but I just need to know for myself. To meet Jamaicans who could share their experiences in those eras, I spoke to local queer friends, and word just got around that I was looking. Because it’s a novel and not a documentary, a lot of people wanted to talk to me. They were very forthcoming about their lives. I even spoke to Jamaicans in New Orleans, Toronto, and Montreal who helped fill in the blanks, recalling what I never knew about Jamaica. For example, given the country’s reputation as homophobic, I was shocked that, at one point, there were five gay bars in Kingston at the same time. They had wonderful names like Fanny Hill. There was Marshall’s—and then another Marshall’s because the co-owners had a falling out and they both refused to give up the name. There was The Closet, but then the people there also had a falling out, so some of them went to form their own club The Interim Closet. And there was Andante. Andante was a jazz bar, but everybody knew that by 9 p.m. the drag queens would perform. Celebrities and the brother of the prime minister would go to see the shows. But by the late ’80s and ’90s they were all gone. With the AIDS crisis, homophobia really exploded in Jamaica. As a religious country, we believe what preachers tell us, and they said AIDS was God’s punishment. The gay nightlife went underground, there were still parties, but the bars and clubs never lasted very long. Talking to the older gays, I learned they’re just trying to get back to where Jamaica already was in 1972. I wanted to interview this guy who I think is 90, which would make him the oldest gay in Jamaica right now. He owns this artists’ retreat called Mountambrin, about an hour from Montego Bay. He started it as a hotel primarily for queer people, but he opened it up because he needed more guests and money. It’s still around and it’s for everyone, but you walk in and he has a lot of phallic art and statues of naked men, as one does. Gays are actually staying in Jamaica, which tells me there’s now a sort of hopefulness. In the past so many queer and trans people had to leave just to survive. With the kids, I find there’s more ease. I visited my alma mater the University of the West Indies and talked to their queer students’ association, which I was shocked existed. I started to give them my whole “it gets better” speech, and they were like, “We don’t want to hear that shit. Do you know Beyoncé?” I loved it. They reserve the right to be 19, to have their crisis be “Beyoncé or Rihanna?” and not “will I be shot today?” One of the guys I interviewed for The Disappearers showed up in pink hair extensions and a pink jumpsuit. I asked, “Where are you going dressed like this?” and he replied, “I just got off the bus.” All right, girl. But I don’t want to paint too rosy a picture. I also spoke to lesbians who said men threaten to rape them every week. Shit’s still going on. We have the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays [now Equality for All] for a reason—it’s an uphill battle. To live in Jamaica is to confront history, which is all around you. But also it's hard tracking down that history. I've been trying for years to find just one piece of footage showing a drag ball in Jamaica. It has to exist. I haven't given up. But I get it because part of how past generations tried to stay safe was by destroying the evidence—actually, maybe the guy who owns Mountambrin has a massive trove. The Disappearers is loosely based on a gay bashing that I knew happened in the late ’80s, but I didn’t have material proof. I kept asking Jamaicans if they remembered it, until finally someone in my interviews corroborated my memory of it. Again, I just needed to know for myself. So my characters are fictional—composites of people I’ve met or heard of and whatever’s in my imagination—but some of them could have existed. There are Jamaicans who will read The Disappearers and recognize these characters, maybe even know people just like them. This is the most personal book I’ve written. I do want it to serve as a record. That’s what fiction can do: fill in the blanks that history can’t or doesn’t want to. History books, to an extent, are only the story of famous people and politicians. You don’t always see how regular people get through their lives, how extraordinary ordinary people are. This is the first time I traveled specifically for a book project, but some travels have inspired other stories. Traveling naturally makes me more curious. To feel like I’m really experiencing a place, the first thing I do is unpack my bags completely, everywhere I go. It makes me feel less like a tourist, I guess. When I settle in, I find that I’m more prepared to take a country on its own terms.” —As told to Matt Ortile

item.title: 11 National Parks That Are Even More Beautiful in the Fall
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.26
I’ve traveled far and wide through America’s national parks, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some landscapes are simply better with a little fall color. Come September and October, sweeping valleys turn gold, forests flare in riots of red and pops of orange, and high country trails welcome that crisp, exhilarating drop in temperature that makes you want to keep trekking a little farther. Even parks we know and love in summer feel completely transformed: the sunsets shine differently, wildlife activity changes, and the seasonal crowds begin to give way to a quieter, more immersive experience. Thanks to the breadth of terrain across the US national parks, there’s no single version of how to experience fall. You might be leaf-peeping beneath the peaks of the Tetons, winding through Acadia’s brilliant coastal forests, hiking Yosemite in the cooler weather, or watching the aspens flicker across the Rockies. And when the sun goes down, the day doesn’t have to end: there are campfires to linger around, stars to seek out, and hot springs to slip into. Below, I’ve rounded up 11 national parks that are particularly spectacular in autumn. Take note: Fall may be shoulder season, but don’t assume that means easy availability—lodges, campgrounds, permits, and popular activities can still book up, so check current park conditions and reservation requirements before you go. —Jessica Chapel This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 16 Best Resorts on Private Islands for an Ultra-Exclusive Getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.23
For many, true relaxation looks like dropping off the map—settling down on a secluded, sparsely populated island where no one knows anything about you, save for your favorite tropical cocktail. The very best private island resorts balance downtime and adventure; personal space and hospitality; rugged, natural beauty and state-of-the-art facilities. Scattered across the turquoise waters of Indonesia, the Maldives, and Turks and Caicos, some of these properties are wonderfully far-flung, while others, like Little Palm Island Resort & Spa in Florida and Lovango Resort and Beach Club in the US Virgin Islands, don’t even require a US passport. No matter where you decide to book your bungalow, you can rest assured that exclusivity and quietude take top priority at the properties on this list. Offering everything from fresh meals tailored to your preferences to bespoke spa treatments, these resorts are built on the idea that it’s all for you. Whether you’re seeking an open-air villa that floats above crystal-clear water, a luxury ecolodge powered by wind turbines, or a safari-style escape where jungle hikes are always on the table, these are the world’s best private island resorts—each the very definition of paradise. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tetiaroa, French Polynesia Actor Marlon Brando’s legacy lives on at his former private getaway in French Polynesia, now a hyper-exclusive, eco-minded retreat where travelers come to escape it all. Relax in one of 35 stylish, palm-thatched villas, each a grand fusion of indoor and outdoor space, the beach just footsteps away (alternatively, go even bigger with the island’s sole over-the-top residence). Enjoy island bike rides, treatments in the stickwork cocoons of the Varua te Ora Polynesian Spa, and French-tinged, Polynesian-influenced dining by French celebrity chef Jean Imbert. Nature tours led by in-house researchers offer a deeper connection to the island, while daily cultural experiences like Polynesian dance classes, ukulele lessons, and traditional weaving sessions introduce guests to local traditions. Make sure to save time to explore the other islands of the Tetiaroa Atoll, which also belong to the Brando family, where untouched beaches, preserved reefs, and thriving seabird colonies are as gorgeous as when Brando first encountered the location in 1960. All meals, libations (including Champagne), in-room dining, and daily spa treatments are bundled into the all-inclusive rate, allowing for carefree indulgence at every turn. And although The Brando immerses guests in barefoot ultra-luxury, it also quietly stands as one of the world’s most sustainable resorts—powered by solar energy and cooled by innovative seawater systems—preserving the paradise Brando so deeply loved for generations to come. —Antonia Quirke - Read Full ReviewLocation: Little Torch Key, Florida This adults-only private island is a study in tropical chic, redefining the castaway fantasy right on American soil.
