There are a total of 30 thatched-roof bungalow suites (some freestanding, some within larger bungalows) across the four-acre island, many with four-poster beds and outdoor copper bathtubs. Thanks to a smart layout and smarter landscaping, you’ll encounter other people less often than you’d expect (a strict cap at 60 guests helps). All suites have water views, outdoor showers, and furnished decks; most also overlook private slivers of white-sand beach and are kitted out with hammocks, loungers, and firepits. The Dining Room has sweeping sea views, and the spectacular SpaTerre complex is underscored by a breezy two-story atrium. Paddleboard or kayak through mangrove mazes as eagle rays swim by, laze the day away on a beachfront hammock, or simply enjoy the day resting on a poolside lounger. Also, don’t miss a snorkeling trip to Looe Key Reef, part of the third-largest living coral reef in the world and site of ongoing reef restoration efforts by MOTE Marine Laboratory & Aquarium, a Florida-based nonprofit marine research institution. Little Palm Island has partnered with the organization to create the “Paradise with a Purpose” package, which includes a half-day in Looe Key Reef, a donation to MOTE Marine, accommodations, and breakfast. —Paul Rubio - Read Full ReviewLocation: Yaukuve Levu Island, Fiji Located in the untouched Kadavu Islands, a 45-minute seaplane flight from Nadi International Airport, this private island balances romance and multigenerational travel in Fiji. Straddling the renowned Great Astrolabe Reef, the waters near Kokomo teem with colorful fish, manta rays, sea turtles, and thriving coral gardens, making underwater exploration a must for any visit (don’t miss the marine biologist–led manta snorkel excursion). Twenty-one beachfront villas range in size from a couples-friendly one-bedroom to larger two- and three-bedrooms, each with a private plunge pool, private walled garden with outdoor shower, and direct beach access. Meanwhile, five hilltop luxury Grand Residences welcome larger families to multi-bedroom homes, inclusive of a private butler and nanny. Guests can also anticipate other water activities like sailing and kayaking, and three memorable meals daily, made of locally sourced produce from Kokomo’s 5.5-acre farm and hydroponics garden, and seafood from a sustainable, caught-to-order island initiative. —Adam H. Graham - Read Full ReviewLocation: Anambas, Indonesia There are drop-dead gorgeous private island resorts, and then there’s Bawah, an entire nature and marine reserve comprising 6 islands, 3 blue lagoons, and 13 unspoiled white beaches in the heart of Indonesia’s Anambas Archipelago. Sustainability lies at the core of the reserve with no compromises on luxury. In fact, the entire resort was constructed by hand using sustainable bamboo and locally sourced natural building materials, and decorated with works from local artisans. The reserve oozes natural splendor, which can be enjoyed from the comfort of a swoon-worthy rustic-chic tented suite, overwater bungalow, or pool villa. Come here for Indonesian coastal cuisine perfected, dinners in the treetops, spectacular sunsets, hikes through the jungle, island-hopping via transparent kayaks, and sublime snorkeling. To access Bawah’s remote location with ease, the reserve offers a door-to-door transfer from Singapore airport with short components by road and ferry, followed by a 75-minute seaplane that lands directly in paradise. —Michelle Jana Chan - Read Full ReviewLocation: Peter Island, British Virgin Islands From the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island, the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, turns up the volume on the wellness-minded, pastoral strains of Caribbean life, and in no time, you might just find yourself humming along to the tune. With just 52 rooms and 2 villas, you’ll never have to battle for privacy and discretion, yet the company of fellow guests is always welcome. In 2017, Hurricane Irma tragically destroyed homes and upended lives throughout the Virgin Islands. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75% of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavor of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favorite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. —Kat Chen - Read Full ReviewLocation: Mnemba Island, Tanzania Just shy of two miles off the coast of Zanzibar’s main island, Mnemba is a tiny, casuarina-forested sanctuary surrounded by a private marine reserve. Home to just 12 shell-shaped, thatched bandas, designed with understated elegance by Fox Browne Creative and Jack Alexander Studio, it’s the antithesis of bling. A seven-month rebuild in 2024 expanded the villas into curvaceous, nautilus-like spaces, blending natural materials with breezy open-air design. Guests can explore turquoise shallows on catamarans, dive vibrant reefs, or simply lounge in private beach bandas watching noddies and plovers whirl above the sandspit. The spa, yoga deck, and Oceans Without Borders education center enrich the experience, while chefs curate custom menus that range from sushi boxes to lobster ravioli served under the stars. Service is impeccable, with a charming butler, a jovial bar team, and Tanzania’s first local dive master leading ocean explorations. Despite Zanzibar’s tourism boom, Mnemba feels like a world apart—exclusive, untouched, and deeply serene. With a staff-to-guest ratio of over 3:1, every detail is handled, leaving you to do exactly what you’re meant to here: absolutely nothing. —Lisa Grainger - Read Full ReviewLocation: Nosy Ankao, Madagascar A nothing-is-impossible hideaway for adventurous high-fliers, Miavana by Time + Tide is set on remote Nosy Ankao in northern Madagascar, only reachable by helicopter. With ease, the private island merges barefoot luxury and a deep commitment to conservation and community support. Just 14 villas, built from sun-bleached Malagasy wood and hand-hewn limestone, sprawl across private gardens and powder-soft beaches. Interiors channel a beachy Palm Springs vibe, with sunken bathtubs, pastel Smeg appliances, and fully stocked kitchens, offering a luxurious home-away-from-home feeling. The central Piazza serves farm-fresh menus that change daily, while off-menu requests are happily fulfilled. Though there’s no stand-alone spa, therapists deliver seashell massages and herbal body wraps directly to your villa. Service is breezy yet impeccable, with butlers anticipating every need—whether folding laundry, crafting green juices, or lending sunglasses. Miavana by Time + Tide’s eco-efforts are serious: villas rely on natural ventilation, solar panels power much of the resort, and local conservation programs protect turtles, lemurs, and coral reefs. While private island life is great, take time to explore mainland Madagascar’s iconic baobab forests or Tsingy formations (both can be arranged by helicopter safari from the island). —Chris Schalkx - Read Full ReviewLocation: Islas Secas, Panama Set within the jungle-cloaked splendor of Panama’s Gulf of Chiriquí, Islas Secas offers an exclusive, eco-friendly escape across a private archipelago of 14 untouched islands. At its heart, the resort’s eight light-footed accommodations—including casitas, safari-style tents, and open-air mansion Casa Cavada—blend flawlessly into the landscape, each with sweeping hilltop views and living spaces that celebrate the outdoors. Guests have exclusive access to this entire island chain, blanketed in tropical flora and fringed by white- and gold-sand beaches. Days unfold as you please across the various islands: kayak through emerald waters, snorkel vibrant coral gardens, hike jungle trails to ancient artifacts, or island-hop to wide, sparkling beaches where staff can arrange private beach barbecues. Water adventures abound, too, from fun on pricey water toys like hydrofoils, flyboards, and Seabobs, to fishing and whale-watching, all included in the resort’s personalized, all-inclusive program. On the main island of Isla Cavada, find a stunning open-air beachfront restaurant, a swoon-worthy jungle spa, a Hemingway-inspired bar, and an infinity pool perched high above the rainforest coastline. —Andrea Whittle - Read Full ReviewLocation: Necker Island, British Virgin Islands Necker Island is the creation of Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson, who has transformed what was once a scrubby, 74-acre British Virgin Island cay into a fortress of lush greenery, serene Balinese villas, exotic animals ranging from local flamingos to endangered lemurs and tortoises, and solar panels and wind turbines that make the island self-sustaining. The resort is accessible only by boat from nearby Tortola—no private-plane runway here—which makes it feel more approachable and refuge-like, especially compared to some other private-island hospitality projects. Every inch of the place feels like a Bond hideaway: Tropical canopies give way to white-sand beaches all your own, lagoons filled with flamingos, infinity-pooled suites, and cozy lounges. A sprawling hilltop Great House has far-flung views of the azure waters around the island; there's also a billiards table, board games, a bar (just one of many on the island, including the self-serve one in your own villa), and dining nooks with incredible views where five-star, family-style dinners and healthy à la carte breakfasts are served. —Shannon McMahon - Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos Located off the main chain of Turks and Caicos, Ambergris Cay achieves billionaire-level relaxation with its serene azure waters, rugged nature, and waterfront villas. The 1,100-acre island is home to a collection of expansive villas, from 1-bedroom beachfront bungalows to 10-bedroom homes. All meals and house beverages are included, meaning you’ll never go hungry—or thirsty—with cocktails made from fresh ingredients and a floating rum bar called The Hangover accessible only by boat. Suites sit on the sugar-sand beach leading into the Caribbean Sea, while sprawling villas are perched on craggy hilltops overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Interiors are beach house chic, with wood-plank floors and shiplap walls. Guests roam the island via golf cart between the spa, tennis courts, beach activities, and state-of-the-art fitness center encased in 180 degrees of glass. Service is breezy but attentive, with 24/7 concierge support via WhatsApp. The private island resort also houses one of the longest runways in the region, making it easy for outdoor-minded billionaires and professional athletes to arrive in private jets for instant immersion into the tropical good life. —S.M. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lovango Cay, US Virgin Islands Located across St. John’s legendary Caneel Bay on an island all its own, this unpretentious seasonal resort (open December through July) features the USVI’s only private island beach club and eco-chic accommodation in the form of wooden treehouses, explorer-style tents, and one- to three-bedroom villas. Views of the surrounding jewel-toned waters abound, peaking at Treetops Lobby Tent, where bird's-eye views of St. John proper and St. Thomas can be admired in a single panorama. Indulge in island cuisine and rum-spiked fun at the resort’s Waterfront Restaurant (get the smoked pineapple old- fashioned and the signature Caribbean lobster paillard) or its fast-casual counterpart, Sand Pit, which services Lovango’s Beach Club and its cabana-lined swimming pool. For active and gastronomic pursuits in greater St. John, take the ferry to Cruz Bay, which runs regularly; for another incarnation of beach bliss, hop on the five-minute ferry to St. John’s Honeymoon Beach, which runs on select days. —Todd Plummer - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lhaviyani Atoll, Maldives This Yuji Yamazaki–designed property in the Maldives’s Lhaviyani Atoll is a next-generation ultra-luxury experience like no other, underscored by a mind-blowing “Anything, Anytime, Anywhere” fixed price policy, where few things are off-limits—nor cost extra—from floating breakfasts to most top-shelf Champagne to private fitness training. The island’s 15 ryokan-inspired overwater residences epitomize contemporary Japanese ocean elegance, offering ample room to relax and play against the backdrop of the Maldives’ lazuline beauty (units start at 3,300 square feet). At Kudadoo’s core lies The Retreat, an impressive open-air minimalist overwater pagoda crowned by 984 solar panels (that power the resort in its entirety) and housing the island’s bar, restaurant, spa, fitness facilities, and lounge areas. Thanks to the Anything, Anytime, Anywhere policy, your residence, The Retreat, and the surrounding nature become your muses for fulfilling the utmost island fantasies. Request to be marooned on nearby Dream Island for a luxury-draped Robinson Crusoe experience or ask for a private toes-in-the-sand beach lunch on Kudadoo itself. Snorkel with giant mantas alongside a marine biologist or try your hand at jet-skiing, parasailing, or fishing. Pencil in plenty of time for spa treatments—they are unlimited, after all—before or after you figure out how to manage an entire staff of butlers, cooks, personal trainers, and yoga masters at your beck and call. Suffice to say, Kudadoo is the ultimate castaway narrative come to life—and the script is yours to write. —L.G. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Moskito Island, British Virgin Islands While everyone knows about billionaire Richard Branson’s original private retreat, Necker Island, the Virgin founder purchased another exclusive playground just two miles away called Moskito Island. But instead of using it for himself and his high-powered pals, the mogul built a home and sold nine other plots for others to build their dream beach houses. While most are only inhabited by the estate owners themselves, three of the remarkable properties—The Branson Estate, The Oasis Estate, and The Point Estate—became available for rent in October 2021. Although more expensive than your average luxury hotel, Moskito Island makes living the life of a billionaire a tiny bit more accessible. Five-star restaurants are swapped for private chefs, hotel suites for exclusive estates, and concierges for dedicated house managers capable of making nearly anything you want possible. The only guests in sight are those in your immediate party—that is, unless you decide to venture to the communal Manchioneel Beach, complete with a floating trampoline and bartenders at the ready, or the Beach House, a community recreational area where you can play a round of tennis and mingle with estate owners (you may even spot Richard Branson himself). —Jordi Lippe-McGraw - Gold List 2018, 2019, 2020Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos As COMO’s sole property in the Americas, Parrot Cay's renowned luxury experience makes it an unrivaled property in Turks and Caicos. The pinnacle of bespoke solitude, it's located on a private island enmeshed in the wilderness. You arrive after a 15-minute chauffeured drive from Providenciales International Airport, then a 20-minute panoramic boat ride through cays and turquoise waves hugged by mangroves. It’s primeval in nature and worlds away, despite its ease of access from the main island. The private, white-sand beach—with miles of clear-water sandbars inviting you to walk across, float around, and laze about for ages—is the main reason why the property has been dubbed by locals as "the Maldives of the Americas," despite being entirely singular in the impression it makes. If you’re seeking a romantic getaway inspired by an itch for an immersive nature escape, this is the place to go—and I recommend booking a private beach house with your own plunge pool for the full immersive experience. —Bridget Knowles FAQ: How we choose the best private island resorts in the world Every resort on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Hertz Promo Codes: Up to 30% Off Rentals | Condé Nast Traveler
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.12
As air travel continues to be unpredictable, there’s never been a better time to hit the road. There are plenty of reasons to embark on road trips both big and small in 2026, from the 100th anniversary of Route 66 to the World Cup games taking place across the country. And car rental company Hertz is a reliable favorite, whether you’re hoping to cut costs on summer travel or make plans with more flexibility. Choose from a shiny catalog of cars, from family-friendly minivans and pickup trucks to luxury Porsches and electric vehicles. This spring, the company is adding the sporty Ineos Grenadier to its fleet; its many compartments make it ideal for tailgating summer concerts. Hertz was founded by Walter Jacobs in 1918, who kicked things off with 12 used Model T’s. The company was then purchased by the eponymous John D. Hertz in 1923, who pioneered the “Hertz-Drive-Ur-Self” System. Hertz’s first airport car rental office opened at Chicago’s Midway Airport in 1932, and has been fueling adventurous travels ever since. Now, with over half a million rental cars in the US alone, the company boasts over 10,000 locations worldwide. Here’s how to save on your next rental car with promotions, free upgrades, and member discounts. And when you're done checking out what Hertz has to offer, make sure you have a look at the deals for Budget Rent a Car, Avis, Alamo, and Enterprise. Book with Hertz for your next adventure this fall and get a 20% discount code If you’ve got a leaf-peeping road trip in the works, get rewarded for planning early. Book a car for two or more days by September 14 and get 20% off your rental, with the pickup window running until December 15. The discount applies to all vehicles, excluding large SUV's, Dream cars, cargo, and box trucks. Be sure to use the code 212271 at the time of reservation. Get one day free with seven+ day bookings with this Hertz coupon From now until September 30, 2026, you can receive 1 free rental day when you rent from Hertz’s newest fleet for 7 or more consecutive days (with a 27-day maximum) across participating Hertz locations in the US and Canada—perfect for those lengthier, cross-country trips. Just be sure to use the promo code 210751 at the time of booking, otherwise the offer will be void. Get up to 20% off at Hertz with a military & government discount code Active duty military, veterans, and government employees can save up to 20% on base rates when booking leisure car rentals. This includes space-available upgrades and a complimentary Hertz Gold Plus Rewards membership, which gives you access to perks like skip-the-line and free rental days. Military members, be sure to use the specific Hertz discount code 2306779. Save up to 20% with the 50 Plus Car Rental Program Hertz’s 50 Plus Car Rental program allows travelers aged 50 and over to enjoy 20% off base rates on a wide range of vehicles for scenic rides across the country. If you’re one of these seasoned travelers, make sure you book with CDP# 2007815. Save $50 on weekly SUV & minivan rentals with this Hertz discount code Got a family trip in the works? Rent an SUV or minivan for seven consecutive days and get $50 off. Make sure you use the promo code 212131 at the time of booking, valid for reservations from now through September 30, 2026. 10% off EV and hybrid rentals with this Hertz promo code If you're traveling with the environment in mind, Hertz is making it a bit easier on you. Those renting EV and hybrid rentals can save 10% off as long as pickup occurs by September 30, 2026. Use the promo code 212157 and keep in mind the discount applies to rentals of three days or more. Free one-car-class upgrade on your next trip with this Hertz promo code You’re on vacation, which means you deserve to drive in style. From now until September 30, enjoy a free, one-car-class upgrade when you reserve a medium sedan or higher. Be sure to use the promo code PC 211748 at the time of reservation. Up to 25% off with the Hertz student discount If you’re a student looking to get on the road, you can save up to 25% everyday base rates via Corporate Shopping. This includes a waived additional driver fee for a spouse or domestic partner in the US. To take advantage of this discount, make sure you enroll in Hertz Gold Plus Rewards. Save up to 20% on base rates with a Hertz AAA discount Thanks to its partnership with the American Automobile Association, AAA members can unlock benefits year-round, like 20% off base rates worldwide and 10% off prepaid fuel. Additionally, AAA members can save an additional $50 off monthly rentals and get one free day when they join the Hertz Gold+ loyalty program. It’s time to put that membership to good use. Save extra with the Hertz Gold+ loyalty program If you’re renting cars on the regular, consider signing up for the Hertz Gold+ loyaly program, which is entirely free to join. Members are able to skip the line at select locations, earn rewards points towards redeemable free car rental days, and receive extra perks like free additional drivers. The membership operates on a tier system, and the higher you go, the more additional perks, like larger selection of vehicles and free upgrades: - Gold gets you 1 point for every dollar spent, plus skip-the-line and members-only rates - Five Star promises 1.25, as well as a wider selection of premium vehicles and free upgrades - President’s Circle goes all the way to 1.5, with the largest selection of exclusive vehicles, guaranteed upgrades, and a dedicated customer service line How to fix a Hertz discount code that’s not working If your Hertz coupon code isn't working, be sure to check for typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization, as well as any terms and conditions. You can also try clearing your browser’s cache and cookies, or switching devices or browsers. When all else fails, Hertz's Support Hub is there to help.

item.title: Where was Practical Magic 2 filmed? An insider's guide to the long-awaited sequel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.80
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Practical Magic 2 filmed? In 1998, burgeoning Hollywood starlets Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock played Gillian and Sally Owens, two sisters in possession of special powers in Practical Magic, a film adapted from Alice Hoffman’s novel by the same name. Set in the witch (history) rich state of Massachusetts, the ingenue outcasts attempt to lift the ancestral curse that strikes dead any man who falls in love with an Owens woman. As they embark on this harrowing journey, spells are cast, “midnight margaritas” are made, and matriarchy reigns supreme. At the time, the film’s reception was middling at best – with a New York Times review describing it as “Barbie Joins a Coven” – and its performance at the box office not much better. With a little room to breathe and bask in nostalgia’s rose-colored glow, the movie has transformed into a feminist cult classic with Gen X and Gen Z fans alike. From 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple to The Devil Wears Prada 2, 2026 has been a year of follow-up films. In that same vein, Kidman and Bullock have reunited in Practical Magic 2, a sequel directed by Susanne Bier that promises to delight fans and take us across the pond to a whole new continent of spooky locales. Another generation of coven-loving will live on in Practical Magic 2, which picks up after a sizeable time jump but with more of the same kooky hijinks. A generous interpretation of time – and a little movie magic – lands Sally’s daughters Antonia (Maisie Williams) and Kylie (Joey King) in their early twenties. Up until now, they have lived their lives ignorant of their powers, which their mother has deliberately shielded them from. Antonia, a medical student, most closely resembles her mother, while Kylie, now a Harvard student, is a bit more of a free spirit. When Kylie falls for sweet Gideon (Xolo Maridueña), and then he falls into a coma, she follows her mother’s path of attempting to right things. Counselled by the recently uncovered Book of the Raven, Kylie sets off to her family’s ancestral home of England, bringing much of the story to English territory. While the original movie was shot in Coupeville, Washington, on Whidbey Island, as a New England stand-in, the sequel's production moved to the UK. Here are all the places where Practical Magic 2 was filmed. Leavesden Studios, Hertfordshire, England The Owens women remain the main characters in this film, but fans of the original film will recall the outstanding Victorian-style Owens family home. The house itself has reached cult status with its cutesy cottagecore aesthetic, and its recreation was crucial to making the sequel. Practical Magic 2’s production notes explain the importance of the house's revival. Producer Denise De Novi felt that bringing the house back to life was one of the most rewarding components of making this movie, “The house in this movie is just a phenomenon,” she noted. In the first film, the exterior of the house was built on San Juan Island in Washington, and the interiors were created on a soundstage in Los Angeles. Those structures no longer exist, so this time around, production designer Tom Burton determined that the most economical option was to build the house from scratch on the back lot at Leavesden Studios. Great care was taken to ensure that the replica was consistent with the original home, including establishing the same sun position so that the sun would set in the same place as it did in the original film. Once the house’s construction was almost complete, the greens team descended upon the set to bring the renowned garden to life, with over 4,000 plants brought in. While about half of the 55 shooting days were spent at Leavesden Studios, the remainder were shot at several notable locations in and around London. Village of Hambleden The quaint village of Hambleden, just west of London, served as the town of Thornfield. The centre of the village is filled with old picturesque brick and flint cottages, all with the signature dormer windows. The Royal Standard of England, Beaconsfield British viewers might take notice of this historic pub, which serves as the exterior of the fictional Thornfield Inn just northwest of London. The Royal Standard, which has been around for over 900 years, claims to be the oldest pub in Great Britain. Located in the Chiltern Hills, the scenic old pub is filled with charm and has been featured in numerous films and television shows including The Theory of Everything, Hot Fuzz, and Too Much. Oysters, fish and chips, and a robust beer list are on offer and quiz night is every Tuesday. Langleybury Mansion in Hertfordshire Langleybury is a vacant 18th-century period house that has served as a backdrop for several notable productions including Downton Abbey, The Crown, and Paddington. The crew utilised this mansion to stand in for rooms at Harvard University as well as some of the UK lodgings. Wormsley Estate in Buckinghamshire The private 2,700-acre estate boasting an opera pavilion, cricket grounds, and a walled garden served as the backdrop for the cottage of Tom Lockland (Solly McLeod), the longtime magic student of Thornfield. Black Park Country Park Practical Magic 2 features sweeping views of the British rolling hills and conifer forests. Black Park, a large park with woodland trails, horse riding, and a lake, was filmed as the forest surrounding Thornfield. The Royal Chelsea Hospital The historic Royal Hospital Chelsea in London is a retirement and nursing home for British Army veterans who have reached the state pension age. The hospital was founded by Charles II in 1692, and it has maintained its grand estate while modernising to meet the present-day needs of its inhabitants. The impressive grounds, with brick buildings and Roman columns, were used in the film for a flower market and for shots meant to be Harvard University exteriors. The Victorian flats of Cromwell Buildings The tattoo-covered Professor Ian Wright (Lee Pace), who quickly becomes Sally’s love interest, is one of the more charming updates in this sequel. His apartment, was shot at these flats.

item.title: Secret objects have been found under the floorboards at Buckingham Palace during renovations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.66
Buckingham Palace is undergoing a major £369m refurbishment that began in 2017 and is set to be completed in March 2027, after its infrastructure was deemed to be in “urgent need of a complete overhaul”. The refurbishment has turned out to be a real archaeological endeavour. During the work, objects dating back more than a century have been discovered beneath floorboards and in other hidden corners of the palace. Some of the objects seem to have belonged to the palace staff, like a pair of black hobnail boots that had seen better days, but also old Christmas cards, blank Littlewoods Football Pool betting slips from 1957, and a fragment of West End theatre listings published in The Standard in 1889. Pages from a 1966 edition of the Daily Express were also discovered, including an article about the prison where the Great Train Robbers were serving their sentences. “The men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings,” the article stated. Another discovery offers a glimpse into the workings of the Royal Household – a document detailing Queen Elizabeth II's schedule during a diplomatic reception in 1977, her Silver Jubilee year. The typed document read: “The British guests will be distributed throughout the State Rooms, except the Music Room and West Gallery, where they should be encouraged to talk to the Diplomats.” The project, the Buckingham Palace Reservicing Programme, was launched to overhaul Buckingham Palace's ageing infrastructure. The royal residence features 775 rooms: 19 state rooms, 52 royal and guest bedrooms, 92 offices, 188 staff bedrooms, and 78 bathrooms. The Royal Family’s official website stated that “The Palace's electrical cabling, plumbing and heating have not been updated since the 1950s. The building's infrastructure is in urgent need of a complete overhaul to prevent long-term damage to the building and its contents.” King Charles III and Queen Camilla will not move into Buckingham Palace after the restoration is complete, but will instead continue to live in Clarence House. This will allow greater public access to the palace, but Buckingham Palace will nevertheless remain the official centre of royal life and the Royal Household's primary workplace, hosting official events and receptions

item.title: Where was Pressure filmed? Behind the scenes of the war epic starring Andrew Scott
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.64
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Pressure filmed? On 6 June 1944, the largest seaborne invasion in history took place on the shores of Normandy, France. After years of global conflict, the Normandy Landings – now known as D-Day – paved the way for the Allied victory on the western front. But the build-up to the operation was nothing short of monumental. Behind the scenes of the deployment of more than 150,000 troops was an intricate web of logistics. Despite meticulous planning, the landings largely depended on the weather – if a storm had rolled in, the results could have been very different. This is where Scottish meteorologist James Stagg (played by Andrew Scott) comes in. With millions of lives at stake, General Dwight D. Eisenhower enlists Stagg to set a timeline for the landings. In doing so, Stagg faces opposition from fellow meteorologist Irving P. Krick and Eisenhower, putting him under immense pressure to deliver an accurate forecast that supports the war effort. This is the tale playing out on the big screen right now, as a stellar cast enacts a crucial but forgotten wartime story that ultimately saved countless lives. But filming a war epic isn’t plain sailing. Here, we take a look at the locations across England used to bring the story to life. Rand Bros Farm Founded in the 1930s by a trio of brothers, Rand Bros Farm, on the edge of Royston, was transformed into the London-to-Portsmouth route seen in the movie’s early scenes. Mentmore Towers Director Anthony Maras scouted more than 100 buildings for the Allied Headquarters – the centrepiece of the movie. While Southwick House, the real-life war headquarters, was considered, its status as an active military base, surrounded by post-war buildings, made it an unsuitable candidate. Mentmore Towers was deemed the best fit – a 19th-century country house built for the Rothschild family. RAF Halton Airfield The airfield featured in the film is one of the oldest and largest in the UK, founded in the First World War and an active training base to this day. St Mary's Church, Mentmore The church featured in the movie sits just beyond the gates of Mentmore Towers. Mentioned in the Domesday Book, it’s likely a wooden structure stood here before the charming medieval structure that stands today. The Historic Dockyard Chatham This historic dockyard stands in for the port of the D-Day embarkation, as troops and submarines headed towards the coast of France.

item.title: 19 best hotels in Sri Lanka including design-led boltholes and beachside resorts
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.34
Sri Lanka has had a rough ride at times, but this teardrop island is now thriving — and easier to reach than ever, with British Airways launching new direct flights from the UK in October 2026. And where better to enjoy this sublime sunny destination than at one of the best hotels in Sri Lanka? The country is as dynamic as it is diverse with gorgeous beaches, serene hill country and ancient ruins. There are also splendid national parks teeming with elephants, leopards and a dazzling array of birds. However, it’s not just about the places. Then there are the people, who are warm, generous and quick to make you feel at home. The delicious spice-laden food, accompanied by a cup of famous Ceylon tea, rounds off the appeal. When it comes to places to stay, there are myriad options. Heritage homes and hotels, often sporting a tropical modernist look spearheaded by star Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa, have long set the tone. But things are changing and the past decade has seen new design-led hotels crop up, pushing the boundaries of hospitality and bringing fresh energy to the country. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Sri Lanka - For honeymoon: Kahanda Kanda, Galle Fort - For families: Cape Weligama, Weligama - For beach: Amanwella, Tangalle - For a south coast location: Kayaam House, Rekawa What is the best part of Sri Lanka to stay in? Cosmopolitan capital Colombo is a quietly rising scene of stylish coffee shops, dynamic art galleries and independent boutiques. But really you want to spend your time on the southwest coast, with its idyllic beaches. There is a brilliant selection of oceanfront hotels around Galle, bringing in fresh seafood, laid-back cafes and toes-in-the-sand luxury. There are equally good properties a short tuk-tuk ride inland for more peace and quiet. While it's tempting to stick to the coast, Yala National Park has excellent lodges, with superb game viewing to go with it. If you have the time, continue up the country to one of the charming, restored colonial properties in the Hill Country, particularly around Ella and Hatton. Then there's the Cultural Triangle, which includes both Kandy, home to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, one of Buddhism's most sacred shrines, and the extraordinary Sigiriya Rock. What area of Sri Lanka is best for first-time visitors? Sri Lanka is compact enough to explore in two or three weeks. Begin in Sri Lanka’s Cultural Triangle, with its ancient cities and temples, before boarding the famous scenic train from Kandy into the island’s lush hill country. Wind through emerald tea plantations to Nuwara Eliya or Ella, then head south for a safari in Yala National Park where elephants and leopards roam wild. Finish on the laid-back south coast, with golden beaches, palm-fringed shores and sparkling ocean views. If you're short on time, then focus on the southwest coast around Galle, particularly if you have family in tow. It's accessible from Colombo airport (two to three hours) and you can experience much of Sri Lanka's best in one fell swoop: glorious beaches, Bawa architecture and colonial history. Just save a night or two for wildlife spotting in Yala National Park. Which part of Sri Lanka is best for beaches? The southwest coast is lined with fantastic beaches, from lively surf hubs to quiet, palm-dotted bays. Highlights include Mirissa for whale-watching and the turquoise waters of horseshoe-shaped Hiriketiya Beach with its trendy cafes and surf vibes. Beginner surfers should head to Weligama Beach, known for its gentle, consistent waves. For simple beach bliss, choose the quiet coastline near Tangalle or the buzzier Unawatuna and Dalawella, with sea turtles wallowing near the shore. When the south coast is out of season (March to December), turn your attention to the beaches on the east coast such as Trincomalee for its deep natural harbours, historic sites and rich underwater biodiversity. Further south is Passikuda, with its shallow, calm coastline, and flourishing Arugam Bay, ‘A-Bay’, Sri Lanka’s surf capital. Where should I stay in Sri Lanka for wildlife? Yala National Park is Sri Lanka’s big hitter, with sightings of elephants near guaranteed, alongside sloth bears, water buffalo and deer. Leopards are also a possibility, though harder to spot. For less crowds, choose under-the-radar Gal Oya National Park, just east of the Hill Country. One of the country’s most unspoilt parks, swimming elephants are the main attraction plus it’s a paradise for bird lovers. How we choose the best hotels in Sri Lanka Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: The ultimate guide to finding 20°C+ sunshine all year – without a long-haul flight
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.17
As summer in the UK simmers to an end, our collective eyes start to wander, considering where we can find a much-needed boost of Vitamin D once dark evenings and wet mornings roll around. There are, of course, the winter sun big-hitters: Thailand for Christmas; the Maldives at New Year's; the Caribbean for a hit of February sunshine. But if you're clever, you can find little pockets of sunshiny joy closer to home all year-long. For true sun-seekers, this is your calendar of how to chase the sun from January to December – without ever boarding a flight for more than four hours. January: Lanzarote, Spain Average January temperature: daytime highs of 22°C The wild coastline of Lanzarote might not register on the radars of those left with the (wrong!) impression that this Canary Island is still a place for soulless package holidays. All the better for those who know better – that hangover from the ‘70s means that when this dramatic volcanic island reveals its true beauty, it comes as something of a joyful surprise. There’s a thriving artsy scene, a smart clutch of cool boutique hotels (we particularly like Cesar Lanzarote) to check into, and unspoilt beaches to explore. In January, expect minimal rainfall and daytime highs in the low 20s (although pack for cooler, breezy nights). February: Madeira, Portugal Average February temperature: daytime highs of 20°C The archipelago of Madeira, cast away off the coast of Portugal, is known for its subtropical climate (meaning hot summers and, crucially, mild winters), as well as its eponymous wine and craggy landscapes. There are also some fabulous hotels to check into – Reid's Palace, A Belmond Hotel, has a knockout pool carved into the coastline and acres of colourful gardens; while Savoy Palace is the smart choice for those looking for an all-inclusive fly-and-flop. February isn't peak season to visit, which means fewer crowds, but temperatures can still skim into the low 20s in the day, and any rainfall is short and sharp. March: Seville, Spain Average March temperature: daytime highs of 21°C The Andalucian city of Seville is a favourite among many Traveller editors – for its old-school restaurant scene, where the best mealtimes are spent hopping between bars, eating melty slithers of Jamón Ibérico washed down with white wine while stood at the bar of a tiled taberna; for the gorgeous Moorish architecture; and for the weather, which promises positivity for much of the year. I've visited twice, once in late October, and once in February: both were warm enough to sip sherry on the street and wander the orange-scented gardens at a leisurely pace, so I feel confident vouching for March, when the afternoons will be balmy without the intense heat that blankets the city in summer. April: Crete, Greece Average April temperature: daytime highs of 21°C The biggest Greek island is, some say, at its best in spring. Emerging from a surprisingly chilly winter, by April you can expect daytime temperatures around 21°C (by the end of the month, perhaps skimming the mid-20s) as well as blossoming flora and fauna. Local hotelier Nikos Tsepetis recently shared his guide to Crete's green heart during spring, without the crowds with us – after skimming for inspiration, check the best hotels in Crete for somewhere smart to stay. May: Malta Average May temperature: daytime highs of 24°C By May, much of Europe has defrosted, promising sunny days and warmer temperatures. Take your pick of destinations – ours is the island of Malta, beloved for its honey-hued Baroque capital city, Valletta, its glittering swimming spots and its enviable climate – Malta gets more than 300 days of sunshine every year. Wandering around the cobbled, UNESCO-listed streets, it's obvious why so many Hollywood productions have chosen the islands as their backdrop: spot them doubling as Ancient Rome in Gladiator and King's Landing in Game of Thrones. June: Alentejo, Portugal Average June temperature: daytime highs of 27°C Portugal's Alentejo region is a place to make the most of summer by slowing down and living a little better. Here, you won't find the crowds you might expect in other corners of the country in peak season: instead, you'll find peaceful countryside, golden-tinged rolling farms, pretty little villages like UNESCO-listed Évora, and a thriving food scene that spotlights traditional dishes, farm-to-table cooking (and not in a performative, zeitgeisty way) and local produce (and wine!). In June, days are warm without hitting the mega-temperatures starting to appear in other parts of Europe. July: Sweden Average July temperature: daytime highs of 22°C If there's one fantasy the Traveller editors keep rehashing at the moment, it's the idea of a Scandi summer – somewhere it's sunny but not too hot; where the days are long and spent soaking up nature without the crowds. Enter the archipelago of Sweden. Summer here is a jumble of bike rides, swimming in lakes, boat trips and festivals. August: Tallinn, Estonia Average August temperature: daytime highs of 22°C As one of the oldest cities in Europe, Tallinn is – perhaps unsurprisingly – drastically pretty. The Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There's a thriving food scene here – the best restaurants in Tallinn reflect the best of Estonia's produce and traditional recipes. In the summer, head up Toompea Hill for widescreen views of the city, take part in Tallinn's sauna culture or take a waterfront cycle. September: Athens, Greece Average September temperature: daytime highs of 29°C After a long, steamy summer, the Greek capital starts to emerge into the (relatively) cooler autumnal months in September. That still means temperatures close to 30°C at the beginning of the month, nine and a half hours of sunshine a day, and positively balmy sea temperatures of 25°C. Spend a long weekend in Athens seeing the Acropolis, wandering around Plaka, the oldest neighbourhood in the city, or culture-hopping around the brilliant museums. The best hotels in Athens, for our money, include The Dolli in the city and Four Seasons Astir Palace Hotel Athens on the Athenian Riviera. October: Sicily, Italy Average October temperature: daytime highs of 24°C The Italian island of Sicily is at its best in the autumn. The sea is at its most inviting, having been warmed by the blazing Mediterranean sun all summer long. Many of the crowds are gone, but there's still a buzz about the coastal towns like Taormina, made (more) famous by The White Lotus, and frenetic cities like Palermo. Our pick of the top hotels in Sicily: Villa Sant'Andrea, A Belmond Hotel, for an enviable seafront setting and Braccialieri Val di Noto for a bright, cheery stay. November: Southern Turkey Average November temperature: daytime highs of 21°C Turkey’s glitzy southern coast draws sunseekers all year long. Peak season might be over by the time November rolls around (bringing with it puffer-jacket and brolly weather at home), but the weather in some of our favourite spots like Bodrum is still enviable enough to tempt us for one final jaunt on these shores. Check into a perennial Traveller favourite, Macakizi, and forget about the winter blues for a few days. December: Malaga, Spain Average December temperature: daytime highs of 19°C Finding genuinely hot weather in Europe by the time we're nearing Christmas isn't easy. But there are corners to seek out where the climate is far better than our own. Case in point: the southern Spanish city of Malaga, where mild winter sun is all but guaranteed and rain is sparse. The city goes all-out for Christmas, with impressive festive lights and sweet Christmas markets to explore without the crowds.

item.title: UK cities could soon be allowed to implement a tourist tax – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.07
Regions and cities across the country are set to benefit from extra funds following the latest announcements regarding the UK tourist tax – officially known as the overnight visitor levy. In a statement published by the UK Government on 10 September, it was announced that mayors and local leaders would soon be handed the power to introduce the overnight visitor levy to maximise the benefits of tourism to the country. The new fee on overnight stays may then be invested to boost tourism and drive growth, supporting local communities. Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said: “Our amazing towns and cities, and our picturesque rural and coastal communities welcome millions of visitors every year – local leaders should have the power to make the most of that popularity.” “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most. It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.” While early reports suggested that the UK tourist tax, as it has since been dubbed, would be uncapped, the statement released on 10 September made it clear that budget staycations would be protected. Rather than a flat fee or rate, the levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of the accommodation – but UK citizens won’t be exempt from paying the fee in other UK regions or cities. This is just the latest in a growing number of fiscal devolution reforms that see local authorities have more power over their areas following the appointment of Andy Burnham as Prime Minister. Steve Rotheram, Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said, “This is something I’ve been calling for over many years, so I’m really pleased the government is taking forward plans to give Mayors the power to introduce a visitor levy locally. “Our visitor economy is already worth more than £6.8bn a year and supports more than 55,000 jobs across the Liverpool City Region. A modest levy on overnight stays could potentially raise up to £18m a year – money that would stay here and be reinvested directly into the events, culture, experiences and infrastructure that bring millions of visitors to our region. “Visitor levy mechanisms are often used in many great cities across the globe to improve the visitor offer and attract even more people to enjoy the experience. It would give us more money to support the things that make our visitor economy such a success, while helping our businesses and communities to benefit from its continued growth.” Will there be a London tourist tax? While plans are yet to be confirmed, including how much visitors will need to pay on arrival in the capital, it’s expected that there will be some form of London tourist tax. In the 10 September statement, the Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I strongly welcome the Government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. This needs to happen sooner rather than later. London’s visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally. “A well-designed, modest levy has the potential to provide an important additional source of funding to support growth, strengthen London’s offer to visitors and help us remain globally competitive. It would allow us to reinvest in the places, infrastructure, culture and experiences that make London one of the world’s greatest cities to visit, while helping manage the pressures that come with welcoming tens of millions of visitors every year. “I will work closely with London’s boroughs, accommodation providers, hospitality and tourism businesses and other partners, before final decisions are taken.”

item.title: 17 best places to see autumn leaves in the UK
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.95
As another glorious summer comes to an end, the arrival of autumn leaves season transforms national parks, commons, and secret gardens across the British Isles. The lush greenery and beds of wildflowers wilt, turning popular picnic spots into kaleidoscopic paintings. Wild ponies navigate the changing landscapes of the Brecon Beacons, amblers take to the New Forest for bracing strolls before hiding out in cosy pubs, and Londoners wrap up for weekend markets and strolls around historic parks. As they change from bright green to a spectrum of red, orange and yellow, these are the most beautiful places in the UK to take in the spectacle. When can you see autumn leaves in the UK? Depending on how long the summer sunshine sticks around, autumn leaves can be found falling across the UK from mid-September. That said, for guaranteed colours – and spectacular photos – the best time to explore is between mid-October and mid-November. Where are the best places to see autumn leaves in the UK? London's parks put on pretty fabulous displays of colour, but the footfall through the capital's central green spaces means the combination of rain- and leaf-fall can make things a little slushy. Head a little further out for undisturbed scenes, such as the nooks and crannies of Richmond Park and beyond into the rolling Surrey Hills, where there are many attractions and towns to stop off at. The Peak District and Lake District are wonderful places in the autumn. Cosy fires roar in pub corners, hot chocolates keep amblers toasty on hiking trails, and pretty villages offer holiday cottages and bed and breakfast spots to get a good night's sleep. Further north, over the Scottish Border, you'll find some of the UK's last true wildernesses. Glide through the lochs and look to the hills, where auburn autumn leaves drift onto dewy grass, and keen walkers reconnect with nature.

item.title: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.44
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (18 - 20 September) 1. Shuck and slurp at the Oyster Championships 18 September Bentley’s Oyster Bar and Grill’s annual London Oyster Championships return this Friday, celebrating the start of the native oyster season. Swing by for bucket loads of Champagne, oysters and entertainment as two competition categories – the ‘Speed Shucking Oyster Open’ and ‘Best Dressed Oyster’ – get foodies going from afternoon into the evening. VIP tickets include exclusive access to an Oyster Masterclass hosted by Tristan Hugh Jones, the grower of the Rossmore oysters used in the competition. Address: Bentley's Oyster Bar and Grill, 11-15 Swallow Street, Piccadilly, London W1B 4DG Website: londonoysterchampionships.com 2. Honour the life of a music legend Until 15 October Mark 20 years of one of the most iconic albums of the century as a free outdoor photography exhibition in King’s Cross celebrates the life, music and legacy of Amy Winehouse. King’s Cross Group, in partnership with Universal Music and the Amy Winehouse Estate, has transformed 30 of King’s Cross' signature art benches in Granary Square and King’s Boulevard, creating an open-air gallery for all to enjoy. Address: King’s Cross, London Website: kingscross.co.uk 3. Secure a spot at a hot new opening Open now The exciting openings keep opening their doors in London. Among the hottest new dining spots is Le Café LPM at The Lanesborough – the new Riviera-inspired café concept from La Petite Maison. The exclusive year-long residency captures the joie de vivre of the Côte d'Azur through an all-day menu packed with favourite dishes, from indulgent classics such as croque-monsieur and veal milanese through to seafood delights like grilled octopus and prawns in herby butter. Elsewhere, Gordon Ramsay has added yet another address to his portfolio with the launch of Gordon Ramsay at Sea Containers. Slurp oysters and work through a menu celebrating British produce, seafood and the grill – on the open-air riverside terrace, should you choose to soak up the final run of summer. Address: Le Café LPM at The Lanesborough, Park Corner, Hyde, London SW1X 7TA; Gordon Ramsay at Sea Containers, 20 Upper Ground, London SE1 9PD Website: oetkerhotels.com; gordonramsayseacontainers.com 4. Indulge in one of London's best burgers With queues that stretch down Bethnal Green Road and plenty of virality, it was inevitable that Dumbo Shoreditch would soon have a sister site. Now, lovers of the smash patty can get their burger fix in Soho, as the brand-new site has opened its doors at 37 Berwick Street. Charles Ganem and Samuel Nataf’s Paris-born concept, credited by many foodies for bringing the smashburger concept to Europe, is the ultimate grab-and-go indulgence. Choose from a cheeseburger with onion, pickles, ketchup and mustard, an earth burger with ‘special sauce’, nuggets and French fries, and tuck in. Address: Dumbo Soho, 37 Berwick Street, London W1F 8RS Website: dumboparis.com 5. Enjoy a moment of reflection 19 - 20 September The Water Lantern Festival transforms Clapham Common into a tranquil haven this weekend, with live music, food and drink and activities for all the family, offering time to pause and reflect. Enjoy all the action throughout the afternoon before wrapping up warm for the evening’s spectacular, as hundreds of lanterns illuminate the water. Address: Clapham Common, Windmill Drive, London SW4 9DE Website: waterlanternfestival.com 6. Feast on Asian flavours along Brick Lane's curry festival 20 September The Brick Lane Curry Festival returns this Sunday, spicier and livelier than ever before following its triumphant 2025 comeback. The celebration of Bangladeshi and South Asian food, culture and community sees Brick Lane transform into a lively street festival as restaurants and vendors spill onto the iconic street. Expect traditional lion dancing, puppet shows and plenty of DJ shows between endless al fresco feasting. Address: Brick Lane, Tower Hamlets, London Website: eventbrite.co.uk 7. Get cultured across Chelsea 16 - 20 September Chelsea Arts Festival brings five days of film, literature, visual art, theatre, music and performance to venues across one of London’s glitziest neighbourhoods this week. Highlights include an exclusive Sense and Sensibility conversation at Cadogan Hall, with Fiona Shaw, Bodhi Rae Breathnach and screenwriter Diana Reid discussing the new adaptation ahead of its UK cinema release. Literature lovers can hear from Bernardine Evaristo, Katherine Rundell and Asa Butterfield, while Gavin Turk explores the role of rubbish in art at Saatchi Gallery. On Sunday, Duke of York Square becomes an open-air market home to artists, live music and workshops. Address: Across Chelsea Website: chelseaartsfestival.com 8. Savour a Sunday feast with a difference Sundays from 6 September If things still feel a little too balmy for a Sunday roast, make your way to Manteca, where Chris Leach’s team are serving special spreads sure to banish the dreaded scaries. The new, regularly changing menus are inspired by the family feasts Chris devoured during his journeys through Rome and Naples, designed to be enjoyed by groups. Think starters such as olives stuffed with Italian sausage and seafood fritto miso, followed by a large centrepiece such as a hearty tray of lasagne or spaghetti and meatballs, to be passed around. It’s great news for oenophiles, too, as head of wine Emily Acha Derrington is uncorking different magnums each weekend and pouring glasses all afternoon long. Address: Manteca, 49-51 Curtain Road, London EC2A 3PT Website: mantecarestaurant.co.uk 9. Check out the city’s new adults’ playground Open now Looking for a buzzy new hangout in the city? Look no further than Roxy Ballroom Holborn, which, following its official opening, promises flowing cocktails with a side of competitive chaos. Crazy pool, high-tech darts, basketball hoops, ping pong tables and karaoke booths are just a few of the activities on offer across the 12,000 square foot site, while the bar serves an array of tangy concoctions and American-style bites. Address: Roxy Ballroom Holborn, 246 High Holborn, London WC1V 7BN Website: roxyleisure.co.uk 10. Savour BBQ flavours at The Ned 4 September - 4 October Swanky London hotel The Ned welcomes two Michelin-starred barbecue chefs for a month of flame-kissed flavours from this Saturday. John Bates from InterStellar BBQ and Ali Clem from la Barbecue transform The Ned’s Electric Bar and Diner with Texan scents and flavours, serving a menu showcasing the craftsmanship, provenance and bold flavours that have made Austin one of the world's tastiest destinations. Think sharing trays uniting highlights from each restaurant’s menu, packed with treats such as peach tea-glazed pork belly, tender pulled lamb shoulder, chimichurri beef short rib and chopped cheese sausage. Address: Electric Bar & Diner, The Ned London, 27 Poultry, City of London Website: thened.com

item.title: Behind the scenes with Condé Nast Traveller on its latest fashion shoot in Salzburg, Austria
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.37
A team from the UK, France, Italy, the Czech Republic and Germany travelled to the beautiful lakes, soaring Alpine peaks and historical towns of the Salzkammergut region in Austria to shoot the new Fall/Winter collections. The varied weather, where you can experience all seasons in one day, inspired a rich palette of outfits from faux furs to gossamer silk. Soft leather and chunky knitwear, paired with diamonds and pearls, fit in perfectly with the elegant Salzburg crowd, who didn’t seem surprised to see our model, Ustyna, treat the cobbled street as her catwalk in a full look from Maria Grazia Chiuri’s first collection for Fendi. Here we share a behind-the-scenes peek at the locations and looks. Traunkirchen, Lake Traunsee The village of Traunkirchen lies on the western edge of Lake Traunsee in the Salzkammergut, directly across from Traunstein, an imposing peak that rises dramatically above the water. The dramatic scene is unsurprisingly a favourite spot among Instagrammers and was a shoo-in for the UK cover and a bright Chanel coat. The best view of the mountain is from the dock at Das Traunsee – Das Hotel zum See, whose owner Wolfgang Gröller has a considered collection of vintage boats. From time to time, he enjoys taking lucky guests out onto the water – our model Ustyna being one of them! First on the traditional boat in a national-inspired denim look and then again on the more modern motor boat wearing a very smart Stella McCartney Moire silk suit. Along with its charming shops and old boathouses, Traunkirchen’s town centre draws people with its stone walls and boathouses set amid green meadows. Other attractions include the Belétage restaurant and bar at the Hotel Post am See, a second property from the Gröller family. We recommended the basil cocktail for a refreshing start to an evening of traditional Austrian food. Feuerkogel Not far from Traunkirchen, the Feuerkogel is a must-hike mountain (if you’d rather, you can opt to take a cable car to the top). When there is still snow on the ground at the 5,200-foot summit, conditions can shift within minutes from crystal-clear sunlight to thick fog, a dynamic shoot location to say the least. If the visibility is good, stay on the northern side of the crest where several terraces offer the best views of the region, and a hot drink. If clouds roll in, a short hike takes you to Alberfeldkogel mountain less than a mile west of the Feuerkogel. Fir trees, cliffs and a mist-shrouded icy terrain create a mystical atmosphere like something out of a fantasy film. This was the perfect place to re-enact that twirling scene from The Sound of Music and to Yodel into the void. Our hairdresser Paulo was inspired by Heidi’s twin plaits, and they looked so chic against the snowy vista in a Louis Vuitton jumper dress complete with hood. Konditorei Zauner, Bad Ischl In the spa town of Bad Ischl, around 30 minutes by car from Traunkirchen, you’ll find the Konditorei Zauner, a patisserie with a glorious display case filled with exquisitely decorated cakes. Zauner has been in business since 1832, and to this day lovingly preserves traditional Austrian coffee culture, serving drinks from a milky melange to an indulgent double mocha. Ustyna, dressed exquisitely in Prada, fit right in. They also offer the country’s largest selection of cakes with some 250 creations as well as about 60 varieties of truffles, pralines and chocolates. The Zaunerstollen, a hazelnut and chocolate wafer, and the Ischler Törtchen, a fruity shortbread, are not to be missed. Lake Fuschl Located on the shores of Lake Fuschl, the Rosewood Schloss Fuschl Hotel is truly straight out of a movie… scenes from the famous Sissi trilogy of films starring Austrian-born Romy Schneider were shot here, and there is a small museum on-site. Today it is the hotel, inside and out, that is the star. The bar is one of the most beautiful in the country with dark wood panelling and hand-painted murals, while the clear lake is strikingly blue. It’s also decidedly more peaceful than other nearby lakes as motorboats are strictly prohibited. Every swim (or paddle) in its waters and every stroll through the nearby green meadows and forests feels like a meditative moment. When the weather might tempt you indoors, the oil paintings on display, whisky menu and board games on offer are extensive. Salzburg The most important city in this part of Austria, Salzburg is famous for its cultural highlights – it’s a destination for everyone who loves art, music and cuisine. The Hotel Goldener Hirsch, a Luxury Collection Hotel, is the place to enjoy a morning coffee with the dailies in a gemütlich historic setting – the hotel was first mentioned in a document from 1407. Or head straight to dinner, where backhendl, a traditional Austrian breaded fried chicken, is a delicious treat. A must on every Salzburg itinerary is a visit to the Kirchtag factory in the old Getreidegasse lane where Mozart was born. There you can watch craftsmen make umbrellas by hand. If you ask nicely, you may be able to take in the city views from the rooftop terrace, wearing Burberry, optional of course. It could be one of the most memorable moments of your Austrian holiday.

item.title: Craft x Tech: Shining a light on Japan’s Tokai region at London Design Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.20
What happens when centuries-old Japanese craft techniques meet the imagination of some of the world’s most experimental designers? At this year’s London Design Festival, the answer can be found inside the V&A in South Kensington, where six artisans from Japan’s Tokai region have joined forces with internationally acclaimed designers and artists to create a new generation of objects. The resulting works span ceramics, washi paper, textiles, cloisonné enamel, and braided cord, but share a common starting point: a desire to view tradition as something alive rather than fixed. For Craft x Tech Tokai Project, founded by designer and engineer Dr Hideki Yoshimoto of design studio Tangent, each designer was paired with a specialist maker from one of the region’s long-established craft communities, bringing contemporary perspectives to techniques passed down through generations. It forms one of the key shows at this year’s festival. “Japan has accumulated an extraordinary amount of knowledge through craft – knowledge about materials, processes, nature and making – much of it developed over hundreds of years,” says Yoshimoto. “I wanted to take that knowledge outside the context in which it is normally understood, and see what new relevance it might have when it encounters very different minds.” Tokai, which encompasses the prefectures of Aichi, Gifu, Mie and Shizuoka, has a rich history of making. Its abundant water, natural resources, high-quality clay and position along historic trade routes have fostered a diverse craft culture, while traditional knowledge and industrial innovation have developed alongside one another. Speaking of visitors to the show, Yoshimoto says: “I hope they see that Japanese craft is not one homogeneous culture, but an accumulation of very specific knowledge developed in different places over a very long time. Tokai is particularly rich in this respect, and if the project can bring some of that knowledge into a wider contemporary context, I think that is more important than simply introducing Japanese craft to a new audience.” Here, we speak to the designers behind the collaborations about the makers they worked with, the techniques they encountered, and what happened when their own creative languages met centuries of Japanese craft knowledge. Fushi: David Caon × Yohei Ito For Fushi, Australian industrial designer David Caon collaborated with Yohei Ito of pottery manufacturer Fudogama to explore the possibilities of Mino Yaki ceramics. Together they created a console and lighting piece from modular ceramic elements. “The material drove most of the decisions in the design, especially in terms of form and scale,” says Caon, who embraced the randomness of the glazing process in favour of its “deeply beautiful and emotive” surface. In Tokai, he was surprised to discover that the craftsmen surrounding the process were “young and energetic”, rather than the older, more serious group he had expected. The collaboration reinforced Caon’s belief in putting more faith in a fabricator's advice and not trying to control every detail. The precision lies in the form and structure of the modules, while the Oribe glaze is deliberately left unconstrained. “I hope people get a little lost looking at all the different ways the glaze has reacted across the individual modules,” he says. Websites: @caondesignoffice, fudogama.com Chair in Japanese Nuki and Dami style, The Everyday at the Atelier: Eugene Kangawa x Mayuki Kato Japanese contemporary artist Eugene Kangawa worked with Mayuki Kato of pottery manufacturer Shingama, drawing on the brushwork and tonal variation of the Japanese underglazed porcelain craft Seto Sometsuke Yaki. “The diversity of expression that comes from clay, the handwork of the brush, and the variations created by heat were especially compelling,” says Kangawa. “In particular, the variations within the deep indigo blue were fascinating.” The collaboration evolved through experimentation, with the kiln undertaking tests it had never tried before, while deliberately retaining “a diversity of forms and moments.” For Kangawa, the process reinforced his belief that craft is intrinsically connected to the geology, history and everyday life of a place. “New discoveries often seem to lie within the process of trial and error,” he explains. He hopes the finished work encourages people to recognise that even techniques passed down for generations can still leave room for new findings. Websites: the-eugene-studio.com, store.singama.jp Kasane: Philippe Malouin × Shigeyuki Ando Shigeyuki Ando of Ando Cloisonne and British-Canadian designer Philippe Malouin joined forces to explore the architectural potential of Owari Shippo cloisonné (a type of enamelware). “The first thing that struck me was the precision of the work and the depth of the enamel,” says Malouin. “It somehow feels very precise and technical, but also obviously handmade.” The project took shape around a practical limitation: the kiln's maximum size. Rather than work against it, Malouin designed a series of boxes that could be stacked to form a larger, totem-like object. The pattern began as “very casual marks” drawn randomly with a felt marker, which Ando and his team translated into silver wire and black enamel. Visiting the Tokai region gave Malouin a deeper appreciation of its craft traditions: “I already had a huge amount of respect for Japanese craft, but being in the Tokai region made me understand how closely these techniques are connected to a particular place and to the people who practise them.” Of the finished piece, he says: “I hope that, at first, people see something quite simple and calm. Then, when they get closer, they start to understand how complicated it actually is.” Websites: philippemalouin.com, ando-shippo.co.jp Grid Unwoven: Lanzavecchia + Wai × Takanori Senda Grid Unwoven brings together Takanori Senda of Warabi Paper Company with designers Francesca Lanzavecchia and Hunn Wai of Lanzavecchia + Wai. They have reinterpreted the traditional Japanese shōji – a lightweight sliding screen traditionally made with a wooden lattice and translucent paper – through the material qualities of Mino Washi, a handmade Japanese paper. “We came to see washi not as a surface, but as a living material that holds light within itself,” say Lanzavecchia + Wai. Working with Senda revealed how its fibres, density, and translucency could become architectural qualities. “We were interested in imagining what would happen if that order were touched by nature, as if a ripple or a raindrop had disturbed the grid. The wooden structure begins to bend and soften, while the washi and light amplify this sense of movement,” they explain. Their experience of Tokai also reinforced the connection between Japanese craft and its landscape: “The rivers, the kozo, the workshops, the people all shape the final work. We loved seeing how craft is not separated from everyday life there. It is embedded in homes, architecture, and the landscape itself.” The turning point in their creative process came at a visit to Senda's workshop: “We realised washi could extend far beyond the traditional sheet, into architecture and interiors. That understanding shifted our ambition, from designing a screen to creating a quiet spatial experience.” Website: lanzavecchia-wai.com, warabipapercompany.com Kataginu: Bethan Laura Wood x Hiroyuki Murase British designer Bethan Laura Wood collaborated with Hiroyuki Murase of Suzusan, transforming the colour and texture of Arimatsu Narumi Shibori – a traditional Japanese textile technique that creates patterns by folding, stitching, binding or clamping fabric before dyeing – into illuminated sculptural works. After researching textile shades and volumes, Wood was intrigued to create a family of lighting that retained elements normally removed during the process. She worked with Suzusan to develop colours that would respond to light: “I discovered that the soft, gentle pastel pink transforms into an almost neon colour when lit.” She was particularly drawn to the interplay between control and chance in the technique, from the delicacy of traditional threadwork to the organic effects of reactive dyes. Working directly with Suzusan allowed the project to evolve through testing and experimentation. “It was very important for me to get to visit the company in Tokai to see how they make their work and be able to discuss different directions and possibilities,” she says. “I really enjoyed seeing the crafts in the flesh and getting to have a go…and of course the yummy food.” Websites: bethanlaurawood.com, suzusan.com Yamollo: Atang Tshikare x Tomoyuki Matsuda Created by South African designer Atang Tshikare and Tomoyuki Matsuda of Itogo, Yamollo is a sculptural lighting work informed by the structure and colour of Iga Kumihimo braided cords. “The braiding process made me think about sculpture as a living line rather than a fixed object. I became interested in how repeated strands could create volume, movement and shadow, allowing light to become an active material within the form,” says Tshikare. The precision of the Kumihimo art form also reminded him of African hair-braiding and craft traditions, “where repetition and rhythm are used to create meaning and structure.” A trip to Tokai deepened his appreciation of the patience, discipline, and intergenerational knowledge embedded in Japanese craft, while showing him how preservation and innovation can coexist. The collaboration ultimately became a cross-cultural exchange, with Tshikare preserving the integrity of the Kumihimo technique while exploring it in a new sculptural context. “For me, respect comes from understanding rather than imitation,” he says. “The work is ultimately about finding common threads between different cultures, histories and ways of making, and recognising how craft can become a bridge between them for a brighter future.” Websites: atangtshikare.com, itogo.co.jp Find Craft x Tech at Medieval & Renaissance, Room 64b, The Simon Sainsbury Gallery, V&A South Kensington, as part of London Design Festival 2026. Exhibition runs 12 - 30 September 2026. Free entry. Find out more at craft-x-tech.com and londondesignfestival.com.

item.title: Elinor Dashwood's guide to Devon: wild moors, rickety antiques and historic pubs for the ultimate Jane Austen escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.06
There are few places in the world I know and love quite as much as Devon. I spent much of my youth growing up in the county that’s sandwiched between Dorset and Cornwall, exploring its woods, rolling hills and beaches, as well as its creaking old pubs and other assorted watering holes. With ancient lore baked into its bones, it’s little wonder this corner of the West Country has captured the imaginations of writers for centuries. Among all that verdant countryside, there really is magic at every turn. Jane Austen knew it. She spent time in Devon with her family in the early 19th century and, later, set much of Sense and Sensibility there. After leaving behind the grandeur of Norland, the Dashwoods move to Barton Cottage, on a fictional estate a few miles from Exeter. Their new abode may be considerably more modest than the home they have left behind, but its surroundings are thoroughly romantic: nestled in a valley, backing out onto high hills, and winding lanes, bucolic downs, woods, knolls and streams all around. It is nothing if not idyllic. With a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility heading to cinemas this September, I decided to explore my hometown through the eyes of the book's heroine, Elinor Dashwood (played by Daisy Edgar-Jones in the upcoming film). From windswept walks to antique hunting, these are the places I think a modern-day Dashwood would frequent – and possibly fall in love along the way. Explore Dartmoor National Park Much of the Devon landscape you’ll see in this year’s adaptation is filmed in Dartmoor National Park, where vast stretches of open moorland are punctuated by granite tors, swirling rivers and plenty of wildlife – birds of prey, otters and, yes, Dartmoor ponies. Much of the production was based around Princetown, Tavistock and Gutter Tor near Yelverton, with Edgar-Jones knowingly referring to filming on “stormy Dartmoor” in a recent interview. There are countless walks through the national park, whether you want a gentle ramble or something more dramatic. AllTrails is particularly useful for finding routes on the go, but whichever direction you head in, expect sweeping views and the kind of wild landscape that feels made for an Austen heroine. Follow the antiques trail in Ashburton For furniture, art, books, trinkets and beyond, there is nowhere quite like Ashburton, home to more than 10 antique shops clustered together on the informally named Ashburton Antiques Trail. One can easily imagine Elinor Dashwood picking up a neat walnut writing desk, a stack of books or a pair of candlesticks here, alongside any number of other treasures she happened upon.
