Start along North Street, stopping at The Shambles, The Globe, Catherine Waters Antiques and Denis Perry Antiques and Interiors, where you’ll find everything from sizeable pieces of furniture to smaller decorative treasures. Continue along East Street for East Street Antiques and Alchemy Antiques, before ducking into the tiny shops on St Lawrence Lane, where rummaging is very much part of the fun. You’ll find pieces spanning the centuries – the 19th included – and at all manner of price points. Eat at Emilia Once the antiques have been acquired, there’s no better place to refuel than Emilia, a tiny Italian restaurant and wine bar on Ashburton’s East Street. The menu is designed for sharing, with plates spanning pappardelle with duck ragu and braised pork to pickled fennel and plenty of good bread to mop up olive oil, all eaten on chunky wooden tables. While it’s true that Elinor probably wouldn’t have been particularly au fait with Italian cuisine, it’s a lovely, rustic, cosy visit for anyone in the area – somewhere I'm fairly certain a modern-day Dashwood would surely adore. Wander around RHS Garden Rosemoor If you were to picture the perfect Austen-worthy garden, RHS Garden Rosemoor might be it. Like Barton Cottage, it sits in a valley, and encompasses everything from carefully designed formal gardens to sprawling woodland filled with ancient trees. It’s an ideal place to wander, lost in thought – a pastime of which any Dashwood sister would surely approve. Thanks to clever planting, there is something to see in every season, although late spring and summer are particularly lovely. Don’t miss the two rose gardens, home to more than 2,000 roses, both old and modern, which provide as much fragrance as they do colour. The cottage garden, complete with thatched summer house, is similarly enchanting. Together, they make for a very pretty way to while away a few hours. Go horse riding When in Rome, do as the Romans do – and in Devon, many would consider horse riding a crucial part of country life. In the novel, the Dashwood sisters sadly have to give up their horses when they leave Norland for Devon, but with a little artistic licence – and given that Elinor is depicted on horseback in Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation – it seems safe to assume she’d take the opportunity to ride across the moor if she could. Close to Widecombe-in-the-Moor is Shilstone Rocks, a family-run riding centre where I learned to ride way back when. As well as mastering the basics in its – mercifully sandy-floored – arena, you can head out on hacks across the surrounding moorland. Few things make you feel more immersed in the Dartmoor landscape. Have lunch at Riverford Field Kitchen While we don’t know Elinor Dashwood’s modern culinary preferences, I’m willing to bet she’d be a farm-to-table kind of woman, preferring local produce for its taste and health benefits. Riverford Field Kitchen, on Riverford’s organic farm near Buckfastleigh, feels like an obvious choice. Here, organic vegetables take centre stage in generous, seasonal dishes, which are brought out to the whole restaurant at the same time. With dried flowers punctuating wood-clad walls and much of what’s on the plate grown just outside, it’s an excellent – and delicious – way to get your five a day. Stay at Glebe House Once a vicarage, Glebe House is now a Georgian guest house set within 15 acres of beautiful East Devon countryside overlooking the Coly Valley. There’s a kitchen garden, where produce is grown before making its way onto guests’ plates, an outdoor swimming pool and the sort of pastoral views Elinor could happily lose herself in. Inside is just as charming. With interiors that nod to Charleston, the rooms are layered with pattern, paintings, wooden armoires, antique furniture and inviting fireside spots made for reading. It’s colourful and characterful rather than overly polished – exactly the sort of country house one imagines a Dashwood sister settling happily into. Have a pint at the Pilchard Inn Given Elinor’s fondness for walking and the outdoors, she’d be impressed by the enormous beach at Bigbury-on-Sea, particularly at low tide, when great stretches of sand and rock are exposed for exploring. It’s then that you can walk across to Burgh Island, the island famously associated with another female writer, Agatha Christie, who used it as inspiration and a setting for some of her novels. Perched on the island overlooking the sea is the tiny Pilchard Inn. Dating back to 1336, it’s an atmospheric, slightly ramshackle pub that has welcomed fishermen, smugglers and countless other characters over the centuries. Today, it makes an excellent stopping point for a pint and a bowl of chips before heading back across the sand. Browse the Devon and Exeter Institution As an avid reader, Elinor would have loved the Devon and Exeter Institution, a historic independent library on Exeter’s Cathedral Green. Founded in 1813, just two years after Sense and Sensibility was published, it is home to two spectacular Georgian library rooms, lined with books and topped by cupolas. Today, visitors can buy a day membership or join one of the Institution’s free guided tours on Wednesday afternoons, providing the perfect excuse to lose an hour or two among the leather-bound books – including some of Austen’s oldest works. Explore Killerton For another dose of history, head to the National Trust’s Killerton, a grand Georgian country house just outside Exeter. Surrounded by thousands of acres of farmland, woodland and orchards, the house is also home to the National Trust’s largest fashion collection – an archive of more than 20,000 items spanning centuries of dress. Think 18th and 19th century clothes – the sort of garments Elinor herself might have worn – alongside pieces belonging to Queen Victoria and 20th-century couture. Not everything is displayed at once, but changing exhibitions offer a fascinating glimpse into the way people have dressed over the centuries. For a heroine known for observing the world around her rather carefully, it feels like a fitting final stop.

item.title: Inside the £1 billion renovation of London’s most glamorous new hotel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.04
If you peer through the leafy canopies of Green Park, you’ll spy a grand mansion proudly standing watch. From its Piccadilly vantage point, Cambridge House has welcomed some of the capital’s grandest residents across its threshold, from Queen Victoria and Lawrence of Arabia to author Ian Fleming. For more than two decades it was home to Prince Adolphus, Duke of Cambridge, then became the townhouse residence of prime minister Lord Palmerston, before finally acting as a base for the Naval and Military Club (otherwise infamously known as the In & Out Club). Now, this 18th-century landmark is entering its newest lease of life – this time, as a magnificent, marble-draped hotel. Condé Nast Traveller has the exclusive first glimpse inside the Cambridge House, Auberge Collection, and we can confirm it’s as glamorous as you’d expect. Think marble-veined hallways, Palladian-style courtyards, majestic sweeping staircases and gilded suites, complete with views across Piccadilly and sprawling Green Park beyond. Fresh off the back of their work on The Twenty Two, Burlington Arcade and Admiralty Arch, British businessmen and hoteliers the Reuben Brothers have embarked on a £1 billion regeneration project for this area of Mayfair, turning this Georgian mansion into one of London’s glitziest hotels – Auberge Collection’s debut hotel in London. “Our vision for the Piccadilly Estate is to preserve what makes this part of London so special, while giving it a renewed sense of purpose,” reads a statement from the Brothers. “Cambridge House is an exceptional piece of London’s heritage, and its restoration has been approached with the care and respect that such a building deserves. We have sought to retain the character and integrity of the house while bringing a fresh perspective to the way it can be experienced today.” Leading the design team were Jean-Louis Deniot (Waldorf Astoria NYC) and Laura Gonzalez (Casa Monti in Rome, Byblos in Saint Tropez), bringing together modern, sleek interiors with decadent trimmings and regal allure in equal measure. In the Augusta Suite, for example, shades of duck egg blue and soothing cream tones are offset by dazzling chandeliers, gold-rimmed mirrors and plush furnishings, while the Adolphus Suite – an ode to the building’s original Duke of Cambridge resident – is a chic, grey-toned affair. On the ground floor, Major’s is rumoured to be London’s hottest new dining space. The team behind Carbone and Torrisi have created the ultimate American chophouse-style restaurant in the restored Georgian ballroom. Diners can expect towering seafood platters, formal caviar service, and an impressive steak selection from British farmers and hunters, all served in one of Mayfair’s most glamorous dining rooms – or outside in the jasmine-fringed courtyard. The signature bar is also causing a stir in London's drinking scene, with Gonzalez guaranteed to deliver a fittingly lavish space for guests to sample bottles from an impressive wine cellar. Major's will have a cocktail menu featuring no fewer than 10 takes on the martini – perfectly suitable for a former Fleming drinking den – while the bar itself is sure to have a stellar drinks menu, too. There will also be a wellness club and spa area. Spread across three floors, the bathhouse will feature hydrotherapy facilities, heated swimming pool, six treatment rooms, a gym, and a relaxation lounge. Later in 2027, the hotel will unveil a members' club. Cambridge House, Auberge Collection is set to open its doors in early 2027, with room rates starting at £1,250. “For us, this is about more than restoring an important building,” says the team at Reuben Brothers. “It is about giving Cambridge House a new chapter, one that respects its past, embraces its future and ensures that it remains an important part of London for generations to come.” For more information, visit auberge.com/cambridgehouse.

item.title: El Niño is returning – here's how it could affect your travel plans
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.03
El Niño has officially arrived – at least according to Japan – and some forecasters are suggesting it could eventually develop into a rare “super” event capable of dramatically altering weather patterns across much of the planet, from the safari plains of East Africa to the coral atolls of the Indian Ocean. For travellers, that could mean everything from a quieter Atlantic hurricane season to worsening wildfire smoke in Southeast Asia, stress on reefs in the Pacific and floods, landslides and transport disruption across parts of the Americas – with the most significant impacts likely to emerge from late 2026 into 2027. Previous El Niños have brought major devastation across continents. From 2015 to the following year, severe drought affected parts of southern Africa, Ethiopia and Central America, vast fires burned through drought-stricken Indonesian forests and peatlands and exceptional ocean heat contributed to the longest global coral bleaching event then recorded. More recently, the strong El Niño recorded in 2024 helped propel that year to the highest global temperature yet measured, with extreme rainfall and flooding killing more than 180 people in southern Brazil and displacing around 600,000. In June 2026, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) stated that “In Europe, this El Niño could be strong enough to flip the pattern: instead of colder-than-normal autumn temperatures that typically accompany it, Europe may experience warmer-than-normal conditions, with that warmth building towards spring 2027”. The House of Commons Library reports that the meteorological effects of El Niño on Europe could result in more extreme winter weather in the UK in 2027. Jump to… In an update issued on Wednesday, 10 June, the Japan Meteorological Agency became the first major national forecasting organisation to confirm the onset of the phenomenon, declaring that El Niño conditions had been present across the equatorial Pacific since spring 2026. Sea surface temperatures in the agency’s closely monitored Niño 3 region were already 1.2C above normal during May, while unusually warm water beneath the Pacific continued to spread eastwards and the trade winds above it weakened, laying the foundations for what could become the dominant climate story of the next 18 months. That's significant because other global agencies have so far stopped just short of formally announcing that an El Niño event is underway – but the World Meteorological Organisation now puts the probability of El Niño developing between June and August at 80 per cent, rising to around 90 per cent or more through the autumn, and has told governments that the time for preparation has already begun. What makes people so apprehensive of El Niño is that it rarely stays where it starts. A patch of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific can eventually influence everything from rainfall in Kenya to drought around Victoria Falls, wildfire risk in Indonesia and winter storms in California. “We need to prepare for a potentially strong El Niño event,” World Meteorological Organisation secretary-general Celeste Saulo warned this month, pointing to the prospect of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves both on land and at sea. UN secretary-general António Guterres was blunter, saying El Niño would “pour fuel on the fire of a warming world”, allowing its effects to travel farther and strike harder. The most alarming forecasts raise the possibility that the event could eventually cross into “super El Niño” territory, an unofficial term generally applied when temperatures in a key part of the tropical Pacific rise at least 2°C above normal, with such events occurring only around once every decade or so, and historically leaving a trail of droughts, floods, fires and failed harvests across several continents. “When you have an El Niño over what climate change already brought, the risks are enormous,” Francisco Aquino, head of the climate centre at Brazil’s Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, told Reuters. Piers Forster, professor of physical climate change at the University of Leeds, meanwhile described the developing event as a potential “window into the future” – a preview of weather extremes that may become increasingly ordinary as the planet continues to warm. Here's everything travellers need to know about this year's El Niño weather system. What exactly is El Niño? El Niño is a recurring warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can disturb weather thousands of miles beyond the ocean where it begins. Under usual conditions, easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards towards Indonesia and northern Australia. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the depths off Peru and Ecuador, while the warmer western Pacific produces some of the world’s most dramatic tropical rainstorms. During El Niño, those trade winds weaken, and the great reservoir of warm water begins sliding back towards the east, suppressing the cold upwelling off South America and dragging the principal zone of tropical thunderstorms across the Pacific with it. That interferes with the Walker circulation – the vast loop of rising and sinking air above the tropics – and sends a series of atmospheric ripples around the planet, with results that can appear entirely disconnected from their source. Is El Niño now officially underway? According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, yes. On Wednesday, 10 June, the organisation said El Niño conditions had been present since spring 2026. Sea surface temperatures in its monitored Niño 3 region were 1.2°C above normal during May and warmer-than-average water extended beneath much of the equatorial Pacific as the trade winds over the central Pacific had weakened. Japan now considers it virtually certain that El Niño will persist through the northern hemisphere autumn. Other global agencies have been more cautious, although they are moving towards the same conclusion. NOAA’s latest full assessment continued to classify the Pacific as neutral while giving El Niño an 82 per cent chance of emerging between May and July and a 96 per cent chance of persisting into the coming winter. The World Meteorological Organisation placed the probability at 80 per cent for June to August, rising to around 90 per cent or more after. Why is this particular El Niño attracting so much attention? Most international models currently suggest that the event will become at least moderate, with a strong event also possible. Some longer-range projections extend into the much rarer territory sometimes described as a “super El Niño”. That's generally used for an exceptionally powerful event in which temperatures across an important section of the central tropical Pacific rise roughly 2°C or more above average – and only a small number of modern El Niños have reached comparable strength. All three became associated with severe and simultaneous weather disruption across several continents. Yet the most extreme projections for 2026 remain just that. NOAA has said there is still substantial uncertainty over peak strength, with no single category dominating its probabilities. Stronger El Niños also make certain consequences more likely rather than guaranteeing them. The amount of heat already sitting beneath the Pacific explains why forecasters are watching so closely – and the WMO has urged governments to prepare for a potentially strong event capable of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves on land and at sea. When will travellers begin to notice the effects? The first visible signs for travellers may be slightly subtler – unusually dry conditions in Bali, greener-than-usual safari landscapes in East Africa, or a quieter Atlantic hurricane season than forecasters had expected. El Niño usually develops between spring and early summer, strengthens through autumn and peaks between November and February. Its effects often then continue through the following spring or summer, while slower consequences – such as depleted reservoirs, damaged reefs, altered river levels and stressed wildlife populations – may last considerably longer. During summer and autumn 2026, travellers could begin seeing the first shifts in tropical cyclone activity, Southeast Asian rainfall, wildfire conditions and the Asian and African monsoons. From around October, attention is likely to turn towards East Africa’s short rains, drought risks in southern Africa and Australia, and the possibility of heavy rain across Peru and Ecuador. The influence on the US, Canada and parts of East Asia usually becomes clearest during the northern hemisphere winter, particularly between December and March. Yet its effect on global temperature may peak later still. El Niño releases heat stored in the tropical Pacific into the atmosphere, meaning the year after an event develops can be exceptionally warm. The strong 2023-24 El Niño helped push 2024 to record global temperatures, and the return of the phenomenon has already raised concerns that 2027 could challenge those records again. What could happen to travel during the 2026–27 El Niño? The potential impacts are wide-ranging and vary dramatically by country. The same climate pattern that brings blue skies to Bali could contribute to flooding in Peru, while travellers enjoying greener safari landscapes in Kenya may be doing so during the same season that drought grips southern Africa. Across Indonesia and parts of maritime Southeast Asia, suppressed rainfall could initially look like ideal holiday weather, but as the dry season deepens, the same conditions can produce water stress, forest and peat fires, and smoke capable of spreading into Singapore and Malaysia. East Africa may face the reverse problem later in the year. Stronger October to December rains could turn safari landscapes a magnificent green while reducing roads to mud, flooding airstrips and complicating transfers to remote camps. Southern Africa may become hotter and drier, improving wildlife visibility around shrinking waterholes in the short term but placing animals, rivers and communities under increasing strain if drought persists. According to analysts, at Victoria Falls, reduced upstream rainfall could eventually reduce the thunderous curtain of water pouring over Victoria Falls, although the effect would be delayed by the vast size of the Zambezi catchment. Coral reefs are another major concern. The world has only recently emerged from the most extensive global bleaching event recorded, during which heat stress affected more than 80% of reef area – and further Pacific warming could expose already weakened reefs to another damaging season before they have had time to recover. Does El Niño mean the weather will be bad everywhere? No – and some destinations may experience conditions travellers actually consider favourable. The Caribbean could have fewer hurricanes, California ski resorts could receive substantial snowfall and drier weather may produce long stretches of sunshine across Indonesia. The danger lies in the point at which favourable weather becomes excessive – for example, with snow closing mountain roads, rain carrying away bridges crossing it, or sunshine becoming drought. Could El Niño affect safaris in Kenya or Tanzania? Quite possibly – and not necessarily for the worse. One of El Niño’s most consistent signatures is heavier short rains across East Africa between October and December. The East African savannah can look extraordinary after rain as dust settles and grasslands turn emerald green – with migratory birds arriving in huge numbers. Yet tracks that are easily navigable in August could become axle-deep mud by November, and small bush airstrips may temporarily close after particularly heavy downpours. During the 1997-98 El Niño, exceptionally heavy rain caused widespread flooding across East Africa, washing out roads and bridges in Kenya and leaving parts of the country difficult to reach. The most recent event offered another warning, as across Tanzania, the rains of 2023 and 2024 damaged 63 bridges, more than 800 kilometres of road and hundreds of culverts. Could El Niño affect the Maldives? The Maldives sits atop one of the world’s most celebrated coral reef systems, making it one of the destinations most exposed to El Niño’s effects beneath the surface rather than above it. During the enormous 1997-98 event, sea temperatures rose so dramatically that large areas of coral across the Indian Ocean bleached, and scientists estimate that some Maldivian reefs lost more than 90 per cent of their shallow coral cover. The good news is that many reefs have since recovered remarkably well, but the bad news is that they are now entering another potential El Niño after enduring the most widespread global coral bleaching event ever recorded between 2023 and 2025. Marine life remains spectacular even on reefs that have experienced bleaching, but conditions may vary dramatically between atolls, and some reefs could face renewed stress if ocean temperatures climb significantly during late 2026 and early 2027. More widely, the Maldives may experience warmer seas, periods of unusual calm and changes in rainfall patterns, but it is unlikely to see the kind of extreme droughts or floods that could affect parts of Africa, South America or Southeast Asia. What could happen in Japan during El Niño? The country that first declared El Niño’s arrival may end up feeling relatively modest impacts compared with many tropical destinations. Historically, El Niño winters in Japan have tended to be warmer than average, which can be good news for city-break travellers exploring Tokyo, Kyoto or Osaka, but less welcome for ski resorts that are dependent on deep snowfall. The bigger concern for travellers may be summer heat. Japan has already experienced a succession of exceptionally hot summers in recent years, and El Niño’s tendency to boost global temperatures could make future heatwaves more intense. Could Thailand have a better winter than usual during El Niño? Thailand often sits on the drier side of El Niño, and during previous events, rainfall has decreased across much of the country while temperatures climbed higher than average – which means more reliable beach days in Phuket and Krabi and fewer interruptions to island-hopping itineraries. Yet there is another side to the story. The powerful 2015-16 El Niño contributed to one of Thailand’s most severe droughts in decades, with reservoirs reaching critically low levels and agricultural regions facing water shortages – so ultimately, what feels like perfect weather for a holiday can create serious challenges for the communities living through it. Should travellers to Bali and Indonesia be concerned? El Niño often brings Bali some of its most glorious weather: weeks of blue skies, lower humidity and uninterrupted sunsets. The problem is what can happen when the dry season refuses to end. The devastating Indonesian fire seasons of 1997-98 and 2015 were both closely linked to strong El Niño conditions, with vast areas of forest and peatland burned, producing smoke that spread across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia. The smoke often originates hundreds of kilometres away, yet visitors can still feel the effects through disrupted flights and deteriorating air quality. Could El Niño affect European holidays? Europe sits far enough from the tropical Pacific that El Niño’s influence becomes considerably weaker and less predictable. However, strong El Niños often contribute to record global temperatures, and Europe has become increasingly prone to severe heatwaves regardless of what happens in the Pacific. The summer after the 1997-98 event was, at the time, the hottest year ever recorded globally, and the 2015–16 event helped produce another global temperature record. The most recent El Niño contributed to 2024 becoming the hottest year in modern measurements. Mediterranean destinations that were once comfortably warm in the shoulder seasons of June or September may increasingly become the sweet spot, while July and August edge further into heatwave territory. Could El Niño affect Mauritius, Seychelles and Zanzibar? During the 2016 bleaching episode in the Seychelles, between 69 and 99 per cent of coral was bleached at monitored locations, followed by an estimated 50 per cent reduction in hard coral cover – and another marine heatwave would affect those ecosystems as they recover from earlier damage. Mauritius has also experienced El Niño-related bleaching, including its first recorded mass event in 1998, although mortality was considerably lower at many sites than in the Seychelles. The 2023–24 El Niño, meanwhile, brought above-average rain to Tanzania across two successive rainy seasons, contributing to severe floods, landslides and extensive damage to roads and bridges.

item.title: The world's busiest airport is no longer Dubai
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
The world's aviation landscape looks a little different this year, with South Korea's Incheon International Airport outranking Dubai International as the world's busiest for international passengers. According to preliminary data from the Airports Council International (ACI), released by Incheon, the South Korean airport served 38.4 million international passengers during the first six months of 2026. Once confirmed by the ACI in its World Airport Traffic Report (to be released next month), the airport will now rank as the world's busiest for the first time since opening in 2001. Dubai International Airport is expected to place outside the top five this year, despite ranking first for international traffic for the past 12 years. The decline in international footfall follows the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which reconfigured the globe's skies when it began on 28 February, with ACI data showing the UAE travel hub fell from 7.4 million passengers in February to just 2.5 million in March. Incheon also reported an 18 per cent increase in transfer passengers this year, as many who previously transferred in the Gulf on their way to Europe had to rethink their route amid airspace closures. This year, London Heathrow is set to rank in second place, recording 37.79 million passengers in the first half of the year, followed by Singapore's Changi Airport, which has seen 34.53 million international passengers pass through its terminals during this period. It's not just the war that's contributed to Incheon's sharp rise in numbers. According to the airport, an infrastructure expansion (which was completed in 2024) has enabled it to handle a larger traffic load – now serving 101 airlines flying to 158 international destinations. And with a growing global interest in Korean culture, from its TV shows to its music, food, beauty and fashion, it's little wonder the airport has continued to climb the ranks, placing fifth in 2018 to being named third busiest in 2024 and 2025, and now reaching the top spot. Before the conflict, Dubai's global status as a tourism hotspot and destination for transfers was increasing year on year. In April, it was named the world's busiest airport for international passengers in 2025, with 95.2 million international passengers landing in the city over the course of 12 months. The figure marked an increase of 3.1 per cent from 2024, and a 10.3 per cent rise from pre-pandemic numbers in 2019. In February, the emirate was also named the world's best-connected city by Mozio, which compared the journey time from arrivals to a central landmark in 50 of the world's most-visited cities. With tensions continuing and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) extending its conflict zone advisory for the Gulf until 31 August, it remains unclear when air traffic in the region will return to its pre-war levels.

item.title: The best family-friendly hotels in Sicily, recommended by a parent of three
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.43
The Sicilians are, by and large, remarkably welcoming of bambini, who are embedded in their psyche as a blessing, not an inconvenience. As such, the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily are also some of the island's most lauded. Expect cooing, overly expressive signs of affection and a society that is unabashedly pro-children, being integrated into every facet of life. Even the most elaborate hotels welcome children warmly – perhaps not the sort whose parents turn a blind eye to their darlings smudging pistachio cannoli filling into Zoffany upholstered sofas, but here, first-rate kids' clubs buy parents plenty of off-duty time. Time, that is, to enjoy a sun-dappled terrace framed by crumbling columns and palms, a haze of distant blue ring-fencing the green hills braided in olive groves and vineyards, and the irresistible waft of orange blossom and freshly baked arancini washed down with crisp Etna wines. Sicily is a wildly romantic island, layered in history, wrapped in surreal blue waters, caught in the crosshairs of civilisations, and intensely varied in its landscape, cuisine and culture – depending on which region you pootle a few kilometres over to. Wild spirits can run free on the island’s abundant argiturismos, free of the formalities and precariously balanced 17th-century busts of the high-end hotels. Where you choose to stay depends on your children’s ages, proclivities and really, how you like to holiday. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. Editor's picks of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily: Best for luxury: Villa Sant'Andrea, A Belmond Hotel Best for children at different ages: Veruda Best for teens: Bracciallieri Best kids' club: Veruda Best all-inclusive: Mangia's Costa Ragusa Borgo 5 tips for visiting Sicily with children Prepare for the heat Small children will struggle outdoors in Sicily in peak summer from about 11am-4pm. Unless they’re aligning with Sicilian siesta law or are under a shaded kids’ club, it would be wise to consider shoulder season for pre-schoolers. What’s more, many of the Baroque Sicilian towns and cities’ ancient cobblestones aren’t designed for prams, so remember to bring a good baby carrier, backpack or hop on one of their sweet family train rides that introduces children to grand Baroque architecture, pointing out the best gelato spots, chocolatiers and the gargoyles peering down from atop their palazzi. Pack smart Invest in a wide-brimmed sunhat and long-sleeved, long-legged swimsuits for tinies to save their skin from the fierce Sicilian sun. Always check with your hotel for minimum kids club age, and what time their restaurant opens – what's worse than a 7.45pm restaurant opening time when you’re children are used to eating at 5pm and being tucked up two hours later? Hire a car Unless you’re staying solely in Palermo or Catania (where Sicily’s two airports are based), it’s worth hiring a car to explore, though don’t expect the rental company to procure age-specific carseats (even if this has been agreed). I have experienced this hiccup numerous times and on my last trip, invested in two Cybex foldable Solution G2 carseats for peace of mind. Even if you book a smart transfer with hotels, you really have to emphasise the ages of your children and reconfirm to avoid the booster seat for a six month old scenario. Embrace day trips Older children and teenagers will enjoy exploring Siciliy’s maze-like towns and villages, diving into its Slim Aarons-looking pools and aquamarine swimming spots, and hopping on boat trips for uninhabited islands and caves. The beauty of Sicily is that, no matter where your hotel is located, much of the island can be explored via day trips, though families would be forgiven for indulging a little Dolce Far Niente, poolside or under the shade of the citrus trees. Take your time Having travelled to Sicily as a family multiple times, the best formula for a successful 10 days or two-week break is, unquestionably, combining a family-friendly hotel with a villa stay. Hotels provide parents with all the pampering they’re so desperately in need of (the spa facilities, the elevated dining, the kids’ club or babysitting), then a villa serves up all that precious family time and, crucially, the privacy to let children run wild and the room space to ensure everyone’s banking ample sleep. It works particularly well for multi-generational groups and opens up new areas of the island for everyone to explore. How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. For more inspiration on where to stay in Sicily and Italy, visit About the author Rosalyn Wikeley is a regular contributor to Condé Nast Traveller and a ski and Sicily expert. Former Creative Content Editor for the publication, Rosalyn has written for the Financial Times, the Telegraph, The Times, Vogue, House & Garden, the London Standard and consulted on content for leading luxury brands and hotels. She beelines for Sicily's Baroque South East every Autumn to seek out new hotels and arty enclaves, and also writes extensively on Paris, family-friendly stays and skiing.

item.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.39
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown. Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact. Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format? Alex McCoy: We [already] had a permanent space in Petworth that we were building out [for our brick-and-mortar restaurant]. There was another restaurant space down the street that was slated to be demolished, so we talked to the landlords and they were like, “It’s yours until your space is ready or our project starts.” We thought it was a great opportunity to train our staff, test the food, and work through the menus while our spot was in construction. It was in a quiet part of town, and we just really wanted to have fun with it, but it ended up becoming this cult sensation. We were packed for months in advance. We had Vogue writing about us. Bon Appetit called it one of the top new restaurants in America. But it was really only about six months total that we had the place open, which is kind of wild. We closed the pop-up in 2017. That Petworth space didn’t end up working out for us, so we had to look for a new space. In the meantime, we were doing pop-ups in New York, D.C., London. We spent a lot of time overseas and some of the bigger pop-ups were in London with our buddies at Carousel. In that time, we were always looking for a new venue, and it was the time in Europe that really evolved the brand into what it is now. How did that time on the road shape the concept and operation plan? After COVID… everyone was struggling to try to figure out how to make restaurants work. With operating and staff costs going up, people were coming up with these creative service styles with [fewer] servers and less table service and more QR codes. The math isn’t mathing, you know? It seemed to me that the model should be similar to the way things operate in Europe with these little hole-in-the-wall places in Paris and London. Chefs don’t own six or seven restaurants; they’re in there [in one place] with one or two people. Not only was that the heart and soul of what Alfie’s always was, but it felt to me to be the way forward with the brand. After we did our last pop-up in London, we found this funky little spot in Georgetown, which is a neighborhood that feels the most European of anywhere in D.C. to me. It’s this incredible 25-seat space in an alleyway behind the hustle and bustle of M Street. It’s a little gritty. You step down into the alleyway and you have to dodge cars. It’s a really cool, funky space with a lot of character. So immediately it was like, this is the spot. This encapsulates the vibe and the ambiance and the feeling and the energy of what we’re trying to do. Have things changed since running the restaurant as a pop-up? It’s very much still a pop-up mindset. Justin, myself, and Ian, who is our sous chef, we’re 90 percent of the staff at this restaurant. From a cooking perspective, twenty-five seats is perfect because it gives us this opportunity to really [pore] over small batches of food. If we’re making a curry for the day, we’re [only] making 30 orders. We’re able to look at the menu on a daily basis and assess based on what ingredients come in. If our local fishmonger has five beautiful seabreams that he’s bringing in, we’ll just throw them on the menu because we have that ability to be scrappy and change things up and make adjustments and not have to retrain the staff and everything. That also plays into Thailand’s market culture, which is the ethos of our brand. We want to challenge ourselves to make dishes utilizing what’s available around here: rockfish, soft shell crab, foraged asparagus from the Eastern Shore, morel mushrooms, things like that. Does your drink menu also play off of local ingredients? When you go to France or Italy or another wine-producing region, you go to a bar or restaurant and you’re drinking what was made in the town or right around it. You don’t often see that in D.C., even when Virginia wineries are making spectacular stuff, literally 15 to 20 minutes away by car. The majority of our wines by the glass are from Virginia and we have more than 2,000 local producers by the bottle too. Our bottles, for the most part, are between $35 and $75. We only have a couple that top that. I think a lot of people go out to eat dreading the check. But I want people to come in and just get lost in the experience and not have to worry that they can’t take a chance on something that they haven’t tried before because it’s too expensive. They don’t have to be thinking about the price of everything they’re eating and drinking while they’re here. Alfie’s also has a wine club. How does that work? Alfie’s has always [drawn] a lot of regulars, and we’ve always tried to facilitate this vibe of being your other living room. If you love wine, we want this to be a place that you want to spend a lot of your time and cater that a little bit more. Our wine club has 19 spots, and for a monthly fee of $150, you basically get a rack of your own [in the restaurant]. If you have a great collection at home, you can bring it in. Or if you have specific tastes and things that you enjoy when you come here, we can curate the wine locker for you so you can actually purchase wine at a steep discount that we don’t have on the list. If there are special selections that are too expensive for us to put on the menu, we can get those for you, and you’ll pay 50% less than standard restaurant prices. After releasing the first few days of reservations, you immediately had 700 bookings. Were you expecting that kind of reception? I wouldn’t say I expected anything. [But] I was hoping for it, and I kind of felt it. Sometimes in this industry, you can feel when something is gonna hit. Leading up to [opening] and seeing some of the interest on social media, it seemed like it was gonna go that route so we were trying to plan for it. Alfie’s scratches an itch that [D.C. diners] haven’t been able to scratch at least since 2020. The city is getting burnt out [by] small businesses being replaced by big corporate restaurant group spots, and we’re very much the antithesis of that. You walk in, and Justin and I are in the kitchen, so we can say hi to you and run food to the table. I think it’s a vibe that D.C. hasn’t had in years.

item.title: Secrets of the C-suite smoothie
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.17
Secrets of the C-suite smoothie Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Julia Baldet was a “burned out” 27-year-old pulling 100-hour weeks when she spotted the opportunity for a new kind of drinks brand last year. “I was working in finance, I was sick from stress, I didn’t have time to eat properly. But I also didn’t want something off the shelf from the supermarket.” The result was Elevate, a café in the City’s Royal Exchange that serves nutritionally enhanced smoothies in packaging that wouldn’t look out of place in a Space NK boutique. Bestsellers include The Glow (£8.90), a strawberry-pink mix of berries, yoghurt and skin-improving collagen. Muscle-boosting creatine – featured in the high-protein Lean Berries – “has also been trending”, says Baldet. A suite of £1.30 add-ons includes MCT oil (quick energy), lion’s mane (focus) pitaya (anti-oxidant) and prebiotic fibre. The brand recently opened a second café in Selfridges and is on target to hit £1mn in sales by the end of 2026. Functional nutrition is now one of the fastest-growing sectors in a wellness market worth $1.8tn globally. The rise of GLP-1s combined with an “always-on” culture means that more of us are skipping meals, and the comfortingly slurpable, customisable smoothie looks primed to fill the gap. Smoothies are also a cornerstone of the regime at Exalt, an “on-the-go nutrition” brand co-founded by Dan Wilson-Vaughan after 15 years in the banking world. Just like athletes, he says, deal makers are now looking to nutrition to give them the competitive edge. “Athletes want recovery and performance,” says Wilson-Vaughan, whose clients range from Premier League football clubs to City types. “Corporates traditionally needed a meal that actually replaces the one they skipped. They now want both.” What a lot of time-poor workers need most is protein, he says: “20g+ [a day] is a must alongside fibre and the right fats. We are also pushing the use of ashwagandha as a way of alleviating stress.” At Earthbar in Silicon Valley, the go-to smoothie is The Protocol ($14.95), a green, protein-packed blend of fruit, spinach and yerba mate (a natural source of caffeine, supposedly without the crash), plus blue spirulina, creatine, collagen and whey protein. There is also a choice of almost 50 further “add-ons”, including B12, probiotics and bee pollen, as well as L-carnitine, a supplement which some believe can help burn fat. As for whether we actually need all these add-ons, the jury is out. “Smoothies can be useful to deliver large amounts of a particular ingredient,” says James Collins, managing director of the INTRA Performance Group, which provides nutrition advice to both athletes and Fortune 500 CEOs. “However, we don’t recommend ‘functional smoothies’ for general, unstructured use. Marketing leads people to believe that a supplement can be the silver bullet for better health and performance without addressing the wider principles of nutrition, exercise and recovery.” Perhaps, just sometimes, all one needs to do is close the laptop and go out for dinner with some friends. Comments

item.title: Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.74
Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago When I say Chicago isn’t a celebrity town, that cuts both ways. We have limited tolerance for Instagram culture, we roll our eyes at round-the-block queues and, for most of us, the very notion of $20 trend smoothies triggers an allergic reaction. On the other hand, we can be provincial. At a recent concert at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, the Jumbotron cycled through drone footage of American skylines. At the sight of Chicago’s, the crowd exploded. At all others, including a glimmering and handsome New York City? Crickets. Chicagoans have a funny relationship to fame. Seeing a celebrity out and about is not just another Tuesday for us: it’s day-derailing. We’ll ignore the cardinal rule imparted by our peers on the coast and bug the hell out of them, then spend the rest of the day calling our cousins’ cousins. We keep our local celebrities close but feel inordinately stung when they decamp for another city. To better understand this hot-and-cold city, we spoke to eight cultural insiders who know it better than most. Some were forged in Chicago. Others enthusiastically adopted it. And many of them still choose to live here, even when New York and LA beckon. Jump straight to . . . Sandra Cisneros, writer and author of ‘The House on Mango Street’ (born and raised in Chicago; based in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Aon Center. After going to a concert downtown in Grant Park, we would walk over to what was the Standard Oil Building, now the Aon Center, on East Randolph Street. In the plaza’s sunken garden is the most fabulous treasure: wind sculptures by Harry Bertoia. They look like reeds, and at the dedication ceremony in 1972, the artist climbed inside the installation and “played” them. Bertoia was a furniture designer, too. When his sculptures were displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1975, it was the first and only time I’d seen a sign that said, “Please touch.” I like the idea that he thought about the poetics of these sculptures moving and making these wonderful sounds. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Hot dogs. If you haven’t had a Chicago hot dog, you haven’t had a hot dog. You have to have a bun with little poppy seeds on it, it has to be bundled in waxed paper and the french fries have to be good. Now, there are even vegan hot dogs. Recently, my family and I got some at Portillo’s late at night, and they were really good — I was surprised! One more thing I didn’t realise until two years ago that the flowers in Chicago’s public parks were so much a part of the city. To me, lilacs, peonies and lilies of the valley are the quintessential flowers of Chicago. Jeff Tweedy, musician and lead vocalist/guitarist of Wilco (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The parks. If you want to soak up what the city and culture are really like, I’d pick any of the Chicago Park District parks, like Independence in Irving Park or Gompers in North Park. Have a picnic and see how Chicagoans really recreate. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand “Dibs”. The concept of saving your parking spot, especially in heavy snow. Technically not legal, but ultimately, pretty fair and moral. If you’re the one who broke your ass shovelling snow, you should get to keep that spot for at least a day or so. What Chicago teaches you When you grow up in a smaller town like I did, there’s a belief that it’s a kinder way to live and that you can’t get that in a city. It’s not true. When I moved to Chicago, I knew more people in my neighbourhood than I did growing up — it’s all about block parties and meeting up with neighbours. Chicago has problems like everywhere else, but it’s a city that facilitates community. Rick Bayless, chef and restaurateur (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The National Museum of Mexican Art. Rather than establishing the museum downtown, the founders chose Pilsen — a predominantly Latino neighbourhood — and they chose to keep this world-class collection free to all. NMMA is not only one of our city’s best museums but an integral player in this vibrant community. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Storefront theatre. Yes, we have grand old theatres that host Broadway touring companies, and yes, we have the internationally acclaimed Steppenwolf, Goodman and Chicago Shakespeare companies. But Chicago is a city of neighbourhoods, and most of them are home to a host of storefront theatres. One of the best is TimeLine Theatre Company, which does historical pieces that have contemporary relevance. Hungry yet? Forty years ago, when we opened Frontera Grill, farmers’ markets hadn’t taken off in Chicago. Today, with local chefs championing local products, there are over 40 and growing. Now communities are hosting “alternative” farmers’ markets that start at 3pm or 4pm and sell until around 7pm on specific weekdays, rather than weekend mornings. Eve L Ewing, author, scholar and co-owner of Build Coffee & Books in Woodlawn (based in Chicago) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The South Shore Nature Sanctuary and Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary. Our city motto is urbs in horto — city in a garden. Away from all the noise and the hubbub, the marshlands and prairie are also part of our identity. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Community. The city is famously corrupt, but there’s a more generous way to understand the “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” way we do things, which is that Chicagoans look out for each other and take care of one another. If you’re my neighbour’s cousin’s pick-up basketball buddy, you’re in the circle and I’ve got to take care of you. The hill she’ll die on Everyone likes to share their (mostly ill-informed) opinions on Chicago pizza, but through and through we’re a taco city. Our ratio of great tacos per capita is off the charts. I grew up going to El Cid, a Mexican restaurant in Logan Square, while El Milagro in Pilsen both sells tacos and manufactures the best tortillas and chips. Enrique Mazzola, conductor and music director of the Lyric Opera of Chicago (divides time between Chicago and Paris) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Driehaus Museum. This small museum just off the Magnificent Mile focuses on the art, architecture and design of the American Gilded Age and the Art Nouveau period. Inside is a magnificent auditorium with interesting and diverse programming. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The walks. One of my favourites goes from downtown along the Lakefront Trail to Lincoln Park. Only a true Chicagoan can understand how beautiful this itinerary is. In general, I love walking around the city — I even walk to work at the Lyric Opera of Chicago and enjoy following the Chicago River every day. Bonus recommendation Wander around the boutique shops and cafés in the North Side neighbourhood of Andersonville. You’re still in Chicago but removed from the tourist areas and high-rises of downtown. Isaiah Collier, saxophonist and composer (divides time between Chicago and New York) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago 63rd Street Beach. The city has its madness, but it also has its tranquillity, usually by the water. Cats will get together here for drum circles — they’ve been doing it for decades. It’s therapeutic and uniquely ethnic. The overview of the city that you see from down there is kind of mythical, very cinematic. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Concerts at Pritzker Pavilion. No matter where you’re from in the city, I think we can all agree there’s something special about being able to witness a proper concert at Pritzker Pavilion. Not amateur stuff, but a full production from start to finish. It’s one hell of a location. A brutal truth We’re the most segregated major city in America. That residual effect has made people feel there are not enough opportunities. It can be disheartening for creatives. Grant Achatz, chef/creative director and co-owner of Chicago’s Alinea restaurant Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Primitive on Jefferson Street. It’s a massive showroom packed with rare antiquities from all over the world. I’m into medieval and Egyptian history, so for me it’s a rabbit hole I can lose an afternoon in. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The grit. When I showed up in 2001 with this weird, modernist way of cooking, this city embraced the risk and let me build. People here get that ambition runs quiet, that the winters bond everybody together, that nobody’s impressed with you until you’ve put in the work. You can’t feel any of that from a postcard. You’ve got to live here a while. Tasha, singer-songwriter and poet (born and raised in Chicago, based in New York) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Promontory Point. We just call it The Point. I don’t think people who aren’t from Chicago really know the secret, stunning beauty it has, especially on the South Side. There is nothing more romantic than jumping from the rocks at sunset on a sticky, hot summer day, the sky pink behind the city skyline, cicadas buzzing. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Being from the city proper. I love the way we bond over that. Not the suburbs. Not the surrounding counties. Definitely not Indiana. A love letter No matter where I end up in the world, Chicago will always be my home, the place I return to, the place that understands me, that holds my whole family and first gave me courage. Chicago forever. What do you love most about Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. item.title: Rose Chalalai Singh’s dinner with the dervishes
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.51
Rose Chalalai Singh’s dinner with the dervishes Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I first went to Turkey four years ago and have gone back every summer since. I have friends in Istanbul – sisters Başak and Defne Kocabıyıkoğlu – who I met in Paris. Together they run Nackiyé, a family-owned fashion brand inspired by the eastern Mediterranean. It was Defne and Başak who introduced me to the whirling dervishes, a Sufi Muslim group founded in the 13th century by the poet Rūmī. They practise a form of meditation and worship called Sema, where they spin in circles while dressed in long, buttonless skirts. Defne and Başak’s great-grandmother, Seyyare, was the first woman to whirl at their family’s dervish lodge in Kutahya (now a mosque). We decided to host a dinner and go to a dervish performance afterwards. The first place I head to when I land in Istanbul – and the last place I go before I leave – is Pandeli, a legendary restaurant above the Egyptian bazaar. It’s an institution; everyone has been there, from politicians to tourists. Fergus Henderson told me it’s his favourite restaurant. The walls are fitted with beautiful blue tiles, and there are framed photographs and notes from all of its visitors; its founder Pandeli Çobanoğlu was a very elegant man. I suggested it as the location for our dinner. Defne and Başak weren’t sure it was going to be possible. In its 125-year history, Pandeli has rarely opened for dinner; the gates to the bazaar usually close at 7pm and it’s right near a mosque. But I asked them to try. A few days later, Defne called me up with the good news. In exchange for a donation to the mosque, they would give us the space for the night. We just needed to have good security on the gates. At 5am on the day of the dinner, we went out on a little taxi boat to go fishing in the Black Sea, just as the light was coming in. It was magical. We caught lots of horse mackerel, a pretty blue fish, and brought it to the restaurant. I coated it in a mix of ginger powder and toasted chilli from my kitchen in Paris, where I mostly use Thai flavours, and fried it almost like tempura. We served it over a bed of yoghurt with fresh herbs and a tomato salad dressed in coriander, dry lemongrass and some seaweed. Abdullah Sevim, the chef at Pandeli, cooked grilled lamb, aubergine and baby okra for a Turkish accompaniment to the fish – Istanbul has amazing vegetables. There’s also a seventh-generation spice store in the bazaar where I went absolutely crazy. I think I spent €800 on Turkish spices, including carob and blue nila powders for food colouring, and around 10kg of pistachios. We dressed the table with pink roses, embroidered napkins and matching pink Chini ceramics from Nackiyé (every plate was drawn, painted and gold-rimmed by hand). The 21 guests were all friends, including art director Katia Hakko and photographer Johan Sandberg. We drank rakı all night from a special narrow highball glass, before finishing the dinner with flan and cherry sorbet. The next night we went to see a dervish performance at Kasımpaşa Mevlevihane, a historic lodge that hosts ceremonies three times a week. It felt like a theatre for religion. The performance was about an hour long, and the dervishes turned to the sound of the ney, an ancient reed flute, which helps create a sense of contemplation. I loved the costumes – the camel-hair hats and swirling white skirts, which symbolise the shrouds of the dancers’ egos. It’s a beautiful act of devotion. Dervish dances are performed to Mevlevi music, which we also had playing at the dinner. Defne and Başak invited two classical Turkish music teachers from Haliç University to play a series of pieces on the ney and the kanun, a stringed instrument that produces a delicate shimmery sound. It is some of my favourite music because it is all about pleasure. What I love about the dervish dance is that it makes you feel calm and silent. It brings you into something that’s very focused. Comments

item.title: Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.21
Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago I’m sick of talking about Italian beef. I don’t even remember the last time I ate it — partly out of stubbornness. But Chicago is not only about dripping beef sandwiches or doorstopper deep-dish pizza. In the almost 20 years I’ve lived here, and 15 writing about the city’s food scene, I am more frequently on the hunt for a standout banh mi or jibarito. Pounding the pavement of my hometown, I’ve come to know the delicate shatter of a Cantonese chicken wing fried to perfection and the quivering wobble of just-set chawanmushi seasoned with wild local alliums. I’ve eaten the best Mexican food in Chicago, slurping goat birria stained red from chillies in a hole in the wall, or wolfing tender lengua tacos in the middle of a grocery store. I’ve wept over corn smut-filled ravioli that honours every iota of this lifeblood crop down to its hairy silk. Chicago is a city of immigrants, proud natives and hearty blow-ins. Almost a quarter of our residents are foreign-born, meaning you can feast aplenty on traditional Sonoran, Sichuan, Pakistani, Polish, Korean, Greek, Ethiopian, Laotian, Colombian dishes and more. You can also taste what it’s like for someone to have to straddle two identities and cultures. In order to experience Chicago’s best culinary thrills, you have to get out of shuffling distance of the beef sandwich and deep-dish chains, away from the tourist attractions dotted amid The Loop’s glistening monoliths. That’s the other thing you need to know about Chicago. It’s a city of neighbourhoods — 77 of them to be exact. Here’s how to eat across three of my favourites. Logan Square I’ve spent much of the past two decades living four-ish miles north-west of downtown in Logan Square, an intoxicating and maddening nexus of contrasts, home to wide, tree-lined boulevards and some of the city’s finest cooking. Low-slung stone structures housing indie cafés, dives, taquerias and a historic jewel box of a movie theatre butt up against ugly, sprawling apartment complexes with lower floors occupied by chains proffering $18 grain bowls. Gentrification has ebbed away some of the neighbourhood’s grittier bits and charm. But with reinvestment have come delights like the 606, a 2.7-mile, foliage-lined walking and cycling trail on a derelict former rail line. The Logan Square Blue Line station deposits you in the neighbourhood’s beating heart. A towering Doric marble column overlooks a circular plaza that has been refurbished to create more walkable space and redubbed La Placita in honour of the neighbourhood’s Latino heritage. On the other side of the plaza is Chicago’s original farm-to-table restaurant, Lula Cafe. Jason Hammel and Amalea Tshilds opened this indie icon in 1999, and now it spills across three storefronts, faithfully churning out inventive seasonal cooking and comfy standbys such as Pasta “Yia Yia”, aka feta-laced, cinnamon-scented bucatini. It’s thanks in part to Lula that the neighbourhood remains a magnet for dynamic, heartfelt seasonal cooking, and why I consider it prerequisite eating to understand what makes Logan Logan. We’ll (officially) start three-quarters of a mile north-east of Lula at Cellar Door Provisions. This decade-old slip of a restaurant has, at various times, been a café and bakery, tasting-menu restaurant and wine bar, all under the same name, and with the same corner perch on a leafy, residential street. It’s now a bistro, and it’s restless, scrappy and exciting. The hyper-seasonal à la carte dinner menu, from chef-owner Ethan Pikas and chef de cuisine Alex Cochran, changes constantly and occasionally startles. You may get red wine-braised lamb’s tongue with herbaceous salsa verde, a pert, luscious burger or grilled mackerel with preserved mussels in sauce Américaine. The wine leans light, bracing and a little weird. Some 350 feet away from Cellar Door is Superkhana International, an Indian-ish restaurant from chefs and co-owners Zeeshan Shah and Yoshi Yamada that blurs lines with joyful abandon. Is their tangy, creamy Palak paneer pizza (with creamed spinach, chilli oil and crispy shallots) pizza or naan? Is their Maggi noodles bolognese umami (that’ll be the Maggi liquid seasoning), warmly tangy (that’ll be the achar masala) — or both? Don’t overthink; just indulge. And always add shareable chaat, which cleverly rotates with our challenging Midwestern seasons. Like the hot-pink-painted Superkhana, Mi Tocaya Antojería, a 15-minute walk south-east, is a riot of colour and bustling energy, though the latter holds a bit faster to dogma in the name of preserving Mexico’s gastronomic heritage. To walk in — Spanish mingling with English, the sizzle of marinated carne and mole-soused tortillas chiming with the metallic maraca of shaking cocktails — is to enter a kind of multicultural Chicago utopia. At the heart of this place is the outspoken chef and proprietor Diana Dávila who recreates the regional Mexican cooking of her childhood, hair swept into a braided crown, laugh reverberating from the pass. A Chicago native born to Mexican immigrants, Dávila would be the first to tell you that her luscious mole negro, comprising some 30 ingredients (and lately enveloping braised pork shank and celery root), is “f****** dope”. Here costra (cheese-crusted) tacos taste like Mexico City and beets get roasted in coffee and heaped on garlicky Mayan pepita spread. Don’t be surprised if you spot beloved Chicago chef Margaret Pak stopping by for a post-shift steak burrito. The big-hearted co-owner of the excellent Keralan restaurant, Thattu, in neighbouring Avondale, swears by this comfy handheld meal, with good reason. Revel in its grilled skirt steak, local black beans, queso chihuahua and sour cream. I’ve been known to wax poetic on Giant’s crab tagliatelle to anyone who will listen. This tangle of al dente pasta slaps the taste buds with sweet, brackish crab, fiery chilli butter and acidity. For almost a decade, I’ve darkened the door of this narrow joint on West Armitage Avenue, bound for a bar stool in the back overlooking the tiny galley kitchen that radiates heat and sweat. Chef Jason Vincent’s boisterous little restaurant has a gift for exceptional, likeable food (think ruffly layered lasagne and pork schnitzel). For summer 2025, this restless crew of creatives upped the ante with a Test Kitchen menu. This is the brave, invigorating food they cook for themselves and that we get to eat: Laotian steamed fish, green garlic chawanmushi with bonito flakes and black sesame and pistachio-studded pâté en croûte with foie gras. Other excellent Logan Square restaurants - Omarcito’s Latin Cafe for tangy marinated steak sandwiches and crispy consommé-drowned chicken tacos, doled out from a bright yellow shipping container. - Bungalow by Middle Brow for thick rafts of sourdough bread and cleverly topped char-speckled pizzas, washed down with house-brewed beer and house-made natural wine — all made from ingredients grown in and around Illinois. - Osteria Langhe for unfettered northern Italian cooking. - The Radicle for late-night pizza and tinned fish snacks, washed down with aperitif-heavy cocktails. - Longman & Eagle for a stiff whiskey cocktail and superb smashburger. Uptown There’s a nostalgic grandeur to Uptown that you can almost conjure into a grainy old film in your mind’s eye as you gaze up at the soaring, Prohibition-era Art Deco buildings. “Of course, Al Capone drank here,” you think, scooching into a beat-up, half-moon booth at the longstanding Green Mill Cocktail Lounge, as you await Chris Foreman’s Friday evening jazz piano set over an eye-poppingly stiff Old Fashioned. A century ago, this booming nightlife and entertainment district even housed the studio that produced a Charlie Chaplin film, but it struggled subsequently for decades after discriminatory housing practices sent property values plummeting. Yet the institutional malfeasance and low rents produced a richly diverse demographic with a penchant for social justice. JOIN (Jobs Or Income Now), an activism group that challenged racist welfare practices, was born here. Vacant storefronts remain, but Uptown is rising (read: gentrifying), as evidenced by the arrival of a Target where a burnt-out rail and bus yard once stood, but also by the bold cooking making a home here. The wind blows a bit harder and chillier up here. All the more reason to pop in for pho in one of the outstanding Vietnamese restaurants concentrated on West Argyle Street. (For a handheld delight, consider the ham and head cheese banh mi on a shattering baguette at Nhu Lan Bakery.) But the stalwart Hai Yen, its stark greyscale facade hiding amid shinier Little Saigon storefronts, is the one Chicago chefs will send you to for bò lá lốt (lemongrass-scented beef and pork sausage grilled in betel leaf) and phở đặc biệt with beef in half a dozen guises bobbing amid slippery rice noodles. I like prefacing said beef injection with a few springy tapioca shrimp dumplings. I’m admittedly not the biggest fan of a tasting menu, but one of the few exceptions is Cariño, whose executive chef and owner, Norman Fenton, nabbed a nomination for Best Chef: Great Lakes at the 2026 James Beard Foundation Awards. This Detroit-born chef, who previously cooked at WILD Tulum in Mexico and then at Grant Achatz’s world-renowned cocktail lounge The Aviary and the inventive, Michelin-starred Schwa in Chicago, has a gift for zhuzhing the stuff of everyday nourishment with imagination and humour. The familiar flavours of tacos al pastor jolt the senses when reimagined as a marinated lamb tartare tostada. Cariño’s dozen-plus-course tasting menu ($200 per person) moved me and made me think, laugh and, yes, cry, just once. (See the aforementioned tear-inducing corn smut ravioli, filled with the truffle-like corn fungus huitlacoche, a Mexican delicacy.) If you don’t mind a 10pm dinner, Cariño performs a more affordable second act in the form of an eight-course taco omakase ($125 per person, including drinks), a masa-centric romp through tetelas, tacos and quesadillas set to a thumping, upbeat soundtrack. The crackly-edged, suadero carnitas taco will change you. Chicagoans can’t go too many days without an outstanding sandwich. Fortunately, Ragadan, a deliciously uncommon mash-up of Jordanian street food joint and Midwestern diner, has several cures for that. Owner Danny Sweis’s parents hail from Amman, Jordan. He was born and raised in his family’s diner in Oklahoma City, hence the menu’s OKC burger, with shaved onion caramelised right into the minced beef. Anything between bread is superb here, but the sandwich that keeps me biking five miles to get there is the falafel ka’ak. Craggy outside, achingly soft inside, the falafel pucks exhale warming spices, layered amid bright, crunchy veg, sharp pickles and silky hummus. And oh, that Levantine bread: wispy, airy, caked in sesame seeds, and sourced from the Latin American and European bakery Markellos. Ask for a za’atar mayo side for dipping. If you don’t, Sweis may deposit a little cup alongside your sandwich anyway. Other excellent Uptown restaurants - Kie Gol Lanee for soul-soothing Oaxacan cooking (get the chapulines if they’re not sold out). - Demera for expert traditional Ethiopian cuisine and aromatic house honey wine. - Sun Wah BBQ for the off-menu Beijing (Peking) duck, starting with the whole crispy-skinned bird and ending with duck-fried rice. - YooYee for lip-tingling braised beef soup with fat hand-pulled noodle ribbons. Chinatown At the corner of Cermak and Wentworth, a landmark red gate denotes the technical start of Chicago’s Chinatown. But you can smell and feel that you’re here the moment you emerge from the Cermak-Chinatown Red Line station. Chinatown breathes and bustles impatiently, its residents endlessly streaming by laden with plastic Thank You bags. It smells, surprisingly perhaps, like Portuguese tarts baking and five-spice and fish. This 30,000-strong community is spilling into proximate districts and evolving as younger generations make their mark. In 2022, Lily Wang and Joe Briglio decided to fix a problem in Chinatown: there wasn’t, and had never been, a dedicated cocktail bar here. The couple took the reins at the classic Chinese restaurant Moon Palace, a 50-plus-year neighbourhood fixture owned by Wang’s parents. They shifted the restaurant into a permanent takeaway operation and built a sultry bar, Nine Bar, where the dining room used to be. You walk into what resembles any other brightly lit, tile-and-wood carry-out, save for a formidable metal door. You’re then deposited into a dim, neon-lit lounge that feels both lively and intimate, bar staff deftly mixing cocktails that mingle Japanese, Chinese and tropical influences, from the MSG-laced martini to a Sichuan peppercorn-spiked margarita called the Paper Dragon. A few doors down, Yao Yao provides a decidedly bright and turquoise-hued contrast to Nine Bar. Tuck yourself into a booth and prepare for the day’s simplest order: pickled fish, a soup of sharp pickled greens and mild, tender bass bobbing in a deliciously tacky broth. Order it mild if you want to feel the Sichuan tingle without missing all the beautiful nuance. Even the smallest size is too large for two, so prepare for leftovers. I like adding toothy thin glass noodles for heft. They come in little knotted bundles. Because we must end on a sweet note, follow your nose to the oldest bakery in town. The family-run, cash-only Chiu Quon Bakery has been open since 1986. It was founded by Pui Yip and Cora Chiu with recipes that Yip brought from Hong Kong, and the second generation owns it now. I’ve never been here when there wasn’t a queue, though I’m grateful for time to ponder my order from the packed wraparound case. For starters, I’ll take an always fluffy, sweet-savoury BBQ pork bun, custardy Portuguese egg tart and a bouncy mochi ball. Uncomfortably full? Me too. I’d suggest a ramble through Ping Tom Memorial Park, a former rail yard turned native prairie park that hugs the Chicago River. Paved paths and raised boardwalks carry you through rewilded grasses and past colourful murals. Glance north at every available opportunity, then gasp. Is that not the most gorgeous view of the skyline? Other excellent Chinatown restaurants - Dolo Restaurant and Bar for traditional and modern dim sum. - MCCB for charcoal-grilled whole fish and twice-cooked pork with leeks. - 3 Sauces Hainam Chicken Rice at the Richland Center food court for, you guessed it, Hainam chicken rice: soft, toothsome poached thigh meat served chilled over chicken fat-flavoured rice. - Yummy Yummy Noodles to slurp shrimp wonton noodle soup. Which is your favourite neighbourhood restaurant in Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And read more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: What Backpacker Splurges in Thailand Really Cost
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.18
Backpacking through Thailand has earned a legendary reputation for being incredibly cheap. You can easily find five-dollar hostel beds, tasty two-dollar plates of Pad Thai on street corners, and overnight buses that take you across the country for next to nothing. However, after following a strict daily budget for a few weeks, almost every tourist reaches a point where they want to trade instant noodles and shared dorms for a special experience. Thailand is one of the best places in the world to treat yourself because your money goes much further here than back home. If you wonder what major budget splurges cost now, here is a realistic look at popular activities, from scaling limestone cliffs in Krabi to teeing off at Thailand's top golf courses. Popular Activities in Thailand Rock Climbing on the Cliffs of Railay Beach Railay Beach in Krabi Province is world-famous among outdoor enthusiasts. Towering limestone karsts rise straight out of turquoise waters, creating some of the most dramatic climbing routes on the planet. Even without climbing experience, local gear shops make it safe and easy to get onto the rock face. A half-day guided climbing program in Railay costs 1,200 to 1,800 Thai Baht ($36 to $55 USD). This covers all equipment, including harness fitting, special shoes, chalk, a guide, and climbing on beginner-friendly walls such as Muay Thai Wall or Diamond Cave. If you want to climb multi-pitch routes on the Thaiwand Wall, it will cost approximately 6,500 to 9,000 Baht ($198 to $274). Budget an extra 100 to 150 Baht ($3 to $4.50) each way for the longtail boat ride from Ao Nang Pier because Railay is cut off from roads by giant cliffs. Getting PADI Scuba Certified in Koh Tao or Phuket If you want to dive beneath the waves, taking a scuba course in Thailand is a rite of passage for travelers. The small island of Koh Tao is one of Thailand's most affordable places to get your PADI Open Water certification. The full price for the Open Water Course lasting more than one day at Koh Tao is 9,500 to 11,000 Baht ($280 to $325). It includes classroom theory, pool dives, four ocean dives, and gear rental. If you take the certification course in Phuket or Koh Lanta, the cost is slightly higher, ranging from 12,000 to 14,000 Baht ($350 to $410) due to larger dive boats and marine park entry fees. For certified divers who want a single day of fun diving, a two-tank boat trip typically costs 3,200 to 4,200 Baht ($94 to $123) and usually includes a freshly cooked hot lunch on the boat deck.
