Roasted Fennel and Farro Salad | Radicchio Salad With Crunchy Shiitake Mushrooms and Barley | Roasted Mushroom and Broccoli Grain Bowls 7. Add a pop of sweetness Adding a bit of sweetness — with vegetables like corn or roasted squash, fresh or dried fruits like apples or raisins or a drizzle of honey or maple — feels like a little surprise. The pop of something sweet turns your grain bowl into a treasure chest you’ll want to dig into again and again, hunting for another treat.

item.title: The Famous 1983 Plum Torte Gets a Remix
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 5.07
Advertisement First published in September 1983, Marian Burros’s plum torte has become one of the most popular recipes in the history of The Times, and it’s no mystery why. It’s easy, it’s practically no-fail and it’s endlessly adaptable. Here are five ways to make the 43-year-old recipe your own, drawn directly from readers who have done just that. Recipe: The Original Plum Torte 1. Toss in almost any fruit “Made this for the first time using 4 cups of blueberries and raspberries (mixed). It was perfect!” Apricots, halved and pitted; cranberries or any summer berry work beautifully, as do sliced apples, nectarines, peaches and pears. Canned and frozen fruit can happily stand in for fresh. 2. Experiment with spices, herbs and extracts “I added a teaspoon of finely minced fresh rosemary to the batter. Nice, subtle flavor.” Depending on your mood, add vanilla extract, almond extract, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom, rosemary, orange or lemon zest for a subtle twist. 3. Play with flours “Made this last night after tasting the one made by our daughter. Used raspberries and blackberries, one basket each, instead of plums, and ⅓ cup cornmeal and ⅔ cup flour. Fantastic!!! The cornmeal adds a very sophisticated ‘Italian’ character to it, very slight crunch, and amazing flavor.” For a different texture, consider a half-and-half mixture of almond or cornmeal flour and all-purpose flour. (Melissa Clark made a version with whole-wheat flour.) Or swap in gluten-free flour blends, with excellent results. 4. Change up the pan “Make it in any Pyrex, casserole, anything.” The torte can be baked in any dish provided it’s around 8 to 10 inches in diameter and oven-safe, so spring-form pans, skillets, ceramic casserole dishes will all yield happy results. 5. Double, triple, even quadruple it “Think about making two … one is not enough.” The batter scales up like a dream, and the baked cake freezes well. In 2023, Ms. Burros recounted the time she once made two dozen and asked her friend to store 12 in her freezer. She got 10 back. item.title: Turn Eggs Into Dinner With This Salsa de Chorizo Recipe
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 3.13
Advertisement In the sun-washed kitchen of Hacienda San Lorenzo at Casa Madero Winery in Parras, Mexico, Mari Medina places two eggs in an oil-slicked pan and turns the heat on low. As the whites slowly set, she ladles a chunky, brick-red sauce that smells of roasted tomatoes, toasted chiles and its rich, smoky main ingredient: chorizo. Recipe: Salsa de Chorizo Ms. Medina, who has cooked at the hacienda in the state of Coahuila for more than 18 years, and whose family has lived in Coahuila for six generations, said that guests travel great distances. They’ll have the salsa de chorizo for the first time and request it again the next morning. Coahuila, the vast Mexican state that stretches from the Texas border to deep into the Sierra Madre, is one of Mexico’s underrepresented culinary regions. Its most famous dish, nachos, was invented in the border city of Piedras Negras in the 1940s and went on to conquer the world. Salsa de chorizo, on the other hand, has been nourishing Coahuila for generations — Ms. Medina learned to make it from her mother, who learned from hers, who learned from hers — but almost no one outside the state knows its name. Whether you call it salsa de chorizo or caldillo de chorizo, which is technically soupier, the idea is the same: chorizo as the base of a stellar sauce, scooped with torn pieces of warm corn or flour tortilla. Though it’s often served alongside eggs or a small bowl of frijoles de olla, the dish began as a meal on its own. Coahuila is an arid place, settled by miners and ranchers who needed food that was nutritious, would not spoil and, above all, rendidor, a word that means yielding, or able to feed many from a little. Cooking the chorizo into a salsa meant that a family could eat well from only a modest amount of meat. The chorizo that cooks in Coahuila seek out above any other comes from a town tucked into a remote corner of the state: Ciudad Melchor Múzquiz. Múzquiz, as everyone there calls it, was founded in 1739 by Basque soldiers looking for silver and gold, and it was shaped by those mining and ranching families. Yolanda Elizondo Maltos, the city’s official historian and chronicler, who was born there and traces her roots to the first Spanish settlers who arrived in Coahuila about 450 years ago, describes the town as “un rincón en el mapa de Coahuila.” A nook on the map of Coahuila. That isolation, she said, further necessitated smart ways to preserve food. “The chorizo has been made here for centuries because it is a way to conserve meat,” Ms. Elizondo Maltos said. “With the spices and the vinegar, it holds for long periods without refrigeration.” Families in Múzquiz follow closely guarded recipes. There’s no one single way to make chorizo, but the common denominators are quality pork butt, as well as dried chiles that are toasted, rehydrated and puréed with fresh garlic, oregano, cumin, black pepper and vinegar. The mixture is then oreada, left to air under a fine cloth to marinate deeply before being packed into casings. People buy their chorizo from the same butcher their entire lives, the one their mothers and grandmothers used. When they cook it, it tastes like home. The chorizo of Múzquiz is so prized that chefs and restaurants across northern Mexico are starting to call it out on their menus. “Rather than make our own chorizo at our butcher shops, I realized it was better to source it from a place that really knows how to make it,” said Anuar Yutani Morales, the owner of Super Carnes Coahuila in the neighboring town of Sabinas, who runs the state’s Festival de la Carne Asada. “The artisanship is incomparable.” In 2019, Múzquiz held its first Festival del Chorizo, which brought together about 30 chorizo-making families. Ms. Elizondo Maltos, who helped organize the event, wants to bring it back. “It marks the city as unique,” she said. At the hacienda, Ms. Medina makes her salsa with chorizo, tomatoes, onion, garlic and jalapeño. She roasts everything until deeply charred. That is, she said, the secret. “It is very homey food,” she said. Once salsa de chorizo enters a kitchen, it tends to stay. Pair it with sunny-side-up eggs, or scramble the eggs directly into the salsa. Poach it like a smokier and meatier shakshuka. Use it to sauce crispy tacos and tacos sudados, filled with mashed potato or shredded beef. Pair it with quesadillas, rice and beans. With potatoes, it becomes an even more filling guisado. Or, pair two of the region’s classic dishes and use it to top nachos. Asked what it would mean if salsa de chorizo were to reach the fame of nachos, Ms. Elizondo Maltos did not hesitate. “Nuestra identidad reconocida,” she said. Our identity, finally recognized. After a pause, almost teary-eyed, she said: “Mucho orgullo.” A lot of pride. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: A McDonald’s Toy, Pokémon Cards, and 25,000 Other Items Dropped in Yellowstone’s Geysers
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.29
An assortment of items collected from Yellowstone geysers shown on a table, includes an Uno card, Polaroid pictures, cameras, and race car toys (Photo: NPS and Jerrad Scoggins/500px via Getty Images) Visitors dropped more than 25,000 items into Yellowstone National Park geysers in 2026, setting a new record for the amount of stuff lost to the world’s most famous hydrothermal features. In all, scientists removed more than 20,100 pieces of trash, 5,600 rocks and sticks, and nearly 300 hats from the park’s hydrothermal areas in 2026, according to a September 14 report published by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). This year marks a new record for debris removal in the park, and comes on the heels of a busy tourism season. More than 2.64 million people visited Yellowstone between January and July 2026, nearly tying the park’s most-visited year in 2021, according to National Park Service (NPS) data. “The more foot traffic an area gets, the more trash will be there—but this is especially true in wide open geyser basins with narrow boardwalks,” Margery Price, the report’s author and a park physical science technician, told Outside. “Midway Geyser Basin in particular is our biggest hat collector.” Among the tonnage of lost personal items were more than a few wacky finds: 15 fake fingernails, eight miniature race cars, two rubber ducks and a McDonald’s toy from 2010—and that’s just the beginning. By mid-September 2025, Yellowstone’s geology team used poles, including one with a 16-foot extendable handle, strainers, hand rakes and shovels to remove more than 13,000 pieces of trash, 4,000 rocks and sticks, and 300 hats from hydrothermal areas. The 2026 haul marks a 50 percent jump over last year’s loot. Objects lost in 2026 include what you might expect to find near the world’s most-visited geysers: camera lens caps, hair ties, and too many sunglasses to count (OK, there were three dozen). More obscure objects also littered the hydrothermal features, like golf tees, Legos, dental retainers, and not one but three lapel pins given to passengers on Delta Airlines flights. Crews also found Polaroid photos of the same hydrothermal features where they were recovered, a two-inch copy of The Vampire Diaries, and a single UNO card. The 2026 cleanup covers nearly all of Yellowstone’s developed, front-country hydrothermal areas, Price told Outside. Crews work everywhere from smaller sites like Frying Pan Spring and Clearwater Spring to Black Sand Basin, Artist Paintpots, Mammoth Hot Springs, Midway Geyser Basin, and Old Faithful. Experts say human objects can irreversibly harm the natural ecosystem. “Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature,” Price wrote in the 2026 report. Trash can clog a geyser’s water supply or block its runoff channels. Restricting hot-water flow can also lower a spring’s temperature, change its color, and hurt the heat-loving microorganisms that call these features home. In extreme cases, debris can even alter a geyser’s eruption schedule. Early 20th-century visitors at Yellowstone’s Minute Geyser clogged its largest vent by tossing in rocks. Eruptions that once happened every 60 seconds and could reach up to 50 feet are now smaller and irregular. NPS says these rocks have since been cemented together by mineral deposits and can’t be removed without risking further damage. Yellowstone has been trying to undo that kind of damage for decades. According to USGS, the first major thermal clean-up effort began in 1942 when a park geologist found features choked with rocks, logs, and materials visitors tossed in. Todd Walton, director of sales and marketing for Yellowstone National Park Lodges and a former park guide, told Outside that visitors should be mindful of their belongings, taking special care with “anything that can get blown off by the wind, like hats and scarves.” “I’ve seen gloves, cups, and sunglasses also, he said. “Hold onto your stuff.” Price told Outside there’s no reliable way to estimate what percentage of lost objects crews recover because conditions vary dramatically from one spring or geyser to another. “Some areas are shallow, and we can see most if not all of what’s in them,” she said. “Others, it’s just not possible for us to retrieve stuff that is too deep, at a challenging angle, or too far out from the edge. Most things sink eventually—especially once they get saturated with minerals.” Yellowstone geologist Liam Rogers told Outside that dropped items can sink quickly—but sometimes come back up. In September 2018, Ear Spring erupted and expelled coins, cans, plastic cups, cigarette butts, and other debris, including coins later dated to the 1930s, according to NPS. If visitors drop something in or near a geyser, Walton said to stay on the boardwalk and contact park staff. “People don’t realize how dangerous it is in these areas despite the numerous warnings and signs saying so,” Walton said. Many thermal areas in Yellowstone are between 150 and 200 degrees Fahrenheit, and although the surrounding ground may look solid, it can quickly give way. Multiple visitors have died in the park’s thermal features over the years. In August 2022, the body of a 70-year-old man was found in the 140-degree Abyss Geyser in the West Thumb Geyser Basin, and more than 20 people have died from burns caused by entering the park’s thermal features since the park began counting.

item.title: ‘High Ground’ Documentary Uncovers the True Story of the 1977 Yosemite Weed Plane Crash
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.00
(Photo: Ron Lykins) You would think a movie about a plane crash with three tons of illegal Mexican weed onboard, two fatalities, a run-in with the Drug Enforcement Agency, and a classic climbers versus park rangers clash would be filled with bad guys. A lot of bad guys. But as it turns out, it is possible to make a feel-good movie about the “legend of dope lake.” Aside from the death of two pilots, could the drug plane crash of 1976 actually have had a positive ripple effect through Yosemite Valley? At a time when we’re all sorely in need of feel-good stories, the new documentary High Ground—the first full-length film about this storied incident—delivers a dose of optimism. How can the tale of a Howard 500 aircraft with three tons (over 6,000 pounds) of weed on board crashing into Lower Merced Pass Lake be uplifting? For that answer, we asked one of the climbers who scored a bale of Mexican weed for himself. Produced by British film production company Dash Pictures, the one-and-a-half-hour doc sheds ample new light on the legend through in-depth interviews with park rangers, a widow of one of the pilots, a U.S. customs agent, the former head of Yosemite Search and Rescue, and climbers who fetched bales of wet marijuana from the lake over the course of a few months. One of those climbers, Ken Yager, founded and now leads the Yosemite Climbing Association, which runs a small museum in the park. Today, the museum displays seven pieces of airplane debris from the crash. For Yager and several other climbers interviewed in High Ground, this is the first time they’ve come public with their stories from the drug rush of 1997 (the plane crashed on December 8, 1976, but wasn’t discovered until January 27, 1977). “People have talked about doing this story for a long time,” Yager told Climbing, adding that several production companies have inquired with him about filming documentaries. How did a bunch of non-climbing Brits end up being the first to produce a feature-length film on the subject? In short, Leo Houlding. Director Daniel Sharp met the pro climber a decade ago through a mutual friend. When Sharp moved to California in 2016, Houlding relayed the tale. The first person Sharp met in Yosemite was climbing photographer Dean Fidelman, who shared his account of what went down decades ago. Fidelman’s report led to more people and more sides of the story, ultimately convincing Sharp that a proper documentary was in order. Sharp calls Yager “the single most key” person when it came to finding other sources and getting “a sense for the project.” Most climbers and rangers involved, including Yager, had decided that 50 years was enough time passed to come out of the woodwork. Only two sources were still unwilling to talk, according to Sharp. “We did a lot of work to reassure people the statute has long since passed,” he told Climbing. One person declined involvement because they were still employed with the park. “We also did a lot of work to reassure people from all sides that we wouldn’t make them look silly, that we wanted to tell a balanced and true story, and that we deal with what’s fact, what’s rumor and what’s memory, and how that changes over time.” Some of the interviewees have died since filming. Dale Bard, a talented climber who established the Sea of Dreams climbing route on El Capitan, passed away on October 1, 2025. (You can read a posthumous letter to him from a former climbing partner here.) Ranger Rick Smith died in July. “We wanted to capture this generation of Yosemite climbers and rangers while they could still tell the story themselves, contradictions and all,” Sharp said. Another less-discussed fatality related to the Yosemite plane crash incident (besides the pilots) is the climber Jack Dorn—a thread that High Ground explores, but doesn’t resolve. Dorn allegedly became enmeshed in a dark web of contacts found in the pilot’s recovered “black book.” Soon after, he died in a fall from a hiking trail at night. But some, including Bard, speculated that he may have been pushed. We sat down with Yager to find out why he finally felt ready to come forward with his account. He also revealed whether that frozen plane weed was any good, and how he thinks the plane crash inadvertently may have shaped Yosemite climbing history. CLIMBING: Why did you choose to remain quiet about your participation in the Yosemite plane crash incident until now? Ken Yager: I’ve talked about it before, but always with an alias. The first time I talked about it publicly, I did an interview with Men’s Journal and it’s called “The Legend of Dope Lake.” My alias was Chuck Strader; I didn’t make it up, they made it up. I didn’t talk about it before using my name for a couple reasons: One, I had a young daughter who wasn’t 18 yet. In case there was any blowback or repercussions, I didn’t want to embarrass her. The other reason was that I was still pushing hard to get a permitted space in the park for the museum. What made you decide to come forward as a source after all these years? First of all, I’ve done everything I wanted to do. I got the park partnership and the museum. I started all these things that have been big dreams of mine for 35 years or more. Then I realized something two years ago, when I opened the museum. The National Park Service (NPS) interpretive teams and law enforcement came down and got tours. The thing they were most interested in was seeing the airplane parts. They’re buying airplane shirts. I said, “You used to chase us for the silliest little things. Were you guys bored or what?” They pretty much said, Oh yeah, we were bored and you were a challenge. It was like a game for them. Now I’m friends with them—sort of. I mean we don’t hang out or anything. Enough time has passed that we can talk about it and chuckle about it and go, Wow, times have really changed. How do you feel about the film, now that it’s premiered? I really like everything about it—how Daniel with Dash Productions is releasing it, how he’s respectful to everyone. It’s Daniel’s 33rd documentary and he said this is the one he’s most excited about. An American director would have had an antagonist. To me, it was a really relatable human story about everyone involved. Nobody looks bad. The plane crashed three days after I showed up in the valley. It’s like it crashed just for me. The whole thing is bizarre, but it helped a lot of people. In your perspective, is that sentiment that the film portrays—no antagonists—accurate? With the park service, the thing fell in their lap and they did the best they could. It’s more just a set of circumstances where everyone was trying to do their thing. For the climbing community, they couldn’t resist. Some people did it for the money, some did it for the thrill. And some did it just to get weed because it was highly illegal back then in every state, let alone on federal property. It was a whole different world back then. It’s still illegal federally in the park. It was a crazy time and nobody knew what to do. We were all in over our heads. I had just turned 18 and I would be tried as an adult. I just wanted some weed. The turn of events just got more and more serious. I lucked out and realized I never wanted to be involved in that business. I just really like the fact that [Sharp] didn’t make anybody bad. Nobody wanted it to escalate. What did you buy with your plane weed profits? How much cash did you walk away with? Some of the weed, I didn’t know what to do with. I gave it to a friend of mine from high school who did. I did buy a $500 Volkswagen. Then I traded a bunch for all the climbing gear I needed that I didn’t have. I used it to climb El Cap. I climbed El Cap four times that year with hip belays and no cams. Those were the days. Just stoppers, hexes, and pitons—it’s a trip. I did ascents of Tangerine Trip and Zodiac. I was the first nobody to do them. They became trade routes. If that hippie can do them, then we can do them. A year or two later, they got done all the time. Was the weed any good? It’s hard to imagine the marijuana being in decent condition after soaking in a lake filled with plane debris and dead bodies—and covered in jet fuel. I remember well. First of all, as I mentioned, weed was highly illegal back then. Most American weed was horrible. Back then, the best weed were Thai sticks and stuff from Mexico—Acupulco Gold, Panama Red, or whatever. They were all high-end, south-of-border pots. The bags were burlap sacks with three layers of plastic around them that of course didn’t work. They all had a label on them. The one I found was 27 kilos (2.2 pounds) before it got wet. The one I had was Double A Grade Mexican (it goes up to triple grade). It dried out and it was still very, very potent. Some of the bales were worse than others. There were bales really close to where the fuel puddle was under the ice. If you peeled off an inch or two out of the bales, the center of the bales were damn good. Just wet. For us, it was a great thing. A little smell of airplane fuel, but most of it evaporated off. The film portrays the lake as quite a scene, by turns spooky, weird, fun, and legitimately dangerous. What was the vibe like at the lake in your experience? I was scared shitless. When I went up there, I got in and out in 22 hours. My mom and her husband were visiting with my stepbrothers and sisters. I was supposed to be spending time with them. So I told them I was going to be climbing at Mount Starr King. My brothers and sisters all knew what was going on. As you’re going up to the lake, wading through icy rivers, you arrive soaking wet. I remember it being windy, cold. You could see planes flying over, not down low, but you’re thinking they’re just watching you up there. I was super paranoid. When I walked up on the shore, you could see insulation, fuel lines, metal wrapped around the trees. And you could smell the oil and hydraulics and fuel, too. It’s super spooky. You know there’s death there. Are there any notable milestones in climbing history that you would correlate with the plane crash? I would say a lot of people did. People did climbing trips to Colorado, went up in the Cirque of the Unclimbables, or they went to Europe. A lot of people went on to climb in other areas they might not have been able to make it to because it involved plane fare. As far as big climbs since then, certainly people stayed around and did first ascents or lots of other climbs, Mike Corbett being one of them. El Cap routes—hard El Cap routes. Sea of Dreams got done the following year. Around that time was Bill Price’s 5.13—a lot of hard free climbing happened then. People were doing some really good climbs at that time, but whether it was because of the airplane I can’t really say. I’m sure it influenced it. A lot of people benefitted from it. People were very generous with it. It’s a little different than nowadays. My God, I can still remember the taste of it. What does the Yosemite Climbing Museum have as far as exhibits related to the plane crash? I have seven pieces of the airplane wreckage. The biggest you can see at the very end of the credits in [the documentary] Valley Uprising—that’s me holding a piece of the fuselage. It could be part of the wing, I have no idea. It’s a sheet of aluminum that’s maybe three feet by five feet. I’ve got a hydraulic pump, some pieces of fuel line. Piece of fuselage or wing. We also sell airplane t-shirts. What is your theory about what happened to Dorn on the Yosemite Falls Trail? I don’t think he was pushed. It just seems a little far-fetched. It was speculation. The way I understand it is that my friend Sean Plunkett actually had the book. He was up there when [Dorn] got the money. My girlfriend at the time worked at the bank. I knew there were soaking wet bills they brought to the bank to exchange. Everywhere I turned, I was involved in it. Everyone was involved. Even if they didn’t go up there, they had friends that did. As the unofficial historian of Yosemite climbing history, how do you view this incident? I think it’s the crowning piece of history as far as the seventies go—it was a very tumultuous time. It started in 1970 with the riots. That scared the park service. Shortly after, they created the LEO [Law Enforcement Officer] arm of the park service—in other words, people carrying guns. The people who had the sit-in at the meadow that caused the riots all looked like the climbers of the seventies—or we all looked like them. We had long hair, we had beards, we’re up there climbing with very little money. The last thing we’re going to do is go get a haircut or buy a razor. I’ve never even owned a comb. There was prejudice there. We’d get harassed. There wasn’t really anything going on. We were the eyesore of the community and looked like bums. Also the law enforcement and park service and Curry Company people, a lot of them didn’t like us because quite honestly they weren’t really fit. Climbers always had girlfriends and a cabin to stay in during the winter. There was a lot of jealousy there. Climbers weren’t having to work and they were. Climbers were having fun and all the female employees seemed to really like them and they didn’t like that. I kind of get it. The other thing I’ll say is that the park service harassing the climbing community and the climbing community pushing back became this kind of cold or invisible war. When I first moved up there, I was a little kid but I learned pretty quickly to stay away from that guy, listen for the radio, and so on. There were undercover people up there to listen in on you—it’s really weird. How did the dope plane crash change that dynamic? In some ways, it created a little bit of a truce and was kind of the turning point to eventually getting along. First of all, we didn’t want anyone to know we went up there. We were scared. Number two: If I was an NPS person investigating that, I’d feel like I screwed up. I wouldn’t want that story to get out either. We were all like: Let’s pretend this didn’t happen and go back to where we were. What really turned it around was the Facelift [a volunteer cleaning event] and the movies lately and a lot more climbers working for the park service and the concessionaire. But it was the culmination of that antagonist relationship between the park service and the climbing community. It took many, many years before it got to where it is now, but I think it was the start of it. Was the Yosemite Facelift inspired in any way by the mess left by the crash? I’ve never been afraid to clean stuff up. I lived off of canning too for a while. A nickel a can back then with everyone not recycling was so easy—then you could go out for dinner and get a beer. I made up to $80 one day. Back then, that was a lot of money. I started [Facelift] because I was a climbing guide and one of my jobs was to talk about Leave No Trace principles. Sort of hard when you’re tip-toeing on the trail and behind every rock there’s a bunch of toilet paper and cigarette butts. I just felt like I was being hypocritical by ignoring it. I’d get so mad, but I’m not going to pick up toilet paper and put it in my climbing pack. I thought: I can be mad about it for the rest of my life, or I can turn it around and do something about it. Interview was edited for space and clarity. High Ground premiered at the Yosemite Cinema in Oakhurst, California, on September 5. It will be playing again during the weekend of Yosemite Facelift—an event established and spearheaded by Yager through the YCA—from September 23-27. The documentary will also screen at the San Diego Film Festival on October 16 and 17. Dash Pictures expects small theatrical releases, as well as additional film festival screenings in the next few months, but can’t announce details yet. It will likely be available to stream or rent online in early 2027. Follow @highgroundmovie for updates.

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape.” Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.85
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management (BLM) order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from a BLM order this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to reclassify livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species of its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led American Prairie to cancel its public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here, and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: 5 Yoga-Inspired Foot and Ankle Exercises to Help You Move Better Outdoors
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.32
(Photo: Canva) Bad news: your feet are likely chronically compromised. When it comes to stretching and strengthening, the feet are easily one of the most overlooked parts of the body, despite the fact that you rely on them for literally each step you take. Runners and other outdoor athletes are especially vulnerable to foot issues. “The foot is the body’s primary interface with the ground,” says Devon Crahan, yoga teacher and owner of Intentional Yoga, a hot yoga studio based in Michigan. According to Crahan, research continues to demonstrate the influence of the foot on movement quality throughout the body. Over time, the dozens of intricate muscles, tendons, and ligaments in your feet naturally weaken and atrophy. Without that structural support, your inner arches start to flatten, making your ankles roll inward. As a result, it’s natural to subconsciously dump more of your weight into your knees and ankles. Eventually, this repetitive strain can compound and become a painful issue throughout your body. Crahan explains that when you rebuild the structural strength in your feet, your knees and hips function more efficiently since the foundation beneath them is better able to absorb and transmit force. It’s possible to improve the mechanics of your feet and ankles with simple stretching and strengthening exercises. An unexpected benefit of bringing more awareness to the feet is paying attention to how you land on them. “I’ll often see practitioners lean too much weight forward into the front toes, which presents itself as pinched-up, or overflexing,” Crahan says, explaining that this can cause cramping. “Learn to lean your weight back a bit, using the front toes strictly for fine-tuning your balance. When practiced consistently, even a simple 5-minute foot yoga routine can help protect your feet, your body mechanics, and your balance in everyday life and on the trails. Regularly stretching and strengthening your feet not only brings more steadiness to your everyday life, but also helps you find more stability on your mat during a yoga class or on the trails. When balancing on the balls of your feet in a squat, you transfer the entire weight of the body onto the arches and toes, which activates the stabilizing muscles to build strength. Focus on: The intense activation in your toes and arches. Lift your heels as high as you can rather than letting them hover. Keep your spine straight and keep your chest from rounding forward as you steady your balance. Continue to breathe. An increasingly common pose in yoga classes, Toe Squat is a variation on Thunderbolt Pose (Vajrasana) that stretches the plantar fascia, the muscle that runs along the bottom of your feet, and strengthens the stabilizing muscles of the toes and ankles. Focus on: The intense opening along the bottoms of your feet. Send your awareness into the center of the tightness, focusing on slow, steady breaths and extended exhalations. This dynamic variation of a simple standing pose strengthens the calves and trains the ankles to stay centered and steady under pressure. This counteracts the tendency to roll the ankles slightly inward, which can compromise knee alignment. Focus on: The alignment of your ankles and the shifting distribution of weight. Notice if your weight spills outward toward your pinky toes and actively press down through the balls of your big toes to keep your weight more centered toward the midline of your body. In yogic tradition, pada bandha (foot lock) is the intentional act of rooting down through the four major corners of the foot (the ball of the big toe, the ball of the little toe, the inner heel, and the outer heel) while actively lifting the inner arches upward like a dome. This practice teaches you to track the exact boundaries of your feet while training you to evenly distribute your weight as you stand. Focus on: The physical sensation in your feet. Feel your arches lift away from the floor as the edges of your feet, heels, and toes press into the mat as if they were glued down. Think of it as an energetic bridge that draws energy up from the ground through your feet. Slowing down and practicing heel-to-toe walks help you consciously track where you place most of your weight. In turn, this can help you rewire any subconscious walking habits that could lead to chronic foot strain. Focus on: The urge to rush. Take your time. Also note the precise micro-moments of skin contact with the floor. Draw your mind entirely into the rolling sensation of your weight transferring from heel to toe. Over time, those daily five-minute foot exercises and foot stretches will build a resilient, lasting capacity of your feet to carry you gracefully, on the mat and on the trails. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston said. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW teams have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without breaks. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the five-year average, and euthanization is up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as he spoke on the phone with Backpacker. “It’s been a busy year,” he said. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he said: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston pointed to the record-low snowpack that caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston said, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he said. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explained. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston pointed out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also said that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze black bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston said. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: Off-Road Vehicles Are Cool But Loud as Hell. Can Polaris’ New Transmission Fix That?
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.50
Overview: Outside tested the Polaris Xpedition, a side-by-side off-road vehicle, on 4WD roads in South Dakota’s Black Hills National Forest. The Xpedition features Polaris’ new NUMATIX Controlled CVT transmission, which uses air pressure to manage the clutch and reduce cabin noise by a claimed 40 percent compared to previous models. The vehicle has 114 horsepower, a 999cc engine, and 14 inches of ground clearance. The two-seat XP model starts at $40,499; the tested ADV5 model seats five and includes an enclosed rear cargo area. The rain storm comes on quick and turns to hail even quicker, so within a few minutes the dirt roads I’m driving in South Dakota’s Black Hills National Forest become bogged with thick mud and slick rock gardens. It’s perfect. I’m testing Polaris’ new Xpedition, an all-terrain vehicle designed to tackle tough 4WD roads while keeping the driver and passengers as comfortable as possible. The off-road capability is only half the story of this side-by-side. I’ve driven my share of off-road vehicles over the years, from four wheelers on my buddy’s farm to snowmobiles in Colorado and my cherished 4Runner built for overlanding. But the side-by-side is a unique category of off-road vehicle. Instead of the open-aired all-terrain vehicles that are designed to get one or two people from point A to point B through rugged terrain, the side-by-side is designed to tackle the same rugged terrain in relative comfort, with closed cabs and surprisingly plush seats. During the last several years, side-by-sides have gotten more posh, with climate control, power windows, sound systems, and infotainment screens. These side-by-sides are so capable, and so comfortable, that there are people in Utah and Arizona (where it’s legal to drive them on the roads) that use them as their primary vehicle. I know a guy that drives his side-by-side to the golf course on a regular basis here in North Carolina. But there’s always been one glaring issue with these enclosed-cab side-by-sides. They’re loud as hell. The engines have to work at such high RPMs to power these machines through technical terrain that your entire ride is accompanied by the high-pitch sound of an engine working overtime. Imagine a car stuck in second gear at 40 mph. That’s what these side-by-sides sound like, and that ever-present hum gets trapped inside the enclosed cabs with no place to go. The first time I drove a side-by-side, I thought the transmission was broken and the vehicle wouldn’t shift. Some side-by-side owners will muffle the sound through after-market sound-proofing, while others wear ear plugs. The loud noise of the engine is enough to turn some people off of the vehicles altogether, so Polaris decided to address the issue, taking a big leap forward in terms of comfort with their latest innovation, the NUMATIX Controlled CVT. This new transmission uses air pressure to manipulate the clutch and deliver a quieter engine at cruising speeds. I’m not going to pretend to understand the engineering principles behind governing the transmission with pressurized air, but I will tell you that the new Xpedition is noticeably quieter than the previous model. Polaris claims that their new side-by-sides with NUMATIX are 40 percent quieter than previous models. You can experience the difference first hand by toggling back and forth between Comfort mode (with the NUMATIX engaged) and Sport mode (NUMATIX disengaged) while driving. The difference is immediately apparent, especially when you reach cruising speeds on a dirt road. The vehicles aren’t as quiet as a minivan, but they are significantly quieter than any other side-by-side I’ve ever driven. What this means is you can hold a conversation with passengers in the vehicle. You can tell your daughter to get off her iPad without raising your voice. You can listen to an audiobook. I drove the Xpedition for several hours through the Black Hills and listened to music the entire time. The Xpedition has had a bluetooth-enabled speaker system for a while, but there was no point using it in the past because the engine noise drowned out anything you’d play. But with the NUMATIX engaged, I could hear every word and note from Tyler Childers as I dropped into big mud puddles and climbed rock gardens. (Side note: You should always listen to country music while driving off-road.) And the Xpedition still performs like a champ in rugged terrain, providing plenty of power to muscle through technical situations. It has 114 horsepower in a 999cc engine that offers plenty of torque for rock crawling, and 14 inches of ground clearance so you won’t get jammed up in the rock garden. For comparison, the race-inspired Polaris RZR Pro R4 has the same horsepower but in a 1997cc engine and 16 inches of ground clearance. So the Xpedition might not be the vehicle you’re looking for if you’re hoping to compete in the Baja 1000, but for the majority of off-road users, it has plenty of power to get us where we want to go. And that’s the real draw of these vehicles. They’ll go pretty much anywhere you want to go in a very user-friendly “point and go” package. You don’t have to be an experienced off-road driver to operate this side-by-side through the gnarly bits. Yes, you can get in trouble—I’ve seen people roll their side-by-side because they carried too much speed through corners with loose tread—but for the most part, these vehicles open up hard-charging, off-road adventures to average drivers like myself. Going from a 4WD vehicle, like my F-150 truck, to a side-by-side is like moving from a cruiser bike to a full-suspension mountain bike on technical singletrack. The terrain is so much less intimidating and you’re no longer limited by the tool at your disposal. That leads me to the ultimate question with a niche vehicle like this: Who is the new Polaris Xpedition’s target consumer? First, it’s for someone with money to spend. The Xpedition ain’t cheap. Starting at $40,499 for the two-seater XP, it’s no wonder some people use these side-by-sides as their daily driver. But there are plenty of people reading this column that have dedicated off-road vehicles, and the new Xpedition might be an option for those off-road enthusiasts that want a vehicle dedicated to exploring gnarly backcountry. The Xpedition goes places a 4Runner, or even a Jeep, can’t go. And it can haul plenty of your gear and your people along the way. The Xpedition ADV5 that I drove fits five (or four and a dog) and has an enclosed rear cargo area (36″ long x 47″ wide and 13″ tall) big enough for your Yeti cooler and camping gear. You can load your bike rack into the hitch and even put a roof rack on top. I’ve driven models of the Xpedition while toting rooftop tents deep into the Grand Canyon backcountry through narrow canyons I would never take my 4Runner. And with the new, quieter Xpedition, you can have a vehicle that offers that same kind of access and carrying capacity without having to wear ear plugs and scream over engine noise.

item.title: Review: Lems Trail Thrasher Pro Shoes
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.18
The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a zero-drop shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole for people who want a hiking shoe that is more robust than a trail runner but less technical than an approach shoe. With a large toe box, durable Nubuck upper, and waterproof membrane, the Trail Thrasher Pro is a versatile, durable shoe that works well for day hikes, wet-weather walks, travel, and everyday outdoor use. - Gender: Men's (Women's Available) - Weight per shoe: 15.2 oz - Wide sizes: No - Drop: Zero - Stack height: 16mm - Outsole: Vibram Megagrip - Waterproofing: Yes - Upper: Nubuck - Fit: True to Size Fit and Comfort The shoe’s most noticeable feature is its generous toe box, which lets your toes spread and splay naturally. The zero-drop platform lets your foot move more like it would barefoot, reducing fatigue and improving balance on uneven ground. Cushioning is modest but adequate. If you prefer more support or more underfoot padding like a max trail runner, these will feel too minimal. Break-in time is immediate. I could wear them right away without any fit issues. Protection I don't look at my feet when I hike, so I like good toe protection just in case I bash into a rock. Like all serious hikers, I've had my share of broken toes and toenails. The Trail Thrasher scores high in terms of toe and foot protection with hefty front-toe kicks and a nubuck upper that's unlikely to split or get shredded at the corners of the toebox. Waterproofing The waterproof lining helps keep feet dry when worn in wet grass, shallow puddles, and muddy conditions. The tongue and upper also help prevent water and trail debris from entering around the laces. Because this is a low-cut shoe, it cannot protect against water that rises above the collar. Deep puddles and stream crossings will likely leave your feet wet. The waterproof construction can feel warmer than a non-waterproof shoe in hotter weather, but warmer when there's a chill in the air. Nevertheless, for ordinary wet-weather hiking and daily walking, the protection is useful. Traction and Trail Performance The Vibram Megagrip outsole provides solid grip on packed earth, gravel, roots, and rocky inclines. The shoe is stable on maintained trails while remaining comfortable when the route varies between roots and rocks, gravel, or pavement. But the Trail Thrasher is not as flexible a shoe as many zero-drop trail runners and is much sturdier, somewhere in between a trail runner and an approach shoe. That takes a little time to get used to, but it's useful if you want to use them across a wide range of surfaces, from trails to gravel and pavement. Recommendation The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a comfortable and versatile choice for day hikers and walkers who prefer a wide, natural zero-drop fit. Its strengths include a zero-drop platform, a spacious toe box, waterproof protection, a grippy Vibram outsole, and durable construction. If it has one weakness, it's the styling. Its plain black look is not the most appealing, even compared with the outlandish color palettes of trail runners and other athletic shoes. Disclosure: Lems donated shoes for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. The non-waterproof version appears to come in much better colors, if that isn’t a must have feature for you I wonder if this would be a good choice for the Arizona Trail, maybe without the waterproofing because of the heat. I’m thinking a bit more resistant to grabbing sharp spiny things, better at keeping pebbles out, and sturdier instead of the mesh-toed Topos I use now. What do you think? If it’s hot, they’d be on the warm side.

item.title: Review: Tarptent Moment Tent Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.31
The Tarptent Moment is an ultralight, single-person tunnel tent with dual side vestibules that doesn't require trekking poles to pitch. If it's raining, you can set up the rain fly first, independently of the inner tent. You can also set up the rain fly and use it like a tarp shelter, without the inner tent. Finally, you can set up the inner tent by itself for stargazing in fine weather, though it takes a little extra configuration and isn't the main reason you'd buy this tent. - Type: Double-wall Tent (with Fly first option) - Poles: 1 (no trekking poles required) - Doors and Vestibules: 2 - Interior Pockets: 2 - Model tested: Siliconized polyester with carbon fiber pole - Weight: 29.85 oz / 846 g - Rain Fly: 15D 100% silicone-coated ripstop high-tenacity polyester (5000mm+) - Floor: 20D 100% silicone-coated ripstop high-tenacity polyester (5000mm+) - Inner tent dimensions: 84″ x 42″ (center) tapering to 24″ (ends) with 39″ of height - Outer (covered) dimensions: 102″ x 72 (center) tapering to 24″ (ends) with 42″ of height - Seam-Sealing: Required (have Tarptent do this for you) - Minimum number of stakes to pitch: 2, more recommended. I first encountered the Moment when I met Tarptent's owner, Henry Shires, in Scotland during the final days of my first coast-to-coast backpacking trip in the 2010 TGO Challenge, as our routes converged in Glen Esk on the way to the east coast town of Montrose. Henry tested a prototype of Tarptent's Moment Tent on that hike, and I've wanted to test the final product ever since. This was my chance. Variations The Moment is available in several fabric versions, including siliconized polyester, Dyneema Composite Fabric (26.05 oz / 738 g), and Challenge Sailcloth UltraTNT v1.5 composite fabric (31.5 oz / 893 g). It's also available with two different inner tent options: one with mesh walls for warm weather, and the second with solid walls to retain greater warmth in winter conditions. Similarly, there are three pole options: the carbon fiber pole works well in moderate conditions, while the aluminum poles are recommended for high winds or heavy snow loads. For three-season use, most US-based users will opt for the tent in whatever material you prefer, the mesh inner tent, and carbon fiber tent poles. I prefer a siliconized polyester tent over Dyneema because it's more compressible, and I don't feel the weight savings are worth spending twice as much on this tent. Dyneema tents also tend to let in a lot of light, which makes it hard for me to sleep on long summer days, whereas the inside of a silpoly tent tends to be darker. Fly First Setup If it's raining, you can set up the Moment rain fly before the inner tent, but you'll typically keep the two connected and set them up at the same time. The inner connects to the fly with toggles, so you can disconnect it if it's raining out and pack it first while staying under cover if you want to keep it as dry as possible. When you set it up again, you can raise the wet rain fly and reconnect the dry inner tent underneath: there are 11 dowels and two mitten hooks to connect. Most double-wall tents sold in the US don't have this capability, although it's fairly common on tents manufactured by European companies (Hilleberg, Exped, Terra Nova, and others.) To pitch the Moment, you insert a collapsible tent pole into the center sleeve to create the hoop. Then you pull the two tent ends out and stake them. You really only need two tent stakes to pitch the tent on soil you can get a stake into, although more stakes can be added to loops positioned along the hoop and perimeter of the tent. Each end of the tent forms a triangular space, created by short carbon fiber struts that slot into channels at the ends. These are called pitchlocks, and they create tunnels at each end of the tent for enhanced airflow. They also lift the tent ends off the ground and increase interior space. Without them, the rain fly would touch the ground, much like the sides of a pyramid tent, and shorten the effective length of the tent. Tarptent uses them on many of its other tents, and they're a signature feature unique to the brand. The ends of the pitchlocks are covered with solid fabric, secured along one side with Velcro. You can also roll the fabric open to let more air flow through the tent, without worrying about rain getting inside, because the ends of the inner tent are recessed. When packing, you can remove the carbon fiber struts that form the pitchlock from their channels, but most people leave them inserted and roll them up inside the tent body. Removing them makes the tent more compressible if you want to store it horizontally in a narrow backpack, but it increases setup time. To remove the center hoop pole in one piece, keep it sharply curved as you slide it out of the sleeve. This prevents the ferrules from separating, so you can pull it out in one continuous length before breaking it down and packing it up. It took me years to learn this trick (credit: Tim at Slingfin), and it really works. The regular setup time is incredibly fast with the Moment (provided the inner and outer tents are already attached), since you only need to insert the center pole and stake out the ends. It's really astounding. It's even fairly manageable in a stiff breeze, as long as you stake out one of the ends and keep the hoop close to the ground before staking out the second end. That said, you'd still want to add a few more stakes if there is any wind, using the numerous anchor points surrounding the body tent. While the Moment isn't a freestanding tent, its hooped structure makes it feel like one. To make it truly freestanding, you can add a long carbon fiber pole (extra $$) that arches over the length of the tent and slots into the end guyout points, so you can pick the entire tent up and move it around freely. This freestanding mode can be particularly useful for added strength for snow loads in winter, reducing flapping in high winds, or for places where it's difficult to stake down the ends of the tent, like a beach or rocky ledge. I don't consider it a must-have for normal use. Once erected, the tent opens along the center zipper, allowing you to open both vestibule side doors completely or partially for great airflow. The center zippers on both sides are reinforced at the bottom by buckles to take pressure off the zipper, since zippers are the most delicate part of any tent. Top vents also help vent water vapor, and magnets secure the vestibule doors when rolled up instead of old-school toggles. Unlike many ultralight tents, the sides of the Moment also reach the ground in the style of British tents. This blocks wind and rain and provides better heat retention. Many ultralight tents made for the US ‘audience' leave a much larger gap between the rain fly and the ground, which helps explain why the Moment and other Tarptent models, such as the Tarptent Scarp, are favored by UK hillwalkers and wild campers. Recommendation The Tarptent Moment is an excellent choice for solo backpackers who want an ultralight tent without relying on trekking poles. Its fast, simple pitch, two vestibules, excellent ventilation, and useful fly-first setup make it especially practical in wet and changeable weather. The ability to use the fly on its own also adds flexibility for winter trips, while the solid construction and low-sided design provide better protection from wind and rain than many ultralight tents. Spacious and comfortable, the Moment provides a versatile shelter for the discerning backpacker who wants to stay “in the Moment.” Disclosure: Tarptent loaned the author a tent. I had the first Dyneema version of this tent and loved it. I was super sad to sell it because it’s difficult to change clothes inside due to a lower ceiling height. It is a rock solid design in bad weather. I spent a couple nights on the shore of Lake Superior in October with the mesh interior and slept comfortably despite the cold wind. I had the cross pole for freestanding capability, and it’s extremely useful in rocky conditions like northern Minnesota. No stakes needed to drive into the impossibly rocky ground. In fact I rarely used stakes, just the poles. Great tent, just make the ceiling higher.

item.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.81
‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food. The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended. “Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home. Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses. Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work. Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli. Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from. At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed. At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations. But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills. Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce. At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930. Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs. At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.” In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie. Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses. Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb. It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious. It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. Högbo Brukshotell has doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&B Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: ‘I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine’: readers’ favourite foodie experiences in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.00
Simple sardines in the Algarve Last August, the smoky aroma of grilled sardines drifting over the beach in Portimão woke me up from my sunbathing on the beach. Attracted by the aroma of barbecued fish, we found ourselves in the old port where, for €12, I was served two delicious sandwiches on rustic bread of sardines in garlic and olive oil, with a small cold beer. I sat down, ate and chatted with locals on benches at simple communal tables. The important thing seemed to be to enjoy food together. The next morning, a reenactment of the fishing boats arriving loaded with fish, as they once were, was a real spectacle – complete with guitar playing, drum-banging and excited seagulls whirling and wailing above in the hope of a feast. Later, concerts and dancing animated the town as the party for the sardine festival went on well into the night. Cooking demos and dishes including sardine-based soup and salads, added to the enjoyment. I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine. Joe A family dinner in the Faroe Islands My wife and I visited the Faroe Islands a few years ago, where we took part in heimablídni, a concept where traditional Faroese food is served in a home. We found it to be one of the best ways to experience the Faroes and a unique experience to share a meal with a local family. Homecooked dishes showcase ingredients from the surrounding sea and mountains. We were served smoked salmon from the host’s own smoker, lamb, potatoes and traditional specialities, all accompanied with great conversation about Faroese life and traditions. Sitting around a family table makes the experience feel personal and authentic. Mike A vegan feast in Sicily As a vegan who loves trying local cuisine, the combination of warm hospitality and a high proportion of locals with a lactose intolerance makes Sicily the ideal foodie getaway. Having hiked to the top of Monte Pellegrino in 35C heat, we popped into a small nondescript street-food shop (the only place that was open) and were delighted to find panelle – delicious crispy chickpea-flour fritters served in sesame bread. We ate them overlooking Palermo harbour. That evening, we tried Haiku, a vegan restaurant with reimagined classics based on dishes such as carbonara and tiramisu. It was so good we kept ordering more and more courses until we could barely move. Esther Strong spirits and small plates in Greece The city of Volos is famous for its Tsipouradika – tavernas that serve tsipouro, a strong spirit made from pomace, the stems, skins and seeds that are left over from wine making. It comes plain or infused with botanicals and anise, and is served with ice and water. Each glass you order arrives with a different small plate or meze. It could be grilled peppers, sundried octopus, a spicy cheese spread or smoked mackerel. You take pot luck as to what the patron fancies dishing up that day. Barbara The perfect snack to pair with Lithuanian beer In Vilnius, we came across the ultimate food pairing for the fantastic beers available there in the form of kepta duona – deep-fried rye bread with garlic and cheese. Every bar has a slightly different version – raw, roast or confit garlic with cream, melted or simply grated cheese. A heavenly snack that could easily become your main meal. Natalie Vegan delights in the patisseries of Paris Being an unfortunate combination of a foodie and a vegan, I was prepared for a weekend of staring longingly into patisserie windows when heading to Paris earlier this summer. I was not prepared for the unbridled joy awaiting me at the Land & Monkeys boulangeries/patisseries scattered across the capital. It began with an outrageously creamy raspberry petit gateaux from its Montmartre branch, followed by the unbelievable fluff and flake of a croissant aux champignons in the Marais the next day. A parting madeleine for the Eurostar on our last day was the pièce de résistance. Elinor Pasta with pears in Bologna It was in Bologna, Italy’s self-proclaimed food capital, where I sampled the city’s signature dish of tortellini. We stumbled across Rosarose Bistrot, enticed by tables with red-checked cloths set in the middle of a cobblestone road. I enjoyed shells stuffed with tangy gorgonzola cheese and chunks of caramelised pears, a fruit I would usually avoid, but I placed trust in the regional delicacy. The fruit’s sweetness blended harmoniously with the strong cheese flavour; crispy and soft fried bread known as crescentine, was used to soak up the remaining sauce. It was only right to mark this culinary experience with a small tortellini keyring from a nearby gift shop, filled with various merchandise emblazoned with the pasta shell. Caitlin Catalonia’s ultimate slow-food festival Last year, I discovered the ultimate slow-food festival – the Snail Feast of Lleida (L’Aplec del Caragol), 100 miles west of Barcelona. Over a long weekend, there was music, dancing, cooking and feasting, all in celebration of the tiny mollusc. Entrance to the festival is free, and visitors can enjoy traditional snail dishes in tents, local restaurants or simply in the town squares. I had two helpings of snails a la gormanda, cooked in a sauce of spicy paprika and herbs. Since attending the festival, I have been treading carefully in my garden in case I harm what I discovered are delicate and delicious creatures. Helen Heavenly cakes in Slovenia Having travelled by train from Bristol down through the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Italy, we reached our penultimate stop, Lake Bled. We’d been awed by the beautiful Swiss alpine scenery, but Bled took it up a notch. After a day of cycling from Bled to Lake Bohinj and back, we refuelled on the local delicacy, Bled cake, a sumptuously smooth set custard encased in the lightest of mille-feuille pastry and topped with whipped cream. Imagine an English custard slice, only a million times better. It was so welcome after a day in the Slovenian mountain air, we made it a holiday habit. A Bled cake a day until we had to come home! Sara Winning tip: delicious seafood soup in Spain Few meals linger in the memory like a proper Asturian sopa de pescado y marisco (seafood soup). After kayaking 10 miles down the Sella River, my reward in the town of Arriondas wasn’t a humble bowl of soup – it was a whole pan! Every flavour shone through in a broth packed with white fish, prawns and sweet crab claws, so extraordinarily rich it almost brought me to tears. I devoured it all, skipping the rest of the courses without regret. Years later in Gijón, history repeated itself. Even my soup-sceptical husband declared it the best he had ever tasted. In Asturias, fish soup isn’t a starter. It’s an obsession in a pot. Oksana Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west Sweden
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.94
I wasn’t exactly in “Sunday best”, but I had made some effort. Well, I’d changed my underwear for the first time in a couple of days and given myself a baby-wipe bath. Still, as we filed into the chapel at Alkavare, I felt more a member of an expedition than a congregation. We sat on the low wooden benches, waterproof jackets rustling and leather walking boots stamping on the flagstone floor to keep warm. Fortunately, the priest, Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen, appeared to be a “man of the Gore-Tex”, as well as a man of the cloth, as he unzipped his own black rain jacket to reveal his dog collar. As the service began, the Arctic wind whipped through cracks in the dry stone walls, insulated only with reindeer hair, and candles flickered in their brass sconces. I had hiked to Alkavare following the Präststigen, or “Priests’ trail”, a 37-mile (60km) route from Kvikkjokk that could stake a claim as Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route, and certainly one of its most beautiful. The Präststigen follows the path that priests would once have taken to the chapel, built in 1788, to perform a service each summer, and today, on the last weekend in July, intrepid hikers and perseverant pilgrims can attend that same service. Alkavare sits on the western border of Sweden’s Sarek national park, home to many of the country’s highest mountains and steepest valleys, yet with no campsites or tourist huts and only scant sections of the more famous Kungsleden trail. There are no other marked paths and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventure.
