It was described by famed Swedish diplomat Dag Hammarskjöld in 1926 as vår sista stora vildmark – “our last great wilderness”. “I hate it when people use the term ‘wilderness’,” Christian Heimrot from Laponia Adventures, a local guiding operator, told me, as I joined him on the research exhibition for a new Präststigen group trip launching next year. “This is a living landscape, people have lived, worked and shaped this land for thousands of years.” Indeed, Sarek national park, (as part of the wider Laponia region), was recognised as a Unsesco World Heritage Site in 1996 for both its cultural and natural value. The Sami, Europe’s last Indigenous population, have braided themselves into these landscapes as tightly and beautifully as the thread of pewter in their traditional handicrafts. The Sami word for the Laponia area is Sápmi, the same word they use to refer to themselves, highlighting the indelible link between people and their environment. Sarek sits on the Sami’s traditional reindeer herding grounds. While they might now use motorcycles and snowmobiles to follow and herd the reindeer, their knowledge of and kinship with this landscape remains undimmed. So, not wilderness, then, but certainly wild. To even reach the start of the Präststigen, I had crossed the Arctic Circle on the road north from Luleå, met with Christian at his warehouse in Jokkmokk (home to the famous Sami winter markets each February) to load up our rucksacks for the six-night trip, and journeyed an hour farther west to the town of Kvikkjokk. From there the trailhead was a short boat ride across Sakkat lake. The first section of the trail climbed steeply, switchbacks tightly coiled in birch woodland; wild blueberries and cloudberries littered the path. Eventually we left the woodland and reached the ridge for our first proper view of Sarek. Away to the north was the cloud-covered summit of Bårddetjåhkkå, where in 1911 Swedish geologist Axel Hamberg built an observatory to conduct meteorological and glacial studies. We slept soundly, as we eased into the rhythms of wild camping – water collected from a gin-clear lake, a hearty supper of reindeer stew, and an eye mask to keep out the midnight sun. The next day we hiked deeper into Sarek via the Vállevágge, the skies the blue of the Swedish flag, the silence only disrupted by the occasional breath of wind. We were following the guidebook Priest’s Path by Hans Fowelin (currently only published in Swedish), and while there was no marked trail, Fowelin had plotted a path of cairns we were supposedly to follow. While some were solidly built square towers, most were little more than one rock propped up against another, mere whispers of waymarkers in a landscape of scree and moraine. Alongside the familiar buttercups and heather there were bright blue blossoms of mountain gentian, red ptarmigan berries and otherworldly looking wild angelica, a source of vitamin C for the Sami. Sarek was visited by botanist Carl Linnaeus during his epic expedition through northern Sweden in 1732, and the first part of the Priest’s trail is sometimes referred to as Linnaeus’s trail. On our fourth day of hiking Alkavare chapel appeared on a bluff above the glacial blue waters of Alggajavvre lake, surrounded by high peaks and valleys. It was utterly beautiful. I had a grin on my wind-burnt face for most of the day, one that even wading across rivers (a common feature of hiking in Sarek), shin-high in glacial meltwater, failed to dim. After rowing across the Miellätno river, using one of the rowing boats left on each bank by the park rangers, we climbed up to the chapel late on Saturday evening where Jacobsen greeted us with a beaming smile. Over tea, he told us he had been dropped off by helicopter at Alkavare with his family on Friday morning and this was his first time leading the service here. Others in the diocese no longer volunteered. “It is physical, hard work and the days are long,” he said, before heading off to re-tar the chapel’s roof and fix one of the rowing boats that had come loose and floated away down the river – returned, later, swinging beneath a helicopter. Sunday mass began promptly at 11am the following morning for our small band of pilgrims (we numbered 11 in total, including the priest). The altar had a simple wooden cross and cloths on loan from the church in Jokkmokk. They were in the poster paint palate of traditional Sami clothing and a reminder that it was for the Sami that the chapel had been originally built – not an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation and eradication of their shamanistic beliefs in the 18th century. After the service we sat outside for coffee and pastries, before beginning our hike home. Christian was keen that we hiked via Sweden’s point of inaccessibility or otillgänglighetspunkten, just over the border from Sarek in the Padjelanta national park. This is the country’s point furthest from any road or town, about 31 miles (50km) in fact, and is often cited as western Europe’s remotest too. Marked with no cairn or monument, just a circle of quartz stones and a trio of reindeer antlers, it felt no more or less remote than most of the previous week’s hiking. And I was struck that what made Sarek and the Präststigen special wasn’t just the scenery, as beautiful as it was, it was the people – the Sami, Hamberg and Linneaus, and the motley congregation we’d briefly joined, and it was a route firmly deserving of more visitors. “I told you,” Christian said, grinning, “It isn’t a wilderness.” The trip was provided by Laponia Adventures, which will lead a guided, small-group trip along the Priest’s Path to Alkavare in July 2027, and offers equipment rental and advice for independent hikers. For more information on Sarek national park and northern Sweden, visit arcticsweden.com Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.45
‘I don’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio. “It’s not the same.” Savio is a very opinionated foodie, so I take his words with a pinch of good Puglian sea salt (see below). He was adamant about the superiority of the stretched-curd cheese from his home turf. Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredient du jour burrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, but despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches, it is often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia. So I asked Savio’s company, Unexpected Italy, an app that calls itself the antidote to overtourism, to organise a trip to the area. About a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter (burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps (stracciatella) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese. There are now several burrata makers in Andria, the most famous being Caseificio Olanda, which offers demos, tastings and a museum. Late one morning, we watch Riccardo “Dino” Olanda, son of the founders, work his magic. He adds almost-boiling water to the curds, then mixes with hands red from doing this every day. As he stretches and massages the curds, a smooth velvety mass forms. “See how it’s shiny?” he says. “Means it’s ready.” Working quickly, he squeezes out round lumps between thumb and forefinger into the familiar mozzarella balls. This action is mozzare, hence the name. He also makes little knots and plaits before moving on to burrata. Taking a warm mozzarella ball, he works it into a hollow bag with his fingers then fills it with cream and stracciatella before tying the top with string. Afterwards, a dairy-heavy meal totally worth the cholesterol and calories: mozzarella and burrata to start, then bread with chunks of caciocavallo (a stretched-curd cheese), and a dessert of heart-shaped fresh ricotta with strawberry jam or cocoa. And, I have to say, Savio is right. The mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a gorgeous cheesy, umami flavour; the salt and flavour leached out by the whey the cheeses later sit in. How will I ever settle for Tesco Finest after this? Over the next few days, eating our way around the province’s restaurants and food producers, I wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way round. Barletta sees few foreign tourists, but it is full of Italian life. There are lots of independent shops, a Norman castle and cathedral to visit, and every evening people pour into the bars, clubs and gelaterie of the sette strade, seven parallel streets in the old town. Down the coast, Trani, with its sea-facing romanesque cathedral and pretty harbour, attracts some tourists, but they are not in evidence at 7am when the fishing boats return. The men complain of rough seas and a poor catch, but from the back of the boats they’re soon selling mullet, octopus, skate, fat sea snails, monkfish and palombo (small shark) to restaurateurs and fishmongers. Thirtysomething Nicola says he went out at midday and got back at 3am. When does he sleep? “Never.” A fifth-generation fisher, he began helping on the boats aged six. We’ll eat fish later, but today is for pizza. Portento in Barletta is run by food nut Luigi Lacerenza. He has us try so many local products as antipasti – caprino goat’s cheese tasting of green mountains, grilled caciocavallo from an old couple who make just six a week and small-batch salami – that we’re almost too full for pizzas. But they are wonderful: one with sausage, olives, oyster mushrooms and yellow tomatoes; another with aubergines and grated cacioricotta. In Cerignola, west of Barletta, Rosario Didonna used the money he won on a TV standup competition to turn his family’s deli into a cosy, wood- panelled restaurant, U’ Vulèsce (dialect for “peckish”). Rosario knows fishers by name, works with small farmers and wine producers, and invites nonne from all over southern Italy to demonstrate recipes in his kitchens. We start with tasty goat prosciutto and plum-sized local olives called bella di Cerignola. Then an unforgettable prawn tartare served in sea urchin shells, hairy crab spaghetti (“the juice is better than lobster”), octopus with bean puree, and sea bass with orange mayo. He waves away our thanks: “I’m doing the best job in the world!” Nicola Barbera at Masseria Barbera, a farm restaurant in the Alta Murgia national park, is equally inspired, but rather by what grows on the estate founded by his great-great-great-great-grandfather Riccardo, who fought with Garibaldi. Exuberantly bouncing us around the farm – it produces 90% of what the 100-cover restaurant needs – he shows us olives and vines, but also the “weeds” growing around them. “They’re eatable,” he says, grabbing handfuls of peppery rocket, and bitter but delicate wild chicory. From the abundant kitchen garden, he makes eight varieties of tomato sauce. We tuck into a lot of this for lunch: a pie with white onions, anchovy and sultanas; courgettes with mint and garlic; spaghetti with yellow tomatoes. (“I call it bastard sauce,” says Nicola. “Those tomatoes take three times as long to pick.”) Then, something I never thought I’d eat: grilled donkey fillet. I feel bad about the patient, mild-tempered beasts, but this is healthy, low-fat food, never intensively farmed. It’s also the best meat I’ve ever tasted. Good food is made better by good olive oil, and producers here include Muraglia, known for organic oil in hand-painted, rainbow-stripe ceramic bottles, and Sabino Leone, offering tours of its ancient groves and oil mill for €15, plus tastings. This area also offers plenty to do between meals. Barletta was the home of Italian painter Giuseppe De Nittis, who hung out with Degas and Manet, and took part in the first impressionist exhibition in Paris, in 1874. Over 200 of his works are now displayed in the 16th-century Palazzo della Marra (€6). At Europe’s biggest salt pan, Salina Margherita di Savoia, there’s an expanse of peaceful ponds with a snow-white salt mountain to climb. Another day, an exhilarating ebike ride in the Alta Murgia with Filippo Tito of Cycling ’n’ Trek, through dense forest to peer with awe into an old bauxite mine that resembles a mini grand canyon. We get back ravenous, but in this corner of northern Puglia, that’s a blessing. Where to stay Until this century, Barletta had little tourist accommodation. Pick of the few B&Bs is Antica Dimora (doubles from €97), a restored 17th-century palazzo run by Lilly and Riccardo Manna. There are three smart bedrooms with lots of plants and breakfast features different local specialities each day. Lama di Luna (doubles from €230) is an organic farm in deep countryside, with six rooms set around an 18th-century stone courtyard. A well and solar panels make it energy and water self-sufficient; half of its 200 hectares are left wild, the rest are planted with olives, vines, almonds and cherries. There’s a cinema, a library and a large pool shaded by 600-year-old olive trees. Where (else) to eat Barletta’s 60-year-old Mosé bakery is revered for its krapfen filled doughnuts and sourdough croissants. There are also chocolates, ice-cream and cakes, all housemade, and great coffee. Puglia has hundreds of gelaterie but experts rate Scoop in Canosa (which is called Puglia’s “Little Rome” for its catacombs, temple ruins and Roman bridge). Francesco Di Nunno makes ice-cream with local seasonal ingredients: raspberry and strawberry sorbets are available only in early summer; percoca yellow peach until mid-August. There’s affordable fine dining at chef Luciano Matera’s Il Turracciolo in central Andria. Highlights for me are broad bean and chicory “meatballs”, bright green inside; a “hidden mushroom” under baked eggy topping; and pasta discs with whole and pureed green beans and peas. At A Sud dell’Anima, chef Nadia Tamburrano uses modern techniques and hyper-local ingredients to make food of astonishing quality for a small hilltop town (Minervino, population under 8,000). Her antipasti explode with flavour thanks to house-cured capers and homemade mustard, syrups and purees. A main of sweetbreads wrapped in intestines feels a bit out-there, but is delicious, the intestines crispy as crackling. The trip was organised by Unexpected Italy, which offers personalised itineraries for Barletta and the surrounding area Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Air Canada’s Aeroplan program: The ultimate guide to earning and redeeming points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.48
Air Canada’s Aeroplan program: The ultimate guide to earning and redeeming points Editor's Note Air Canada's Aeroplan loyalty program is one of the most valuable Star Alliance airline programs — and it's one worth knowing, even if you don't travel to Canada. Aeroplan still uses published award charts for most partner flights, a rarity in a loyalty world increasingly driven by dynamic pricing. Plus, it charges low fees on award tickets and lets you add stopovers to one-way tickets for just 5,000 extra points. It's easy to earn Aeroplan points — even if you live in the U.S. — since the program partners with most major transferable points and miles programs, so you can earn Aeroplan points with your everyday spending. Here is everything you need to know about Air Canada Aeroplan. Related: Why Air Canada Aeroplan has become my favorite Star Alliance loyalty program Aeroplan pros and cons Pros - There are published award charts with low redemption rates for most partner airlines. - No carrier-imposed surcharges apply. - You can enjoy one stopover per direction of travel, including on one-way tickets, for 5,000 extra points. - Transfer partnerships with most major transferable rewards programs are available, all at a 1:1 ratio. - You can pool points with up to eight family members, and credit card preferred pricing is shared across the pool. - Generous lap infant pricing is available, and there's no fare within Canada or between Canada and the U.S. Cons - Air Canada's own flights are priced dynamically and can be extremely high on busy dates. - Change and cancellation fees are steep. - Complex stopover itineraries often have to be booked by phone, which carries its own fee. - Points expire after 18 months without activity. - Partner premium cabin availability can be hard to find. Air Canada Aeroplan partners Air Canada is part of Star Alliance, the world's biggest airline alliance. You can earn and redeem Aeroplan points on any Star Alliance airline, making it easy to get just about anywhere in the world. You'll find Star Alliance hubs in some of the world's largest airports, including Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Frankfurt Airport (FRA), Istanbul Airport (IST) and Tokyo's Haneda Airport (HND). The following airlines are Star Alliance members: - Aegean Airlines - Air Canada - Air China - Air India - Air New Zealand - All Nippon Airways - Asiana Airlines - Austrian Airlines - Avianca - Brussels Airlines - Copa Airlines - Croatia Airlines - Egyptair - Ethiopian Airlines - EVA Air - ITA Airways - LOT Polish Airlines - Lufthansa - Shenzhen Airlines - Singapore Airlines - South African Airways - Swiss - TAP Air Portugal - Thai Airways - Turkish Airlines - United Airlines Aeroplan also has partnerships with many carriers outside of Star Alliance, including: - Aer Lingus (codeshare only) - AirBaltic - Air Creebec - Air Dolomiti - Air Inuit - Air Mauritius - Air Serbia - Azul Brazilian Airlines - Bamboo Airways - Bearskin Airlines - Calm Air - Canadian North - Cathay Pacific (select routes only) - Central Mountain Air (codeshare only) - Discover Airlines - Edelweiss Air (codeshare only) - Emirates - Etihad Airways - Eurowings - Flydubai - Gol Airlines - Gulf Air - Harbour Air - Helijet - Juneyao Air (Star Alliance connecting partner) - Lufthansa City Airlines - Middle East Airlines (codeshare only) - Olympic Air - Oman Air - PAL Airlines - SriLankan Airlines (codeshare only) - SunExpress - Virgin Australia Be sure to review the information on Air Canada's airline partner page to understand the full scope of each carrier's partnership. For example, as noted, some of the airlines listed above only have codeshare partnerships with Air Canada; other partnerships — such as Cathay Pacific — are limited to specific routes. Air Canada Aeroplan elite status Air Canada Aeroplan rewards its frequent flyers with valuable perks like seat upgrade certificates, free checked bags and other benefits across five different status tiers. Likewise, Air Canada elite members receive reciprocal benefits on Star Alliance partner airlines. Earning Air Canada Aeroplan elite status Aeroplan recently changed how you qualify for elite status. It used to require earning a combination of Status Qualifying Miles, Status Qualifying Segments and Status Qualifying Dollars to earn status. Nowadays, the airline awards elite status solely on the number of Status Qualifying Credits you earn in a single calendar year. SQCs are earned based on how much you spend on an Air Canada flight or vacation package: - Economy Flex or higher: 4 SQCs per Canadian dollar spent - Economy Standard fares and eUpgrade add-ons: 2 SQCs per Canadian dollar spent - Air Canada Vacations packages: 1 SQC per Canadian dollar spent You can also earn 1 SQC for every 5 Aeroplan points earned with most partners, including Star Alliance partner airlines, up to 25,000 SQCs per year. For example, earning 10,000 Aeroplan points on a partner flight would also earn 2,000 SQCs. Exclusions apply for Aeroplan eStore earnings, bonus points and points converted from hotel or credit card programs. Additionally, nonalliance partner airlines do not earn SQCs. Here's a look at the requirements for each status tier: - Aeroplan 25K: 25,000 SQCs - Aeroplan 35K: 35,000 SQCs - Aeroplan 50K: 50,000 SQCs - Aeroplan 75K: 75,000 SQCs - Aeroplan Super Elite: 125,000 SQCs You can also earn Aeroplan 25K status by earning 100,000 Everyday Status Qualification points in a single calendar year. You'll earn 1 ESQ for every 1 eligible Aeroplan point earned with Aeroplan partners. This includes the Aeroplan eStore but excludes bonus miles and point conversions. Earning status with Aeroplan credit cards The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (see rates and fees) can be a big help when earning Aeroplan elite status. That's because it includes automatic Aeroplan 25K elite status for as long as you have the card. Plus, you can upgrade to Aeroplan 35K status by spending $75,000 on your card in a given calendar year. Cardmembers can also earn up to 25,000 SQCs per calendar year with the Aeroplan card. It includes 5,000 SQCs as an annual bonus, 10,000 SQCs after spending $25,000 on your card in a calendar year and another 10,000 SQCs after spending $50,000. Aeroplan elite status requirements The higher your status, the more benefits you can enjoy when flying with Air Canada and its partner airlines. Below you'll find an overview of the Core Benefits awarded at each status level. You can also earn additional benefits when you earn Milestone Benefits, which we outline in the next section. Aeroplan 25K - Priority airport check-in, when available - Priority standby - Priority boarding with Air Canada, United and Lufthansa - Ability to earn 2 points per dollar spent on Air Canada-ticketed flights - Two complimentary checked bags on Air Canada flights - Complimentary handling of sports equipment - Preferred seat selection at check-in on eligible Air Canada routes - Avis Preferred Plus status match - Five eUpgrade credits - Star Alliance Silver status Aeroplan 35K All Aeroplan 25K benefits, plus: - Priority baggage handling on Air Canada flights - Priority security screening, where available - One extra complimentary checked bag on Air Canada flights - Ability to earn 3 points per dollar spent on Air Canada-ticketed flights - 10 eUpgrade credits Aeroplan 50K All Aeroplan 35K benefits, plus: - Access to Maple Leaf lounges and Air Canada cafes - Access to Virgin Australia lounges when flying Air Canada or Virgin Australia - Access to Emirates business-class lounges in Dubai when flying between Canada and Dubai - Preferred seat assignment at booking for Canada and U.S. routes on eligible Air Canada flights - Preferred seat assignment at check-in for other routes - Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status match - Ability to earn 4 points per dollar spent on Air Canada-ticketed flights - 15 eUpgrade credits - Star Alliance Gold status, which includes partner lounge access Aeroplan 75K All Aeroplan 50K benefits, plus: - Preferred seat selection at booking on all eligible Air Canada fares - Ability to earn 5 points per dollar spent on Air Canada-ticketed flights - 20 eUpgrade credits Aeroplan Super Elite All Aeroplan 75K benefits, plus: - Access to the Arrivals Lounge in Terminal 2 of London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) - Complimentary changes and cancellations on Aeroplan award tickets - Complimentary inflight refreshments in economy - Two status passes to share elite perks with a friend for a single itinerary - Gift your eUpgrade credits to someone else - Avis President's Club status match - Ability to earn 6 points per dollar spent on Air Canada-ticketed flights - 30 eUpgrade credits Milestone Benefits Milestone Benefits provides another way for Air Canada frequent flyers to earn eUpgrade credits (which can be used for flight upgrades) and other perks. Members start unlocking Milestone Benefits after earning 10,000 SQCs. You can pick benefits at some levels, with choices ranging from Maple Leaf Lounge passes to bonus points, status passes to share with friends and discounts on award tickets. How to earn Air Canada Aeroplan points It's surprisingly easy to earn Air Canada Aeroplan points, even if you're not flying Air Canada. Here's a look at some of the ways to earn them. Fly with Air Canada You'll earn Aeroplan points based on how much you spend on your Air Canada flight, with elite members earning bonus points. Members without elite status earn 1 point per dollar spent, and elite members can earn up to 6 points per dollar spent. Note that this is calculated based on your ticket price before taxes, fees and third-party charges. | Elite level | Points earned per dollar spent | |---|---| | Member (no elite status) | 1 | | Aeroplan 25K | 2 | | Aeroplan 35K | 3 | | Aeroplan 50K | 4 | | Aeroplan 75K | 5 | | Aeroplan Super Elite | 6 | Earning rates are based on the ticket cost in Canadian dollars. If you pay in a different currency, Air Canada will convert the cost of your ticket to Canadian dollars using an "industry-standard exchange rate" before calculating your earnings. Fly with Star Alliance and nonalliance partners Partner flights still earn Aeroplan points based on the distance flown and the fare class you book. Every partner airline's earning rates chart is listed on Air Canada's airline partner page. Find your partner airline on the list, and click on it. Here's how this works. Say you book a one-way United flight from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) on United's website, and your ticket is booked in D-fare domestic first class. According to Aeroplan's United earning chart, this ticket earns 150% of the miles flown. This flight clocks in at 719 miles, meaning you'd earn 1,079 Aeroplan points. Earn points with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card Air Canada offers multiple credit cards in Canada and one here in the U.S. New Chase Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card applicants can earn up to 115,000 bonus Aeroplan points: 75,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus an additional 40,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first 12 months from account opening. In our September 2026 valuations, TPG values Aeroplan points as worth 1.5 cents each, making this welcome bonus worth $1,725. Know, though, that such a valuable welcome bonus comes with an annual fee of $195. With elevated earning rates in multiple categories (most notably, up to 5 points per dollar spent on Air Canada flights made with the card as an Aeroplan 25K elite member), plus up to $100 in annual Air Canada statement credits (up to two $50 semiannual credits), a 15% award discount when booking an itinerary with at least one Air Canada-operated flight and complimentary Aeroplan 25K elite status, this card is incredibly valuable, especially if you ever fly Air Canada. Transfer credit card points to Aeroplan You can transfer the following credit card rewards to Aeroplan at a 1:1 transfer ratio: - American Express Membership Rewards points - Bilt Points - Capital One miles - Chase Ultimate Rewards points This makes it easy to earn Aeroplan points on your everyday spending, as many transferable points and miles credit cards offer bonus points or miles on everyday purchases and large welcome bonuses. The following cards all currently offer strong welcome bonuses with points or miles that you can transfer to your Aeroplan account: You'll sometimes even find limited-time transfer bonuses when transferring points to Aeroplan. Related: Why transferable points and miles are worth more than other rewards Earn Aeroplan points at airport shops and restaurants Aeroplan added Club Avolta, which includes airport retail brands Hudson and Dufry, as an earning partner on June 30. Members who link their Aeroplan and Club Avolta accounts in the Club Avolta app earn 1 Aeroplan point for every CA$2 spent in store and on preorders placed through Avolta's Reserve & Collect service. More than 900 Avolta locations take part. In Canada, that includes Toronto Pearson Airport (YYZ), Vancouver International Airport (YVR) in British Columbia, Calgary International Airport (YYC) in Alberta and Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport (YTZ). In the U.S., it includes Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and ORD. Avolta says the partnership will extend to its HMSHost dining outlets before the end of 2026, taking the network to close to 1,900 airport retail and food-and-beverage locations across North America. Earn with retail partners Air Canada has an online shopping portal that lets you earn Aeroplan points through third-party vendors such as Apple and Uber Eats. You can click through the merchant's link on the Air Canada eStore before you make a purchase and earn a set number of points per dollar spent. This can be a great way to earn bonus points on everyday purchases. However, not all Air Canada retail partners are valid for points-earning purchases in both the U.S. and Canada. Some are limited to Canada, so double-check your merchant's terms and conditions before using the eStore. Air Canada for Business Air Canada has a business rewards program called Air Canada for Business. Businesses can use this program to earn additional Aeroplan points on every flight and get a 5% discount on Flex fares and higher. Additionally, companies using Air Canada for Business earn 500 SQCs for every $5,000 spent on eligible fares. These SQCs can be allocated to employees, helping them reach a higher tier of elite status. Do Aeroplan points expire? Aeroplan points expire after 18 months of inactivity. Air Canada suspended that policy during the coronavirus pandemic and has extended the suspension several times since. Points that would otherwise have expired are protected through Nov. 29, and the standard policy returns the following day. Any earning or redeeming activity resets the clock on your entire balance, so a single small transaction protects a 500,000-point account as effectively as a 5,000-point one. Qualifying activity includes crediting a paid Air Canada or Star Alliance flight to your account, converting points from a credit card program, booking a hotel or car rental through Aeroplan, shopping through the Aeroplan eStore and redeeming for any Aeroplan reward. Members with Aeroplan elite status are exempt, as are primary cardholders of an Aeroplan cobranded credit card. Aeroplan Family Sharing Aeroplan lets up to eight verified family members pool their points into a single shared balance while keeping their individual accounts. Spouses and partners, children, siblings, in-laws, parents and grandparents can all join. The member who creates the pool is the family lead, who must be 18 or older and must have held an Aeroplan account for at least six months. Every point each member earns goes into the shared balance, including the points they already hold, and members cannot contribute only part of a balance. The family lead decides which members can redeem from the pool and which can only contribute to it. Redemptions come out of every member's account proportionally rather than from one person's balance, and any member with redemption privileges can book a reward for anyone, including someone outside the pool. If one member of the pool is the primary cardholder of an Aeroplan credit card, everyone in the pool sees that cardholder's preferred pricing on Aeroplan flight rewards, which can save thousands of points on a single booking. How to redeem Air Canada Aeroplan points You can use your Aeroplan points to fly worldwide; Air Canada offers a bevy of routes of its own, but its extensive alliance and nonalliance partner network expands this list even further. The program uses a standard award chart for most partner flights, pricing flights based on region and distance. However, Air Canada's own flights and those operated by select partners — including United, Emirates and Etihad — are priced dynamically. This means you can book many partner award flights at a predictable price. Aeroplan doesn't add fuel surcharges to award tickets, so you'll only pay minimal taxes, plus a CA$39 (about $28.70) partner booking fee (if applicable). Aeroplan's award chart As mentioned, Aeroplan employs a hybrid distance- and region-based award chart. You'll pay based on your flight length, but pricing varies based on the region you fly to and from. Each region is broadly defined. To find the cost of an award ticket booked by a nondynamic partner, first determine the regions you're flying from and to. Then, calculate the distance between your origin and destination using a tool like Great Circle Mapper. Next, find the award chart for your region pair in the Air Canada award chart to determine the cost of your flight. You can also search for your flight on Air Canada's website to view the price, as most partners are bookable online. Here is the chart for travel from North America to the Atlantic region, which includes flights from the U.S. to Europe. Flights on Brussels Airlines are priced based on the "All other partners" rates above, meaning they're based on the standard award chart. As such, a flight from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Brussels Airport (BRU) is 3,650 miles long, meaning it'd cost 60,000 points plus taxes and fees in business class. Things get trickier with Air Canada flights and those operated by the "select partners" that Aeroplan prices dynamically. This includes flights operated by United, Emirates, Flydubai, Etihad, Canadian North, Calm Air and Bearskin Airlines. In these instances, the figures listed on the award chart serve as a floor; you'll have to check Air Canada's website to find award costs for these airlines, and pricing can vary radically day to day, especially on Air Canada flights. Aeroplan award fees, changes and cancellations Air Canada does not charge a booking fee when you book a flight reward on its website. Booking through the Aeroplan Contact Center costs CA$30 per ticket, and that fee is nonrefundable and still applies when an itinerary cannot be completed online. Any award that includes a flight operated by a partner airline incurs an additional CA$39 partner booking fee per ticket. Change and cancellation fees depend on the fare option you book rather than the cabin, so a flexible economy award can be cheaper to cancel than a lowest-price business-class award. Same-day changes at the airport are priced separately. Changes and cancellations must be made at least two hours before departure. Booking awards for infants and children An infant under 2 at the time of travel who does not occupy a seat still needs their own ticket, but what that ticket costs depends on where you are going. For travel wholly within Canada and for travel between Canada and the U.S., no fare applies. For every other itinerary, including flights between the U.S. and Europe, Asia or South America, the fare is CA$25 or 2,500 Aeroplan points per direction of travel. Taxes, fees and charges still apply on top. Only one lap infant is permitted per adult traveling. The best ways to redeem Air Canada Aeroplan points The Aeroplan award chart is full of interesting sweet spots and great deals. Here are some of the best ways to maximize the award chart and the program's interesting features, such as stopovers on one-way award tickets. Book Air Canada flights on off-peak dates Aeroplan's system for dynamically pricing Air Canada-operated flights is unpredictable, but it can still lead to good deals on off-peak dates. This is especially true for short-haul cross-border and Canadian domestic flights, which are frequently priced at under 10,000 points one-way. Just note that fees can be high on cross-border flights, so make sure to compare the cost of an award ticket to buying a ticket outright. Meanwhile, on peak dates, the prices are often unreasonably high and not a great redemption option. This is especially true for flights from North America to Europe and Asia. However, if you are willing to travel on off-peak dates, you might be able to find a good deal on longer flights. Try booking seasonal flights in the first and last month of the season (you can use Air Canada's Wikipedia page to check which destinations are seasonal) for attractive pricing on low-demand dates. Book a mini round-the-world trip with stopovers You can add one stopover to one-way tickets or two stopovers to round-trip tickets for 5,000 points apiece. These stopovers can be anywhere in the world, and Aeroplan lets you get creative with your routing. The only major restriction to know is that your total distance flown can't exceed twice the nonstop distance to your destination. Stopovers are not permitted within Canada, the U.S. or China, and no stopover can run longer than 45 days. You can make some interesting itineraries with Aeroplan's flexible routing rules. For example, you can book a mini round-the-world trip that includes two stopovers and multiple 24-hour layovers. You can book stopover tickets online, but you may need to call to book more complex itineraries with additional layovers. If you choose to book a complicated itinerary with long layovers, make sure to find award space on Air Canada's website before you call to book. Related: The complete guide to Aeroplan's stopover and routing rules Fly partner airlines from the East Coast to Europe Many flights from the East Coast to Western Europe fall into the 0 to 4,000 miles tier on the North America-to-Atlantic award chart, and there are plenty of partner airlines flying across the Atlantic that regularly release seats to Aeroplan. This includes popular airlines like Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Lufthansa, LOT Polish Airlines, Swiss and TAP Air Portugal. These flights cost just 60,000 points in business class (Lufthansa recently stopped releasing first-class seats to partners like Aeroplan), so they're a great way to cross the Atlantic in style. If you're eyeing a longer flight to Europe, business-class flights cost 75,000 points for itineraries up to 6,000 miles. These options are cheaper than those offered by other Star Alliance programs, such as Avianca Lifemiles and United MileagePlus, for the same flights. Fly business class to India for 85,000 points You can book Star Alliance partners like United, Air India and Turkish Airlines between the U.S. and India for just 85,000 points each way in business class or 50,000 points each way in economy class. Bottom line Air Canada's Aeroplan loyalty program is great. Solid redemption rates, flexible stopovers and no fuel surcharges mean you can get some excellent deals on award tickets. The program also partners with many of the largest transferable points and miles programs, so it's easy to rack up Aeroplan points through your everyday spending. Even if you aren't planning to visit Canada or fly on Air Canada, you should consider the program for your next points transfer or major redemption. TPG featured card | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent on purchases at restaurants worldwide, on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent at US supermarkets, on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 5X | Earn 5X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid hotel stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™. | | 3X | Earn 3X Membership Rewards® points on flights booked through AmexTravel.com, the Amex Travel App™, or purchased directly from airlines. | | 2X | Earn 2X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid car rentals booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™ and cruises booked and paid through AmexTravel.com. | | 1X | Earn 1X Membership Rewards® point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. |

item.title: Who's eligible for the Chase Ink Business Cash and Unlimited's $1,000 cash-back welcome offer?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.44
Who's eligible for the Chase Ink Business Cash and Unlimited's $1,000 cash-back welcome offer? If your small business is looking for an affordable way to earn cash back or boost its Ultimate Rewards balance, the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are two great choices. Currently, both cards are offering their highest-ever welcome bonuses, which could be even more valuable if you have an eligible Ultimate Rewards card that provides access to Chase's transfer partners. It's important to know whether or not you're eligible for a welcome bonus. You don't want to waste a hard pull on your credit just to find out you didn't meet Chase's requirements from the start. Current offers on the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited Currently, the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited have the same welcome offer: Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months of account opening. These best-ever offers end on Sept. 17 at 9 a.m. ET, so I recommend applying sooner rather than later. We haven't seen offers this good on either of these cards before. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, this welcome offer could be worth up to $2,050 if you hold a card that offers access to Chase's transfer partners, such as the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees) or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees). That's because you can combine the rewards you earn on your Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited with that account and redeem them with any of Chase's partners. Am I eligible for the Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited's welcome bonus? When considering whether you're eligible for a welcome bonus on either card, there are several factors to keep in mind. Chase 5/24 rule Chase's well-known 5/24 rule states that you may not be approved for a new Chase card if you've opened five or more personal credit cards over the past 24 months. While small-business cards like the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited don't count toward 5/24, Chase will still take that rule into consideration when deciding whether to approve you. No-annual-fee Ink family rules Chase has gradually tightened its eligibility rules for cards in the same family. For the Ink Cash and Ink Unlimited, you can earn a welcome offer on either card, but not both. That rings true even if you earned a welcome bonus on one of these cards before the rules changed, or if you closed your account years ago. In addition, you likely won't be able to earn a second bonus on the same no-annual-fee Ink card. For example, if you previously earned a welcome bonus on the Ink Unlimited, you probably can't earn another one on that card. Do I need a business to open the Ink Cash or Ink Unlimited? You don't need a traditional business, such as an LLC, to open a small-business card like the Ink Cash or Ink Unlimited. However, you do need a side hustle or similar gig at a minimum. Freelancing, pet sitting, driving for a ride-hailing service and reselling are all examples of work that may qualify you for a small-business card. Related: How to get a business credit card Can I hold both the Ink Cash and Ink Unlimited at the same time? Yes, but remember that you likely won't be able to earn a welcome bonus on both cards. Since both cards have identical welcome offers right now, you don't need to worry about which card offers greater value with its bonus when deciding which to apply for first. If you don't want to hold both cards, your choice will come down to how your business typically spends. Since the Ink Business Cash earns bonus rewards at office supply stores and on common utilities, dining and gas (dining and gas subject to a spending cap), it's a better choice for business owners who frequently make those purchases. The Ink Business Unlimited earns 5% cash back on Lyft (through Sept. 30, 2027) and 1.5% cash back on all other purchases. That makes it an ideal choice for businesses that make a wide variety of purchases or whose spending habits shift regularly. Bottom line It's always important to check whether you're eligible for a card and its welcome bonus before applying. Credit card issuers will almost always perform a hard pull on your credit report when you apply; too many hard pulls on your credit report can lower your credit score. Given that, you don't want to waste a hard pull on a card you more than likely aren't eligible for. That said, if you meet the eligibility requirements for either the Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited, now is a great time to apply. Both of these cards have a best-ever welcome offer that's ending on Sept. 17 at 9 a.m. ET. To learn more, check out our full reviews of the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited. Apply here: Chase Ink Business Cash Apply here: Chase Ink Business Unlimited

item.title: 7 reasons you might want the Amex Business Platinum instead of the Amex Platinum
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.03
7 reasons you might want the Amex Business Platinum instead of the Amex Platinum Editor's Note Thanks to its stellar portfolio of perks and all the incredible uses there are for American Express Membership Rewards points, we often focus on the American Express Platinum Card®. Some folks even forget that the card has a counterpart, The Business Platinum Card® from American Express, that offers many of the same benefits as the personal card, along with some that make it a great choice for small-business owners. Using a business card like the Amex Business Platinum for work-related purchases can help you separate your personal and business expenses so your end-of-year accounting is a bit easier, too, which is a factor in its favor. Here's a quick look at both cards side by side and a helpful list of reasons why the Amex Business Platinum might actually be a better choice for some folks. Related: Is the Amex Business Platinum worth the annual fee? Comparing the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum Let's start with a quick snapshot of both cards and their benefits. | | Amex Platinum | Amex Business Platinum | |---|---|---| | Welcome offer | Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. | Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 300,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. | | Annual fee | | | | Earning rates | | | | Unique benefits | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | As you can see, each card offers a robust slate of benefits specific to its own cardmembers. But the two cards also have a menu of similar perks to be aware of, which will help you with your decision about which card to get. Related: 9 things to do when you get the Amex Business Platinum Card Perks offered by both cards Here are the benefits that both the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum cards offer — meaning you will be able to take advantage of these no matter which card you opt for (enrollment is required for select benefits): - Up to $600 statement credit each calendar year (up to $300 biannually) on prepaid bookings at Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection properties made through Amex Travel (minimum two-night stay requirement for The Hotel Collection) - An airline fee statement credit of up to $200 per calendar year on charges with the eligible U.S. airline you select - Get $120 as a statement credit for a Global Entry application fee or a statement credit of up to $85 for TSA PreCheck once every four years - Receive a statement credit per calendar year to reimburse your annual Clear+ membership fee (up to $219 per calendar year; subject to auto-renewal). - Eligible cardmembers can access the American Express Global Lounge Collection, which includes Centurion Lounges, Priority Pass™ lounges, Delta Sky Clubs (limited to 10 annual visits; when flying on a same-day Delta flight; except basic economy flights; spend $75,000 in a calendar year to unlock unlimited flights), Aspire lounges, Escape lounges, Plaza Premium lounges and Lufthansa lounges - Complimentary car elite rental status with Hertz President's Circle, Avis Preferred Plus and National Emerald Club Executive - Complimentary Gold elite status with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, plus Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World - No foreign transaction fees (see rates and fees for the Amex Platinum and rates and fees for the Amex Business Platinum) - Benefit from various travel protections and purchase protections Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum Reasons to choose the Amex Business Platinum over the Amex Platinum Now that you have a full rundown of benefits to refer to, here are some key reasons and spending habits that might lead you to choose the Business Platinum Card instead of the Amex Platinum. 1. You have or already had the personal Amex Platinum If you currently carry the personal Amex Platinum Card, or even if you previously had it but no longer do, you might not be eligible to earn its welcome offer. That's because, like many other issuers, American Express has restricted who is eligible for the welcome bonuses on its cards. So, if you already have, or previously had, the Amex Platinum, you might be blocked from taking advantage of its current welcome offer. If you want the card's benefits and the chance to earn hundreds of thousands of additional Membership Rewards points, however, you might opt for the Business Platinum instead, since currently or previously carrying the personal Amex Platinum should not preclude you from being eligible for the Business Platinum's welcome bonus. Related: 10 things to do when you get the Amex Platinum 2. You spend enough to earn the Amex Business Platinum's higher welcome offer The Business Platinum welcome offer requires some strategic spending, as the requirement is $20,000 in purchases within the first three months of card membership. That's a considerable sum, but it's not outside the usual operating budget of some small businesses. By contrast, the Platinum currently has a lower spending requirement of $12,000 within the first six months of card membership to earn its welcome offer. And note: You have double the time of the business version to reach it. The personal card's terms might work better for your spending habits. However, the fact that you can potentially earn nearly twice as many points with the Business Platinum is a worthwhile consideration (not everyone will be targeted for the same welcome offers). 3. You spend a lot on flights and hotels, specifically The two cards have very similar earning structures when it comes to travel, with two subtle but significant differences. The personal card earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked through Amex Travel and directly with airlines on up to $500,000 in purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent after that. The Business Platinum earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked through Amex Travel (not directly with airlines) with no spending cap. Both cards earn 5 points per dollar spent on prepaid hotel bookings with Amex Travel. If you tend to book flights directly with airlines, the personal card might be a better choice. However, if you use Amex Travel for a lot of your travel plans — or if you have that option — then you won't miss out by charging your reservations to the Business Platinum. Plus, if you book a lot of flights, or more than $500,000 worth per year, specifically, with your card, then you're definitely better off with the business card since its bonus-qualifying spending isn't capped at that amount. Just remember that the Amex Business Platinum only earns bonus points on flights booked through Amex Travel, unless the charge is for $5,000 or more (subject to a spending cap). Related: The best credit cards for paying taxes and fees on award tickets 4. You can maximize the Amex Business Platinum's large-transaction and business category bonuses If you tend to make a lot of high-dollar purchases or spend a lot in certain categories, then the Business Platinum's earning structure can really set you ahead. The card accrues points at the following rates. - 2 points per dollar spent on purchases of $5,000 or more - 2 points per dollar spent on U.S. purchases from construction material and hardware suppliers, electronic goods retailers, shipping providers, and software and cloud system providers There is a combined $2 million spending cap per calendar year (then 1 point per dollar spent). If these are the types of business purchases you tend to make — or if you regularly use your card for transactions of more than $5,000 — then the Business Platinum blows the personal version's earning rates out of the water. You might also find creative ways to leverage these bonuses on one-off purchases. Related: The top 7 credit cards to maximize large purchases 5. You use Amex Pay with Points for premium travel One major way the two cards diverge is that the Business Platinum Card offers cardmembers a bonus 35% of the points back they redeem through Amex's Pay with Points feature, while the personal version does not. There are a few stipulations, though. First, you only receive the 35% points bonus on flights booked through Amex Travel on the same qualifying airline you designate for the up to $200 per calendar year airline fee statement credit. The good news is, the ticket can be in any cabin class, not just a premium one. Second, you can only receive up to 1 million points back per year. To max that out, you'd have to be redeeming nearly 2.9 million Amex points, though, so this cap shouldn't impact most people. Even if you seldom redeem Membership Rewards points this way, this one benefit can save you tens of thousands of points on a single ticket. 6. You prefer the business card's statement credits The personal and business versions each offer many annual statement credits. Some are the same, but many are unique to each card. The personal card offers quite a few lifestyle statement credits. But if those aren't things you actually use normally, why bother trying to track them while juggling the card's steep annual fee? The Business Platinum offers thousands of dollars in annual statement credits with popular business-related merchants. (Enrollment is required for select benefits; select benefits are subject to auto-renewal.) Plus, with the Business Platinum, you'll earn up to $1,200 in Amex Travel flight statement credits and up to $2,400 in One AP statement credits (valid from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31 of the calendar year after meeting the requirement), after spending $250,000 or more on eligible purchases in a calendar year. While this is a substantial spending requirement, if you can meet it through your regular spending activity, the Business Platinum could be a better option. That said, these benefits aren't substantial enough to make it worth going out of your way to spend that much on the Business Platinum. Related: Who should (and shouldn't) get the Amex Business Platinum? 7. You are interested in adding employee cards The personal Amex Platinum Card allows you to add up to 10 active authorized users. You can either add them as additional Platinum Card holders at a cost of $195 per card per year (see rates and fees) with some of the card's travel benefits, including lounge access, or as Companion Card holders with no annual fee (see rates and fees) and very limited benefits. By contrast, the Business Platinum allows you to add up to 99 additional Employee Cards. Full Business Platinum additional cards with some of the same benefits afforded to the primary cardmember carry a $400 annual fee each (see rates and fees). Employee Expense cards have no annual fee (see rates and fees). All card activity can be tracked through Amex. For business owners who need to track employee spending (and who would like to earn points for themselves on all that spending), the Business Platinum lets you have many more cards under your umbrella and allows you to track them easily. Bottom line Both the Amex Platinum and the Business Platinum are excellent rewards cards with a variety of benefits from which members can reap tremendous value. Consider which card best matches your financial habits and needs, and which card's other perks you're most likely to leverage year after year. And after all that, you might even want to consider carrying both the personal and business Amex Platinum cards since there are plenty of ways the two cards don't overlap. To learn more, check out our full reviews of the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum. item.title: Sports travel is having its 'Eras Tour' moment. Airlines have noticed
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.72
Sports travel is having its 'Eras Tour' moment. Airlines have noticed Next month, the reigning national champion Indiana University Hoosiers head to Lincoln, Nebraska, for a college football showdown against the University of Nebraska Cornhuskers. United Airlines is planning to help with the fan frenzy. The carrier plans to offer a rare flight between Indianapolis and Lincoln on game weekend. Normally, it wouldn't connect those two cities with nonstop service. There are more flights like that one, too. That same week, United will also offer unusual nonstop service between Eugene, Oregon, and Columbus, Ohio, catering to a high-stakes University of Oregon-Ohio State University matchup. Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines has added a full slate of flights this fall, specifically to carry fans to away games. And later this month, American Airlines will go bigger and farther: When the Dallas Cowboys head to Brazil for an NFL game, American will offer a special flight from Dallas to Rio de Janeiro on one of its large Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Everywhere you look right now, airlines are leaning into sports. For good reason, too. "The local market in sports is so popular right now, and so much money is being spent," Joe Esposito, chief commercial officer at Delta Air Lines, said last month when speaking on a panel in Texas. "No matter where you look in this country — whether it's college, pro, WNBA — everything is packed," he added. "It's an insatiable business." Sports travel is booming In 2025, fans spent $51.1 billion traveling to spectator sporting events, according to the Sports Events and Tourism Association. And keep in mind that was before fans flooded major U.S. cities this summer for the FIFA World Cup. In Austin, one out of every six hotel room nights is now owed to sports-related travel, tourism leaders say. "It drives summer. It drives weekend[s]," Tom Noonan, CEO of Visit Austin, said last month. "It's a big part of Austin's future." It's about how fans are traveling Of course, fans following their teams around the country is nothing new. Rose Gray, a Wisconsin-based travel adviser, has helped Green Bay Packers fans book trips to away games for more than 40 years. What has changed, she said, is how fans are choosing to travel. Gone are the days of scoring cheap tickets, staying in budget motels and tailgating to beat traffic. Now, fans are asking Gray to send them to Formula One races in Monaco with prime seats and meet and greets with their favorite drivers. "They may say, 'I don't want to just stay in some Motel Six an hour away from the Masters," Gray, of Fox World Travel, said. "They're looking for an experience. It's not just a game. It's talking to the locals. Learning about the local cuisine. Being as close as possible." It's a cultural phenomenon cut from the same cloth as the all-in approach Taylor Swift fans took while booking trips to The Eras Tour in 2023 and 2024: expensive hotels, luxe dinners and high-end experiences. In the face of stubborn inflation and higher borrowing costs, it might be the latest sign that consumers are refusing to sacrifice travel even as they face difficult spending decisions. "I don't think the splurge is necessarily people that are all really wealthy," Wendy Zajack, adjunct professor who studies consumer behavior at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said. "I think people are willing to save for a big trip or a big moment," Zajack added. "And when they do it, they're going to do it all in." Airlines bet big on the big game Airlines have taken notice. Southwest is planning unique nonstop service between Oklahoma City and Jacksonville when Oklahoma State plays the University of Florida in November. The weekend before Thanksgiving, there's a flight between Columbus and Omaha when Ohio State plays Nebraska. To be fair, these football-focused flights aren't actually new. United has been strategically adding unique routes to college football games for nearly a decade. But in recent years, the Chicago-based carrier has doubled down on finding opportunities to add one-off routes, even ones that don't touch its major hubs. A prime example is the flight between Birmingham, Alabama, and Baton Rouge, Louisiana, which it added for the Nov. 7 Alabama-LSU matchup. "We've developed a much deeper understanding of where fans want to go and how they prefer to travel," Michael Weeks, United's managing director of domestic schedule development, told TPG. "That experience," he said, "has helped us become more strategic in identifying the right games, matching capacity to demand, and creating schedules that work well for customers." More than a game The deep link between sports and travel goes well beyond Saturday college football games, too — especially as leagues launch games to more alluring destinations. The NFL is planning its biggest international tour in 2026, following this past week's first-ever game in Australia. Next summer, the MLB plans to host another game on the Iowa farm that was once the set of the film "Field of Dreams." Meanwhile, ticket sales are already underway for one of the biggest draws of all: the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. At a time when so much in life now happens on a screen, traveling to these "in-real-life" games increasingly feels like a splurge worth planning a larger trip around, according to Zajack. "I think in our world right now we are really craving unique time-bound events," she said. "I don't see an end to it right now." TPG's tips for booking If you're planning to book a trip to see your favorite team, it helps to be an eagle-eyed schedule-watcher. Begin searching flights and hotels as soon as your team's schedule drops. If you're hoping to use points, the best award deals are sometimes available 11 months or more in advance. Just be sure to book reservations you can change if the price later drops or if your plans change. Consider protecting your trip with a travel insurance plan that covers major events like sports games or concerts. And, when possible, add another layer of protection by purchasing your travel with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance. Because flight prices typically surge around major events, plan to land a few days early and leave a couple of days after the final whistle. This can add peace of mind if you get delayed and help you avoid high-demand ticket prices. Plus, you'll get to experience the destination more fully. Finally, be strategic when using points and miles. While award bookings can reduce your out-of-pocket expenses on flights and hotels, consult our valuations to ensure you're not handing too many hard-earned points over at once. Related reading:

item.title: Delta ends 19-year Monterey hiatus, returns to Central Coast with 2 routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.52
Delta ends 19-year Monterey hiatus, returns to Central Coast with 2 routes Delta Air Lines is returning to California's Central Coast for the first time in almost 19 years. In December, the airline will launch service from the Golden State's Monterey Regional Airport (MRY). It's a return that's certainly a long time coming. Delta last operated regular service to the airport in January 2008. Now, most of its top competitors — including American Airlines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines — have flights from the airport. Delta's latest go-around in Monterey is set to begin on Dec. 19, right as the holiday season kicks off. Delta's 2 routes from Monterey The carrier plans to offer nonstop flights to two of its western hubs: - Twice-daily service to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Daily service to Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) Both routes will be served by Embraer 175 Delta Connection regional jets. Sardines, Steinbeck and sea otters: TPG's guide to exploring Monterey, California Monterey Regional Airport: What to know MRY is a tiny airport just miles from the California coast that gives travelers easier access to destinations like Monterey County, Carmel and Big Sur, not to mention the scenic Highway 1, along the state's rugged Pacific coastline. If you can find a fare that fits your budget, flying directly to Monterey is a great way to reach the area without a long drive or risking traffic. In comparison, Monterey is about two hours from the region's largest hub at San Francisco International Airport (SFO). Meanwhile, the drive from MRY to San Jose Mineta International Airport (SJC) takes about an hour and a half. Monterey's airport only has a small handful of gates, and the terminal can certainly get busy when you get a couple of flights departing around the same time. So I'm curious to see how the airport fares when another major carrier joins the mix. However, adding one of the nation's three biggest airlines — and service to two major hubs — will certainly be good news for travelers in the region. Tip: If you're flying from MRY, I'd suggest getting to the airport a little early. There's a local restaurant outside security, and you can grab a bite to eat and do some sightseeing (or planespotting) on the large observation deck. Read more: What makes a good destination for a company retreat — and why TPG chose Monterey How the competition stacks up Delta will have competition on one of its routes, as United already offers flights between MRY and LAX. With these two routes, Delta will serve all but one of its western hubs. Left out of this route announcement is Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), which already has MRY service on Alaska Airlines, Delta's top Pacific Northwest rival. Related reading:

item.title: Quarterly statement credits and bonus categories: Maximize these Q3 benefits before Sept. 30
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.37
Quarterly statement credits and bonus categories: Maximize these Q3 benefits before Sept. 30 Quarterly benefits are among the more challenging credit card perks to keep up with. When it comes to quarterly statement credits, you have three months to use them up before they expire. With quarterly bonus categories, you have to memorize a new set in each quarter to ensure you're getting the best return for your spending. With the end of the third quarter approaching, now is a good time to check which benefits you still have left to use. Most Q3 statement credits and bonus categories reset after Sept. 30, meaning you have just a few weeks left to maximize them. Here are the perks you'll want to use before the end of September 2026. Bookmark this article, and come back in October when Q4 begins. American Express There are a few Amex cards with quarterly benefits you'll want to take advantage of. Here's what to know. The Business Platinum Card from American Express The Business Platinum Card® from American Express has two statement credits that reset each quarter. These help offset the Business Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees). - Up to $90 statement credit per quarter (up to $360 per calendar year) for eligible Indeed purchases in the U.S.: Business owners can use this statement credit toward subscription plans, sponsored job posts, advertisements on the platform and more. - Up to $50 statement credit per quarter (up to $200 per calendar year) for eligible Hilton purchases: This statement credit can be used for any eligible purchase at a property in the Hilton portfolio. Note that you must be registered in the Hilton for Business program to participate. Enrollment is required for select benefits. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Business Platinum. American Express Platinum Card With the American Express Platinum Card®, there are a pair of quarterly statement credits that help offset its $895 annual fee (see rates and fees). - Up to $100 statement credit per quarter (up to $400 per calendar year) for Resy: Pay with your Amex Platinum at an eligible U.S. Resy restaurant. No reservation is required. - Up to $75 statement credit per quarter (up to $300 per calendar year) for Lululemon: Pay with your Amex Platinum and receive the statement credit for purchases made at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online. Enrollment is required for select benefits. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum. Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card The Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card has one quarterly benefit you'll want to maximize. - Up to $50 in flight statement credits per quarter (up to $200 per calendar year): Pay for a flight directly with an airline, through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™ and receive up to $50 in statement credits each quarter. To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Aspire. The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card The quarterly statement credit on The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card is a highlight perk. - Up to $60 Hilton statement credit per quarter (up to $240 per calendar year): Receive up to $60 in statement credits each quarter on purchases charged directly with the Hilton Business Amex toward a property within the Hilton portfolio, including bookings and incidental charges, such as dining and spa services. To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Business Amex. Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card The Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card's quarterly statement credit is one of the card's top benefits. - Up to $50 Hilton statement credit per quarter (up to $200 per calendar year): Receive up to $50 in statement credits each quarter on purchases charged directly with the Hilton Surpass card toward a property within the Hilton portfolio. This statement credit is similar to the one on the Hilton Business Amex. To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass. Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum Chase Two Chase cards provide rotating quarterly bonus categories for cardholders to maximize. Chase Freedom and Chase Freedom Flex If you have the Chase Freedom Flex® (see rates and fees) or legacy Chase Freedom® (no longer available to new applicants), you have access to bonus categories that change every quarter. - Up to 5% cash back: From July 1 through September 30, you can earn bonus cash back on gas stations and electric vehicle charging, public transit, select live entertainment and donations to United Way. You'll receive bonus cash back in these categories on up to $1,500 of combined spending each quarter (then 1% back). You must activate your categories to receive this higher earning rate. If you haven't activated your Q3 categories yet, don't wait: You have until Sept. 14 to activate. The quarter ends Sept. 30. To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Flex. The information for the Chase Freedom has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Citi One Citi card provides rotating quarterly bonus categories. Citi Dividend Card If you hold the Citi® Dividend Card (no longer available to new applicants), here are the Q3 categories you need to keep in mind. - Up to 5% cash back: You'll earn 5% cash back this quarter on purchases made at gas stations and home improvement stores. Citi Dividend cardholders earn 5% bonus cash back on up to $6,000 of spending across the year (then 1% back thereafter), so you can maximize your bonus categories for the whole year during a quarter that has the best bonus categories for your individual spending habits. You must activate your categories each quarter. These categories will run through Sept. 30. The information for the Citi Dividend card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: Ultimate guide to the Citi Travel portal Discover Discover has one card that earns bonus cash back in a new set of categories each quarter. Discover it Cash Back The main perk of the Discover it® Cash Back is its rotating bonus categories. - Up to 5% cash back: Discover's third-quarter bonus categories are gas stations, transportation and drugstores. Cardholders earn 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined spending on rotating categories each quarter (then an unlimited 1% cash back thereafter). You'll need to remember to activate your current categories. This quarter ends Sept. 30. The information for the Discover it Cash Back has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: The best first credit cards for beginners U.S. Bank If you're a U.S. Bank fan, there's one card with a quarterly benefit you can maximize. U.S. Bank Cash+ Visa Signature Card With the U.S. Bank Cash+® Visa Signature® Card, you'll receive bonus cash back each quarter you activate. - Up to 5% cash back: This benefit is flexible each quarter. You'll earn 5% cash back on up to $2,000 in combined spending on two rotating categories (then 1% back) of your choice after you activate them. The categories covered this quarter are cellphone providers, department stores, electronic stores, fast food, furniture stores, ground transportation, gyms and fitness centers, home utilities, internet, movie theaters, select clothing stores, sporting goods stores, streaming services and TV. The current quarter runs through Sept. 30. The information for the U.S. Bank Cash+ has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: 11 credit cards that can get you $1,500 or more in first-year value Bottom line If you're focused on maximizing your card benefits, now is the time to check whether you have any Q3 statement credits or bonus categories left to use. Benefits can reset monthly, quarterly, biannually or annually (either each calendar year or cardholder anniversary). It's important to know when your statement credits begin and end to get the most out of your rewards cards. Many of the benefits above reset after Sept. 30, so take a few minutes to review your cards and make sure you aren't leaving any value on the table. Then, check back in October for a rundown of the quarterly benefits you can maximize during Q4.
